#6229. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

A.R. Kunik, et al. The ‘‘dark magic mushroom’’ co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin. Current Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

#6227. Anker’s New Power Station Is the Most Efficient I’ve Tested, Capable of Running My Fridge for 2 Days

My capacity test showed the Solix S5000 is nearly 97 percent efficient.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

How long a power station lasts has the most impact on your experience when using one, whether you’re experiencing a blackout or enjoying a weekend off the grid. This year, Anker has upped its game with the S-series stations. Advanced algorithms have improved how its inverters deliver power and extend battery life. Not long ago, I reviewed this technology in the small but powerful S2000 and was impressed. Now, I’ve put the newer and larger S5000 power station through its paces, and it didn’t disappoint.

For context, I also compared the S5000 to Anker's other large power station, the F3800 Plus (now only available as a bundle with other home power accessories), which has been on our list of the best portable power stations. Each model offers both 120- and 240-volt output, but the S5000 has a much larger battery capacity of 5,024 watt-hours (compared with 3,840 watt-hours with the F3800 Plus), and the S5000 is much smaller in size. While it offers less total power output (4,500 watts versus 6,000 watts for the F3800 Plus), I think the S5000 represents an overall improvement for those looking to buy a home backup station that’s more powerful than a typical portable power station.

This is what I cared about the most because better inverter efficiency is the primary feature Anker touts with the S5000. To evaluate its efficiency, I ran two tests. The first was to turn on the AC output and let it run overnight with nothing plugged into it, making sure to deactivate any auto-off features. I did this because, even when idling, most power station batteries lose some stored energy. But after 18 hours, the S5000’s battery capacity was still at 100 percent—that’s impressive. To make a comparison for context, I ran the F3800 alongside it for the same amount of time, and its battery capacity dipped to 81 percent.

For the second test, I plugged a watt meter into the station and plugged a space heater into the meter. I then ran the heater at full power, drawing around 1,500 watts, until it drained the battery fully. Using a resistive load like this (a device that turns energy to heat) can drain a battery pretty quickly, but this also gives you a good read on a power station's performance. It lasted just over three hours, and my meter measured just under 4,900 watt-hours. Compared with its official spec of 5,024 watt-hours of capacity, I determined that this station is around 97 percent efficient. Many stations hover around 89 percent on average, so this was a big win for the S5000.

The technology behind this ability enables the inverter to throttle itself up and down to meet the demands of the devices plugged into it. This is especially significant for lower-powered devices and cyclical appliances with fluctuating power needs, like refrigerators, because the inverter maintains its efficiency, regardless of what’s plugged into it. That means longer run times across the board. This station could easily power my full-size refrigerator for more than 48 hours.

The size of this station in relation to the battery capacity is its second most striking feature. It’s two-thirds smaller than the F3800 but offers 1,184 more watt-hours. At 99 pounds, I wouldn’t call it light, but with two wheels and a telescoping handle, it’s easy enough to roll around, and it’s not too hard to lift in and out of a vehicle. It would be easy to transport this to and from a second home or a job site.

There are a few other enhancements, as well. The 30-amp, 240-volt connection (great for powering an electric dryer or other 240-volt appliance) has its own on/off button, so it won’t create any unwanted drain when all you need is 120-volt AC power. It also accepts both low- and high-powered DC input, which means you get up to 3,000 watts of solar power if you have enough panels to achieve that.

There’s also a port connection for adding up to five expansion batteries, potentially increasing the total battery capacity to as much as 30,000 watt-hours. That same port can be used to connect to Anker’s Solix 5000 Smart Tri-Fuel Generator for direct DC recharging, which is three times faster than standard AC charging. I had this very generator on hand and was able to test this out. I observed around 4,000 watts of input while the generator was running on gasoline. In an emergency where the power has gone out for several days, you could use this method to fully recharge the S5000 in less than two hours.

The only downside is the maximum total output of 4,500 watts. While that’s perfectly fine for very basic home backup and RV use, it’s not going to power a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, let alone a full bank of circuits on a manual transfer switch, no matter how many expansion batteries are attached (they only add capacity, not output). True whole-home backup would require a larger station.

Sometimes, newer power station models are just more of the same, with only minor tweaks to power output, capacity, or outlet configuration. But the Anker S5000’s inverter efficiency technology is a notable upgrade that delivers on its promise of longer runtime than comparable models with the same capacity.

It’s not a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that) and doesn’t have as much output power as the F3800, but it can bring substantial power during an emergency to several appliances or a couple of critical circuits, and it’s much more portable. And if you’re an RV owner looking for a compact yet powerful station, this should definitely be on your list for consideration.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. #6226. The Sky This Week from November 13 to 20: The Leonids peak

Friday, November 20The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will be 252,040 miles (405,619 kilometers) from Earth.

Already 60° high in the east by 8 P.M. local time is M33, the Pinwheel Galaxy in Triangulum. This lovely spiral glows at 6th magnitude and is technically visible from a dark site with sharp eyes — just wait until after moonset if you want to give it a try. You’ll find it in far western Triangulum, about 4.3° west-northwest of 3rd-magnitude Alpha (α) Trianguli.

Any telescope will show M33, but larger ones are better because its considerable size — some 70’ across along its longer axis — spreads its light out and makes its surface brightness quite low. Instruments 10 inches or larger will show some detail along the spiral arms, including brighter knots of star formation.

Located some 2.7 million light-years away, M33 is the third-largest galaxy in our Local Group, after Andromeda and our own Milky Way. This cosmic neighbor is a classic spiral with no central bar and a round, bright nucleus wrapped by its dusty arms. Oriented more closely to face-on than Andromeda, M33 is a popular target for visual observers as well as astrophotographers.

Sunrise: 6:43 A.M. Sunset: 4:45 P.M. Moonrise: 10:54 A.M. Moonset: 7:55 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (21%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Saturday, November 14Following inferior conjunction early this month, Mercury has reappeared in the morning sky. Now magnitude 0.3, you can find the small planet some 5° above the eastern horizon an hour before sunrise. It lies to the lower left of brighter Venus (magnitude –4.8), which sits alongside Virgo’s luminary Spica, about 12° to Mercury’s west.

This morning, Mercury is less than 1° south of 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis, which should be visible until the sky brightens enough to wash out the star. You can capture both in the same field of view in either binoculars or a telescope. Mercury now appears as a 32%-lit disk that is 8” across. Compare that with Venus, which features a narrower phase just 13% lit but stretches 51” by comparison. The brighter planet lies just 1.4° northwest of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.

Both Spica and Kappa can act as guideposts to help you spot Venus’ and Mercury’s motion, respectively, over the next few days. Mercury is moving east and will pull away from Kappa to the lower left. Venus, which just recently reached a stationary point, is also moving east, but will swing slightly northeast (to the upper left) of Spica for a few days before tracking more directly east.

Mars passes 1.2° north of Jupiter at 10 P.M. EST — we’ll focus on this pair in the early-morning sky tomorrow.

Sunrise: 6:44 A.M. Sunset: 4:44 P.M. Moonrise: 11:33 A.M. Moonset: 8:56 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (29%)

Sunday, November 15Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

Sunrise: 6:45 A.M. Sunset: 4:43 P.M. Moonrise: 12:05 P.M. Moonset: 9:58 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (38%)

Monday, November 16It’s a great night to catch Saturn’s largest and brightest moon, Titan, as it skims south of the planet. Two hours after sunset, Saturn is roughly 40° high in the southeast, outshining all the other stars in this region of the sky. It lies to the lower left of the Circlet of Pisces and to the upper left of the bright star Fomalhaut in Piscis Austrinus.

Zoom in on Saturn with a telescope to first catch sight of its ring system, stretching 43” from end to end and tilted 8° to our line of sight. Currently we are seeing Saturn’s southern side, including the entirety of the planet’s southern hemisphere. The gas giant’s disk now measures 19” across.

Titan is difficult to miss, shining at mid-8th magnitude just south of the ringed planet. Don’t be fooled by a fainter 10th-magnitude field star, which lies just to Titan’s west. The three next-brightest moons, also 10th magnitude, are Tethys, Dione, and Rhea. They lie closer to the planet. Tethys sits about 40” west of Saturn’s center shortly before 8 P.M. EST, while Dione is just west of the limb and Rhea just east of the planet. Dione and Rhea are moving westward, and Rhea will skim just north of Saturn’s pole along the way, standing due north of the planet around 10:40 P.M. EST. Tethys is moving east, and will disappear behind the planet’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 2:35 A.M. EST on the 16th (still late on the 15th along the Pacific Coast).

Sunrise: 6:46 A.M. Sunset: 4:43 P.M. Moonrise: 12:32 P.M. Moonset: 11:00 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (47%)

Tuesday, November 17First Quarter Moon occurs at 6:48 A.M. EST, floating among the stars of Aquarius.

Early this evening brighter targets are best, as the Moon doesn’t set until late. Ready for viewing as the winter constellations start to dominate earlier each day is the Pleiades, an open cluster cataloged as M45.

Known since antiquity and readily visible to the naked eye, the Pleiades contains several bright stars arranged in a tiny dipperlike shape. Located in northwestern Taurus, the cluster is sometimes mistaken for the Little Dipper, although that asterism is much larger and lies in the northern sky, anchored at the end of its handle by Polaris, the North Star. The Pleiades shines with a collective magnitude of 1.6 and spans roughly 110’ — a huge swath of sky. It lies above the sideways V-shape of Taurus’ face as the Bull rises in the east this evening, and is already 30° high by 7:30 P.M. local time. How many stars can you make out with the naked eye? Most observers see six or seven.

Once you’ve taken in the cluster without any optical aid, zoom in with binoculars or a finder scope. (Any higher magnification and you won’t see most of the cluster at once, but instead be limited to a smaller portion.) Many more stars will now pop into your field of view. If you do opt for high magnification, look for a faint grayish haze around the stars — this is nearby dust reflecting the stars’ light, and requires clear, dark conditions to make out.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight, with the best meteor viewing overnight into the early-morning hours of November 18, as the Moon sets around midnight and the radiant rises higher. Check out tomorrow’s entry for more detail.

Sunrise: 6:47 A.M. Sunset: 4:42 P.M. Moonrise: 12:56 P.M. Moonset: — Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (57%)

Wednesday, November 18The peak of the Leonid meteor shower, caused by the dusty debris of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is best seen early this morning after the Moon has set and the shower’s radiant rises high in the hours before dawn.

Two hours before sunrise, Leo is high in the southeast, with bright Jupiter and Mars joining the curved shape of the Sickle asterism. The Leonids’ radiant is located just inside the cuved blade’s inner edge, near 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Leonis to the upper left (north) of Mars and Jupiter. The two planets appear roughly side by side in the sky around this time, with ruddy Mars at left and more golden-yellow Jupiter at right. Regulus sits just to their lower left.

To catch the most meteors, you’ll actually want to look a little ways away from Leo, about 40° to 60° to the left or right of the constellation. This is where meteors with the longest trains will also occur. Although this shower isn’t particularly strong, you can expect to see roughly a half-dozen or more Leonid meteors per hour. The Leonid shower produces some of the fastest-moving meteors we experience all year, streaking through the sky at some 44 miles (70 kilometers) per hour.

Sunrise: 6:49 A.M. Sunset: 4:41 P.M. Moonrise: 1:19 P.M. Moonset: 12:03 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (67%)

Thursday, November 19The solar system is a dynamic place. Let’s return to the predawn sky today to check out the inner planets’ progress relative to the stars of Virgo. An hour before sunrise, both Mercury and Venus are again well above the eastern horizon, with the stars around them still visible before twilight brightens too much.

Compared with earlier in the week, Venus now sits to the upper left of Spica, rather than directly above it. Venus will pass 1.8° due north of Spica later today at 6 P.M. EST. Now moving steadily east, it will track along the ecliptic, slowly headed for Libra. Mercury has already reached the Balance, sitting within its domain and to the far lower left of Kappa (κ) Virginis, as opposed to the pair’s close proximity a few days ago.

Pull out your telescope to see how the planets’ appearances have changed, too. Mercury is now 55% lit and 7” across, while Venus is 18% lit and has shrunk more noticeably, now 47” across.

Sunrise: 6:50 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 1:41 P.M. Moonset: 1:07 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (76%)

Friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

From Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

Mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST. We’ll check out the planet in the predawn sky in next week’s column.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%)

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.

#6224. Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

#6221. These Music City Airbnbs Exude All of Nashville’s Southern Charm

In the two decades I’ve lived in Nashville, I’ve seen a lot of changes. When I first moved, my friends and family would ask why I lived here; now, they’re asking when they can come visit. And as the Music City grows, so does the number of gorgeous places to stay. Travelers can choose from vacation rentals in any neighborhood for any group size, whether that be large bachelorette parties looking to hang out near the honky-tonks, or solo music lovers who want to catch a show at the Grand Ole Opry. Houses with vast yards are good options for folks with kids, dogs, and songwriter friends who want to pull out the guitar, and some even boast private pools that let you keep the summer heat at bay. Nashville, of course, is known for its street of honky-tonks, and securing a modern condo downtown with a bird’s-eye view of all the action offers a one-of-a-kind experience that you won’t soon forget. No matter what type of stay you’re after, there’s an excellent Nashville vacation rental worth holing up in. Read on for some of my favorite vacation rentals in the city I call home.

It’s the perfect spot for those who like to balance their big-city trips with a bit of solitude and relaxation after a long day. At home, expect great views, a delicious breakfast, and the chance to truly disconnect—there’s no Wi-Fi or TV.

Location: Ashland CityThings to do nearby: Hiking trails on property, Beaman Park, Cumberland River kayaking

Spend the day at home watching movies on the outdoor projector and eating pizza from the wood-fired oven. There’s also a guitar if you want to pick your way through some songs, and vinyl records from the nearby record shop, The Groove. When you’re ready to head out, the neighborhood is full of bars, boutiques, and restaurants, and you’re a quick bus ride, bike ride, or Uber from Lower Broadway.

This two-bedroom guesthouse sits in a middle ground: There's a $75 fee per small or medium dog, who will have to hang out in a crate if you leave them home alone. There's a small backyard for your pup to explore (with a firepit for humans), and the neighborhood has wide sidewalks for safe, on-leash adventures. It's also perfectly located for a visit to Franklin (a 20-minute drive), one of my favorite day trips from the city, and Arrington Vineyards for wine tasting. Inside, the two-bedroom home has a washer/dryer, room-darkening shades, and a bathtub. It's only about a 10-minute drive to downtown Nashville and 15 minutes from the Grand Ole Opry. Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Access to laundry, early luggage drop-off, elevator access, high ceilings

This industrial loft is among a variety of rentals in one of downtown Nashville's century-old buildings—and is run by local company Anchor Rentals, which also manages The Russell, a boutique hotel in a renovated East Nashville church. What that means for business travelers headed here is that they won't have to worry about the hosts canceling or not being in the area. This particular apartment, with its high ceilings, multiple workspaces, and well-equipped kitchen (which includes a microwave, coffee machine, and toaster oven for quick breakfasts), is a great spot for weekday visitors.

Location: Downtown NashvilleThings to do nearby: Ryman Auditorium, Lower Broadway, Frist Art Museum, Dolly Museum Nashville

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pack-and-play, toys for kids, minimalist design, groovy bar cart, French press coffee

Perfectly located 15 minutes away from both Vanderbilt and Belmont University on foot, this apartment in Music Row is an easy home base for parents visiting collegians or touring with high schoolers. With two bedrooms and one bathroom, it has enough space to comfortably fit four people. (If you're traveling with toddlers or infants, the home also offers a pack-and-play and children's books and toys.) There's also a full kitchen complete with a gorgeous Smeg fridge.

Location: Music RowThings to do nearby: Studio B; Vanderbilt University; Belmont University; restaurants, bars and shops in Hillsboro Village and Edgehill Village; Belcourt Theatre

What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Nashville?

East Nashville and Wedgewood-Houston are two busy and buzzy neighborhoods with great dining scenes, music venues, and fun shopping. They’re also a quick Uber or bike ride to downtown, making it easy to experience it all. If you’re looking for something a bit quieter, check out the leafy Sylvan Park neighborhood. For something fit for families, head to Donelson, with easy access to parks and the Opryland attractions.

When is the best season to visit Nashville?

There’s no bad time to visit Nashville, but spring and fall offer more temperate weather, when it is easier to hike, bike, and paddle, or just stroll down Broadway without the steaminess of a southern summer collecting under your hat. Most people want to be in Music City during the warmer months to take advantage of outdoor concerts and street festivals, but if you come in winter, you’ll get to cheer on the NHL’s Nashville Predators and see the holiday magic of the five million lights at Gaylord Opryland.

In my opinion, a trip to Nashville should be about five days long, which offers you enough time to expand your vacation beyond Broadway and the honky-tonks. You’ll have enough time for a day or two in town—you can boot-scoot under the neon lights of Lower Broadway—and still have a few days for exploring the surrounding parks, greenways, museums, shops, and music venues away from the crowds.

#6219. The Sky Today on Friday, November 13: Spot Mirach’s Ghost

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Celebrate Friday the 13th with something spooky: a ghost in the constellation Andromeda. This evening, point your telescope toward 2nd-magnitude Mirach (Beta [β] Andromedae), already nearly 60° high in the east by 7 P.M. local time. One of the Princess’ brightest stars, Mirach is a cool, reddish M-type giant. It lies some 200 light-years away and shines nearly 2,000 times as brightly as our Sun.

But Mirach is not quite our target — we’re looking for its so-called ghost, just 6.8’ northwest of the star. You’ll need a big scope to see it, but look carefully: Can you spot a faint smudge of light, about 4’ across, close to the star? This is the Ghost of Mirach, a far more distant elliptical galaxy glowing at 10th magnitude and cataloged as NGC 404. It lies some 8 million to 10 million light-years away, just beyond the gravitational bounds of our Local Group of galaxies. It’s called a ghost because it appears almost like a ghostly image of the bright star Mirach, which dominates the view.

Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6217. Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Asteroid defense is the mission’s top priority, but there’s also fascinating science to be done.

The Hera spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera captured this black-and-white image of Didymos and Dimorphos from about 60 kilometers away. The photo shows the far side of Didymos compared to the DART impact.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

#6216. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

Friday, November 13The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will be 252,040 miles (405,619 kilometers) from Earth.

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#6215. The 9 Best Multitools for Fixing Things in a Pinch

Cut, tighten, loosen, open, and twist your way through whatever challenges crop up.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

For situations where you don’t have your full tool kit by your side, jump into action like a real-life MacGyver using a multitool. These handy pocket-size companions have come a long way from the Swiss Army Knives of yesteryear, boasting major improvements not just in overall design, but in the quality of tools, materials, and the total number of features offered. Modern-day multitools are designed to be twisted, wrenched, and squeezed with just about the same force that any regular item in your toolbox endures.

A good multitool is typically made of all-stainless steel or equally durable metal with as many as 30 tools integrated into the frame. That said, the majority of them still fit comfortably in a pocket and weigh less than a half pound.

There are dozens of multitool manufacturers, so we got our hands on models from established, popular brands like Victorinox, Gerber, Leatherman, SOG, and more to find out which stood out from the pack. Following our tests and in-depth research, these are the multitools we pick up for fixing nearly anything in a pinch.

It’s hard to nail down one aspect of the Arc that I like best, because it does just about everything well. The opening and closing mechanism is responsive and every tool is accessible from the outside. Plus, the 20 listed functions all work well, as opposed to those on some other multitools that feel like afterthoughts for the sake of an eye-popping marketing claim. This effectiveness across the board is precisely why it is our new best overall pick.

In comparison to our former best overall pick, the Victorinox Spirit X, the Arc shines the brightest when looking at its blade. Unlike the Spirit X, which is made entirely of stainless steel, the knife on the Arc is made of MagnaCut. That means it’s more resistant to corrosion and rust and retains its edge longer.

Beyond this, the blade is simply wider, longer, and based on a pretty basic touch test, feels a lot sharper. In my hands, it made it easier to poke through boxes sealed with duct tape and slice off a chunk of an apple.

The Arc also comes with a larger set of scissors, a thicker saw, and a larger file. Furthermore, it’s equipped with a hip clip that slides directly onto your pants while the Spirit X requires a holster that must be looped through your belt to carry it on your person outside of a pocket.

RoverTac’s 12-in-1 initially caught our eye because it has a good number of useful tools—and it’s affordable, too. While it might be bulky and heavy, we have to admit it’s a decent value. We don’t expect it to hold up to intense use, but in a “save your butt” kind of capacity, it’s certainly holds up to light use.

The long-nosed pliers, wire cutter, and wire stripper all worked reasonably well, as did the can and bottle openers and various screwdrivers. RoverTac claims the tool includes a saw blade, but it’s more like a serrated knife, which worked—just not very well.

The plain knife blade is sharper than it looks and easily cut through rope and twine during our tests. The 12-in-1 comes with a sewn nylon sheath to attach to your belt. Don’t expect this to be the pride of your tool collection, but when you need it most, it will be there.

While no multitool can replace a set of full-size hand tools, the Gerber Gear Center-Drive multitool is by far the closest that we’ve tested. The foldable center-axis provides a lot more length in comparison to the average multitool screwdriver, which gives you extra reach for tight spaces.

The blade on the Center-Drive is also the longest of any that we’ve tested. It feels large enough to take on real cutting responsibility like thick rope or small branches. The high-carbon steel also ensures long-term durability so you don’t have to worry about constantly sharpening the blade between uses.

The Center-Drive is bulkier than other options on this list, but the included nylon sheath is designed to slip onto your belt. Another plus is that there’s a full bit set included.

Fresh out of the box, the Swiss Tool Spirit X impressed us with its design and finish. The tools are packed into the frame very closely, like scientific instrumentation. All the tools—save one—deploy from the outside of the frame, so you can access them without much hassle. The company claims 24 tools in this multitool, but we counted 23, including one that’s simply a hook for a lanyard.

While the needle-nose pliers, wire cutters, scissors, three standard screwdrivers, and can opener work well, it was the less common tools that really impressed us. This is the first multi we’ve seen with a metal saw, which is on the edge of the file. It cut through mild steel hardware surprisingly well, and the file did a nice job cleaning up the edges when we were done.

The Phillips screwdriver shank flares out at the end so that all four points on the head are the same size, making for very solid engagement. The Spirit X’s bottle opener is made from wide stainless steel stock, which keeps it flat on the bottle cap so it doesn’t slip or cut into the cap. The combination reamer-punch efficiently opens up holes in wood, leather, and soft metals, and it can drill holes through 3⁄4-inch pine board.

An all-around great pick, this multitool will get the job done, no matter what that job happens to be.

Full Victorinox Swiss Tool Spirit X Multitool Review

The next iteration in one of Leatherman’s most popular lines comes with a weighty price tag. But it’s justified, since we had a hard time finding fault with the Wave Alpha.

The multitool comes with a standard knife blade, a saw, a file, and a pair of scissors. The file worked well smoothing out nails, and the saw comfortably powered through small branches.

However, we were most pleasantly impressed with the scissors. They’re much larger than any other pair of scissors we've seen on a multitool (“the largest cutting surface ever on a pliers-based Leatherman,” according to the brand). Because of their size and the spring that pushes the handle back up after every snip, we were able to hold the bottom still in hand and easily use our thumb to press down on the blade to cut. This simplified cutting through large pieces of paper, even for those of us who are lefties (since nearly no scissors are designed for cutting with our dominant hand).

The classic pocket knife is made of MagnaCut steel, which is corrosion-resistant and has great edge retention. During testing, we focused on everyday items like twine, paper, cardboard, and zip ties and opening sealed packages. We never needed more than one stern pull of the blade to get through any of them.

The central tool of the Wave Alpha is the plier-wire cutter, which we found easy to use thanks to the biting grip of the ridges and the ergonomic handle.

Though Leatherman lists 16 tools, we counted closer to 12. For instance, the file is designated as two separate tools, with the traditional flat side counting as one and the diamond-coated edge counting as another. That’s a fairly common embellishment with multitool descriptions.

Full Leatherman Wave Alpha Multitool Review

With its svelte, minimalist frame featuring three main tools, this Gerber cuts down on the unnecessary junk and keeps its tools simple and effective.

As a pocket knife–based multitool, it features a full 3-inch, locking plain blade. Although it isn’t the sharpest right out of the box, it cut cleanly through paper, plastic, rope, twine, and steak, and was adequate for some light whittling.

The side opposite the blade features a hex bit driver and scissors. The driver has a reversible bit in a magnetic holder—we love this because you get legit flat and Phillips screwdrivers that just plain work.

The scissors are a bit larger than those found on other models and were easy to control when cutting out intricate shapes from paper to medium cardboard. Between the scissors and the driver is a sharp, narrow awl. We weren't able to use this to drill holes in wood and plastic, but it works well, as intended, to poke holes through leather and canvas.

Rounding out the eight functions is a nice bottle opener that pivots off the end of the tool frame. It doubles as a pry bar (the bottle opener flipped over) and a “hammer” (the wide base of the bottle opener). Is it less a hammer and more just a flat surface for hitting things? Sure. But when you need to finish tapping in a tent stake or small nail, it’ll do.

The plier-based Leatherman Signal comes with several standard items, including a stainless steel blade and a serrated saw. However, it impressed us most with its several outdoor-specific functions.

These include a detachable ferro rod that, in combination with the serrated saw, creates sparks for your campfire. The ferro rod also doubles as an emergency whistle. During testing, I was particularly pleased with the carabiner on the bottom of the multitool. While not a major feature, being able to clip it onto my hiking backpack and forget about it made it so much easier to carry with me than other options.

Perhaps the only major downside is the hammer tool. It functions more like a blunt, flat end you can use in a pinch.

Everyday life doesn’t always require a saw, hammer, or bulky pliers. The Leatherman Micra is a keychain tool, and it doesn’t pretend to be anything else. The Micra hosts a number of items that are still quite handy when small and, importantly, are often the most useful in day-to-day life.

The multitool is built around a pair of scissors, which are the perfect size for cutting tags and snipping loose threads. Tools on the body include tweezers, a nail file and cleaner, a small screwdriver, and a bottle opener, among others.

While carrying the Leatherman Micra around, I was genuinely astonished at how often I used it. I frequently pulled it out for small tasks like picking something out from under my nails, plucking a small hair out of place, or tightening the screws on my sunglasses’ hinges.

The Micra works so well because it knows what it is. The convenience and portability make it hard to go anywhere without it.

With its wide frame and large plier jaws, the Dual-Force is a beast of a multitool. You can open the pliers and slip the pivot to spread the dual-position jaws extra wide to grab large fasteners or objects. The jaws feature three separate gripping areas: two for large or small round objects and one for gripping flat things. We appreciated their versatility for holding well in a variety of situations.

One of our favorite things about the Dual-Force is that all the other tools are accessible when the pliers are closed. This multitool also features a bit holder with two Phillips and one plain screwdriver bit. We regard these among the most useful multitool screwdrivers available, although they are sometimes difficult to use in tight spaces.

The Dual-Force is rounded out with a large knife, a saw blade, and a three-sided file. The knife blade is reasonably sharp out of the box, and we easily cut through thick rope with it. We used the saw blade to cut both green and dried-out sticks and branches with relative ease. We were able to use the file on both wood and metal, although it was better suited for the metal.

While the number of tools and functionalities on your multitool isn’t the only measure of how helpful it’ll be, it does give you a sense of its versatility. The multitools we recommend have anywhere from five to 20 or more different functions.

Note that, in their descriptions, manufacturers often count different capabilities of a specific tool individually to arrive at a higher number of “tools.” Pliers, for example, may be counted three or four times if they can function as needle-nose pliers, regular pliers, wire cutters, and wire strippers.

It’s key to pay attention to the quality of each tool and, of course, how often you’ll use them. For instance, a multitool with a screwdriver attachment is great, but if that multitool’s grip doesn’t give you the leverage to twist off seized screws or only comes with one screwdriver bit, it’s far less effective in practice.

We recommend starting your search by listing three or four tools you use most. Then, opt for a multitool that performs well at those functions. A multitool that has a few tools you use frequently will end up being more valuable to you than one packed to the brim with tools you don’t use much at all.

One of the key reasons to own a multitool is for its portability and convenience compared with carrying a full set of tools. So, if you can’t fit it in a pocket or in the center console of your car, it’s probably too big. That said, size isn’t everything. Each item on a multitool needs enough space from the others to work effectively, and you need to make sure you have a good grip for leverage.

The weight of a multitool only becomes a problem if it is too heavy to comfortably clip onto a belt or slip into a pocket. The majority of the tools on our list are made of stainless steel, which is durable yet relatively lightweight.

Can a Multitool Replace a Tool Kit? In short, no. Multitools are useful in a pinch or when you just need them for a quick fix, but they cannot replace a full tool kit. The biggest utility of a multitool is its convenience. It can function well enough for small repairs or to get by when you’ve got nothing else nearby.

We designed our tests to utilize every tool and function of each model. We carved white pine boards and maple branches. We opened bottles, cans, and shipping packaging. We disassembled and reassembled an old British carburetor, an electrical junction box, and a standard three-prong outlet.

We cut rope, twine, lamp wire, 14-gauge indoor branch circuit wire, maple saplings, branches, paper, and plastic. We also stripped the wires we cut and crimped electrical connectors. With the pliers, we gripped, squeezed, twisted, and turned various bits of hardware. Finally, we filed wood, metal, and even our own fingernails.

During these tests, we paid close attention to the performance of the tool in the given task, the ease of use, how each multitool ergonomically fit in our hand as we worked, and how we expect each tool to last over a long period of time. After all that was said and done, we noted our impressions to compile our final list.

For testing across the board, we evaluated each tool in common situations. For instance, the saw isn’t likely going to cut through 2x4s, so we opted for small branches, twine, and cardboard boxes.

#6214. Singapore Airlines Unveils the ‘Largest Double Bed in the Sky’ As Part of a $1.6 Billion Redesign

Getting a good night's sleep on a long-haul flight isn't easy, even when you're lucky enough to be flying first class. But Singapore Airlines—consistently voted as one of the best airlines in the world by CNT readers—is taking things to a whole new level, unveiling what it claims will be “the largest double bed in commercial aviation” as part of a major revamp of its long-haul cabins.

The airline announced the $1.6 billion redesign on Friday, November 6, with the first aircraft expected to enter service in the second half of 2027.

Singapore Airlines's new first class cabin

And the luxury doesn't stop there. The new suites will feature Italian Poltrona Frau leather upholstery, personal wardrobes, dedicated dining spaces, and 32-inch 4K entertainment screens. Passengers can also expect proper bedding, including cotton sheets, duvets, a choice of pillows, and mattress toppers from German bedding specialist Paradies.

The new business class seats also come with adjoining seats, offering the option to sleep alongside a traveling companion.

But what about those of us traveling farther back? Premium economy will benefit from additional personal space, adjustable leg rests, dedicated storage, and larger entertainment screens. Meanwhile, economy passengers can look forward to redesigned seats with more leg space, adjustable headrests, and new storage compartments.

The new economy class will feature more leg space, adjustable headrests, and new storage compartments.

The upgrades will be introduced gradually across Singapore Airlines's new Boeing 777-9 aircraft and 41 retrofitted Airbus A350-900 aircraft, including its ultra-long-range fleet. The latter will also receive first class cabins for the first time.

There's no confirmed date yet for when passengers will be able to try the new double beds, but one thing is certain: cuddling up at 35,000 feet has just become a little more appealing.

#6213. Nov. 13, 1971: Mariner 9 orbits Mars

On May 30, 1971, Mariner 9 launched, setting off on its mission to Mars. On Nov. 13, 167 days later, it entered orbit around Mars, making it the first spacecraft to orbit another planet.

With Mariner 8, Mariner 9 was one half of the Mars 71 mission. But when Mariner 8 launched on May 9, it failed to achieve orbit and tumbled out of the sky after five minutes, crashing into the Atlantic Ocean. As a result, Mariner 9 inherited all of 8’s goals in addition to its own, giving it an extensive list of objectives: surface mapping, atmospheric monitoring and analysis, surface data collection, and returning around 3,000 photographs.

When Mariner 9 arrived at Mars, it encountered a global dust storm. Because it had been designed for longevity, the orbiter was able to wait out the storm and begin its mission afterwards. (Soviet spacecraft Mars 2 and Mars 3 did not fare as well.) Over the course of about a year, Mariner 9 returned 7,329 photos and mapped 85% of the martian surface. It also revealed a dynamic and active world – including shield volcanoes, dry river valleys, ice at the martian poles – and gave researchers close-up views of the surfaces of Phobos and Deimos.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6212. The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A new study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.
