#6210. REVIEW: Spectrum Optics SkyPilot 127

The smart telescope revolution has grown rapidly over the past few years. Most of these scopes focus primarily on electronic imaging, though, and while amateur astronomers may marvel at the images, they also still enjoy the simple pleasure of looking directly through a telescope.

That’s where the SkyPilot 127 from Spectrum Optics ($999) takes a different approach. Rather than replacing direct observing with a screen-based experience, the SP127 combines a traditional 5-inch (127 millimeters) f/15 Maksutov-Cassegrain telescope with a smart guidance and imaging system.

At first glance, the SP127 looks like a conventional catadioptric with a standard finder on a motorized alt-azimuth mount. But looks can be deceiving.

The secret lies in that “finder.” On closer inspection, it is not a finder at all, but a 2.1-inch (53 mm) f/4 ED refractor outfitted with a digital camera. This second optical tube is the heart of the SP127’s electronically assisted system, serving as both guide scope and imager. The guide scope determines the telescope’s position through plate solving, slews to selected targets, maintains tracking, and captures images. Spectrum Optics also includes the same intelligent camera and 53 mm refractor in its separately sold SPi53 Smart Telescope system.

The camera is built around a Sony IMX662 CMOS color sensor with 2.9-micrometer pixels and a resolution of 1920×1080 pixels. It includes 64 gigabytes of onboard storage.

The MirroSky app, available for iOS and Android, is central to the SP127’s operation. It controls target selection, image capture, live stacking, and display, while the guide scope and camera work together to find objects and produce live-stacked images.

Meanwhile, the Maksutov is dedicated primarily to visual observing. The optical tube weighs approximately 6.5 pounds (2.95 kilograms) and measures 14.6 inches (370 mm) long. A Vixen-style dovetail makes it easy to remove the optical tube from the mount. Total weight for the assembled SP127 is about 26 pounds (11.8 kg).

In addition to the guide scope/imager, the SP127 comes with a 25 mm Plössl eyepiece, a 90° 1¼” star diagonal, a screw-on visual back, an adjustable tripod with steel legs 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) in diameter, cables, an AC adapter, and a Bahtinov focusing mask for the guide scope. The camera’s nosepiece is also internally threaded to accept standard 1¼” filters.

In its standard configuration, the included camera photographs through the 53 mm refractor rather than the Maksutov. Although the camera is removable, Spectrum Optics recommends a separate camera for imaging through the Maksutov because its long focal length and narrow field are not well-suited to the included camera’s plate-solving system. That doesn’t mean you have to invest in more equipment, though; I took some very nice shots of the Moon simply by holding my iPhone to the Mak’s 25 mm eyepiece.

The SP127’s hybrid arrangement works well in practice. After the user selects a target in the app, the guide scope directs the mount to the correct location, then tracks the sky. The observer can view the target visually through the Maksutov while the guide scope stacks and displays images via the app. A word of caution, however: Be careful not to shake the instrument when looking through the eyepiece. Even a slight motion will blur the image being photographed.

Like most Maksutov-Cassegrain systems, the SP127 excels at medium and high magnifications. Its 1,900 mm focal length is especially well-suited for observing the Moon, planets, planetary nebulae, and double stars.

(11.8 kg) Mount Payload: 9 lbs. (4 kg) Connectivity: built-in Wi-Fi, 2.4 and 5 GHz Camera Storage: 64GB onboard storage Tripod: Full-size adjustable steel-leg tripod Eyepiece: 25mm Plössl Price: $999.99 Contact: Spectrum Optics 2175 S Grand Ave Santa Ana, CA 92705 1-888-879-5143 spectrumoi.com

For this review, I arranged to receive a sample SP127 directly from Spectrum Optics. It arrived securely packed and in perfect condition.

Setup was easy, thanks to the well-illustrated paper manual that came with the scope. After I aligned the guide scope with the Maksutov during the day, as the instructions suggested, the scope was ready to go. I had everything together in under half an hour.

Control is handled entirely through the MirroSky app. To initialize the scope to the sky, the system uses onboard sensors combined with date, time, and location information supplied by the connected smart device. The camera includes dual-band Wi‑Fi capability supporting both 2.4 and 5 gigahertz connections. During use, the app’s interface was straightforward and easy to navigate. Target acquisition was quick and accurate. Chosen objects were always centered in the field of view. The app also provides guided tours and a database containing more than 100,000 stars, solar system members, and deep-sky sights.

Tracking performance was accurate for visual observations and short-exposure imaging. Since the SP127 uses an alt-azimuth mount, field rotation may become evident around the edges with longer exposures.

The SP127 can be powered by eight user-supplied AA batteries in the mount, a suitable external 12-volt power source, or the included AC adapter.

I found that the Maksutov performed very well. Lunar views were well-defined, with crater walls, rilles, and other surface features standing out crisply. I was especially impressed when, in moments of steady seeing, the SP127 detected a few of the craterlets on the floor of Plato. It passed another tough test by resolving Schröter’s Valley, a sinuous rille near craters Aristarchus and Herodotus.

Planetary performance also proved impressive. Multiple cloud bands as well as the Great Red Spot were clearly visible on Jupiter, and shadows cast by Galilean moons could also be seen on the planet’s cloud tops.

Double stars were another strong point, thanks to the long focal length. The Trapezium in the Orion Nebula, for instance, was striking. The included eyepiece did well, but the view really sparkled when I swapped in my own eyepieces with shorter focal lengths.

Throughout it all, I was very impressed with the crispness of the images, showing the high quality of the Maksutov’s optics. Like most catadioptric telescopes, the SP127 focuses by moving the primary mirror. This takes tight manufacturing tolerances to maintain a precise focus without tilting the mirror. I found that alignment stayed spot-on after swapping eyepieces and refocusing the view.

I was equally impressed with the imaging results using the 53 mm guide scope. The app allows you to customize settings, including gain, exposure length, number of frames to capture, and dark frames. After I experimented with the settings, the Orion Nebula appeared in vivid color after only two minutes of exposure, even as it was setting in my light-polluted sky. The Pleiades also recorded beautifully, although not all members squeezed into the guide scope’s approximately 1.6° by 0.9° field. The Horsehead Nebula, the Whirlpool Galaxy, the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules, and more displayed details exceeding what you might expect from such a small aperture, especially after post-processing using apps like PixInsight, GIMP, and Photoshop.

The SkyPilot 127 is one of the most original entries in today’s smart telescope market. For observers who still enjoy looking through an eyepiece but appreciate the convenience of app-driven targeting and imaging, the SP127 offers something genuinely special. In a small but growing group of smart telescopes that combine traditional eyepiece observing with integrated electronic imaging, the SP127’s hybrid design makes it an appealing bridge between conventional astronomy and the smart telescope revolution.

Contributing Editor Phil Harrington received the Walter Scott Houston Award in 2018 for his lifelong work in astronomy.

#6209. 14 Best Steakhouses in New York City for Old-School Chops, Wagyu, and the Perfect Martini

No single steakhouse can beat out all the others in NYC. Each has its strengths, and some are certainly better than others. There are the classics—Keens and Gallaghers in Midtown, Delmonico's in the Financial District, Peter Luger over in Williamsburg—that have been here for a hundred years or more, and for good reason. They are dimly-lit, tavern-like, with walls clad in wood. The menus do not change. The new and newish guard variously emulate and do their own thing. Increasingly, we are seeing steakhouses taking the basic assignment—red meat and sides in a formal dining room—and running with it in various cultural directions. Below, we've rounded up our favorites across this board. What's most important is their shared ability to make its diner feel important, a feat that goes beyond (but does require) the ability to gorge on good steak.

Read our complete New York City guide here, which includes:

Seagram Building, 99 E 52nd St, Midtown Manhattan

I am forming the opinion that a steakhouse's cardinal function is to make its diners feel important. No place has succeeded so impeccably in this mission as The Grill, where I was whisked from a downstairs lobby into the glamorous dining room as though a visiting board member come to town to be courted and impressed. I went for lunch, so the metal chain curtains that undulate (yes, they are ever-moving) over the massive windows shimmered in the daylight. Everyone except for me, it seemed, as there on very important business. I was the only male diner that I could see not in a jacket. The menu is very spendy (you cannot get a cocktail for less than $26) and therefore especially reserved for special occasions. Peppered filet mignon and martini, I'd say, are the way to go, but if it's lunch and the prime rib roast beef sandwich is being served, it's a worthy detour. —C.H.

The best thing that happened to me at 4 Charles Prime Rib was that I made a new friend. Steak and martinis and burgers, they're all fabulous—make no mistake. But sometimes it’s the life that comes at you in pursuit of those delicious menu items that leaves you feeling the most full. Too corny? Allow me to elaborate.

4 Charles is one of the toughest tables in town. Like Torrisi, it’s practically a private members' club where the only people who can land a reservation are those who’ve eaten there before. Hopeful walk-ins start lining up over an hour before opening at 4 p.m., and I got there at 2:45 p.m. to find myself second in line. I sat on the West Village townhouse stoop and enjoyed the day, enjoyed the sight of the staff puttering around setting up, glared at the people with reservations who we in line agreed were “line cutters.” When the host began seating people around 3:45 p.m., she told me that I was the first single walk-in and would therefore enjoy the one table by the door that they reserve for such parties. The man behind me, who arrived nary five minutes after I did, was told he would therefore have to wait until I was done. “Can’t I just sit with him?” he asked in earnest bewilderment. “Sure!” I responded.

And so together we unhinged our jaws and ate the 10-ounce double wagyu smash burger with thick slabs of bacon, his with an egg, and together we poured the beef jus over the pink center of the titular 4 Charles Cut and expressed our unexpected delight with the horseradish cream accoutrement. Together we drank martinis—I, a perfect vesper; he, an espresso; and then a chocolate each. If you’re going to try to go, I recommend you do so in this way. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Peter Luger isn't just the Brooklyn steakhouse. It just might be the New York City steakhouse, especially if history carries any weight with you, dear reader. This fine establishment has sat at the same address in the Williamsburg Bridge's shadow since 1887, and the interiors carry about as many frills as your average public house—dark wood, plaster walls, and so on. The menu is just as unadorned, with the most popular menu items being the dry-aged steak for two, steak for three, or steak for four. You can also, rest assured, get a single steak, lamb chops, salmon, or filet of sole. The Luger's sizzling bacon is not to be missed, nor are the sliced tomatoes and onions with Luger's Own sauce (pro tip: they go quite well together.) If you're there before 3:45 p.m., you'd also be wise to order the over-½-lb Luger burger, which is so simple and bloody with optional American cheese that your eyes will roll back in your head. —C.H.

This summer, the Montecito and Malibu staple Lucky's Steakhouse came to roost on a bustling street in New York’s Soho—and has been a fun addition to the city’s oft-stodgy steakhouse landscape ever since. Importantly, it’s a cool counterpoint—with its intimate size, Jazz Age-y murals, sexy date-night vibe, and a menu that accommodates non-steak eaters (i.e. me, a pescatarian). I know what you’re thinking: Why is a non-meat eater reviewing Lucky’s? Well, precisely for the fact that steakhouses can be wincingly non-inclusive, despite often being the restaurant of choice on special occasions. And Lucky’s feels different, not least because of its ambience. On a recent night, we started with the oysters, the peaky-toe crab cocktail, house chips, and Jimmy’s Greek salad (named after a family member of the owner). I then got the salmon, initially a perverse choice—because it usually plays poor country cousin at most steakhouses—but it was excellent. And we really dug into the sides—onion rings, market vegetables, and creamed corn. Both times I ate there, my companions ordered the 10-oz Gene’s Filet and I heard murmurs of firm approval. Whatever your dietary preference, don’t miss Lucky’s martini service, for which multiple servers will shake (or stir) your drinks table-side and in unison—because a little theatre hurts no one.

Head 10 blocks south of New York’s Koreatown (see an itinerary of the neighborhood here), and you'll find Cote, a Korean steakhouse and one of the city’s best and buzziest restaurants. There’s no shortage of a la carte options, but the prix-fixe Butcher’s Feast is where diners should start. For $74 a person, you're treated to seasonal ban-chan, savory egg soufflé, two stews (including spicy kimchi stew), and the house selection of beef, including USDA Prime and Wagyu, cooked on the table with smokeless grills. The restaurant’s award-winning wine list features an impressive Champagne selection, and all by-the-glass pours come from Magnums, the large-format bottles that sommeliers say keeps wines younger and fresher. There's also a second location at 550 Madison that's a bit grander, should that suit you. —D.F.

Gallaghers is the best steakhouse to eat at before a Broadway show. Wood paneled walls covered in framed old photographs (one of singer Perry Comon had to be labeled “this is not Jeffrey Epstein” due to those two men’s shared resemblance) offset the inhumane Midtown environment just beyond the front door. This is a place that’s as good for steak (and it really is good for steak) as it is for all of the accoutrements one expects of a good steakhouse—beyond the bovine, highlights include the old fashioned, the creamed spinach, the house-smoked bacon, and the beautifully browned veal chop parmigiana. Putting it all over the edge is the people watching—real live businesspeople drowning their sorrows at the bar alongside the theatergoers, and haughty waiters doing buttoned-up to the max. —C.H.

The only difficult choice to make when entering Keens is where to look first. Is it up, at the 90,000 pipes lining the ceiling? To the glass cases, where the most famous churchwardens—15-inch pipes—smoked by the likes of Babe Ruth and General MacArthur are stored? In the bar, are you mesmerized by the Miss Keen painting (a nude, lounging on her bear rug) right away, or are you too distracted by the New-York-ad-men-in-the-'50s vibe? This steakhouse, open since 1883, delivers something new to look at every time you go. Keens was originally called a chop house, in recognition of its famous mutton chop, and although that is good and musty and intense, most people are ordering steak. There’s the porterhouse for two or three, the chateaubriand, and the filet mignon—which is actually fabulous here. You want the béarnaise or au poivre sauce on the side, and the creamed spinach, which is less a vegetable than it is dessert. There's also the matter of the burger, which can be ordered up to the dining room from the more casual bar menu. —Alex Van Buren

1271 Avenue of the Americas, Midtown Manhattan

From the moment you walk into Cuerno, there's a sense of importance—the crowd, in suits and slicked back hair, is well-dressed; the dining room is always bustling and full, necks turning to see who else has walked in; and tableside preparations are happening left and right. This is Northern Mexican meat at its finest, in a space that feels true to that spirit—big leather booths, a colorful tile mural of a skeleton riding a bull—and with a menu that won't let you down. There are expected starters, like fresh guac and queso fundido, but also a chicarrón de pulpo bursting with flavor, and a charcoal-roasted cauliflower complemented by truffle and habanero. The main event, of course, are the steaks, like the decadent Taco Taquero with perfect skirt steak, and fire-roasted bone marrow scooped onto each tortilla tableside, or the Norteño-style arrachera served with chiltepin butter and avocado salsa.

Portions are generous, so come in a group of four people minimum to actually try different sections of the menu. And though most steakhouses focus on wine (and the wine list is good here), I like the chance to pair smoky mezcal and tequila cocktails with the heavier food. —Megan Spurrell

355 Metropolitan Ave, Williamsburg, Brooklyn

Not just in Williamsburg, not just in New York City, but truly one of the coziest, best-value steakhouses I’ve ever been to, St. Anselm manages a rare balance: laid-back yet elevated, intimate without trying too hard, and consistently delicious. The space feels like a hidden tavern—dark wood, low light, and just enough buzz and energy to make it feel like a special night out. The Butcher’s Steak is the standout—charred to perfection, tender and juicy inside, and ideal for sharing (for two) alongside fingerling potatoes and long green beans. Go for a group lunch or, better yet, settle in after dark when the candles are lit and the place feels like a warm, secret pocket of the city. Ask your server—or better yet, belly up to the bar—and you’ll get a wine recommendation that pairs not just with the food, but with your mood. —Jessica Chapel

513 E 6th Street, East Village, Manhattan

Buenos Aires earns major points for nostalgia: The tiny dining room is adorned in hanging soccer jerseys, televisions showing live games and commentary, and scarfs and pendants for teams like the Boca Juniors. There are couples on dates, families with kids, and even, in my case, a dude who came in alone and ordered his regular with his headphones in. (Ask about celebrities and they'll bring out an iPad with photos of grinning staff beside countless Latin America soccer players, American actors, and even Matt Damon who apparently hosted two birthday parties here in the early 2000s.) All to say, this isn't the place to bring the corporate account or close the deal, but it is the place to roll up your sleeves and tuck into a massive skirt steak, expertly cooked, and served no-frills—just a great piece of meat on a plate. Do save room for the empanadas (carne cortada a cuchillo, of course); on my next visit, I'm planning to order the sweetbreads as well. —M.S.

Glam, glam, glam with a capital G. Golden Steer's New York iteration—the original is in Vegas, and little of that location's trademark opulence has been sacrificed in adapting the brand for New York. We're not in Midtown either, but in the West Village, and this is a fitting addition to that neighborhood as it increasingly wears its wealth on its sleeve. Entering this crimson bunker is a cinematic experience—long hallways flanked by side quests like the capacious but moody bar. What to get? Sink into your plush booth and go full Sin City: the bloody bull oyster shooter (where a rich beef broth-spiked shot of bloody mary chases the slime), the big ole baked potato, and a Caesar dotingly mixed tableside. Any cut of meat will do. —C.H.

56 Beaver St, Financial District, Manhattan

The definitive downtown steakhouse is also New York City's oldest. Its home since 1837 is 56 Beaver Street, a dramatic triangular lot at the intersection of Beaver, William, and South William in the Financial District. When I visited on a mid-May evening, the exterior was bedecked in American regalia—they were to film an episode of The Gilded Age there the next day (the new season is currently airing on HBO) depicting the ticker tape parade welcoming the Statue of Liberty to the city. All of this history would be moot were the steakhouse inside not very good, which it is from top to bottom—superlative, doting service in the mural-clad dining room, stiff drinks, perfect cuts of meat. As with every steakhouse, there are a couple of signature items beyond steak that you should consider. Here, it's wedge salad and buttery Lobster Newberg, said to have been invented there. Don't miss either, but steak is still the thing, namely the titular flagship cut—a glistening 18-ounce ribeye that stands alone on the plate, needing no accoutrements. —Charlie Hobbs

Dinner and a show in New York City’s midtown sounds fabulous, but in practice usually means settling for a meal that delivers more on convenience than cuisine or atmosphere. Carvesteak, a newish steakhouse on the west side of 48th street, stepped up to all these qualities after I saw The Rocky Horror Show earlier this year. Designed by David Rockwell and the Rockwell Group, it’s moody, mirrored interiors are filled with little nods to the Broadway history it shoulders—including a dramatic velvet curtain that the bartender at the martini bar told me was once part of the set for Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Phantom of the Opera (even if untrue, it certainly looked the part). Speaking of the martini bar, it’s not to be missed: a pocket-sized station to post yourself up at before or after dinner. Food-wise, this is a classic steakhouse menu, but with a little bit of flashiness thanks to the restaurant’s Las Vegas origins (it debuted at Resorts World Las Vegas in 2021): think, prime cuts and aged rib eyes with all the sides and sauces you would expect, but also the option to order a potato and caviar “popsicle.” There’s a pre-theater menu, too, but for the full experience I suggest coming hungry and catching the last call before 10 p.m. —Lale Arikoglu

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

Ice out your opponents with these editor-approved picks.

Whether it’s competitive head-to-head matches or family game night, air hockey tables are an endlessly replayable way to bring the fun of the arcade and the ice rink into your home. Just like pool tables and ping-pong tables, air hockey tables come in several sizes and styles to suit your space and aesthetic.

A basic tabletop air hockey table runs under $100, though for an upgraded model with a frame and legs, expect to pay $300 to $500. For the most premium air hockey tables, you’re looking at what’s essentially a significant piece of furniture that typically costs $750 and up. High-quality tables often have wood or metal frames, LED lighting, and powerful fan motors for smoother gameplay.

While air hockey tables miniaturize the sport, buying one isn’t a small decision. Before you drop some change on a table, check out our list of the best air hockey tables we recommend, plus all the key features to look out for as you shop.

Looking for more games to play at home? Check out our stories on the best PS5 games, the best Xbox games, and the best Nintendo Switch games.

This 7.5-foot-long air hockey table is a perfect size for teens and adults. With a near-regulation 82-inch rink and a 120-volt motor, the air hockey table is both big enough and powerful enough to provide high-level gameplay for even the most competitive players.

The table is bordered by multi-colored LED lights that illuminate the rink as well as the two goals. The purchase also includes two rechargeable LED light-up pushers and a hockey puck for in-the-dark action.

The air hockey table has a built-in scoreboard that automatically registers and counts goals as they happen in real time. This sensor is also synced up to speakers that play upbeat music throughout the game and sound effects whenever you score.

For powerful action without the size and cost of a regulation table, this option from Triumph Sports is well worth considering. The 54-inch-long air hockey table is affordably priced yet still offers many of the features of more expensive choices.

It features a dual-motor blower, LED corner lights that light up when you score, and a digital scorekeeper that automatically racks up goals as they happen. The air hockey table also has a built-in abacus for manually counting your goals.

Similar to other tables on this list, it comes with light-up LED pushers and a light-up LED puck that make it easy to play in dark rooms.

Forget the legs and focus on the gameplay. This space-saving 40-inch-long tabletop air hockey table is a win for your wallet and your game. The tabletop design still offers a high-powered, 100V fan motor that propels air to replicate arcade-quality machines, with quiet, even airflow and a smooth, frictionless surface.

The air hockey table also has two manual sliding abacus scorers on each end, so you can keep track of your own goals as you play. Because it has no legs, the table can be easily stored in a closet or under the couch whenever it isn’t in use, saving valuable space in your game room.

Don’t limit yourself to just one game. This air hockey table also has an attachable top table designed for ping pong. The ping pong table has a mesh net in the center and comes with two paddles and two balls. In order to use it, simply place it on top of your air hockey table and slide it into place.

Underneath that table tennis top is one of the higher quality air hockey tables on this list. It sits at 80 inches long for near-regulation size and comes with NHL logos on the table legs and in the center of the rink.

The air hockey table also has an LED scoreboard built directly into the rail and speakers that play sound effects while you play. An underrated but well-appreciated feature of this table are the leg levelers. This helps maintain a level and fair playing field for both table tennis and air hockey.

For a serious gameroom upgrade, you might want to go with an all-in-one machine, especially if you’re limited on space. This one offers virtually every tabletop game imaginable, including chess, cards, checkers, bowling, and backgammon. In other words, you can host poker night and wind down the night with an intense game of air hockey, with little work involved. It features over 50 accessories to keep game night exciting, and the space-saving design makes it compact and portable for easy storage. This is a two-birds-with-one-stone situation here.

Some people consider air hockey tables an “eyesore.” Or at least my mom did when I was a kid. The Brookdale Air Hockey Table from Wayfair, though, features an elevated, rustic design and blends in well with modern decor. It offers just as much function as form, though, with a strong 110-volt airflow, in-game sound effects, and a built-in control panel for quick, easy play. Sort of the best of both worlds.

Air hockey table sizes range from full regulation length (84 inches), which you see at an arcade, to miniature tabletop options that are not much bigger than a board game. Between the two of them are a large number of mid-sized choices that fit comfortably into game rooms without monopolizing the entire space. If you plan on building a room around your air hockey table, we recommend regulation size. Otherwise, measure out the space you want to place the table in and buy one with dimensions that fit it.

There’s a big difference in the price and quality of the tables we selected below depending on their use case. For casual fun, you can get away with choosing a smaller, less expensive table. Tabletop options that can be set up and stored when not in use are also a great option for the less competitive air hockey fan.

More serious players should stick with larger options, which have powerful motors and well-placed fans that create a consistent feel across the entire playing surface. They should also look for a table with wide, sturdy legs that keep it in place even as you move and dive for the puck.

Many air hockey tables come with more than just a rink and pucks. Several options have LED lights to up the atmosphere or come with a digital scoreboard that automatically keeps track of goals and time. Some air hockey tables even have speakers that blast music and sound effects tied to the game. Several options on our list also provide a set of light-up pushers and pucks so you can even play in the dark.

We kept a range of ages, abilities, and prices in mind when making our air hockey table selections. The goal was to find high-quality products that would suit different space and design needs without absolutely breaking the bank. We researched hundreds of products ourselves, consulted expert assessments, and of course read through thousands of consumer reviews before making our final choices. Our final choices on this list reflect what we believe to be the best air hockey tables depending on your personal needs and budget.

#6207. How to watch Starship Flight 15

SpaceX is set to launch its 15th test flight of Starship on Friday, Nov. 13. For the first time, the company will try to catch both stages of the rocket — the Super Heavy booster and the upper stage, which SpaceX calls “Ship” — with the arms of its launch tower. If it works, Starship will become the first orbital rocket ever recovered in full.

SpaceX is targeting a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (4:45 p.m. CST) Friday from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas, pending regulatory approval. Starship launch dates often slip, so check the company’s Flight 15 mission page for the latest.

SpaceX’s live webcast begins about 30 minutes before liftoff — around 5:15 p.m. EST if the launch holds at the start of the window. You can stream it on the Flight 15 mission page or on SpaceX’s X account.

If you’re near the Texas-Mexico border, crowds typically gather on South Padre Island, across the bay from the launch site. On the Mexican side, the public beach at Playa Bagdad offers a head-on view of the launch tower.

About six and a half minutes after liftoff, Super Heavy should fly back to Starbase and be plucked from the air by the tower’s “chopstick” arms, a catch SpaceX has made three times before. Ship will continue to orbit and release 26 of SpaceX’s next-generation Starlink V3 satellites.

The real test comes the next day. Ship will circle Earth about 14 times at roughly 171 miles (275 kilometers) up before heading home. Until now, Ship’s test flights have ended with a practice landing at sea: it flips upright, and then fires its engines to set down gently on the water. This time, it will run that same maneuver over Starbase and hopefully settle into the tower’s arms instead. SpaceX’s flight timeline puts the catch about 22 and a half hours after launch — around 4:18 p.m. EST on Saturday, Nov. 14, if Starship lifts off on time.

SpaceX says Ship will head for the tower only if flight controllers confirm that every system it needs for reentry, the landing burn, and the final approach is healthy. If not, the company can bring Ship down at preplanned spots in the Pacific, with go/no-go checks built into the flight for splashdowns near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.

#6206. The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Like parrots, Infernogallus could deftly strip the flesh from large seeds

The ‘hell chicken’ Infernogallus (foreground) dines on Cretaceous fruits, sharing its habitat with a Tyrannosaurus rex (background).

Illustrated by Danielle Dufault, © Danielle Dufault, 2025.

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”

Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”

#6205. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 14: Venus and Mercury in Virgo

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Following inferior conjunction early this month, Mercury has reappeared in the morning sky. Now magnitude 0.3, you can find the small planet some 5° above the eastern horizon an hour before sunrise. It lies to the lower left of brighter Venus (magnitude –4.8), which sits alongside Virgo’s luminary Spica, about 12° to Mercury’s west.

This morning, Mercury is less than 1° south of 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis, which should be visible until the sky brightens enough to wash out the star. You can capture both in the same field of view in either binoculars or a telescope. Mercury now appears as a 32%-lit disk that is 8” across. Compare that with Venus, which features a narrower phase just 13% lit but stretches 51” by comparison. The brighter planet lies just 1.4° northwest of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.

Both Spica and Kappa can act as guideposts to help you spot Venus’ and Mercury’s motion, respectively, over the next few days. Mercury is moving east and will pull away from Kappa to the lower left. Venus, which just recently reached a stationary point, is also moving east, but will swing slightly northeast (to the upper left) of Spica for a few days before tracking more directly east.

Mars passes 1.2° north of Jupiter at 10 P.M. EST — we’ll focus on this pair in the early-morning sky tomorrow.

Sunrise: 6:44 A.M.Sunset: 4:44 P.M.Moonrise: 11:33 A.M.Moonset: 8:56 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (29%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time on the 15th, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

#6204. The Best Stocking Stuffer for Jet-Setters Is This Viral Handbag Accessory

If there’s one thing I love almost as much as planning a trip, it’s having a cute lineup of travel gear to help me get there. The perfect carry-on, a reliable travel tote, a passport holder that doesn’t look like everyone else’s—and, as of late, a bag charm (or three). The accessory du jour has officially made its way from our handbags to our airport ensembles, and I can’t think of a more delightful stocking stuffer for the traveler in your life.

Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is showing off Coach's signature cherry bag charm

Bag charms have a longer fashion history than their current moment suggests: Jane Birkin famously adorned her namesake Hermès with personal keepsakes. Hermès then introduced its Rodeo charm in 2005, and Fendi sent its furry Monster charms down the runway in 2013. After a runway revival at Miu Miu and Balenciaga shows in 2024, the look made its way back to stylish travelers everywhere.

It makes sense, really: We put so much thought into what we pack and what we carry, so why not have a little fun with the bags that get us there? A bag charm is an easy way to give a well-loved weekender a fresh look, or make that familiar canvas tote feel a bit more like your own. There are colorful beads, mini leather accessories, nostalgic trinkets, whimsy characters, and even designs with a practical purpose. Some bag charms are simply there to look good; others offer a clever place to tuck away small essentials. And when your suitcase is circling the baggage carousel among a sea of lookalikes, a fun, personal detail is hardly a bad thing.

Beyond the styling, I like to think of bag charms as a new kind of travel keepsake. We’re always bringing pieces of our trips home: a street market find, a knickknack from a beach town, some wonderfully impractical souvenir that means everything to us and very little to anyone else. Rather than tucking them away on a shelf, clip these charms onto a tote or suitcase, and they’ll join you for the next adventure. The same goes for a charm gifted by a friend or one that reminds you of home. Nothing says, “think of me on the road,” quite like this.

Bag charms add a pop of color to a neutral bag or suitcase

And there’s no shortage of ways to make the look your own. Layer a few bag charms together, mixing colors, textures, and shapes, or keep things more understated with a single leather accent or jewelry-like detail. Think of it as accessorizing your luggage with the same consideration you give the rest of your travel outfit. Whether you’re shopping for the friend who’s always planning a weekend away, the family member with an enviable vintage luggage collection, or the frequent flier who appreciates thoughtful detail, there’s something in the mix for just about every kind of traveler.

Bag charms are small, they’re personal, they’re wonderfully extra, and truthfully, a whole lot more exciting to unwrap than another pair of compression socks. (Sorry, compression socks). Ahead, I’ve rounded up the best bag charms to gift this season, from playful fashion finds and colorful conversation starters to travel-friendly designs that do a little more than just look pretty.

A little cherry on top, quite literally. Made from glittery resin and metal, this bright red pick brings a playful pop of color to a tote, backpack, or set of keys. It’s a particularly good choice for the friend whose wardrobe could always use one more fun thing.

For the person who prefers their accessories a little more understated—but still appreciates a good detail—this bad boy pairs deep green beads with gold-tone hardware and a lobster clasp, offering their favorite bag a subtle hit of color and texture.

For the New Yorker in your life, here's some Big Apple nostalgia to take on the road. Kate Spade pays homage to its hometown with this mini MetroCard-inspired design—and for those who remember the ol’ swipe of a subway card, it's a fun yet tasteful piece of the city to carry along.

I’m adding this gold boot gem to my cart. For a little Western flair—minus the need to break in a new pair of boots—the iconic brand Tecovas has turned its Loretta boot into a mini accessory crafted from solid brass with an antique finish. It comes with both a key ring and a D-ring, so it can go wherever its owner does—whether that’s a road trip, a dude ranch weekend, or simply the daily commute.

Talk about chic! Sézane’s Juliette keychain has a caramel-color resin exterior with delicate white lace detailing, but the real treat is inside: a pocket mirror that opens with a pivoting mechanism. It’s ideal for a quick lipstick check before stepping off the train or heading out to dinner.

For the friend who has approximately 1,000 photos of their dog on their phone—and would happily add one more to the rotation. This little Jack Russell is embroidered onto supple full-grain leather, with a debossed Lauren Ralph Lauren logo on the back. A rather handsome stand-in for a four-legged travel buddy.

A handbag for your handbag? I’m listening. This mini zippered pouch is styled like a classic carryall, with leather construction and gold-tone hardware, and clips onto a larger bag to keep small essentials close. It’s available in red, cobalt blue, and silver, and can be personalized with a foil-debossed monogram—making it an especially sweet gift for a loved one.

A little luck for the road never hurts! This Madewell design brings together a wishbone, stone, and moon motif in a red-and-gold-toned cluster, and is finished with a dog-clip closure. It’s a playful pick for the friend who loves a meaningful trinket—or could use a little good fortune on their next big adventure.

For the friend who's always planning their next trip, this miniature version of Away’s signature hard-shell carry-on is made from the same durable polycarbonate shell and opens into two little compartments for small essentials like a spare key or folded cash. It clips onto a bag or backpack, and the Coast Blue shade is a nice nod to the real thing.

Meet the mini-me of one of our editors' favorite travel bags. Calpak's best-selling Luka duffel—this compact zip pouch comes in a pearlescent finish and clips onto a larger bag with a carabiner-ready loop. Better yet, it actually earns its keep: There’s room for keys, earbuds, cash, or whatever small essentials you’d rather not fish around for at the bottom of your tote.

A flower that doesn’t need watering—or a vase. Inspired by the marigolds of Diwali, this three-dimensional design is made from layered Italian leather petals and comes in yellow or orange. The leather leaf can also be monogrammed, making it a thoughtful gift with a personal touch. It’s a lovely way to bring a little color to someone’s everyday bag.

#6203. Nov. 14, 2012: NASA announces an extended mission for Kepler

The Kepler Space Telescope, launched March 6, 2009, was designed to search the Milky Way for exoplanets. Using the transit method, Kepler ultimately observed over 500,00 stars and contributed to the discovery of almost 2,700 exoplanets.

Though Kepler was originally intended for a 3.5-year mission, NASA announced on Nov. 14, 2012, that the space telescope had successfully completed its primary mission and would be embarking on an extended mission. When a second gyroscope (also referred to as a reaction wheel) failed in May 2013 – the first having failed in July 2012 – that mission was in question, however, as it left the spacecraft with limited control for pointing. But engineers were able to craft a workaround using the momentum of the Sun’s light pressure to keep Kepler evenly and steadily directed, and the extended mission using this methodology, dubbed K2, was formally approved in May 2014. Kepler continued to function for a further four years, and was retired in October 2018 when it ran out of fuel. TESS (the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) has since inherited its planet-hunting mantle.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

The U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

"When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

It takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

Experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

The nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in New York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.

#6201. The 7 Best Noise-Canceling Headphones Clear Out The World So You Can Listen to What You Love

These cans and earbuds knock out background noise so you can focus or relax.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Noise-canceling headphones were once a niche category, dominated by high-priced over-ear cans. Throughout most of the 2010s, those seeking to drown out ambient noise distractions at work or during travel had to spend upwards of $300 to get a pair up to the task. These days, that's no longer the case. The market is jam-packed with quality noise-canceling headphones, including reliable models that start below $100. Having so many options to choose from can rightfully be overwhelming even for tech-savvy shoppers. To help you find the best noise-canceling headphones worth investing in, I spent months testing highly-rated options from leading brands and created this buying guide to share my recommendations.

Read more related reviews in our best wireless headphones and best wireless earbuds buying guides.

I’ve been testing consumer tech products, including audio gear, since 2011. Before I began testing, I spent a day sifting through product specs and features to handpick up-to-date products from reputable makers across the price spectrum—from budget to premium.

My testing routine included spending at least a week with each headset on this list. I used it at work, during my daily commutes, and, of course, while traveling domestically and internationally. These scenarios allowed me to properly evaluate the products’ design and ergonomics.

To evaluate the audio performance of the headphones, I streamed a carefully curated Apple Music playlist with tracks in various genres, including live albums. The eclectic music selection helped me experience the ability of the headphones to produce bass, treble, and mid-range. I also used the cans to stream podcasts, watch video content, and play video games.

Traveling by plane and working in a large open office gave me perfect scenarios to test the noise-canceling capabilities of all headphones. I paid close attention to how each set performed in this critical area, keeping in mind its form factor and price tag.

Ambient mode for being aware of your surroundings is just as essential and a key component of my testing routine. I also made sure that the headphones performed well during telephone, FaceTime, Microsoft Teams, and Zoom calls.

Regarding battery life, I meticulously observed how frequently I had to charge each headset. Spending days without battery anxiety was a benchmark for excellence in this department.

Lastly, where available, I tinkered with the companion app of every pair of headphones. I looked for tools to customize sound and additional features that help enhance the overall experience.

With all of the above tips in mind, enjoy a more peaceful daily and travel routine by switching to one of the products I vouch for below.

Bose QuietComfort headphones (and earbuds) have been synonymous with best-in-class noise cancellation for years. It stands to reason, then, that the Ultra cans top this product category.

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2 headphones, which launched in late 2025, offer up to 30 hours of battery life and superior wired playback. The headphones’ ability to tune out ambient noise distractions by generating almost complete silence is commendable and alone worth splurging on. What’s more, their companion app lets you customize its intensity and save the setting for easy access in a specific scenario. Such a level of modularity sets the product apart from its rivals, just as the core feature’s performance does.

On the audio front, the Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones deliver a balanced sound that’s customizable via an app. Dubbed Bose Immersive Audio, the cans’ ability to deliver multi-dimensional spatial sound with optional head tracking is superb and, crucially, easy to access. I like that the feature works with any audio content rather than requiring Dolby Atmos-enhanced audio. I successfully used it to make live music albums and videos more lifelike during my testing.

The 24-hour battery life of the QuietComfort Ultra headphones leaves a little to be desired, as competitors, including those in lower price tiers, can last longer between charges.

With an under-$100 sticker before additional and frequent discounts, the SonoFlow Pro HQ51 noise-canceling headphones by 1More are a legit impulse buy for such a product without skimping on design, ergonomics, performance, and battery life. The cans are surprisingly sleek and comfy, capable of delivering a high-quality audio experience across the board, as well as long battery life.

The sound quality of the headphones thoroughly exceeded my expectations when I put them through their paces. Tuned by a master audio engineer, the cans treated me to a balanced sound that made me feel like I was using a much pricier set. The tools for customizing the sound via their companion app are just as impressive.

When it comes to noise cancellation, the SonoFlow Pro HQ51 is among the best for the money. The headphones did a solid job in tuning out distractions, but couldn’t match the serenity of costlier cans. That’s totally fine considering their agreeable price.

With up to a staggering 65 hours of battery life with noise cancellation, the SonoFlow Pro HQ51 leaves rivals that cost several times more in the dust. I could easily spend a week using them without battery anxiety. And believe it or not, you can get up to 100 hours of wireless playback from the 1More headphones by disabling the core functionality.

The Beats Studio Pro headphones are a must-have for owners of multiple Apple devices. Just like AirPods (and other Beats products), the cans will instantly connect to Apple devices that are linked to the same iCloud account. Once I paired them with my iPhone, I could instantly use the cans with an iPad, a MacBook, and a Mac mini, as well as keep tabs on their whereabouts in the Apple Find My app.

In addition to the seamless hardware compatibility mentioned above, the Beats Studio Pro headphones deserve the attention of Apple users for their ability to deliver a superb spatial audio experience. Accessing the functionality on an iPhone or an iPad is as easy as long-pressing the volume control button in the command center.

The Studio Pro headphones’ audio quality and noise cancellation are among the best in their price category. Their sound is balanced, melodic, and versatile, making it suitable for a wide range of music styles. There is no option to customize it via an app, but I didn’t feel like I had to make any changes while using the cans.

Unlike many competitors, the Beats Studio Pro headphones can deliver lossless audio over a direct USB-C link to phone, tablet, or computer. Listening in higher fidelity doesn’t include noise cancellation. Thankfully, I could access the latter via the standard audio jack when I needed to use the entertainment system during a flight.

The Beats headphones integrate well with Android and Chrome OS hardware, too, but I prefer the Apple experience for its superior spatial audio and because I don't need to install a companion app. Consider the recently released AirPods Max 2 over the Beats Studio Pro if you have a bigger budget for Apple-ready headphones. Their audio performance, craftsmanship, and controls are on a much higher level. However, you’ll have to settle for a heavier headset with shorter battery life and spend extra on a suitable protective case and a cable with a standard audio connector.

On-ear headphones have largely taken a back seat to larger over-ear ANC headphones, which offer more passive noise cancellation, and earbuds for their pocketable form factor. Marshall’s Milton ANC headphones offer a now-rare premium on-ear design that gives you the best version a middle ground between the two, with a lightweight design, great sound quality, and a less ostentatious on-ear fit. With a foldable design and scratch-resistant ear cup covers, the Milton wears really well over the course of long day on the go.

On the audio front, the Marshall Milton ANC impressed me with crisp, energetic sound that's customizable via a companion app. Its noise cancellation is also stellar, though does not generate the same auditory void as my top over-ear picks.

The headphones’ knob and customizable button controls are a benchmark for excellence and miles ahead of their competitors. The same goes for its 50-hour battery life. (Or 80 hours if you turn the ANC off.)

On-ear headphones are especially niche if ANC is your top priority, but it’s a great everyday carry headphone if your earbuds just aren’t cutting it. If you dig Marshall’s look, but would prefer an over-ear solution, the Monitor III ANC has a similar design and controls, but with a heavier, more deeply isolating form factor.

Reviewed: Marshall Milton ANC Wireless Headphones

The Bowers & Wilkins PX8 S2 wireless headphones are, hands down, my favorite wireless ANC headphones for discerning audiophiles looking for something more detailed than the standard options from Sony, Bose, and Apple.

Like the legendary British audio maker’s (very) expensive floor speakers, these over-ear cans produce pristine, infinitely customizable stereo sound that faithfully generates every detail of whatever you’re listening to.

At a time when wireless headphones generally try to earn attention with digital enhancements like spatial audio, the PX8 S2 impressed me with its old-school approach to audio fidelity. (Note: B&W has added spatial audio since my review via a firmware update.) Experiencing the headphones’ sound with noise cancellation enabled is like listening to Bowers & Wilkins speakers in your own private space.

For $800, you know every aspect of these headphones has to work incredibly well, and they do. Its craftsmanship and tactility, headlined by genuine leather and metal accents in several colors, is a marvel for folks with extremely discerning taste... And plenty of disposable income.

The Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones are all about delivering an incredibly powerful bass that’s available and adjustable via a dedicated button on the left cup. The sensory experience is truly remarkable and unlike anything rivals can offer, even though it predictably impacts the overall audio fidelity. The headphones’ noise cancellation is solid, if not on par with pricier sets from leading makers.

I didn’t reach for the Crusher ANC 2 when I felt like streaming classical jazz, but I grinned every time I played my favorite downtempo tracks on the product. Using the cans for playing action-packed games with the bass cranked up was also a ton of fun.

Disabling the thunderous low-end brought me a more “grown-up” sound, customizable via an app. That’s not what I’d recommend the product for, however. This Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 is all about celebrating bass.

The Crusher ANC 2 is also comfy to wear and equipped with convenient button controls. I also like the headphones’ integrated Tile tracker, as well as their sleek design with a contrasting, brightly colored button for activating the Crusher experience. There are tons of color options.

Skullcandy’s Icon ANC wireless headphones are handily the best for exercising on this list. The surprisingly affordable cans have a compact on-ear design, a secure fit, and an IPX4 rating for sweat- and water resistance. These qualities, together with convenient button controls, make the Icon ANC equally suitable for indoor and outdoor workouts.

The default sound of the headphones has an enhanced bass, which helped me stay motivated during my workouts. The Skullcandy app has several presets for customizing the sound, as well as a graphic equalizer to create your own. The noise cancellation worked, but it didn’t stop me in my tracks with its efficiency. That’s hardly a surprise considering the product’s price category.

I found the Skullcandy Icon ANC’s multi-directional control knob to be incredibly convenient during my testing. Their 50-hour battery life with noise cancellation exceeded my expectations, too. I didn’t expect this longevity from a compact pair of wireless headphones.

Skullcandy offers the Icon ANC in several colors. Every set comes bundled with a soft carrying pouch.

Noise cancellation relies on built-in microphones that continuously monitor your surroundings. A dedicated chip processes the sound captured by the microphones before sending its exact aural opposite to your ears via the headphones' audio drivers. This sophisticated technology naturally contributes to the cost of noise-canceling headphones. Translation? The more you spend, the better you'll isolate yourself from your surroundings. Prepare to drop north of $300 if you are looking to achieve (almost) complete silence from your purchase.

High-quality sound is also a must for a great pair of noise-canceling headphones. Support for immersive spatial audio is particularly important for top-shelf headphones. It makes live albums and video content more immersive and the listening experience more lifelike, especially if dynamic head tracking is available. Spatial audio is available on most top-shelf noise-canceling headphones. High-end sets without this functionality make up by producing pristine stereo sound, which makes them worth investing in. Speaking of stereo sound, today's best headphones in this space, including budget-friendly models, support lossless audio over wireless and wired connections. If you are using a streaming service that offers lossless audio, keep an eye out for this feature. It will serve you well.

Your next set of headphones should get you at least 20-30 hours of wireless playback between power-ups with noise cancellation. That’s the bare minimum for these products, with class-leading sets by Apple, Bose, and Sony delivering battery endurance in this ballpark. That’s enough to get you through a long flight or hectic workday in silence.Remarkably, cheaper cans now have much longer battery life. Some will give you double the endurance of the class-leading options with noise cancellation and a three-digit number of hours without it. Those numbers are remarkable, but trust me, stronger noise cancellation and higher-quality sound are worth the more frequent charging sessions.

A companion app for customizing the sound and the noise cancellation, among other things, is essential for any set of wireless headphones or earbuds today, so look for it while shopping. Apple AirPods and Beats products don’t have an iPhone app. Their settings are easily accessible directly in iOS, iPadOS, and macOS.

#6200. In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho, the documentary dives into how oceanographers are racing to understand the world’s changing waters

Aerial imagery of research vessel Star Keys safe harboring in Abel Tasman, New Zealand.

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

#6199. 13 Travel Slippers That Are Comfier Than the Ones From Your Favorite Hotel

After a full day of sightseeing—or an even longer one spent in and out of airports—few things feel better than kicking off your shoes and sliding on a cozy pair of slippers. The complimentary slippers at a luxury hotel are always tempting to take home, but if we're honest, they rarely last beyond a few wears. Fortunately, plenty of more durable—and more comfortable—options exist, from plush, shearling slides and classic wool slip-ons to lightweight travel slippers that barely take up any room in your suitcase. Some have cushioned footbeds and rubber soles sturdy enough for a quick trip outside; others feature soft, suede soles better suited to padding around the house.

Whether you want a warm, fluffy pair by your bed or a foldable option for your next long-haul flight, there’s a slipper for everyone on this list. Read on for the very best pairs to pick up this season from Bombas, Cozy Earth, Ugg, and more.

⁠These lightweight, fuzzy slippers feature a soft, wool-like polyester upper, a breathable lining, and a memory foam footbed for a cushy feel underfoot. The nonslip soles are sturdy enough for quick trips outside to grab the mail or take out the trash, but they're best suited for indoor wear. Available in five colors and backed by more than 10,000 Amazon reviews, they're an affordable option for wearing around the house or packing for a weekend away.

It's easy to see why this under-$25 Amazon find has racked up more than 23,000 five-star ratings. Not only are these slippers ridiculously soft (and just the right amount of over-the-top), but they're also pretty practical, thanks to the thick memory foam insole that retains its shape even after daily wear.

While your winter wardrobe likely contains a cashmere sweater or two, don’t sleep on these cashmere slides from Garnet Hill. Thanks to the slip-on slides’ sumptuous cashmere construction and breathable, thermal-insulating fibers, they’ll keep your feet warm and toasty—but not sweaty—all winter long. The padded footbed provides an extra layer of pillowy-soft comfort.

After a long day on your feet, you'll be glad to have these Quince slippers waiting by your bed. They have a soft suede leather upper and thick Australian shearling lining that feels plush against bare feet. And unlike some fuzzy slippers that leave your feet sweaty, the shearling material naturally wicks away moisture and regulates temperature, so you can wear them year-round.

The soft, moisture-wicking sheepskin wool lining of this classic shoe has made it an all-time favorite from the nostalgic Australian brand. The Scuff comes with a thin rubber sole that has just the right amount of support and stability for being on your feet in the kitchen or just puttering around the house on the weekend. Colors include the popular chestnut (shown above), dark gray, and black.

This luxury slide keeps your feet dry and cool, thanks to its moisture-wicking and temperature-regulating design. They're fluffy and warm, and so easy to slip on when you first wake up in the morning. Plus, they feature a slip-resistant sole, making them one of the sturdiest picks on the list.

One of the little luxuries of a hotel stay is slipping into the plush robes and slippers hanging in the closet. Now you can capture that vacation-level comfort at home with The Ritz-Carlton Frette slippers. Crafted from ultra-soft microfiber, they feel cozy and spa-like, while the nonslip soles make them practical for everyday wear around the house. The embroidered hotel logo adds a touch of opulence, and when they need a refresh, simply toss them in the wash.

These striped slippers from Parachute look like something you'd find at a cool boutique hotel. Made in Turkey from thick, absorbent cotton terry, they're soft underfoot and comfortable to slip on after a shower or while lounging at home. The stripes add a little more personality than your typical spa slippers, and the rubber soles grip slippery floors effortlessly. They're durable enough for everyday wear, too, though you may want to size up for a roomier fit.

Made with ultra-soft sheep fur and a plush shearling lining, these chic slippers provide plenty of warmth on chilly fall and winter mornings. As warm as they are, they're also naturally odor-resistant and breathable, so you don't have to worry about your feet getting too hot. They offer a grippy, durable outsole, so while they're best suited for lounging indoors, they can also be worn outside if necessary; you'll feel a little more secure wearing them out on the Airbnb's deck or down to the hotel lobby than in other pairs. They come recommended by commerce editor Meaghan Kenny, who regularly turns to them for extra warmth on cold weekend mornings at home.

Bombas has quite a few solid slippers from which to choose—including the Gripper Slipper that really blurs the line between sock and shoe. But the Sunday Slipper, with its super-soft faux fur and slip-on, slip-off capability, sits at the top of the heap when it comes to versatility. If you're stumped on what to gift someone for the holidays, the best-selling style is foolproof.

Birkenstock manufactures footwear of fabulous durability and quality, from the popular sandals and clogs that you can wear here, there, and everywhere to the more indoor-friendly Zermatt shearling slipper. Despite being supremely soft, the latex sole offers a boost of support, which is why they make such a great house shoe. They come in men's and women’s sizes, and you can pick between wide or narrow fits for optimal comfort.

The Ugg Tasman slipper might be the most recognizable slipper on this list, and it's popular for good reason: The closed-back design makes it a more practical alternative to the brand's classic Scuff slipper; the plush sheepskin lining and durable suede upper ensure coziness and durability; and the Fair Isle–inspired Tasman braid around the trim adds a hint of character.

L.L.Bean fans rave about these clog-like slippers for their arch support, heel cushioning, and playful patterns, featuring designs ranging from turtles to moose to ombré forest trees. They have a fleece lining and rubber anti-slip sole, and are roomy enough to wear your thickest socks underneath in colder months, making them our top pick for cold feet.

What are the best brands for travel slippers?

Bombas and EverFoams design lightweight slippers that are conveniently packable, while Ugg and Quince offer cozy shearling options that take up a bit more suitcase space. If you love the slippers you usually find at luxury hotels, The Ritz-Carlton also sells its signature Frette spa slippers online, so you can bring five-star comfort right to your home.

Slippers can be a welcome change from sneakers or boots on a long-haul flight, especially if you’re hoping to get some sleep. Choose a lightweight, packable pair with nonslip soles, but switch back to shoes when walking around the cabin or using the bathroom.

What should you look for in the best indoor slippers?

When shopping for indoor slippers, fit and material matter most: Wool and shearling provide warmth without trapping too much heat, while memory foam adds cushioning. Look for a soft, flexible sole with enough grip to keep you from slipping on hardwood or tile floors.
