#6198. The 6 Best Flashlights for Everyday Use

Yes, they’re better than the one on your phone.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Smartphones may give us an easy access to a light source, but for seeing objects at a distance or brightening a workspace in places like the attic or under the sink, you need the power and range of a LED (light-emitting diode) flashlight. Flashlights are vital for navigating the outdoors at night and absolutely essential during a blackout or emergency, when you don’t want to drain your phone’s battery.

We’ve tested a variety of popular models to find the best flashlights, whether you’re looking for one to use in the midst of a blackout or simply want to put a decent one in the glove box of your car, just in case.

Perhaps the most important element of testing flashlights is to ensure they’re as bright as manufacturers claim. Brands typically list a lumen count, though they’re often inflated. Flashlights tend to dim slightly after you turn them on and your eyes adjust, and how quickly they do so is key. It’s not just about the peak brightness, but how long that brightness actually lasts and how bright the light is after it dims.

To measure lumen, you need an integrating sphere, which is an expensive piece of equipment. So for testing flashlights, we built our own. We consulted with product engineers at two different companies to go over our plans. We also used their commercial spheres to verify lumens on calibration lights to make sure that our own sphere sensors would be accurate.

After construction and calibration, we measured each flashlight individually at specific time intervals. We recorded our measurements immediately after turning on the light, every 30 seconds for the first 3 minutes, at 5 minutes, and then every 5 minutes for a full half an hour. Our official figure is based on our measurement at 30 seconds because most flashlights drop brightness quickly after that before eventually stabilizing at a dimmer level.

After completing the quantitative portion of our testing process, we used each flashlight in a variety of real-world applications, noting aspects including quality of build, ergonomics, weight, water-resistance, and other key specs.

Our best overall is an evolution on the classic hefty Maglite you remember in your parents junk drawer that could blind you if you looked directly at it. This model trades in the D batteries for a rechargeable and replaceable battery. Furthermore, the flashlight has an LED bulb that shines just as brightly as the old-school models you remember.

While Maglite lists that the flashlight shines with a brightness of 1,082 lumens, our own testing measured an even higher figure, not dropping below 1,082 lumens for more than three minutes.

Beyond this, I really love how it feels in my hand. It isn’t quite as clunky as the giant models of the past, but it still boasts a similar heft that feels solid and durable. The aluminum frame and IPX4 water resistance rating backs that feeling up.

If raw lumens and longevity are top of your priority list, it’s hard to find a better choice than the Streamlight Polytac X USB. The starting point of 554 lumens is already solid, but in testing, the flashlight settles between 334 and 324 lumens, which is a far higher than nearly all other options we tested.

The relatively compact design doesn’t detract from the overall performance, as the light beam extends for close to 300 feet. That said, the reflector is not adjustable, so you’ll have to look elsewhere for a floodlight.

Beyond this, we liked the nylon polymer body which was grippy and a lot more comfortable to hold in comparison to a fully metal exterior, which can be icy to the touch in cold temperatures.

There are three preprogrammed function sets we were able to access using Streamlight’s Ten-Tap selector switch. The selection process is a little awkward, but most people will likely only use it sparingly to set the preferred programs, which include low/medium/high, high/strobe/low, and high only. We recommend reading the instructions thoroughly to get this right.

From a fully charged state, the Polytac X ran for almost 5.5 hours during our runtime test before going dark.

No, Energizer isn’t just for batteries and Jeep isn’t just for cars. The collaboration between the two brands has led to an affordable, sturdy flashlight with enough brightness to cut through the darkness during late nights on the trails or on the roadside.

While Jeep’s involvement isn’t more than some design elements and a logo, this particular option is part of a larger lighting collection the brand did in collaboration with Energizer, featuring headlamps and other flashlights.

During our lumen testing, the flashlight measured a little less than 20 percent below the 1,000 lumens Energizer claims, which isn’t uncommon given nearly all flashlights fall a little short of their advertised number. It still offers tremendous light, especially in tandem with the reflector and lens, which do a nice job angling the light out in a steady, powerful beam.

Test Editor Bradley Ford noted: “The unique feature on this light is the Power Indicator screen for which it is named. When the light is turned on, or the mode changed, the screen displays estimated runtime for that mode—then it switches to battery capacity, listed as charge capacity remaining. Really a nice feature, and better than typical three or four battery-level indicators that are more common.”

We’ve tested other flashlights from ThruNite and were impressed by their durable, powerful lighting. That’s why we called in the Archer 2A V3 to test.

The flashlight is said to have more than 8 hours of consistent lumen output, higher than many flashlights we tested. Along with brightness, the Archer flashlight is compact and easy to carry around for everyday tasks. Need a quick light to check the back of your shed? Simply reach into your pocket and use the Archer.

The ThruNite won’t be top of the list in any one category but thrives on being pretty consistent across all of them. It’s bright, long-lasting, and durable, which is just about all you really need.

This ArkPro line of flashlights from Olight caught our eye not just for its slim, pocket-sized design, but also for the volume of additional features it offers. The ArkPro Ultra has four different lighting options: a long-range spotlight, a shallow floodlight, a UV light, and a laser pointer.

Furthermore, you can use those lights in combination with one another. For example, you can turn the laser pointer on and off while shining the flood.

During testing, the long-range spotlight and floodlight ended up being our favorite dual feature. We were able to illuminate small dark rooms easily with the shallow floodlight, while using the long-range spotlight for hallways and large empty spaces. Having both in one body is not a common feature. While we might have initially winced at the price tag, the Olight makes a solid case that it has the value of multiple flashlights.

That said, it’s worth noting that our measured lumens fell short of Olight’s claimed 1,700 figure. The flashlight is still much brighter than most other options but did degrade over the 30-minute test.

Another promising feature: the physical display lights on the body that indicate battery, brightness, and a lockout mode. That last one prevents kids from accidentally flashing the laser or other lights in their eyes by locking the device from shutting on and off.

The USB-C charging is also a plus. With nearly every smartphone charger already built in the same design, you’ve likely got dozens of compatible charging cords lying around.

This small, tactical flashlight from ThruNite does a number of key things well. The over 2400 lumens at its brightest setting rivals some of the most powerful options we recommend. At the same time the compact body and hip clip make it a great portable option that easily slips in a pocket or center console of your car.

What sets the TC15 apart from other options is the extraordinary runtime. On its Firefly mode (which is admittedly a very low setting), the flashlight can run for up to 30 days before needing to recharge.

The durable aluminum body is capable of handling a steep drop and the IPX8 rating means you can feel confident using it in the rain.

Traditional light bulbs, while nostalgic, are inefficient and waste a lot of energy. According to the U.S. Department of Energy, as much as 90 percent of the energy required to illuminate an incandescent light is given off—essentially lost—as heat. Halogen bulbs are an improvement on classic incandescent lights, but still generate a ton of heat. Beyond this, the bulbs themselves are also quite delicate. If dropped, they can easily shatter.

In contrast, LEDs are 70 to 75 percent more efficient than incandescent lights. That efficiency doesn’t lead to lower brightness either, with LEDs actually shining far stronger than most classic bulbs. The LED itself is a semiconductor that emits light when current passes through it. Furthermore, without a delicate filament inside, LEDs are far more durable.

While LEDs in flashlights are more efficient than traditional bulbs, they still generate a fair amount of heat. Especially as brands continue to push to create brighter and brighter flashlights, the heat generated grows too. That said, most LED flashlights have circuitry designed to manage power consumption and prevent your light from burning up.

For the most part, as long as you use common sense and don’t max out your light for hours on end, your LED flashlight should be fine. Take care of it responsibly and you’ll never deal with heat issues.

The actual brightness of your flashlight is measured in lumens. Lumens are essentially measuring the total light created by flashlight, with the higher the figure, the brighter the flashlight should shine.

Even accurate figures reported by a company can often refer to the absolute highest possible lumen output, which is not realistically what you end up using most of the time. Being able to measure them ourselves provides a lot of much needed reassurance.

That said, lumens aren’t the end all, be all. A lot of the perceived brightness and clarity of the beam is due to the reflector shape and lens. So, the width and length of the light beam from your flashlight will likely be a better determination of whether it works for you or not.

IP is short for ingress protection, meaning protection from stuff getting inside the flashlight. Those letters will be followed by two numbers: The first digit indicates protection from solids like dust or grit. The second digit indicates protection from moisture, in this case the concern is usually water. Sometimes there will be an “X” in place of one of those numbers, which means the flashlight hasn’t been tested for protection from solids (if the X is where the first number should be) or liquids (if it’s where the second should be).

For the first number, protection from solids, the highest rating, 6, indicates the light should be impenetrable by dust and sand. The highest value for the second number, representing protection from liquid, is 8. The flashlight can be submerged in water deeper than 1 meter for longer than 30 minutes, with no harmful effects.

A flashlight’s IP rating gives a partial picture of its durability. You’ll also want to take into account things like the materials used—ranging from lightweight but less-than-durable plastic to rubberized enclosures to heavy-duty anodized aluminum—and whether the flashlight floats in water in addition to being waterproof, not to mention the warranty.

As our first-hand testing showed, manufacturer estimates for flashlight specs are relatively accurate, especially regarding the peak brightness. It’s important to keep in mind that there are a variety of factors that can influence a flashlight’s moment-to-moment performance, such as its battery life and how long it has run in the past few hours.

As we mentioned, it is normal for flashlights to only shine at peak brightness for a few minutes before sliding back to the middle of their range. The good news is your visibility won’t suffer for that.

That depends on how you’re using your flashlight. Manufacturer Nitecore suggests a range of 1 to 300 lumens should be enough to light up a room or an intermittently lit outdoor area. Look for 300 to 980 lumens for walking in the dark without any additional light sources. Mechanics and other workers who need to see precise details in complete darkness might go a little higher, say 1,000 to 1,300 lumens.

Hunters or law enforcement might use brighter flashlights than that, but it really depends on the task. Furthermore, it’s important to remember that powerful flashlights can be disruptive to other people and wildlife, so choose your light carefully.

Flashlight enthusiasts often recommend making a flash part of your “everyday carry,” keeping it on you at all times as you would with your keys or smartphone. Personally, we recommend being proactive and keeping it around whenever or wherever you think there’s a chance you may need some extra light. For example, if you’re going on a hiking trip or evening walk, it’s a no-brainer.

It’s never a bad idea to stash a flashlight on each floor of your home in case of a power outage or other emergency. That way, you can easily grab it without going up or down stairs in the dark. It’s best to keep them in a place that you know you’ll remember and is easy to find in the dark, such as a small drawer.

We also stronglyrecommend keeping a flashlight in your car, as you never know when you might have a mechanical issue at night, and you’ll want to save your phone battery.

Separately, FEMA and The Department of Homeland Security recommend that you keep an emergency kit with a flashlight and other essentials in a cool, dry place somewhere at home, as well as in your car. In order to keep the kit intact and ready for an emergency, the flashlight in your emergency kit should be a backup, not your primary flashlight.

#6197. These 9 Hotels for Broadway Lovers Put You in the Heart of NYC’s Theater District

As a Californian who discovered the wonderful world of Broadway by borrowing CDs from my local library, it was only fitting that the first trip I ever planned by myself was to New York City—and the entire itinerary revolved around collecting Playbills. Now, after living in the area for more than two decades, I’m that unlikely New Yorker who still claims Times Square as her favorite and most-frequented neighborhood. I just love the Theater District—where else can you find 41 venues featuring the world's best live theater all within a single mile?

In this age of event tourism, Broadway has remained a constant. And seeing a show is about more than just the storyline of a play or the numbers in a musical—it’s an experience that you’re a part of. Over my 20 years as an entertainment editor and journalist, I’ve interviewed numerous Broadway stars, and they always say they feed off of, and are fueled by, audience reactions. You’re not just a passive viewer; your presence drives the show. It's something special to take part in.

If you've got a Broadway trip in your future, chances are you're going to need a hotel that will help you maximize your experience. The list below features properties with themed suites, theater lore, and locations just steps from the Great White Way. Read on for the best places to stay in NYC for a show-stopping Broadway getaway.

Closest theaters: 1-minute walk to Palace Theatre, 3-minute walk to James Earl Jones Theatre and Lunt-Fontanne TheatreWhy we love it: Right across from Palace Theatre, pre- and post-show prix-fixe menus, Studio 54 history

These days, Studio 54 is one of Broadway’s most popular stages (currently home to The Rocky Horror Show ), but back in 1977, Ian Schrager opened it as a nightclub, and it has since come to epitomize celebrity culture for a generation. Schrager brought that same visionary spirit when he opened the 452-room Times Square Edition in 2019, just across the street from the Palace Theatre. One of my favorite spots in Times Square is the hotel's Terrace and Outdoor Garden, a lush dining oasis that offers three-course Broadway Express prix-fixe menus both pre- and post-show. For those looking for an upgraded theater experience, the Edition's Showstopping Stay package—which can be booked up to 10 days in advance—includes two premium tickets to select shows, dinner with Champagne, theater-themed amenities, and house-made snacks.

Closest theaters: 9-minute walk to Studio 54, 10-minute walk to Vivian Beaumont Theater, 11-minute walk to Broadway TheatreWhy we love it: Central Park views, Broadway VIP Experience

Though a few blocks north of the Theater District thrills, the Mandarin Oriental is still less than a 15-minute walk to most theaters—yet it feels a world apart. It overlooks Central Park in one direction, and its 75-foot lap pool has views of the Hudson River. Guests are pampered with a true five-star experience every step of the way, whether it’s raising a glass at The Bar speakeasy or lounging around at celeb-favorite MO Lounge. You can also rub shoulders with the stars via the hotel's Broadway VIP Experience package, which includes an hour-long meet-and-greet with a Broadway cast member over bites and Champagne at the lounge. Also included are orchestra tickets (choose from 13 shows, including Hamilton and Harry Potter and the Cursed Child) and show merch, as well as add-ons like a theater transfer in a Mercedes, a 90-minute guided tour of the Museum of Broadway, or even acting lessons or a private concert with a stage star.

Closest theaters: 3-minute walk to Belasco Theatre, 4-minute walk to Hudson Theatre, 5-minute walk to Stephen Sondheim TheatreWhy we love it: Official partner of the Tony Awards, recently refreshed, early check-in option

If hotels could earn Tonys, the Sofitel New York would be a clear winner. As a longtime partner of Broadway’s iconic awards show, many a theater star has walked through its doors. That includes George Clooney during his Broadway debut in Good Night, and Good Luck, Jonathan Groff during his turn as Bobby Darin in Just in Time, and Mia Farrow while she was in The Roommate. Just last year, the property underwent a full makeover, reimagining its 398 rooms and suites (some with Empire State Building views), as well as its lobby, fitness center, and dining options (including Social 45 Bar & Bistro), drawing on the Art Deco glamour of Paris and New York. While an exclusive Broadway package is currently in the works, the Sofitel does currently offer The Ultimate Manhattan Luxury Staycation experience, which includes a welcome drink, dining credit, signature pastries, and early check-in at noon, perfect for squeezing in an extra Wednesday or weekend matinee.

Closest theaters: 2-minute walk to Eugene O’Neill Theatre, Walter Kerr, and Longacre TheatreWhy we love it: Quiet, designed by a Tony-winning scenic designer, curated theater mementos

Despite being footsteps away from several Broadway theaters, Civilian Hotel manages to create a cozy boutique experience, starting with an entrance just around the corner from Eighth Avenue. One step inside, and you feel like you’ve earned a backstage pass— hotelier Jason Pomeranc teamed up with scenic designer David Rockwell (Hairspray, Legally Blonde, Elf) on a classic theater theme featuring everything from marquee-inspired lighting to dramatic curtains. Even its 203 guest rooms channel vintage dressing room vibes. Rockwell's goal was to create a space for NYC’s creatives—performers, designers, directors, producers, and writers—that paid homage to classic Broadway. Stop by the Blue Vault tasting room and lounge to spot some theater relics, and the Olio Collection rooftop bar for more than 250 pieces of theater-inspired art.

Closest theaters: 1-minute walk to Palace Theatre, 3-minute walk to Marquis TheatreWhy we love it: Location across from TKTS booth, buzzy Sky Lobby

When it comes to Theater District locations, you can't find much better than the 661-room Tempo by Hilton New York Times Square. Making its debut in the dense area in August 2023, it snagged a prime spot right across from Duffy Square’s TKTS booth, the bright red discount ticket outlet that sells last-minute show tickets for up to 50% off (psst, check here for today’s offers). Even closer is the Palace Theatre, currently home to the musical The Lost Boys, which the property has partnered with on a themed suite, bookable through September 14, 2027. Inside the suite, you'll find an ’80s seaside feel mimicking the musical’s world of Santa Carla.

Closest theaters: 2-minute walk to Eugene O’Neill Theatre, Walter Kerr, and Ambassador Theatre; half a dozen more a 3-minute walk awayWhy we love it: Vacation vibes at its Bar Sprezzatura, daily complimentary wine in the Living Room Lobby during Evening Social Hour, Roundabout Theatre Company partnership

The first time I stepped off the elevator into Kimpton Theta New York’s Bar Sprezzatura, I immediately craved an Aperol spritz. That’s how much I was transported to the Italian Riviera. The contrast between the lively Midtown streets below (the bar sits on the 15th floor) and the laid-back rooftop bar made me fall in love with the 364-key property instantly, and with multiple two- and three-bedroom suites, it's perfect for families and groups looking to book a foodie-friendly Broadway bonding trip. This November, the hotel launched the Roundabout Theatre Co. x Kimpton Theta package, giving guests 20% off tickets to Roundabout Theatre Co. shows (currently The Rocky Horror Show and Imaginary Invalid) plus pre- or post-show drinks at the bar.

Closest theaters: Attached to Marquis Theatre, 1-minute walk to Minskoff Theatre, 2-minute walk to Richard Rodgers TheatreWhy we love it: Ideal for Marquis Theatre shows, home to NYC’s only rotating restaurant, Broadway Bound Dining Package

For a mega-sized hotel smack dab in the middle of Times Square, the Marriott Marquis still has a sense of character. When I first moved to the area 23 years ago, I used to frequent its eight-floor Broadway Lounge, looking out at Times Square and marveling that I had finally “made it." Nowadays, I still pop in for a dose of nostalgia, gazing up at the 36-floor atrium’s elevators leading to the hotel's 1,900 rooms—a constant in a world that’s changed so much since it opened in 1985. But that throwback feel comes with a new spring in its step, most notably at its 48th-floor spinning restaurant, The View, reimagined by Danny Meyer in 2024. (Note: TodayTix members get free bubbly and bar snacks here, depending on their tier.) But what makes the property so unique for theater fans is that it’s the only hotel ever built with a Broadway theater inside—yes, the Marquis Theatre is literally on the third floor. Also special: The Broadway Bound Dining Package includes the chance to mingle with a theater star!

Closest theaters: 2-minute walk to the Nederlander Theatre, New Amsterdam Theatre, and Lyric TheatreWhy we love it: Themed rooms, located on 42nd Street, close to other attractions

Now here’s a hotel that reflects both “A Whole New World” and “The Circle of Life.” Through its partnership with Disney’s two long-running musicals, Hilton New York Times Square guests can go all in with themed rooms curated by Broadway designer Devin Sparkles Design. Aladdin's Times Square Palace Suite is decked out just like Agrabah, down to a genie lamp, Moroccan magic carpets, and Jasmine-inspired silks. Over in The Lion King’s Royal Suite, it’s all about the wonders of the Serengeti Pridelands, with hand-painted Rafiki-like patterns and bird puppets flying from the ceiling. Both include wake-up calls from each musical’s most iconic characters—the Genie and Rafiki—as well as themed drinks. But perhaps the most valuable part of the package, especially for those driving in? Parking in Times Square.

Closest theaters: 1-minute walk to Hudson Theatre, Belasco Theatre, and Lyceum Theatre

Why we love it: Passageway running between Hudson Theatre’s entrance and stage door, June 2026 refresh

Ever since my first Broadway trip to NYC in 2002, I’ve been stage-dooring shows. The Hudson Theatre shows can be tricky for this, as the theater’s entrance is on 44th Street, but its stage door is on 45th. It wasn’t until I discovered that the Millennium Hotel had a secret passageway—which is also the entrance to the hotel—that I started snagging spots close enough to get autographs (including from Daniel Radcliffe during Merrily We Roll Along). That said, I've always been jealous of those actually staying at the 751-room property, with a trio of theaters literally at their doorstep. Those eager to dive even deeper into the Theater District's history will love that the property is just across the street from the Museum of Broadway.

Is it expensive to see a show on Broadway?

Yes, price tags can be high—the year-to-date average per ticket for 2026 is $122.67. But there are also plenty of ways to find discounts through lotteries, TodayTix, Theatr, and the TKTS Booth. I’ve only paid more than $100 five times in my life—and never more than $200. (That’s why I haven’t been to a movie in nearly a decade, but have seen nearly 40 shows in the last year!)

What show should I see on Broadway this winter?

For last-minute trips, hot tickets right now include Bowen Yang’s record-breaking run in Cole Escola’s Oh, Mary! (Lyceum Theatre), plus A Few Good Men (Vivian Beaumont Theatre), Much Ado About Nothing (Winter Garden), Other Desert Cities (Hudson Theatre), and School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play (Samuel J. Friedman). And of course there are long-running hits like Wicked (Gershwin Theatre), Hamilton (Richard Rodgers Theatre), Harry Potter and the Cursed Child (Lyric Theatre), The Great Gatsby (Broadway Theatre), and Disney’s The Lion King (Minskoff Theatre).

Are there any shows I should plan a 2027 trip around?

As we’re standing on the precipice of one of the most anticipated Broadway seasons, there’s no better time to plan a theater getaway. Coming soon are Dolly: A True Original Musical (opening December 7 at St. James Theatre), the Julia Roberts and Paul Rudd–led Small Mouth Sounds (February 10 at Ethel Barrymore Theatre), Jonathan Groff’s The Amish Project (February 10 at Broadhurst Theatre), Dirty Dancing (February 12 at Lena Thorne Theatre), Evita on Broadway (February 27 at Winter Garden Theatre), Lin-Manuel Miranda’s Warriors (March 9 at Lunt-Fontanne Theatre), Purple Rain (March 12 at Majestic Theatre), The Sound of Music (March 23 at Vivian Beaumont Theatre), Damn Yankees (March 24 at Marquis Theatre), and the one I’m most thrilled about, the West End transfer Paddington: The Musical (March 30 at Al Hirschfield Theatre)—I already have my ticket for the first preview!

Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. In this excerpt from "The Secrets of our DNA," geneticist Turi King examines how DNA was used to reveal the ultimate fate of the last members of the House of Romanov.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In 1917, the Russian Revolution was in full swing. Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated, and he and his family were exiled to a remote Siberian town. There were plans to get the family to the U.K., but King George V (Nicholas' first cousin) and the British government withdrew their offer of asylum over concerns of the ramifications.

After the Russian Provisional Government was overthrown by the more extreme Bolsheviks in October 1917, Nicholas, his wife, their children and several members of the family's staff were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, where, in July 1918, they were executed. Their bodies were hidden and remained lost to time ‪for nearly a century —‬ until modern technology, with some help from the British royal family, unraveled the fascinating story of their disappearance.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of Our DNA: How Genetics Has Changed the World" (Pegasus Books, 2026), author Turi King, director of the Center for Evolution at the University of Bath, looks back at the incredible story of how DNA was used to solve a major mystery of modern history: What happened to the last members of the House of Romanov?

I was sitting in a lecture theatre at Cambridge University in 1994 when one of my lecturers, Erika Hagelberg, spoke about a new study she had just been involved in. It was the first major case to combine both mitochondrial DNA and DNA fingerprinting to identify human remains: those of the Russian imperial family.

But first I need to take you back to Russia in 1917 and the abdication of the tsar following the Russian Revolution.

The Russian royal family, the Romanovs, had been the reigning imperial dynasty since 1617, and three centuries later, Tsar Nicholas II was on the throne. Nicholas was the cousin of George V, king of the United Kingdom, their mothers being sisters, and had married George's cousin Princess Alix (Alexandra) of Hesse, who was apparently Queen Victoria's favourite grandchild. Nicholas and Alix had five children, four daughters (Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia) and a son, Alexei.

The tsar and his wife were not well liked by the Russian population and political unrest culminated in the revolution of 1917, when Nicholas was forced to abdicate. The family were kept under house arrest and in 1918 they were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg with the royal physician, Dr Botkin, and three of their staff. On the night of 16 July, the family, their doctor and staff were herded into the cellar together and executed. Their bodies were then taken to a secret location and placed in a hastily dug communal grave, doused in sulphuric acid in an attempt to disfigure them and hinder identification, and then covered over, the location of the grave being lost for more than 70 years.

The Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, 1919.

Ironically, the new Russian government had wanted to get the Romanovs out of Russia due to the risk of their becoming a rallying point, but a plan to grant asylum to the Romanovs in the U.K. because of their links with the British royal family fell through, owing to a reluctance on the part of George V to grant it. Yet those links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial in their identification.

Fast-forward to 1991, when several skeletons were found in a shallow grave some 20 miles from Yekaterinburg. Many of the bones were badly damaged but it was possible to determine, based on examination of the skeletal remains, that there were nine individuals — two short of the 11 killed that night. The faces of the skulls were badly damaged in all of the skeletons, all of them showing evidence of violence either in the form of bullet holes or bayonet wounds or both. Before the genetic study, Russian forensic scientists had used numerous techniques alongside historical data to tentatively identify the remains as some of the members of the Russian royal family, their doctor and servants.

These included examining the bones, to determine approximate age and sex, and some of the teeth, the expensive dental work, incorporating gold, platinum and porcelain, indicating that certain remains must belong to members of an aristocratic family. The team worked out that the two missing individuals would have been two of the children, one of the daughters (while it was hard to determine which one it would be, given how close in age they were, it was thought that it was either Maria or Anastasia) and the son, Prince Alexei.

The Russian chief forensic medical examiner then contacted a team in the U.K., which included Erika, to see if genetic evidence could be used to confirm the identification. The U.K. team used the amelogenin genetic sex test, now part of standard forensic DNA testing, which confirmed the sex of the skeletons (four male and five female bodies), while an early form of DNA profiling showed that there was a family group here — two parents and three children — and four unrelated individuals. So far, so good.

Next, they needed to prove that this was the Russian royal family, and they did this using mitochondrial DNA analysis. As you'll remember, mitochondrial DNA is passed down by a mother to all her children, male and female, but only daughters can pass it on — so if female-line family members of Tsar Nicholas and Tsarina Alexandra could be found and would agree to give a DNA test, their mitochondrial DNA should match that of their royal ancestors. It just so happened that the late Prince Philip, husband of the late Queen Elizabeth, was related to the tsarina through the female line: she was his great-aunt, his maternal grandmother being the sister of the tsarina. He kindly gave a DNA sample.

The testing that they did was standard for the time in that they looked at two regions known as hypervariable regions 1 and 2 (HVR1 and HVR2). You'll remember that mitochondrial DNA has 37 rather crucial genes on it where any "typo" that occurs as the DNA is being copied could have serious consequences if the mutation is deleterious. By contrast, in those parts of the mitochondrial genome that don't code for anything, such as these two hypervariable regions, mutations can occur more freely without necessarily causing issues, meaning that these regions contain much more genetic variation. These are the sections of mitochondrial DNA that scientists began analysing for identification purposes. While it's not as precise as DNA profiling because many thousands of people will all have the same mitochondrial DNA type, it can be very helpful in a case such as this.

Prince Philip's DNA was eventually used to confirm the identities of the lost Romanov family.

When the team sequenced these two regions, Prince Philip's mitochondrial DNA was found to match that of the putative remains of the tsarina and her daughters. Next they found two living female-line relatives of the tsar, descended from his maternal grandmother: a great-great-niece, Princess Xenia Cheremeteff Sfiris, and a first cousin twice removed, James Carnegie, 3rd Duke of Fife. The mitochondrial DNA from these two matched each other perfectly, and they, in turn, matched that of the tsar, except at one base where there was both a match and a mismatch.

This is because the tsar had what's known as a heteroplasmy at this position: some of the mitochondrial DNA sequences showed a T and others showed a C, his maternal relatives showing a T. Heteroplasmy is known to take place primarily through mutations occurring when the DNA is copied to make new cells in a person's lifetime, but it can be inherited from a maternal ancestor with heteroplasmy. Extremely rarely, it can come from paternal mitochondrial DNA making it into the cell. So the fact that heteroplasmy existed in the DNA sample didn't negate the match, and the probability that these were the Romanovs was still between 70 to 1 through to 840,000 to 1 in favour. But, it did sow some seeds of doubt. Incidentally, we now know that heteroplasmy is fairly common, with potentially over half of the human population having at least one heteroplasmy, albeit at a low percentage in terms of their mitochondrial DNA carrying it.

So, to be doubly sure, in 1996 the remains of the tsar's brother, Georgij, who had died in 1899, were exhumed and he was found to have exactly the same mitochondrial heteroplasmy. Given the very low chance of two people having this particular heteroplasmy if they weren't related, this pointed to the mitochondrial DNA data the researchers obtained being 130,000,000 times more likely if these were the Romanovs than if they were an unrelated family.

The case was solved in terms of identifying the tsar, tsarina and three of their daughters, but the mystery still remained as to what had happened to the two other children. In the scientific paper reporting the results, the authors conjectured that possibly the two children had been buried separately, or that they could have survived the massacre. Incidentally, there was a woman living in the U.S. who claimed to be Anastasia, saying she had managed to escape being executed, and so the fact that two of the children were missing from the Romanov family group only fuelled the idea that maybe she truly was the missing princess.

Then, in 2007, a group of amateur archaeologists, digging a mere 70 metres away from the previously discovered mass grave, came across more human remains. Skeletal evidence showed that they were the remains of two bodies, a young woman aged 15-19 and a probable male aged 12-15. DNA analysis was brought to bear and again showed that the two individuals were siblings and related to the Romanovs already identified. As an extra DNA test, Y-chromosome testing was carried out, the Y chromosome being passed from father to son, to confirm that the Y chromosome of the newly found male skeleton was indeed male and that it matched the Y chromosome of the tsar. This also then matched male-line relatives — a second cousin once removed of the tsar (third cousin of Alexei) through Tsar Nicholas I. The missing Romanov children had been found.

From an award-winning expert on DNA, discover the myth-busting book that opens a dazzling window into the world of modern genetics.

Fascinating, compassionate, and entirely captivating, The Secrets of Our DNA is the essential book that explains how genetics has changed and transformed the world around us.

Turi King is renowned for presenting complex findings on DNA and genetic science in an accessible and compelling way and she has won awards for her public engagement in science. Turi is the director of the Milner Centre for Evolution at the University of Bath. She is an honorary fellow of the British Science Association, a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London, a member of the Chartered Society of Forensic Sciences, and a member of the International Society of Forensic Geneticists. She is well known for her academic work leading the identification of Richard III; advising on the case of Mary Jane Kelly (the last victim of Jack the Ripper); leading the project on sequencing Hitler’s genome; as well as her media work co-presenting BBC’s DNA Family Secrets.

#6194. 21 Best Places to Visit in December in the USA

We’ll never forget the first time we visited New York City in December. We’d seen it in movies, but standing there, seeing the Rockefeller Center tree all lit up for the first time, with skaters below and festive music in the air… it was pure magic.

But December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa. We’ve also spent the holidays escaping to the warmth, trading snow boots for flip-flops.

In fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather. We’ve done so many road trips in the USA and flown almost everywhere, trying to find the best places to either escape the snow or enjoy the winter, you would think we are obsessed. And we want to share all of that knowledge with you.

If you’re looking for the perfect winter getaway, you have a clear choice: either lean into the winter magic or escape it completely. Are you dreaming of a warm-weather escape with sunshine and sand, or a storybook Christmas town that looks like a real-life snow globe?

Based on all those experiences, we’ve put together this list of our favourite places to visit. Whether you’re looking for a festive city, a snowy mountain, or a sunny beach, we’ll help you find the perfect spot.

Here is a quick look at some of the best places for a December getaway in the USA, from festive winter wonderlands to sunny escapes.

December is a month of pure magic and festive energy. It’s the perfect time to use up that last bit of vacation time for the year. The biggest draw is the distinct choice it offers: You can either dive head-first into a winter wonderland, complete with snow and holiday markets, or you can completely escape the cold weather and find yourself on a sunny beach. It’s a month of festive celebrations, incredible decorations, and finding the perfect atmosphere to end the year.

If you’re anything like us, sometimes the best gift in December is a break from the cold. Trust us, we know after living in Toronto, Canada. Those winters are brutal. These are our favourite spots to find sunshine and warm weather, where you can trade your winter coat for a light jacket or even a swimsuit.

We love the laid-back, quirky vibe of Key West, and it’s even more special in December. We have a great memory of biking around the island, seeing the historic inns draped in holiday lights, and then ending the day at Mallory Square for the sunset celebration. It’s a perfect escape from the cold.

Why Visit in December: This is the perfect time to visit. The summer humidity is gone, the weather is sunny and warm (often in the high 70s), and the risk of hurricanes is very low. The whole island is in a festive spirit, with unique events like the “Bight Before Christmas” boat parade.

Where to Stay: We recommend finding a guesthouse or inn in the historic Old Town to be close to the action.

We once went to a holiday luau in Ka’anapali, and it’s an experience we’ll never forget. You’re eating kalua pork and sipping a mai tai, watching a beautiful hula performance… and then Santa Claus arrives on an outrigger canoe. It was the perfect, uniquely Hawaiian way to get into the festive spirit.

Why Visit in December: You get tropical weather, festive holiday luaus, and it’s the official start of the humpback whale watching season. Be aware that this is a popular time, especially around Christmas, so prices can be high and you’ll need to book in advance.

Where to Stay: Look to the resorts in Wailea or Ka’anapali for a classic Maui experience.

We’ll always remember snorkeling the underwater trail at Trunk Bay in St. John. The water was so calm and clear, and seeing all the colourful fish felt a world away from the snow back home. That’s the magic of a Caribbean trip in December, and the USVI makes it so easy for American travelers.

Why Visit in December: It’s the start of the dry season, with fantastic weather and warm, clear water. You get a full-on tropical, warm-weather Christmas experience, all without needing a passport.

Where to Stay: You can choose from large resorts in St. Thomas or more eco-friendly villas and lodges in St. John.

We were not prepared for how magical St. Augustine is in December. We took one of the Old Town trolley tours at night, and seeing the entire historic city, from the old Spanish architecture to the palm trees, draped in millions of white lights… it was breathtaking. It’s a holiday light display unlike any other.

Why Visit in December: The famous “Nights of Lights” festival. The entire city is illuminated, and the mild Florida weather is perfect for walking around and enjoying the atmosphere. It’s one of the most festive and warm places you can visit.

Where to Stay: We recommend a historic inn or bed & breakfast in the downtown district to be within walking distance of all the lights.

While Maui is our go-to for a resort escape, Honolulu is where you go for a vibrant, city-meets-beach holiday. We loved seeing the massive Santa surfing with his reindeer in the fountain at the Iolani Palace. The whole city has this amazing “Mele Kalikimaka” (Merry Christmas) spirit.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect blend of warm beach weather, world-class shopping, and festive displays. It’s also a significant month for history, with the memorial events at Pearl Harbor.

Where to Stay: Waikiki has a huge range of hotels, from historic beachfront properties to modern high-rises.

If your idea of a winter getaway is to truly get away from everything, the crowds, the noise, the stress, then South Padre is a perfect choice. We spent a week there, and our days consisted of long, quiet walks on the beach. It was a total reset and the perfect way to escape the winter blues.

Why Visit in December: The weather is mild, and the crowds are gone. It’s one of the warmest places in Texas and offers a simple, relaxing beach vacation without the high prices or holiday chaos of other destinations.

Where to Stay: You’ll find many beachfront condos and hotels offering great off-season rates.

We thought we knew desert holiday lights, but the “Las Noches de las Luminarias” at the Desert Botanical Garden in Phoenix is on another level. Walking the garden paths lit by thousands of hand-lit luminaria bags, with musicians playing, was a top-tier holiday experience.

Why Visit in December: You get two trips in one: perfect, sunny weather for outdoor adventures like hiking during the day, and stunning, sophisticated holiday light displays at night.

Where to Stay: Choose from upscale resorts in Scottsdale or stylish hotels in downtown Phoenix.

Sometimes, the warm weather destinations just won’t cut it, especially if you are looking for that winter wonderland feel. So, this section is for travellers who want to dive head-first into the holiday spirit. These are the cities and towns that go all-out for December, with millions of lights, Christmas markets, and an atmosphere of pure magic.

We’ve visited NYC many times, but there’s a specific energy in December. We grabbed hot chocolates and walked through the Bryant Park Winter Village, watching the ice skaters zip around the rink under the lights of the surrounding skyscrapers. It felt like being in the opening scene of a holiday movie. There is nothing like New York City at Christmas.

Why Visit in December: It is the quintessential American Christmas destination. From the iconic tree to the world-famous window displays, the entire city is on a different level of festive.

Where to Stay: Midtown is convenient for seeing the main holiday sights, but we also love the West Village for its cosy, neighbourhood feel.

We’d heard Leavenworth was a “Christmas Town,” but we weren’t prepared for the reality. We visited during the Village of Lights festival, and walking through the snow-covered Bavarian-style village while every single building was covered in over half a million lights… it’s not an exaggeration. It’s the closest we’ve ever felt to being inside a real-life snow globe.

Why Visit in December: The entire town transforms into a “Hallmark movie” Christmas village. It’s a full-immersion holiday experience with carolers, festive food, and incredible decorations.

Where to Stay: Book a Bavarian-style lodge or inn right in the village. You must book many months in advance for December.

We love Asheville, but visiting in December is all about the Biltmore Estate. We took the candlelight evening tour, and seeing the main banquet hall with its 35-foot tree, fireplaces roaring, and carolers singing… it felt like we’d stepped back in time into a Gilded Age Christmas party.

Why Visit in December: Christmas at Biltmore is one of the most iconic holiday events in the country. The city itself is a cosy mountain retreat, and the Blue Ridge Mountains are just beautiful with a dusting of snow.

Where to Stay: You can stay on the Biltmore Estate for the full experience or choose a boutique hotel downtown.

Here are the remaining destinations for the “Best Christmas Towns & Festive Cities” section, all written with unique, December-focused content.

We’ve visited a lot of Christmas markets, but visiting the one in Bethlehem, known as “Christmas City USA”, just felt right. We sipped hot cider and browsed the stalls in the old quarter, and you can feel the city’s 250+ years of Christmas tradition. The whole place is lit by the glow of a giant Moravian star on the hillside.

Why Visit in December: This is Christmas City USA. It was nicknamed this on Christmas Eve, 1741. It offers one of the most authentic and historic holiday experiences in the country, blending its Moravian heritage with a European-style Christkindlmarkt.

Where to Stay: Look for a hotel or inn in the historic downtown area to be close to the festivities.

Walking into Solvang in December felt like we’d been transported to a Danish village during its Julefest celebration. We spent the day exploring the half-timbered buildings, windmills, and bakeries, all decorated for the holidays. It’s such a unique and charming way to experience a winter getaway in the middle of California.

Why Visit in December: The town’s month-long “Julefest” (Yule-fest) celebration is in full swing. It’s a one-of-a-kind Danish-style Christmas with parades, markets, and, of course, delicious European pastries.

Where to Stay: Choose one of the charming Danish-themed inns right in the village to be in the middle of the Julefest activities.

We had to see the “Christmas Capital of Texas” for ourselves, and it did not disappoint. The entire historic Main Street is transformed. We loved seeing the vintage railroad, which becomes the “North Pole Express” for the month. They take the “Christmas Capital” title seriously; there are over 1,400 events in 40 days.

Why Visit in December: It is the officially designated “Christmas Capital of Texas”. The sheer number of festive events, light displays, and activities is staggering, making it a top-tier destination for families and holiday lovers.

Where to Stay: The Gaylord Texan Resort is an attraction in itself, or you can stay near the Historic Main Street to be close to the events.

A New Orleans Christmas is an experience all its own. We did a “Reveillon Dinner,” a modern take on a Creole holiday tradition, and it was one of the most memorable meals we’ve ever had. Afterwards, we walked to Jackson Square to see the St. Louis Cathedral all lit up while carolers sang.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience unique Creole Christmas traditions you won’t find anywhere else. The weather is mild, the food is incredible, and the city’s lobbies (like at The Roosevelt) have some of the most elegant decorations we’ve seen.

Where to Stay: We recommend a hotel in the French Quarter to be in the middle of the action and see the decorated lobbies.

We went to Natchitoches (pronounced Nak-a-tish) specifically for its Christmas Festival, and it was a total joy. It’s one of the oldest and biggest in the country. The whole city, which is the oldest in Louisiana, lights up with over 300,000 lights along the Cane River, and the weekly fireworks shows are fantastic.

Why Visit in December: It hosts one of the oldest and most celebrated holiday festivals in the US, running for six weeks. It’s a classic, Southern Christmas experience in a beautiful historic district.

Where to Stay: Book a room at a historic bed & breakfast in the downtown area.

Visiting Colonial Williamsburg in December felt like walking through a living history Christmas card. We joined a candlelight tour, and seeing the historic buildings lit by real candles in the windows, with carolers in period costumes and the smell of woodsmoke in the air… it was absolutely magical.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience a traditional, 18th-century “Colonial Christmas”. The decorations are all-natural (no plastic lights), and the atmosphere is incredibly authentic and charming.

Where to Stay: Stay in one of the historic Colonial Houses or a tavern right in the restored area for the full immersive experience.

Here is the final category of destinations. This section is all about embracing the snow and finding that perfect winter wonderland.

For many, holiday season travel is all about finding that perfect, snowy scene. These are the places to go for world-class skiing, cosy lodges, and that magical feeling of a true winter escape.

We’ll always remember our first “après-ski” in Aspen. We had spent the day on the mountain hitting fresh powder whenever we got the chance, and as the sun went down, the sky lit up with this incredible pink and orange light they call “Aspenglow.” Sitting by a fire, enjoying a glass of Christmas cheer, and watching the snow fall on the historic town, it just felt like the peak of a luxury winter trip.

Why Visit in December: It’s one of the world’s most famous upscale ski destinations, and the town is just as much an attraction as the mountains. The festive atmosphere, high-end shops, and restaurants are all decked out for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Aspen is known for its luxury hotels and ski-in/ski-out resorts.

One of our favourite things about Park City is its history. We loved skiing down to the historic Main Street, popping off our skis, and walking straight into a saloon that’s been there since the silver mining days. It feels like a real Western town, not just a ski resort.

Why Visit in December: It’s a historic mountain town with two world-class ski resorts (Park City and Deer Valley). The historic Main Street is incredibly charming, and the “Snow Globe Stroll” features life-sized snow globes you can walk through.

Where to Stay: You can find ski-in/ski-out hotels or stay at an inn on the historic Main Street.

Jackson Hole in December is just dramatic. We took a sleigh ride through the National Elk Refuge, and seeing thousands of elk gathered against the backdrop of the snow-covered Teton mountains… it was a powerful and wild winter experience we’ve never forgotten.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect mix of rugged “cowboy Christmas” charm and some of the most challenging ski terrain in North America. The town square, with its famous antler arches, is beautifully lit for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Stay at a slopeside resort in Teton Village or in a hotel in the town of Jackson.

We love Whitefish because it feels like a real, down-to-earth ski town. We spent a day snowshoeing in nearby Glacier National Park, enjoying the total silence and incredible snowy landscapes, and then came back to town for a casual dinner. It’s all the beauty, without the glitz. Just what we were looking for in a winter vacation.

Why Visit in December: It’s a laid-back, charming mountain town with a top-rated ski resort and stunning scenery. It’s also right next to Glacier National Park, which is a spectacular place to explore in the winter.

Where to Stay: You can find lodges on the mountain or stay in one of the friendly inns in downtown Whitefish.

This was a trip purely for the fun of it, and it was 100% worth it. You drive down streets named “Santa Claus Lane” and “St. Nicholas Drive,” the streetlights are shaped like candy canes, and you can visit the Santa Claus House and see his reindeer. It’s a surreal and joyful experience.

Why Visit in December: It’s the ultimate Christmas fantasy come to life. The entire town is Christmas-themed, 365 days a year, but it’s most magical in December with real snow on the ground and the added bonus of possibly seeing the Northern Lights.

Where to Stay: North Pole is very small; most visitors stay in the nearby city of Fairbanks, which has a wide range of hotels.

For the best warm weather, your top choices are Southern Florida (like Key West), Hawaii (like Maui and Honolulu), and the desert Southwest (like Phoenix and Palm Springs). The U.S. Virgin Islands are also a fantastic passport-free tropical option.

Leavenworth, Washington, is often considered the ultimate “Christmas town” as it looks just like a Bavarian snow globe. Other top choices include Bethlehem, PA (known as “Christmas City USA”), Solvang, CA (for a Danish-style Julefest), and Grapevine, TX (the “Christmas Capital of Texas”).

Yes, but it depends on the park. It’s the perfect time to visit desert parks like Death Valley, Everglades, and Big Bend, where summer heat is unbearable. However, many mountain parks like Glacier, Yellowstone, and parts of Yosemite are mostly inaccessible due to heavy snow and road closures.

You are almost guaranteed to find snow in the mountain towns of the Rockies, like Aspen, CO, Park City, UT, and Jackson Hole, WY. You’ll also find snow in the Cascade Mountains (like Leavenworth, WA), Alaska, and the mountains around Lake Tahoe.

December is a magical month to travel. Whether you’re chasing the sun, seeking out that perfect snowy scene, or looking for a town that’s full of holiday magic, the US has the perfect spot for you.

We hope this list, based on our own winter travels, helps you plan your next getaway. Save this on Pinterest for your holiday planning! Where is your favourite place to go in December?

From set-it-and-forget-it backyard centerpieces to grab-and-go options for weekend camping trips, we tried well-regarded options from Solo Stove, Breeo, Blue Sky, and more.

Engineered to contain flames and burn fuel more completely, smokeless fire pits deliver ambient warmth with a lot less smoke in your eyes than a traditional campfire. They achieve this through two points of combustion: The first happens at the bottom, where airflow feeds burning wood; the second occurs at the top, where the fire’s smoke and gas output are burned off. And while no smokeless fire pit is 100 percent smokeless, if you use best practices (like burning dry wood) they come pretty darn close.

We tested smokeless fire pits in our New York and Pennsylvania backyards, building fires rather than judging them on specs alone. Along with smoke output, we considered size, which affects wood capacity and where the heat actually lands, as well as how easy each pit was to empty of ash and store once done, among other factors. We also used them repeatedly over time to see how their finishes held up, because a brand-new pit can look very different after several fires.

Solo Stove is the brand most people associate with smokeless fire pits (though Breeo was the first game in town). The latest joiner in Solo Stove’s lineup is the Summit, an upgraded take on the ever-popular Bonfire. Its 23-pound weight makes it just as easy to lift and store off-season, and there’s even less setup required. All-in-all, it’s the best smokeless fire pit for most people who want to enjoy a backyard fire pit that can be stored off-season.

Because the Summit is four to five inches shorter than the Bonfire, it does a better job of keeping your feet warm, one of the major gripes our Test Editor Brad Ford had of the earlier model. He says that while it holds less firewood, it undoubtedly produces a higher flame that extends well above the rim.

Another improvement he points out is the Summit’s integrated stand, which he says is sturdier and allows for better airflow than that of the Bonfire’s detached stand. There’s also a deeper ash pan, which is particularly helpful because the Summit burns through wood fast and needs frequent reloading. In terms of price, the 19.5-inch Summit is $100 more than a Bonfire of the same size, an extra cost that’s well worth the investment.

Full Solo Stove Summit Smokeless Fire Pit Review

After trying out the Breeo X Series 24 for several months, test editor Brad Ford loved it. According to Ford, “One of the coolest details of the X Series 24 is its Corten finish. (It is also available in a stainless-steel finish.) Corten is a structural steel alloy you often see used for bridges or power line towers. It’s designed to oxidize, or rust, creating a natural finish that protects the steel rather than continuing to degrade it. This eliminates the frustration I’ve had with some stainless-steel fire pits that discolor after a couple uses.”

Beyond this, Ford also liked, “that Breeo intended for their smokeless fire pits to be used for cooking from the get-go, which means they’ve got accessories for the X 24 that work very well. And most of their cooking accessories are compatible with all their fire pits. Top this all off with the fact that the X 24 is made right in Lancaster PA, USA, unlike most other popular brands.”

The Breeo X 24 weighs more than twice as much as the other models we’ve tested, so it’s not exactly portable—but it is long-lasting.

As the largest pick of the lot, the X Series was easy to load with wood and start a fire. We fit 18- to 20-inch logs into it, laying them across the raised X in the bottom of the pit. This patented design keeps the logs high, allowing air to flow in and feed the fire from the bottom.

Cleanup required scooping ash out, as the unit is too heavy to dump out easily—Breeo sells a shovel designed to ease this process. The brand also offers several accessories for cooking over the fire, which make the X Series as much a grill as it is a fire pit.

This hefty, all-black fire pit is a great-value addition to an outdoor setup. Its wide diameter gives you plenty of room to build a substantial fire, and the shape and airflow make for a good, largely smokeless burn. It takes both wood and pellets right out of the box, no adapter or switch-up required. And the lift-out ash catch has two handles, making it one of the easiest models to empty. (You still have to reach into the drum to lift it out, though, so wear gloves.)

The black coating is practical, too: Unlike stainless steel, it doesn’t show every fire mark. Once in place, it blends nicely with patio furniture, particularly setups with black metal legs. While it does scratch more easily than others we tested, you can touch it up with high-heat spray paint, just like you would a grill.

Some things to bear in mind: At 35 pounds, it’s heavier than many of the models we tested, so you’re unlikely to move it around much once it’s situated. The price doesn’t include a cover, which you’ll definitely want if it’s going to live outside for the season.

Because the ash catch sits inside the main body, with no separate base beneath it, we’d also place this one on a fireproof mat to be extra safe. And this may be petty, but the branding is the most prominent of any pit we tested: you’ll be looking at the words “Blue Sky” on the base every time you sit down.

If you want to bring the campfire with you wherever you go, the Packfire portable fire pit is an ideal choice. It packs down into a backpack, so you can carry it on your shoulders and set it up wherever your adventures take you. In fact, its innovative design won it a spot in our 2026 Home Awards.

The fire pit is composed of three sections: the base, which serves as a stand and ash pan; the body, which, when fully set up, surrounds the base; and the ring, which holds the body in place. Cleanup is easy: Simply lift the ring and body off the base, pour the ashes out, and break everything back down for travel.

It’s worth noting that even though it’s built for travel, the fire pit is still a bit cumbersome to carry around. While our Director of Product Content, Will Egensteiner was testing the Packfire, he said its 27.5 weight was a factor. “As I heaved it onto my back to put it away, I almost tipped over. And I’m not a small guy.”

The substance of this fire pit starts with the box: One of the largest and heaviest we had to maneuver into location for testing (only the Breeo was heavier), moving it really requires two people or a dolly. Some of that initial box weight comes from the generous bag of wood pellets packed inside, but the pit itself, at 45 pounds with nothing in it, is hardly lightweight.

Assembly is a little less impressive. Attaching the legs required a drill, as, while an Allen key and screws were included, some of the holes weren’t perfectly aligned, making the process more fiddly than it should have been. It does, however, come with spare screws.

Once assembled, though, this thing is a very good-looking workhorse. The large bag of wood pellets kept going for about 35 minutes before burning down to embers; produced virtually no smoke; and the heat output was surprisingly high.

Simply by flipping the inside container, you can also fire up 14-inch logs inside. The exterior frame stayed remarkably cool and, given it’s black, didn’t discolor the way the stainless steel ones did. While the inside picked up some black streaks from the flames, they looked more like evidence of a real fire than damage, which we actually liked.

The ash disposal is a true highlight. You don’t have to lift, twist, or tip the pit to empty it: An ash pan slides out from the side, shovel-style, so you can dump the refuse without moving the fire pit at all. It also comes with a perfectly fitted cover, which is particularly useful given how difficult this one would be to haul away when not in use.

This seriously smart, compact fire pit is made for small spaces and taking on the road. It’s lightweight, straightforward to assemble, and comes with six pieces: a pit and ash can that sit on top of one another; two pieces that twist together to form a fire poker (a little tight to sync up, but ultimately quite a useful piece); and a spark screen with a screw-in knob to lift it (also a very nice extra).

Truly, the whole kit is quite remarkable, given the price. The ash catch is also cleverly designed to fit inside the fire pit for storage, so there’s nothing extra to haul around when not in use. The black finish looks sharp and has the added benefit of hiding burn marks better than lighter finishes. (The downside is, it scratches easily.)

The whole thing packs into a carrying bag with a shoulder strap and drawstring closure. It’s also lighter than any other model we tested, making it an excellent choice for beach parties, camping trips, or anywhere you need to carry your fire pit more than a few feet.

There is one important caveat: Because the pit is so compact, you’ll mostly be limited to twigs, which burn quickly. Use wood pellets instead, for a longer, more consistent fire. The carrying bag also feels flimsy, like it could break down quickly with repeat use, but, for the price, that may not matter.

This one looks like a saucer and comes with just three pieces: a main body that locks securely into the ash holder base and a wind guard that twists onto the rim. It’s also one of the roomier pits we tested, with a wider, more-open design that accommodates both more and larger pieces of wood than many others. The manufacturer says it handles logs up to one pound. We’d have preferred a measurement in inches, but went with 16 inches, which it handled better than the Tiki. You can also add a griddle attachment to turn it into a cooker.

This one really does produce a roaring fire that can warm four people comfortably. The wide, funnel-like shape seems to encourage a bigger, more expansive flame; sitting around it felt more like a bonfire than simply burning wood in a container. After 25 minutes, we still had a substantial fire going. Its lower stature kept our feet warm too.

The biggest downside is ash removal. The pan in the base is relatively shallow, and the wide fire pit is awkward to twist and lift off for cleaning. You’ll want long arms—or a second person—to do it comfortably. The stainless-steel finish also turned a light bronze after just one use. A cover costs extra.

Before lighting a single fire, we evaluated the things that can make or break a smokeless fire pit before you ever use them. We assessed the packaging and how well each pit was protected in transit, weighed every model, and evaluated assembly. We read the instructions, noting whether they were clear, complete, and actually useful.

We considered whether it could be disassembled for storage, and what came in the box versus what required an additional purchase. While We had plenty of outdoor space to work with, safety always came first: we set every pit on heavy-duty pavers and kept a fire extinguisher close at hand.

Then we lit them up. We used comparable loads of seasoned firewood to assess how easily each pit started, how much smoke it produced, how evenly it burned, and how much heat it put out. We paid attention to flame height and consistency, too, and whether the fire actually warmed people sitting around it—not just looked good from a distance. We measured logs to see exactly what each pit could accommodate and tested wood pellets where models supported them.

Finally, we evaluated the less glamorous but equally important details: how easy each pit was to tend, how much ash accumulated, how easily that ash could be removed, and what it took to clean and put each model away. And because a fire pit can be beautiful at 7 p.m. and a pain in the ass at 10 p.m., we tested for both.

Whether you want a smokeless fire pit to heat your outdoor space or be more of an ambient seasonal moment is an important consideration. For long nights by the fire with family and friends, you’ll likely want to invest in a larger model that measures 24 inches in diameter. In testing, models that size and up exuded warmth for several feet, and could easily warm four to six people.

They could also handle 14- to 16-inch-long logs. The trade-off: Models this size are a lot heavier and harder to move. If you’re looking for more of a warming accent, narrower fire pits work wonders. You can also maximize some models’ output by adding a heat deflector that sits above the flames and pushes heat out laterally, instead of letting it escape upward.

Ideally, the smokeless fire pit should work right out of the box, with limited-to-no setup, besides setting the pit on a base. It should also break down easily. If you’ll be storing it between fires or seasons, a model that’s easy to disassemble, carry, and put away is key.

The shallower and wider the smokeless fire pit, the easier it is to make a fire from scratch. You simply have more base room to work with to set up your paper, kindling, and wood, and less depth to maneuver to light your fire once ready. No matter your choice, you’ll definitely want a lighter with a long metal wand and a safety catch. None of the models we tested included one.

Burning pellets instead of wood was the closest we got to a truly smokeless fire during our testing. Made of compressed wood waste like sawdust, chips, and shavings, pellets are easy to light, always bone dry, and produce a hotter, more consistent flame than logs. There are trade-offs, though: They lack the classic crackle and pop of a wood-burning fire and that wonderful smell.

Bags of the stuff also typically cost more than a handful of logs at the hardware store, yet burn about the same length of time. But, if you’re allergic to smoke, don’t want your sweaters to smell of it, have wet wood drying out, or want a reliable and even fire every single time, pellets are an excellent way to go. Some fire pits work with them right out of the box; others need an adapter.

Every smokeless pit burns wood. Many smokeless fire pits can also use wood pellets right out of the box. Some, like Solo Stove, need an adapter, so the tiny pellets don’t drop right through the pit’s air holes into the ashcan below. Some portable options may only be wide or deep enough to handle twigs (pellets may be a better option for those).

Pro tip: Wet or green wood will always be slow to burn and emit a lot of smoke; use a moisture meter to suss out whether your logs are dry enough to light up before putting a match to them.

If you plan to use your fire pit regularly, easy ash removal should be a deciding factor. The last thing you want to have to do is pick up and tip a heavy steel drum over a trashcan in order to empty it of ash. Instead, look for a removable ash pan or tray that allows you to lift the ash out cleanly once the pit has fully cooled (usually 12 to 24 hours after a fire has ended). Otherwise, you’ll need a shovel to scoop out the ash.

If you don’t have space to leave your fire pit outside all year, think about who will move it and how often. Even a small pit designed for camping trips can weigh as much as 20 pounds. Fortunately, these options usually come with a carrying bag, so you can sling them over your shoulder. Meanwhile, larger models can top 45 pounds (the 24-inch Breeo weighs just over 60 pounds), which matters when you have to move it under cover or into the garage at the end of the season. Units that come apart make this easier; having a dolly or hand truck on hand helps, too.

Material affects how long your new pit will look the way it does on arrival. While stainless steel looks shiny and modern from the start, heat from the flames will discolor it, and potentially quite quickly, as some testing showed. (You can restore its original shine with a stainless-steel cleaner such as Bar Keepers Friend, but that’s extra work.) Corten-steel usually costs more but forms a protective rust-colored patina that looks attractively weathered over time. Painted or powder-coated steel usually costs less, but can scratch and chip with repeat use.

Whatever finish you choose, keeping your smokeless fire pit empty of ash and covered when it’s not in use will help extend its life. Rainwater sitting in a fire pit full of ash can create a corrosive, alkaline slurry that accelerates rust and can damage the metal. Some models come with a cover as part of their bundle; others charge extra for it. Our reviews note whether a cover is included in every pick.

Smokeless fire pits can be a lot more than a place to warm your hands on chilly nights. In some cases, you can turn them into an outdoor kitchen. Brands like Breeo, Solo Stove, and Cuisinart have grill grates, griddles, pizza ovens, or roasting sticks that let you cook over an open fire. Other add-ons also make a difference, like a cover, if you plan to leave it outside when not in use; a spark screen, particularly if you have toddlers and pets around (though, warning: they can also get hot to the touch); and fire pokers or ashtray lifters, so you don’t get your hands dirty. Definitely check the accessory lineup before you buy your pit; they’re often model-specific. A pair of fire-resistant gloves is always a good investment.

While product photos often depict smokeless fire pits sitting on wood decks or backyards, it’s worth noting that their bases can get hot enough to scorch or discolor lawns, wood decks, composite, and asphalt. Ideally, yours should sit on brick, concrete, stone, or sand. But in the absence of that, a dedicated base (sometimes included, other times sold separately) helps raise the unit off the ground. For an even safer setup, consider adding a fireproof mat underneath. You should also keep a bucket of water or a fire extinguisher nearby and check for local burn bans before lighting. For more on fire pit safety, check out our story.

Arabella Bowen is a seasoned product tester who specializes in travel, design, tech, home improvement, and outdoor essentials. #6192. 15 Best Grand Canyon Hotels, Rentals, and Glampsites for Sleeping in Style Under the Stars

A mile deep and 277 miles long, the Grand Canyon is a jaw-droppingly majestic chasm in Arizona’s rust-red desert that’s speckled with pinyon pines. Standing on its edge, one can’t help but feel small, watching the mighty Colorado River churn vigorously along the ravine’s bottom. Whether you’re hoping for a challenging all-day hike to the canyon’s floor, a soul-stirring overlook near the visitor center, or a multi-day rafting expedition, this national park has all that (and more) in spades. It’s hardly a surprise that it drew more than 4.4 million visitors in 2025 alone, so you know you'll have some competition when it comes to finding the best place to stay nearby.

Personally, I like to stay as close as possible to the park, to make the most of dreamy desert sunrises and maximize my time on the trails. Grand Canyon is famous for its historic lodges and quirky Route 66 nostalgia, which can make picking the perfect spot for your crew a little overwhelming. Cozy cabin or fancy, family-sized rental? Canvas glamping tent under the stars or a fun getaway that’s in the heart of the action? I’ve sorted through the hundreds of options so you don’t have to.
