When is the best time to visit Grand Canyon National Park?

With an elevation spanning 2,000 feet to 8,000 feet, Grand Canyon experiences a wide range of temperatures on any given day. Thus, the best season to visit greatly depends on what your adventure priorities are.

If you’re planning to raft “the big ditch” with a guide, go between April and October for warm, sunny days that perfectly contrast the 50-degree Colorado River. Hoping to hike to the bottom and camp at Bright Angel? Don your favorite traction devices atop the canyon to crunch through seasonal ice and book a backcountry permit for late fall, winter, or early spring. Auto tourists who want to explore the canyon’s south rim by car can travel in virtually any season—just be prepared for crowds in summer months and occasional snow closures at the height of winter.

Lastly, a good rule of thumb for intrepid travelers hiking down into the canyon is that you’ll gain roughly 5 degrees for every 1,000 feet you descend. Plan on it being 20 degrees warmer at the bottom of the canyon than it is at the rim. The National Park Service (NPS) does not recommend hiking to the bottom of the canyon during summer months, as temperatures at Phantom Ranch often surpass 100 degrees.

How do you get to Grand Canyon National Park?

If you’re planning to fly in, the closest major airports are Sky Harbor International in Phoenix and Harry Reid International in Las Vegas, but both are at least a three-hour drive away, so you’ll want to rent a car and crank up the tunes to brave the journey. Regional airports are scattered around the area, most notably in small-but-commercial Flagstaff, Sedona, and Tusayan. There’s also a vintage train service that runs daily from Williams, Arizona.

Notably, Grand Canyon National Park is a stone’s throw away from one of the most iconic road trips the US has to offer–historic Route 66. Running from Chicago all the way to the Pacific Coast in Santa Monica, California, this legendary trip ventures across northern Arizona on Interstate 40.

What are the best things to do in Grand Canyon National Park?

Spanning 23 breathtaking miles between Grand Canyon Village and the Desert View area, Desert View Drive is the only scenic byway in the park that’s open year-round to private vehicles. Enjoy Mary Colter’s iconic Desert View Watchtower, which was inspired by ancestral Puebloan architecture and features murals by Hopi artist Fred Kabotie, at the park’s far eastern edge.

Another popular drive along the South Rim is the winding Hermit Road, which ends at the historic stone structure of Hermit’s Rest that date back to 1914. The drive is only open to private vehicles in December, January, and February; in all other months, travelers must use the park’s free shuttle system, hopping on and off at popular sites.

Though the hiking distance between the canyon’s north and south rims is a scant 21 miles, the drive to get between the two is a circuitous 220 miles. As a result, only 10% of the national park’s visitors set foot on the just-as-striking North Rim. This high-elevation outpost (over 8,000 feet) and log cabin-style lodge have a shorter visitation season than the South Rim (you’ll have to travel there between May 15 and October 15 most years), but adventurous drivers desperate to escape the crowds should make a beeline for the pinyon and ponderosa pine–studded views of crumbling crimson sandstone along Cape Royal Road. Plus, you’ll be within easy driving distance of Zion, if you’d like to extend your journey.

If you’re into hiking past dramatic vermillion outcroppings, secret waterfalls, and hanging gardens, you’re in the right place. The Grand Canyon also boasts some of the most stunning wheelchair-accessible paths in the country (check out the 13-mile, mostly-paved Rim Trail), as well as hamstring-busting overnight treks into the belly of the ravine.

For an epic out-and-back excursion with much of the expansive red rock scenery you’d find on a longer jaunt, head to South Kaibab Trailhead and venture just under a mile downhill to the aptly named Ooh Aah Point. Want a little more bang for your buck? Continue down to Skeleton Point for a sweeping panorama of the Colorado River (six miles round trip). Bright Angel Trailhead is another iconic starting point for a day hike or overnight trek into the canyon. Lace up your boots for a three-mile round-trip stroll to the shade structure at Mile-and-a-Half Resthouse or, if you’re an experienced hiker looking to sweat, start early for an all-day 12-mile journey to jaw-dropping views of Plateau Point.

Trekking to the bottom of the Grand Canyon and back is the stuff hiking bucket lists are made of. But due to midday heat and the extremely strenuous nature of these hikes, the National Park Service does not recommend aiming to complete such a journey in a single day. It’s highly recommended to nab a backcountry permit and camp overnight at one of the many below-the-rim sites (like Bright Angel Campground or Havasupai Gardens). Pro tip: Use the free park shuttle and create a loop starting at South Kaibab and ending at the Bright Angel Trailhead. Heading for the quieter North Rim? Tramp down the North Kaibab Trail for two miles (one-way) to Supai Tunnel.

Find our full list of the best Grand Canyon hikes here.

It’s rare that a national park offers a designated bike path along its most iconic sights, but at the Grand Canyon, visitors can spin for roughly 13 miles along the park’s dreamy South Rim vistas. BYO-bike or rent one at Canyon Adventures in the village, then steer onto the paved Greenway Trail to South Kaibab. Or, utilize the free shuttle system (yes, they’ve got bike racks) and ride the bus to Monument Creek Vista, then cruise along the South Rim to Hermits Rest.

North Rim visitors hoping to escape that South Rim fervor can enjoy loads of rugged mountain biking. A 12-mile swath of the enormous, 800-mile Arizona Trail runs right through the park.

Are there guided tours at Grand Canyon National Park?

There are dozens of phenomenal guided tours available for guests who aren’t comfortable backpacking alone or want a unique type of experience. Mule rides are a storied part of the canyon’s past and how many early tourists ventured into the canyon (sometimes in full Victorian regalia). Though it might seem like a rough place for a working animal, mules are much better equipped to handle heat and steep, rocky terrain than their horse counterparts. Plus, these rides offer below-the-rim access for visitors with mobility concerns. Today, both short day trips and extended overnight ventures to Phantom Ranch on muleback are available for those looking to pay homage to a bygone era.

For a brag-worthy addition to your hiking checklist, seek out Wildland Trekking’s guided rim-to-rim backpacking journeys (or, in winter, go big and test your skills on a rim-to-rim-to-rim hike). Craving something off the beaten path? The remote, five-day Hermit Loop offers miles of fire-red sandstone plateaus.

I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention the second-to-none river rafting to be had at Grand Canyon National Park. Grand Canyon Expeditions and Western River Expeditions have been guiding for decades and both offer first-class service for intrepid travelers looking to go the distance on the mighty Colorado.

Think that cows are the king of flatulence? There's another animal that likely blows the competition away.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Flatology, the study of flatulence, sounds more like a joke than a serious scientific discipline. But studying farts actually helps biologists understand an animal's diet and digestion.

We know that a host of creatures ‪—​​ from whales, to snakes, to sloths ‪— pass gas. But do we know which animal is the top tooter? Experts told Live Science the answer is blowing in the wind.

"Getting quantitative measurements for farts per animal is pretty difficult," Nick Caruso, a data scientist and co-author of '"Does It Fart?: The Definitive Field Guide to Animal Flatulence'' (Quercus Publishing, 2017), told Live Science in an email.

What we can do is hypothesize using the data we do have. Expelled gas is made partially of methane, so comparing methane emissions produced by different species may provide a clue. However, this method does have limitations, experts pointed out.

Researchers measure the methane animals produce by placing them inside respiration chambers, then inserting a capsule into the stomach that releases a tracer gas while strapping them with a harness that samples their breath. Alternatively, they capture their breath at stations where they feed or are milked.

Research points to livestock, especially cows, as major methane emitters. A recent report puts their total methane emissions at 117 teragrams per year. (One teragram is equal to 1 billion kilograms, or 2.2 billion pounds.) A buildup of cow-generated methane gas even caused a dairy shed in Germany to explode. However, contrary to what many people believe, the "overwhelming majority" of methane emissions from livestock is released through burping, not flatulence, Ermias Kebreab, a professor of animal science at the University of California, Davis, told Live Science in an email.

The reason comes down to where in the gut the gas is made. Herbivores can't break down plant material on their own; they rely on microbes in their guts to ferment it, and that fermentation releases gases such as methane and carbon dioxide, Dr. Marcus Clauss, head of research and co-director of the Clinic for Zoo Animals, Exotic Pets and Wildlife at the University of Zurich, told Live Science in an email. Some of this gas is absorbed into the bloodstream and exhaled. The rest tends to leave by the nearest exit ‪—‬ animals that ferment their food toward the front of the digestive tract mostly burp it out, while those that ferment it toward the back mostly pass it as wind, Clauss explained.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Cows and other ruminants ‪(such as buffalo, sheep, goats and camels)‬ ferment their food in a chamber called the rumen, located near the front of the digestive system, so most of the methane they produce is through belching, Matthew Hayek, an associate professor of environmental studies at New York University, told Live Science in an email.

So if it's not cows, which animal is the top farter based on their methane emissions? The best candidates are hindgut fermenters ‪—‬ herbivores that digest plant matter in the large intestine (the hindgut). Meat eaters, by contrast, typically produce far less methane than herbivores do, Clauss said.

Are cows really the top contender for animal farts?

One possible contender are termites, which break down wood and grass in their hindguts. Their global population is estimated to be around 27 quadrillion (that's 15 zeros) individuals, and they collectively emit 10 teragrams of methane per year.

But, per individual, the title might go to horses. According to a 2019 report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, horses have the highest methane emissions among hindgut fermenters — around 40 pounds (18 kg) of methane per horse each year.

However, Clauss is skeptical. "The ranking of horse as highest is only because it has been measured," he told Live Science in an email. "But there are so many hindgut fermenters not measured, like rhino ... Who knows?"

If we consider methane emissions per unit of bodyweight, the nutria (Myocastor coypus) ‪—‬ an herbivorous, semiaquatic rodent ‪—‬ would have higher methane emissions than the horse, Clauss said.

Clauss also questioned the accuracy of using methane emissions data as an indicator of flatulence. "There is some methane in flatulence, but most likely the majority of methane produced by an animal is exhaled, i.e. it goes via blood to the lungs," he said.

So until scientists figure out how to measure animal farts, any ranking remains speculative. For now, scientists have developed ways to track intestinal gas in people, including swallowable electronic capsules that measure gases inside the gut and clip-on underwear sensors that detect hydrogen in farts.

Methane is a particularly potent greenhouse gas when released into the atmosphere, and the quantities that large herds of cows and other ruminants emit through burping are enough to contribute to climate change. Indeed, scientists are experimenting with ways to reduce methane emissions from cattle — for example, by adding seaweed to their diet.

But animal flatulence is not a major contributor to global methane increases, Hayek said.

Even methane emissions from termite flatulence, while large, do not have an impact, Stefan Arndt, a professor of physiological and ecosystem ecology at the University of Melbourne in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "A large proportion of that methane is then consumed by methanotrophic bacteria in the soil," he said. These bacteria use methane as an energy source, thereby reducing the net methane emissions from termites substantially.

"Their emissions are part of the natural cycle of methane that has always been there for millennia," Arndt added. "The increasing methane concentrations in the atmosphere that are leading to climate change are caused by humans."

#6189. Our Cities Are Shrinking. Does That Mean They’re Doomed to Be Unlivable?

Population decline could leave thousands of cities struggling to maintain aging pipes, roads, and buildings. An engineer says it’s not too late to make the choices that will revive urban life.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Two billion individuals. That’s economist and demographer Dean Spears’ forecast for our human population in 300 years. The last time we belonged to that small of a group was 1927. Now there are eight billion of us, and in 2080, we’re expected to hit our peak—around ten billion people. Yet, for the first time in history, demographers estimate that the average dropping birth rate over the past several decades means our species will no longer be able to replenish our numbers.

Civil engineers say this will cause major instability worldwide, including to the man-made structures of our world—roadways, buildings, safe water pipelines, and more. All of them will likely deteriorate without city residents who can pay to maintain such structures.

But we don’t have to fully reimagine what our infrastructure would look like under extreme population collapse; we can look to a swath of the industrial Midwest, known as the Rust Belt, which saw immense population decline when the steel industry cratered in the 1970s and ’80s. The fallout meant shedding at least 75 percent of the 350,000 jobs lost nationally, and massive population decline in cities from St. Louis, Missouri to Buffalo, New York. For example, in Cleveland, Ohio, 46 percent of the residents exited between 1970 and 2000, a typical scenario.

Depopulation on this scale is an unprecedented situation, but also an inevitable one, explains civil and environmental engineer Sybil Derrible, PhD, a professor at the University of Illinois Chicago. He calls himself an urban engineer, because he focuses on studying how population loss will affect multiple urban infrastructure systems over the coming century. “As far as I know, there's no policies about how to deal with depopulating cities,” he says. “No one’s going to give you $2 million to shrink.”

The total mass of all infrastructure systems humans have built over the past 200 years is truly mind-boggling; it exceeds all living biomass, which is 545.8 gigatons, according to the World Economic Forum. “So when the population goes down, infrastructure will go from being a thing we really need to being a burden. And it's already happening in many cities where there was a lot of infrastructure investment,” says Derrible.

In the 1970s, a massive exodus began in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, when the steel industry collapsed. The city of nearly 700,000 residents shrunk to about half its size between 1970 and 2025, and today more than 20,000 housing units sit vacant.

The engine that keeps a city running is its infrastructure, a vast, interconnected network of housing construction, roadways, public transit, electrical grids, and safe drinking water. But multiple factors, including job loss and a higher cost of living, have been pushing people—including new migrants—out of thousands of American cities for decades, leaving the infrastructure with little financial support. The problem will only worsen as the population fails to replace itself, Derrible believes.

Right now, about 40 percent of the nearly 30,000 U.S. cities are losing their people. In a century, it will be more like 50 percent. The larger ones, like New York City or Chicago, are likely to weather changes in population in the long run. It’s the smaller ones, home to about 10,000 to 20,000 people, that will truly suffer, Derrible says. About 12,000 cities, many of them in the Midwest, are facing infrastructure problems, but at least another 3,000 will be experiencing them by 2100, according to Derrible and his team’s 2024 paper in Nature. While the overall U.S. population is increasing due to immigration, people coming to this country don’t usually move to “small, rural cities,” he says. Instead, they settle in the suburbs.

Yet, policies designed to help people living with weakened infrastructure don’t yet exist, Derrible says. “Those people are completely being neglected. So I'm worried about that. I really want to make sure that we have some policies to be able to help them.”

But Derrible believes the solutions will come. Policymakers, engineers, scientists, city planners, and residents need to put their heads together and do the work, he says.

Here are three core parts of city infrastructure that are already being hit the hardest.

The most dire consequence of a shrinking population is the inability to maintain massive but increasingly derelict water distribution systems, Derrible says. If you don’t have money for upkeep, the result can be crises like Flint, Michigan’s untreated toxic water disaster, which happened after the cash-poor city switched its municipal water source from Detroit’s system to the Flint River to cut costs in 2014. The city has seen a mass departure of people since the 1980s, when the U.S. auto industry closed many plants and downsized operations. By 2010, four years before the water crisis, Flint’s population had dropped to nearly half its former peak.

“[The water problem] is especially overlooked because people don’t think about it too much,” Derrible says. Figuring out solutions to the lurking water crises in cities has to happen now, he says, but no easy solutions exist. Questions about how to deal with water contamination or shortages are many, though: “Do you go back to wells? Are there aquifers?” Derrible asks. And if you need to cut off a totally depopulated part of a city, how do you even do that?

According to industry organization Empowering Pumps and Equipment, aging water infrastructure is the biggest enemy of water, wastewater, and stormwater professionals who maintain and run these systems. The group cites the 2017 American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) Infrastructure Report Card, which says that pipes leak 6 billion gallons of treated drinking water each year, and that about 240,000 water main breaks happen annually. Upgrades and replacements require greater investment—to the tune of $670 billion, the ASCE’s 2025 infrastructure report says—but funding doesn’t come close to meeting need. With two million miles of drinking water pipes across the country, many of which were laid in the early- to mid‐20th century and are now technically at the end of their lifespan, it will take an estimated 200 years to replace the entire system at the current replacement rate of 0.5 percent of pipes per year, according to the 2017 report.

Underutilized roads are cracking and becoming harder to drive on, but also harder to fix in cities with far fewer people. A 2021 paper by Derrible and his team in the journal Environmental Research: Infrastructure and Sustainability reported that driving on rough roads in New Orleans cost about $685 per person each year. The city has lost half its population since Hurricane Katrina.

Instead of stretching thinning budgets to maintain underutilized roads, cities could consider current and future traffic patterns and potentially abandon some roadways. They could even rip out surfaces and turn them back into dirt roads, Derrible says. Each city must look at its individual needs and create its own solution.

Japan is implementing a similar kind of solution, where denser patches of houses and services keep their maintained roads and public transit areas, but in areas with few residents, the mostly unused streets are closed or repurposed.

Several cities in the U.S. have been choosing to remove the interstate highway sections that slice up their cities, most of which entered urban areas in the 1950s and destroyed and divided neighborhoods. One such city is Detroit, Michigan, which plans to replace the wide gray strips with roomy, walkable neighborhoods, in hopes of reconnecting residential areas.

Because fewer people means less tax revenue, cities that are being abandoned have less money to deal with aging or empty infrastructure like buildings. The other side of the coin is that new businesses don’t want to occupy old buildings. “New Costco? They’ll want new land to build it,” Derrible says. “At the same time we have all those abandoned buildings that we're not doing anything with, because it's just cheaper to build on new land than to retrofit an existing building.”

The picture of abandoned buildings doesn’t have to look like a post-apocalyptic nightmare of neglect. Existing buildings that are still in good shape could meet housing needs or become community spaces. For example, urban malls could be turned into apartments that are already conveniently located.

“At the very least, what I think we could be doing when a building is being abandoned is remove all the hazardous equipment, material, appliances, all of that,” Derrible says. Similar to the cleanup after a natural disaster, all furnaces and power and electrical hardware must come out to prevent fires and toxic materials.

Then you could either bulldoze the building and remove the debris, or you could strip the structure for useful parts, such as wood, metal, pipes, and electrical wire. Even skyscrapers could become rich sources of material that the civil engineering industry could mine. “Instead of going to quarries and getting new material, we could go to old skyscrapers or old concrete buildings. We crush them, so we have the aggregates to build new buildings,” Derrible says. The wood could also be reused, or it could become a source of fuel when burned. Derrible foresees abandoned city infrastructure as a potential source of new jobs that mine and process material for reuse. “Isn't that like the core of the American system, to turn any challenge into an opportunity, right?”

#6188. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#6187. Airport Luggage Tag Scam: How to Protect Your Checked Bags in 2026

Imagine walking up to customs after a long international flight and being told that a suitcase connected to your name has been flagged.

Then the officer points to the luggage tag and says, “Then why is your name on it?”

That is the nightmare behind a luggage scam travelers need to understand in 2026. It is called baggage tag switching, and it is exactly what it sounds like: the luggage tag from an innocent passenger’s checked suitcase is allegedly removed and placed onto another bag.

Baggage tag switching scams happen when the luggage tag from a traveler’s checked bag is allegedly removed and placed on another suitcase. To protect yourself, take a video of your suitcase before check-in, photograph the bag on the scale, take a close-up photo of the baggage tag, keep your baggage receipt, place a tracker inside your suitcase, and report any damaged, missing, delayed, or retagged bag before leaving the airport.

According to a W5 investigation, innocent passengers flying from Canada have been detained after their real luggage tags were allegedly moved onto suitcases containing illegal drugs. The investigation focused on flights from Canada and alleged cases connected to Toronto Pearson, but the larger lesson applies to travelers everywhere: once your checked bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting the system to protect your luggage, your tag, and your name.

We have traveled to more than 130 countries on all seven continents, and checked bags have always been part of travel. But the old habit of simply handing over your suitcase and hoping for the best needs an update.

In 2026, protecting your checked luggage is not just about stopping theft. It is about protecting the paper trail that connects you to your bag.

This is part of a bigger shift in how travelers need to think about airport safety, baggage scams, and common airport security mistakes before they fly.

Editor’s note: This article is based on our video about baggage tag switching, which has reached more than 86,000 views on our travel YouTube channel.

Before you check a bag, take two minutes to create proof that the bag is yours.

It also helps to run through a full pre-travel checklist before you leave for the airport so you are not rushing through check-in.

This may sound like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes at check-in. And those two minutes could matter if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

We covered this luggage tag scam in detail in the video below, including the simple two-minute routine we now recommend before checking a bag.

Baggage tag switching is when the tag printed for your checked luggage is removed from your actual suitcase and attached to another bag.

When you check luggage, the airline prints a baggage tag that usually includes your name, flight, destination, routing information, barcode, and bag number. That tag is the airport system’s way of connecting that suitcase to you.

The problem is that once your bag goes behind the counter, you cannot see what happens next.

In the alleged scheme reported by W5, corrupt baggage or ramp workers could remove a legitimate tag from a passenger’s suitcase and attach it to another suitcase heading to the same destination. If that second bag is intercepted, the paperwork points back to the innocent passenger.

That is what makes this scam so dangerous. You may have done everything right: checked your own suitcase, kept your boarding pass, and boarded your flight. But behind the scenes, one strip of paper may now connect your name to a bag you have never seen.

Most airport workers are honest. Let’s be clear about that. The vast majority are doing hard jobs under pressure, moving thousands of bags through complex systems every day. But a baggage system only needs a few bad actors to create a very serious problem.

This story has received attention because of Canadian cases, but this is not only a Canada problem.

The bigger issue is that every major airport has the same basic weak point: you hand over your suitcase, it enters a restricted area, and from that point on, you are relying on the system to protect the tag, the bag, and the records connected to your name.

That is true in Toronto. It is true in New York, London, Paris, Dubai, Bangkok, Mexico City, Sydney, and anywhere else checked luggage moves behind the scenes.

International travel also adds another layer of risk. If your name gets tied to a suspicious bag in another country, you may be dealing with a different legal system, different customs procedures, and possibly a language barrier.

The Government of Canada warns travelers that drug offences abroad can have serious consequences and that you should never carry anything across a border for someone else. The Canada Border Services Agency also specifically reminds travelers that trafficking cannabis or other drugs across the border is a criminal offence and warns people to beware of anyone asking them to carry something.

That is why documenting your own luggage matters. You are not being paranoid. You are creating a simple evidence trail.

Before your suitcase disappears behind the counter, take a clear video of it.

Do a full 360-degree view. Show the front, back, sides, wheels, handles, color, brand, straps, stickers, scratches, dents, or anything that makes your bag identifiable.

Yes, you may feel ridiculous filming your suitcase at the airport. Do it anyway. People film lattes. You can film the thing that might keep you out of a holding room.

This video creates a time-stamped record of what your suitcase looked like before it left your hands. If someone later claims a different bag is yours, you have proof of what your actual luggage looked like at check-in.

When your bag is placed on the airline scale, take a quick photo or video showing the weight.

This matters because weight is part of the paper trail. If your suitcase weighed 19 kilograms at check-in and another suitcase connected to your name weighs 32 kilograms, that difference may matter.

You are not trying to become a detective. You are simply creating a record that says this was your bag, this was the weight, this was the condition, and this was the tag attached to it.

That is the kind of simple documentation that can help if your bag is delayed, damaged, retagged, or questioned later.

Once the airline attaches the baggage tag to your suitcase, take a close-up photo or video of it before the bag goes onto the conveyor belt.

Make sure you can clearly see the barcode, destination airport, flight number, routing, and bag number. Also check that the airline has looped and attached the tag properly.

You are not being difficult. You are checking the one strip of paper connecting you to your luggage. That little tag is doing a lot of legal heavy lifting.

Air Canada’s own baggage information explains that self-service kiosks can print baggage tags, receipts, and boarding passes, and that travelers then attach the tags and proceed to bag drop. That means passengers are often handling or reviewing this paperwork themselves before the bag disappears into the system.

Never throw away the little baggage receipt sticker you receive at check-in.

Keep it somewhere safe. Don’t stuff it in a random pocket, lose it before boarding, or assume the airline app is enough. Put it with your passport or travel documents until your suitcase is back in your hands.

That receipt usually contains your bag number. If something goes wrong, that number becomes part of the evidence trail. That number can help airline staff or investigators compare what you checked, what arrived, and whether someone intercepted or retagged another bag.

This is one of the easiest travel habits to fix, and it costs nothing.

Before you close your checked bag, take one clear photo of the inside.

You do not need to photograph every sock like you are filing a museum inventory. Just take one clear photo of the contents: clothes, shoes, toiletries, chargers, jackets, and the usual chaos of travel.

This helps show what you actually packed. If a suitcase connected to your name contains items you have never seen, you have a record of what was inside your real bag before check-in.

This is especially useful on international trips, where proving what you packed may become more complicated once you are outside your home country.

It is also a good reminder to double-check what not to pack in checked luggage before you leave for the airport.

A luggage tracker will not stop someone from tampering with a baggage tag, but it can help show where your real suitcase went.

We use Apple AirTags, but there are also Tile trackers, Samsung SmartTags, and other luggage tracking options.

The important thing is this: put the tracker inside your suitcase. Do not hang it outside where it can easily be removed.

If authorities are asking about a suitcase connected to your name and your tracker shows your actual suitcase is somewhere else, that becomes another part of your evidence trail.

Trackers are also helpful if your bag arrives late, gets separated from its original tag, or ends up in the wrong baggage area. They are not perfect, but they give travelers one more layer of information when airline systems fail.

We use AirTags in our checked bags, but Samsung SmartTags and Tile trackers are also good options depending on your phone. The key is to keep the tracker inside the suitcase where it cannot easily be removed.

We also recommend pairing a luggage tracker with a few simple anti-theft travel accessories especially on longer international trips.

A plain black suitcase is basically the airport version of camouflage.

Make your luggage easier to identify with a bright strap, ribbon, sticker, or distinctive luggage tag. You want to be able to spot your bag quickly and prove what makes it different from hundreds of others.

But do not put too much personal information on the outside. Your name and phone number are enough.

You do not need your home address waving around the baggage hall like an invitation that says, “Please rob us while we’re in Italy.”

Keep luggage identifiable, but not overly revealing.

This rule has always mattered, but it matters even more now.

Never carry a package, gift, suitcase, envelope, or item for someone else. That means no favors for strangers, no “harmless” packages, and no quick airport errands for someone you barely know.

If you did not pack it, you do not carry it.

The CBSA specifically warns travelers to beware of people who ask them to carry anything and notes that consequences for drug trafficking can be serious in Canada and abroad.

That is the cleanest rule in travel: your bag, your responsibility.

If your checked bag arrives without the original tag, with a damaged tag, with a rush tag, or through a different baggage process than expected, do not just shrug and leave the airport.

Do not rely on a quick conversation at the counter. Conversations disappear the second you walk away. Written reports create a record.

This matters if your bag was mishandled, delayed, retagged, or separated from its original tag.

When your suitcase comes out at baggage claim, do not grab it on autopilot and leave.

Check that it is actually yours. Look at the tag, compare the bag number against your receipt, check your tracker, inspect the condition, and make sure the contents have not obviously been disturbed.

We have seen people accidentally walk away with someone else’s luggage. It happens more easily than people think, especially after long-haul flights when everyone is tired and half the carousel is filled with identical black suitcases.

Before you leave the airport or customs area, take one minute to confirm everything looks right.

Not necessarily. We have traveled for decades, and carry-on only is not always realistic. Sometimes you need to check a bag, especially on longer trips, family trips, cruises, cold-weather destinations, camera-heavy travel, or extended international travel.

For a smoother trip overall, our easy air travel tips can help before you even reach baggage claim.

For longer flights, our long-haul flight tips can also help make the journey easier before you even get to baggage claim.

The point is not to scare people out of checking luggage. The point is to update your habits.

The old way of checking luggage was simple: check the bag, keep the receipt somewhere, and hope for the best.

It sounds like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes — and those two minutes could make a huge difference if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

If authorities ever question you about a suitcase that you do not recognize, stay calm.

Do not guess, don’t joke and do not become argumentative.

Ask for legal assistance and show the documentation you collected: your suitcase video, scale photo, baggage tag photo, receipt, tracker information, and photos of what you packed.

This article is not legal advice, but from a traveler’s perspective, the goal is simple: create proof before there is a problem.

If your name is ever attached to a bag you did not pack, your documentation may help show what your real suitcase looked like, what it weighed, what was inside it, and where it went.

Before every checked bag disappears behind the counter, take two minutes to create a simple record of your suitcase.

That’s it. Two minutes. No drama. No paranoia. Just smart travel.

Most airport workers are honest, and most checked bags arrive without a problem. But airport systems are massive, complicated, and not completely invisible-proof. Once your bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting a chain of people, machines, tags, scans, and systems to keep your suitcase connected to your name.

So before your next flight, take two minutes to protect yourself. Film your bag. Photograph your tag. Keep your receipt. Use a tracker. And never carry anything for anyone else.

The goal is not to travel scared. The goal is to travel smarter.

Because when travelers get smarter, scams get riskier for the people trying to pull them off.

After nine days in space, the Artemis II crewmembers faced their final and riskiest challenge: splashdown. In this excerpt from the book "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space," astronaut Jeremy Hansen describes the moment from his chair.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After nine days in space, the four crewmembers of NASA's Artemis II mission looked out their capsule window on April 10, 2026, and saw the bright-blue Earth below them. The crew had traveled more than 250,000 miles (400,000 kilometers) from our planet — farther from Earth than any humans had ever gone — and now, home was just a few hundred miles straight down.

Only one milestone remained: splashdown, a fast and fiery plunge into the Pacific Ocean that would mark the end of humanity's first crewed mission to the moon in more than 50 years.Mission specialist Jeremy Hansen, the lone Canadian Space Agency astronaut on the crew, had every reason to be confident that the team's Orion crew capsule would hold up just fine. But this was Hansen's first time in space, and his first time dropping through the sky like a fireball at 24,600 mph (39,600 kmh).

It wasn't that he was afraid for himself, Hansen explains in "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space" (Hanover Square Press, 2026), which he co-wrote with John Larsen). Rather, he knew that his wife Catherine and three children would be among the millions of Earthlings watching the most dangerous moment of his mission from below.

In this excerpt from the book, Hansen describes the thrilling intensity of splashdown and the euphoria of knowing that he and his crewmates were going to make it back safely — and make history.

CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen smiles inside the Orion crew capsule during the Artemis II lunar flyby.

Immediately after jettisoning the European Service Module, and exactly half an hour before we were due to splashdown, Mission Control initiated the crew module raise burn. This nineteen-second burn was the first and only burn using the small thrusters built into our Orion capsule. It slightly shallowed our entry trajectory to put us right in the sweet spot while also providing some added distance from the service module, as we'd be hitting the atmosphere in near succession. It, too, went flawlessly. I tightened my straps; it was time for the fireworks.

A re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere is absolutely on the short list of the most incredible experiences of my life. We slammed into it at 7:53 p.m., thundering down at over 10 kilometres [6.2 miles] per second. Per second.

The thrusters fired almost constantly to stabilize the capsule: loud thuds, as if Thor himself were hammering on our spacecraft, as the G-forces quickly began to build, aggressively scrubbing off the velocity we had added to our rocket nine days earlier. Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us. It started red and transformed into a bright, bluish-green, pulsating light. It was breathtaking, the bright colors igniting our senses.

It was insane to think about what we were doing. We all knew how this worked; we all knew the science. But deep inside, I also recognized that astronauts must have a screw loose to do this. Nobody in their right mind would strap themselves inside a metal canister that itself was sitting inside a giant fireball. But there was no other way down, and I had accepted the realities of this journey long in advance.

Although I was at peace, I felt guilty for the stress I was putting on my family. I had talked to them openly about the mission's risks, and this was the highest-risk moment. I tried to send my love telepathically, telling them it was going great.

The Orion capsule drops toward the Pacific Ocean with all parachutes successfully deployed.

As we continued our freefall, it looked like a thousand camera flashes were exploding inside Integrity. I lowered the sun visor on my helmet. There were only centimeters of heatshield and aluminum separating me from the more than 2500°C heat outside. Almost instantly, the heat inside our cramped home also began to rise, an increase that engineers refer to as "thermally benign." All I know is that I couldn't feel it, blissfully wrapped in my thermally controlled garments.

As we continued to fall, the G-forces built up to nearly four times the pressure we feel on Earth. I wasn't too worried, having endured more than five minutes of the same G-force, or more, in the NASA centrifuge trainer. I had half-expected the freefall back to Earth to seem short, but it was a long six minutes before the flames finally ceased and we re-established communications with Mission Control.

It had already been a wild ride, but I also knew another crazy part — parachute deployment and the actual splashdown — lay ahead. My adrenalin kept pumping.

Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us.

"Integrity, Houston. Comms check, post-blackout," we heard from Mission Control. It was music to our ears. It was exactly 8:00 p.m.

"Houston, Integrity," Reid [Wiseman, mission commander], replied. "We have you loud and clear."

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried. For the folks at NASA, it was clear that all had gone well during the descent — a small fleet of NASA and Air Force planes had captured it on high-resolution cameras. But, for me, it wasn't over yet. I wouldn't truly feel safe until our three main parachutes successfully deployed. If they didn't, we'd be a chunk of metal slamming into the ocean at incredibly high speed, and the chances of surviving that would be somewhere between minimal and non-existent.

I've watched many of my close friends return from space, and I find the minutes after surviving the re-entry heat until the parachutes deploy to be the hardest part to watch. When I see a capsule plunge through the clouds with no chutes, I always worry they might not appear at all. That's completely terrifying.

Jeremy Hansen arrives on the deck of the USS John P. Murtha after being recovered from the Orion capsule. All four crewmembers were in perfect health after splashdown.

I thought of Catherine and the kids, sending them a "don't worry, gang" message in my mind. Catherine later told me that she had a very bad feeling about the heatshield, so when we emerged from blackout, she began crying and didn't even focus on the parachutes.

Three minutes later, at an altitude of 7,100 metres, timed explosions released small chutes that pulled off the cover for two larger chutes, called drogues because they are intended to slow our acceleration to a speed that would allow our main parachutes to open without ripping. They did their job perfectly, but it was wild inside the capsule, jerking us back and forth like a ride at the fair.

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried.

One minute later, at only 1,500 metres above the ocean, the drogue chutes cut loose, and, for a few moments, we felt like we were falling backward. Then, in succession, the three main parachutes began deploying, blossoming slowly so they wouldn't tear apart. The rate of our fall slowed as the red-and-white nylon canopies, each 35 metres in diameter, filled with air. The thrusters kept firing, aiming the capsule's base directly toward the point of impact.

"Integrity, we see three good-looking parachutes," we heard from our CAPCOM. Within seconds, our splashdown speed had reduced to 27 kilometres per hour.

That's it, I said to myself. I'm pretty sure we can survive whatever else could be thrown at us now.

Christina [Koch, mission specialist] seemed to agree. We grabbed one another's hands in a moment of celebration.

Excerpted from "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, The Groundbreaking Human Mission Into Deep Space" by John Larsen with Jeremy Hansen. © 2026 by John Larsen, used with permission by HarperCollins/Hanover Square Press.

The dramatic, high-stakes account of Artemis II, the first human journey into deep space in fifty years, told from the perspective of astronaut Jeremy Hansen ... A riveting and intimate account of the iconic achievement of Artemis II, Earthrise—written by author John Larsen and based on extensive interviews he conducted with Hansen—is a testament to what can be achieved with unity, teamwork, and a bold belief in humanity’s ability to reach for the stars.

John Larsen is a former executive-level military public affairs officer who served with the Royal Canadian Air Force during combat operations in Europe. Based in Calgary, AB, he is a business advisor, entrepreneur, writer, and university instructor. He holds graduate degrees in Communications and in Creative Non-Fiction Writing. Earthrise is his second book.

#6185. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

#6184. SeaWorld Parks Promo Codes November 2026

Marriott Coupon CodesYou never forget your first dolphin encounter—and for many kids across the country, that often happens at SeaWorld. The beloved oceanarium puts the “amusement” in amusement parks: orcas leaping in the air, floorless rollercoasters named after sea monsters, and even aquarium sleepovers. With parks in Orlando, San Diego, San Antonio, and Abu Dhabi, SeaWorld’s aquatic allure has no bounds. SeaWorld is a top choice when it comes to taking the family out for some educational fun.

Established in 1964 by four UCLA graduates, SeaWorld began in San Diego with 22 acres, six attractions, and a handful of sea lions and dolphins (beloved orca whale Shamu arrived at the party a year later). In the early 2000s, the parks expanded with thrill rides and rollercoasters, as well as Discovery Cove, allowing visitors to interact with marine animals like bottlenose dolphins. Over the course of its history, SeaWorld has rescued over 40,000 animals and, through the SeaWorld and Busch Gardens Conservation Fund, donated over $19 million to global projects, from restoring coral reefs to preventing coastal erosion. If you want your little ones to have a whale of a time, here are the best SeaWorld Parks promo codes, discounts, and deals.

Take advantage of SeaWorld's Black Friday discounts. Save up to 60% on tickets, fun cards, and passes. Save over 50% on a single-day ticket to SeaWorld San Diego ($65 instead of $130) and enjoy increased flexibility if you visit before March 31, 2027. Combine it with the All-Day Dining option for $40, and you won't have to worry about buying meals. You can also save 40% on a 2027 Fun Card and take advantage of unlimited free visits to SeaWorld San Diego now through 2027 ($78 from $130).

SeaWorld expresses its gratitude for the service of military members through the Waves of Honor program, which grants any US active-duty military, activated or drilling reservist, or National Guardsman one complimentary admission per year, and tickets for as many as three direct dependents. Military personnel can also enjoy a 50% off discount on up to six SeaWorld Orlando single-day tickets, plus a Silver Annual Pass at SeaWorld Orlando (unlimited admission with no blockout dates for 12 months) for $161 instead of $279. Those who can take advantage of this offer will need to verify their identity via ID.Me.

For military personnel who have completed their service, SeaWorld is offering 50% off single-day tickets at SeaWorld Orlando, plus the same Silver Annual Pass discount that active-duty military members get to enjoy. To take advantage of this offer, verify with ID.Me.

If you’ve got a preschooler, give them the gift of maximum aquarium time. At SeaWorld San Antonio, kids under the age of five can enjoy free, unlimited admission to SeaWorld until January 2027, plus unlimited visits to Aquatica for only $39—just be sure to register before the offer expires on May 30. Preschool Cards are limited to Texas residents only.

Because SeaWorld is dedicated to research and education, the theme park offers certified K–12 teachers in Florida free admission. The SeaWorld Florida Teacher Card is valid for unlimited admission to SeaWorld Orlando through September 2, 2027. All teachers have to do is pre-register on ID.Me with a Department of Education (DOE) number. Plus, Florida Teacher Card holders have the option to add Aquatica Orlando for only $49.99.

If you find yourself visiting the dolphins often, consider investing in an annual pass for the lowest cost per visit. Annual passes often include perks like free guest tickets and discounts on food and merchandise. During the sale, prices for passes are reduced for new members: Save up to 15% on the Bronze Pass, 20% on Silver, 25% on Gold, and 30% on Platinum. Using a SeaWorld Parks promo code annual pass deal can pay for itself in just two visits.

To make sure your SeaWorld discount applies correctly, verify the expiration date; many SeaWorld coupons are time-sensitive. Check if the code is park-specific (for example, a SeaWorld Orlando promo code may not work for San Diego). #6183. I’m a Neurosurgeon. My Near-Death Experience Showed Me ‘Universal Consciousness’ for the First Time.

By comparison, it makes our material world feel “murky.”

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

When I earned my medical degree at Duke University, I was taught that consciousness is created out of chemical reactions occurring within the brain, a foundational assumption of scientific materialism, or physicalism—the notion that only the physical exists. After eleven years of rigorous training, I practiced as a neurosurgeon for more than two decades, including 15 years teaching and operating at Harvard Medical School.

I performed surgical procedures that took patients from extreme discomfort to full relief by releasing a nerve blockage or removing a tumor. I could stimulate the brain in awake patients and affect their mental experience, which initially seemed to support my physicalist worldview. At the same time, patients deeply comatose from brain maladies would sometimes become fully alert right before dying. I couldn’t explain these phenomena, and so I dismissed them. That is, until November 2008, when a severe case of bacterial meningitis caused me to spend seven days in deep coma—and later reshaped my view of the universe.

Over three hours, I went from back pain and headache to epileptic fits and coma, as E. coli bacteria devoured my neocortex, or the outer surface of the brain, the part that is most responsible for human mentation. Healthcare professionals use the Glasgow Coma Scale to measure decreases in consciousness, with scores less than 9 indicating deep coma. A corpse would score a 3, the lowest grade on the scale, and my scores were 6 to 7 during most of that week—the doctor was out! Lumbar puncture revealed my cerebrospinal fluid to be filled with pus under pressure, and the glucose level in that fluid was only 1 mg/dl (normally 80-90, with severe bacterial meningitis occasionally as low as 20). CT and MRI scans revealed my entire neocortex was involved, meaning there was no physical functioning brain left to produce a dream or hallucination.

By the tenets of modern neuroscience, my awareness should have been zero. Without a functioning neocortex, my brain was incapable of producing a simple thought or image—and yet, I lived through a vivid, richly-detailed, hyper-real event, by comparison making this material world appear murky and dreamlike. I was unbound by space and time, immersed in universal consciousness, and wrapped in unconditional love. I had visions revealing structure to the non-physical realm that fully relates to and intertwines with our lives here on earth.

Back in the hospital, my prospects for survival were down to 2 percent when, on day seven, I startled everyone as I began to awaken. My doctors were even more surprised when I fully recovered over about two months. As my medical knowledge returned, I reviewed my records and scans, and discussed them with my doctors, trying to make sense of it all. I searched for a physicalist explanation, yet the case was unyielding—no conventional explanation could suffice. I was forced to acknowledge that an expansive model of reality was required to explain my experience.

When my case records were peer-reviewed before publication in the Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, the editors asked the authors to explain my unprecedented recovery. They replied that my miraculous recovery occurred because of my spiritual journey, knowing of similar extraordinary recoveries in the near-death literature. Due to techniques of cardiac resuscitation developed in the 1960s, millions of others have escaped the shackles of the physical brain and body, and reported similar near-death experiences (NDEs) of connection with a non-physical realm. Those descriptions have been categorized and evaluated using Greyson’s NDE Scale (developed by UVA psychiatrist Bruce Greyson), which quantifies the cognitive, affective, paranormal, and transcendental aspects of the experiences.

The vast evidence from these unusual experiences has convinced many former physicalists that their model is outdated. A more sufficient explanation is that the brain serves as a transceiver or antenna for tuning in to a larger, collective consciousness. Renowned Harvard psychologist William James, French philosopher Henri Bergson, and English writer Aldous Huxley, all postulated this “reducing valve” role for the brain in the early 20th century, noting that a shift in the primary physicalist assumption was required to explain these phenomena.

With a growing abundance of data, it is clearer that consciousness is fundamental and influences physical matter from the top down, rather than the bottom-up model of physicalism, where consciousness arises from the brain. Spontaneous remissions and the placebo effect confirm the power of the mind over matter and validate the observer effect seen in quantum mechanics experiments.

The “hard problem of consciousness” remains unsolved because its underlying premise is false.

I believe merging first-person subjective inquiry with rigorous empirical science will take us farther in knowing the true nature of our consensus reality.

To that point, humanity will thrive when science finally acknowledges that we are interconnected through love and part of one larger consciousness, with free will to become the best version of ourselves, both as individuals and collectively. The golden rule is woven directly into the fabric of the universe, providing a moral compass that shows that, ultimately, what matters most is how we treat each other.
