#6096. Air Algerie Business Class Review: An Odd Avion Express Airbus A320 Wet Lease

For the next portion of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, I flew Air Algerie’s Airbus A320 business class on the one-hour flight from Algiers (ALG) to Tunis (TUN). Okay, Air Algerie doesn’t actually operate A320s, so this flight was operated by Lithuanian and Maltese charter operator Avion Express (which Air Algerie is really bad at disclosing during the booking process).

I mean, what can one really say about this flight, especially after coming off of Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, which was possibly the worst long haul business class I’ve ever flown? Truth be told, for a short haul flight this wasn’t terrible, but it also wasn’t good. It was just… whatever. As an aviation geek, I always do love a wet lease adventure!

As I explained in the last installment, I booked an attractive one-way business class cash fare on Air Algerie, even though it didn’t start or end where I actually wanted to go. 😉 I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day)10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

So in the last installment I reviewed Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, and then this installment is my review of the connecting flight.

I’ve already reviewed the Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers, which gives strong furniture store vibes and is nothing remarkable, but is still much better than Air Algerie’s onboard experience.

My flight to Tunis was scheduled to depart at 7:10AM, and my boarding pass indicated that boarding would start at 5:40AM. Yes, 90 minutes before departure… for an Airbus A320. Not surprisingly, that was completely inaccurate. I get that airlines don’t want people to miss flights, but I do find it frustrating when airlines don’t actually tell you when you should realistically be at the gate.

Anyway, my flight was departing from gate nine, roughly a five-minute walk from the lounge. Algiers Airport is fairly pleasant — it feels sterile and there’s not much to it, but compared to some other airports in the region, it isn’t half bad. But of course let me remind everyone that nothing holds a candle to Cairo Airport (CAI), easily one of the world’s finest facilities. 😉

I showed up at the departure gate plenty early, but even by 6:10AM (30 minutes after the alleged boarding start time), there wasn’t actually anyone at the gate.

The crew showed up at around 6:20AM, and boarding actually started at 6:35AM. The boarding process was rather strange on a variety of levels.

For one, before boarding started, the gate agent and security staff walked onto the jet bridge and then lit a cigarette and smoked. Nice… real professional.

Second, when boarding did start, it was just a free for all, with no priority give to business class passengers.

Third, there were three separate passport and boarding pass checks on the jet bridge by airport police. So first the gate agent checked documents, then upon entering the jet bridge a security officer checked both, then 100 feet later another security officer did the same, and then at the door of the plane, another security officer checked. After all that hard work protecting us, they definitely deserve a cigarette!

At the forward door to the plane I was greeted by the crew, and then headed toward my seat. I was flying on an 18-year-old Avion Express Airbus A320 with the registration code 9H-AMJ. While Avion Express is a Lithuanian company, this plane was registered in Malta.

This A320 has seen quite some things, as it started its career in 2008 at Wizz Air Ukraine, then in 2015 it moved to the main Wizz Air fleet when the Ukrainian subsidiary shut down, and then in 2021 it was taken over by Avion Express. Since then, it has flown on a wet lease basis with carriers like Eurowings, British Airways, Viva, and more.

For those not familiar with the concept of wet leasing, this is when an airline leases out its plane to another airline, including the crews. So while it’s sold just like any other Air Algerie flight, and the catering is like any Air Algerie flight, the crew and planes are from Avion Express.

This Avion Express A320 had a total of 180 seats, spread across 30 rows in a 3-3 configuration. Unfortunately unlike most of Air Algerie’s own planes, this one didn’t have a dedicated business class cabin with different seats. Instead, the first three rows were designated as business class, and they just had economy seats with blocked middles. That means business class had the capacity for 12 passengers.

I assigned myself seat 3F, the window seat on the right side in the third (last) row. This was a pretty old school cabin, which is a double edged sword. On the plus side, this meant seats were well padded, which you don’t typically find nowadays, given the emphasis on slimline seats.

Legroom was okay when you consider these are really economy seats, so it could’ve been worse.

The seat had a standard tray table, which folded down from the seat in front.

Given how old school the cabin was, it definitely wasn’t in very good condition, though. I mean, just look at the liner inside the window, and how that was coming apart.

Also, given the age of the cabin, it was clear that nothing had really been updated — there were no power ports, there was no Wi-Fi, and there was no streaming entertainment. That’s of course not a huge issue for such a short flight, but I’m just trying to help people manage expectations here.

The overhead console was typical for an A320, and had individual air nozzles and reading lights.

The cabin stayed really empty — there were only two other commercial passengers, and then one pilot who seemed to be commuting to Tunisia, for whatever reason.

Boarding was really efficient, and wrapped up by 6:55AM, as the flight wasn’t very full. That was still 15 minutes before the scheduled departure time. Before departure, the crew came around with juice or water as pre-departure drinks. I opted for a water, and was also given a packaged refreshing towel.

Ironically enough, on this flight the safety demonstration was exclusively performed in English (compared to my previous Air Algerie flight, where it was in French and Arabic, but not in English).

At 7AM the main cabin door closed, and at 7:05AM we began our pushback (sorry for the quality of the pictures, as the windows were super dirty)…

On the taxi out, we saw another Avion Express A320, which looked identical to ours (we also had an all-white A320).

There were quite a few Air Algerie planes parked on the ramp, as very few seemed to actually be at gates. I’m not sure if Air Algerie’s aircraft utilization is just terrible, or what.

By 7:25AM we made it out to runway 23, and were immediately cleared for takeoff.

Our climb out was smooth, and I loved the views on departure… I wish I could’ve actually visited Algiers, but the visa situation is complicated (and after my review, I’m not sure they’d be happy to have me anyway). 😉

The seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff. At that point the crew closed the curtain between the cabin and galley, and got started with the service.

On this morning flight, breakfast was served. There was no choice, but I was served a hot dish with scrambled eggs, veggies, and some sort of meat. There was also a yogurt, a croissant, and a pastry, and additional bread rolls were offered (though I passed).

It sure seems like Air Algerie instructs Avion Express flight attendants to not deviate from their service protocol, which is to say that everything must simply be thrown on the tray, with zero effort put into presentation. 😉

So I couldn’t help but reorganize the tray a little bit, to make it look a little more presentable.

Drinks were also offered. I asked for a coffee, and it was a rather disgusting powdered coffee that I didn’t at all enjoy.

Before the descent, I checked out the lavatory, located at the front of the cabin. It was very basic and worn, though at least it wasn’t dirty.

Since this was a wet lease, the flight attendants onboard worked for Avion Express. I couldn’t actually figure out what country they were from (and they weren’t really friendly enough that I felt like being conversational). But anyway, they went through the motions, and weren’t rude, and they spoke a little bit of English (more than the Air Algerie crew on my previous flight).

There was also one Air Algerie flight attendant onboard, I guess to “oversee” the service, as is common with wet leases like this. In this case, he just plopped down in a business class seat and relaxed for most of the flight.

Around 30 minutes after takeoff, at roughly the halfway of the flight, the captain made an announcement, informing us we were at an altitude of 10,700 meters (35,000 feet), and that we’d be descending in around five minutes. Sure enough, we started our descent as planned, and the seatbelt sign was turned on 10 minutes after that.

The views on approach were gorgeous. Tunis is of course a coastal city on the Mediterranean Sea, so the views are tough to beat. I fondly remember my visit to Tunisia around a decade ago.

On our approach, we ended up flying out over the Mediterranean, and then circling back to land toward the south.

We ended up touching down on runway 19 at 8:25AM.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival gate, where we pulled in at 8:30AM next to an Etihad A321LR (probably the nicest plane that serves the airport).

From there I cleared transit security, and had an extended layover, before connecting to Marseille (MRS) in Tunisair economy (due to a downgrade from business class).

My Air Algerie flight operated by an Avion Express A320 was perfectly whatever. For an hour-long flight, I thought the meal was quite good. However, the Avion Express A320 wasn’t terribly inspiring in terms of its modernness, seating, amenities, or service. So yeah, I don’t really have strong feelings on this one, other than appreciating that the flight was at least on schedule.

What do you make of Air Algerie business class, operated by an Avion Express A320?

I had a similar experience flying them from Algiers to Constantine. Biz class is just a coach seat (window or aisle) with the middle seat blocked off. Fairly mediocre experience but still miles ahead of Royal Air HardasaRoc, I mean, Maroc. Now that was a craptacular experience.

The tray arrangement does seem to confirm my suspicion they are round-trip catering their TATL flights…!

#6095. How Much Does It Cost To Own & Operate A Cirrus Vision Jet Each Year?

Aerospace Trek | Shutterstock | Simple Flying

The Cirrus Vision Jet is often presented as an accessible entry point into private jet ownership. Its single-engine design, ability to be flown by one qualified pilot, and comparatively compact cabin make it less complex than larger business aircraft. However, a lower acquisition price does not make the annual budget inexpensive. Fuel, maintenance, insurance, hangar space, pilot training, and engine reserves can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to the cost of keeping one available.

Published estimates vary considerably because they do not all measure the same operation. GlobalAir's report estimates approximately $200,000 annually at 100 flight hours, while CRAFT's ownership model puts the figure at over $600,000 for 200 hours. The difference reflects assumptions about crew, management, training, maintenance, and other fixed expenses, rather than a simple disagreement over fuel prices. A realistic budget therefore depends on how often the aircraft flies, whether the owner pilots it, and which services are included.

The most useful way to estimate the Vision Jet's annual cost is to separate fixed expenses from those that increase with flight hours. GlobalAir's operating-cost report estimates $190,462 for 100 annual hours. Its total includes $47,342 in fixed costs and $143,120 in variable expenses, equivalent to approximately $1,905 per flight hour when the annual budget is divided by 100 hours. The report provides a lower-cost reference point, but its public summary does not itemize every assumption behind the fixed-cost figure.

CRAFT's estimate is substantially higher because it uses a broader ownership model. It assigns $310,291 to annual fixed costs and $1,565 to each flight hour. That produces estimated totals of $466,791 at 100 hours, $623,291 at 200 hours, and $936,291 at 400 hours. The model includes professional crew salary, recurrent training, hangar, insurance, management, fuel, maintenance, engine overhaul reserves, and trip-related expenses.

These figures should not be averaged with GlobalAir's estimate. The two providers use different cost scopes, and CRAFT explicitly includes a professional crew and aircraft management. The GlobalAir figure is closer to a narrower operating budget, although its public summary does not allow a direct line-by-line comparison. Buyers should use the estimate that best matches their intended operation, then obtain a tailored quote.

CRAFT's $310,291 fixed-cost estimate is the largest reason its annual totals exceed GlobalAir's. Its model allocates $190,271 to crew salaries and another $19,000 to recurrent training. It also budgets $28,470 for hangar space, $12,050 for insurance, $33,000 for aircraft management, and $27,500 for miscellaneous fixed expenses. The exact amounts will vary by location, aircraft value, pilot experience, and the services an owner handles personally.

Hangar rental is particularly location-sensitive. A heated hangar at a regional airport may cost substantially less than space at a major metropolitan airport, where availability is limited. Insurance premiums also depend on hull value, pilot qualifications, annual utilization, and claims history. Owners with less turbine experience may face higher premiums or requirements to complete additional training before insurers approve them to fly.

Management fees cover administrative work that is easy to overlook, including maintenance tracking, flight planning, scheduling, regulatory compliance, and coordinating pilots. A self-managed owner can reduce this expense, but takes on those responsibilities directly. The aircraft still needs secure storage, insurance, and scheduled oversight whether it flies 50 hours or 400. Consequently, low annual utilization can make the cost of each completed flight disproportionately high.

Private jet charter rates range from $2,000 to more than $20,000 per hour, but taxes, fees, discounts, and passenger count determine the true costs.

CRAFT estimates variable expenses at $1,565 per flight hour. Fuel accounts for $620 of that amount, based on an estimated burn of 81 gallons (307 liters) per hour and a Jet A price of $7.66 per gallon in its October 2026 calculation. Its November 3 update used an estimated $7.55 per gallon, bringing the hourly fuel estimate to approximately $612. Actual consumption varies with altitude, power settings, weather, payload, and the length and profile of individual trips. Fuel prices also differ among fixed-base operators, and contract arrangements may reduce the retail price.

Maintenance is estimated at $400 per hour, with another $200 allocated to engine overhaul reserves. These are planning allowances rather than bills that arrive at a uniform hourly rate. Routine inspections, component replacements, and unscheduled repairs occur at different intervals, while engine reserves accumulate for future major work. An owner who does not set aside money during lower-maintenance years risks facing a large expense when an inspection or overhaul becomes due.

The remaining $345 per hour in CRAFT's model covers crew, landing, and handling charges at $275, plus $70 for miscellaneous variable expenses. Airport fees can vary substantially by destination, while overnight crew costs depend on where the aircraft travels and how long it remains away from home. These figures explain why a short local flight and a longer trip do not necessarily have identical ancillary costs. The published hourly estimate is a useful planning average, not a guaranteed rate for every mission.

Cirrus offers the JetStream ownership program to bundle maintenance and support services into a prepaid agreement. According to the manufacturer's 2024 prospectus, annualized JetStream pricing typically ranges from approximately $96,000 to $225,000, depending on aircraft age, agreement length, and expected utilization. Agreements generally run from one to three years and establish a maximum number of covered flight hours. The program can include normal-wear replacements, recurrent pilot training, subscription renewals, scheduled maintenance, and support from Cirrus technicians.

JetStream is not simply an additional insurance policy or a substitute for every operating expense. It changes how eligible maintenance and support costs are budgeted, shifting some unpredictable expenses into a defined program payment. The owner still needs to account for fuel, hangar space, insurance, airport charges, and any work or exclusions not covered by the selected agreement. Nor should the full JetStream price automatically be added to a model that already includes maintenance and training allowances. Doing so could count some expenses twice.

Cirrus says Vision Jet pilots must complete annual recurrent training to maintain their type-rating privileges, and its program provides access to factory instructors and service centers. The manufacturer's prospectus also describes CAPS parachute-system overhaul coverage as part of the package. For a buyer comparing aircraft, the remaining JetStream term, annual hour allowance, transferability, and covered work can materially affect the value of an individual jet.

The accessories are rather cool, but they don't come cheap.

The Vision Jet was designed around owner-pilots, and Cirrus says its type-rating pathway is tailored to the aircraft. An owner who already holds the necessary qualifications and flies personally can avoid the professional pilot salary that dominates CRAFT's fixed-cost estimate. That changes the economics substantially. Removing the model's $190,271 crew salary does not make the remaining expenses disappear, however. Owners must still budget for recurrent training, insurance, maintenance, hangar space, and the time required to manage the aircraft.

A professionally crewed operation may make sense for an owner who cannot fly regularly, wants a pilot available for every trip, or needs help managing the aircraft. CRAFT's model includes a full crew salary and management structure, so its $623,291 estimate at 200 hours is better understood as a managed ownership scenario than a universal owner-pilot price. A self-flying owner should build a separate budget using actual insurance quotes, hangar rates, training costs, and the selected maintenance arrangement.

The purchase itself is another major expense outside the annual operating totals. AOPA listed a new Vision Jet at $2.85 million in its 2022 aircraft guide, while its March 2026 coverage put the G3 at approximately $3.68 million with available options. Used examples vary by generation, equipment, hours, condition, and remaining maintenance-program coverage. Financing adds interest and fees, while depreciation reduces the aircraft's resale value over time. Neither is included in the GlobalAir or CRAFT annual operating totals. Buyers should therefore model acquisition, down payment, debt service, taxes, and expected resale value separately rather than treating the annual operating estimate as the complete cost of ownership.

The Vision Jet's appeal rests on making personal jet travel manageable for an owner-pilot, but the annual budget depends more on operating structure and utilization than on its single-engine design alone. A pilot who flies 100 hours a year and manages the aircraft personally may spend far less than a professionally crewed owner using a comprehensive management model. Conversely, higher utilization spreads fixed expenses across more trips, even as fuel, maintenance, and engine reserves rise.

Prospective buyers should treat published figures as starting points, not quotations. The next step is to compare a specific aircraft's maintenance history and JetStream status with local insurance, hangar, fuel, and training prices. As more G3 aircraft enter the market and used examples change hands, program coverage and resale values may become increasingly influential in purchase decisions. A careful five-year forecast, including depreciation and financing, will reveal whether the Vision Jet is genuinely economical for a particular owner's travel pattern, rather than merely less expensive than a larger business jet.

#6094. Livery of the Week: Etihad Partners with McLaren

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

While traditional marketing theories advise airlines to avoid sponsoring events such as motor racing because of perceived associations with “danger” and “uncertainty” — concepts that could reflect negatively on air transport operators — the past couple of decades have seen several airlines establish partnerships with Formula One teams and events.

Today, some carriers are title sponsors of their home Grands Prix. Gulf Air, for example, has been the title sponsor of the Bahrain Grand Prix since its inception in 2004. Singapore Airlines, which has held the same role at the Singapore Grand Prix since 2014, has extended its commitment through 2028.

Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways has been the title sponsor of the UAE Grand Prix since the race’s debut in 2009. This year, it also entered into a partnership with McLaren Racing, bringing together “two organizations with a shared commitment to innovation, ambition, and delivering exceptional experiences for fans and customers around the world”.

To mark the partnership, Etihad has painted one of its Boeing 787-10 aircraft in a special livery, taking McLaren Racing’s distinctive color to the skies.

The livery features McLaren’s signature papaya orange across most of the fuselage — the same color used on its racing cars and team uniforms. The “Etihad” and “McLaren” names appear side by side above the cabin windows, while the McLaren logo is displayed toward the rear of the aircraft against a black background. The tail fin retains Etihad’s signature mosaic pattern, with its colors adjusted to complement the fuselage’s black-and-orange scheme.

Papaya has taken flight 🧡✈️Keep your eyes on the skies and let us know if you spot us 👀#McLarenF1 | #BeyondBorders | @etihad pic.twitter.com/NCHxsdAMTi

The aircraft chosen to showcase the special livery is a Boeing 787-10, registered A6-BMI. It was delivered to Etihad directly from the manufacturer on Oct. 14, 2020.

The aircraft features one of Etihad’s older cabin designs, introduced in 2018. It has 327 seats in a two-class configuration: 32 business class seats in a 1-2-1 layout and 295 economy class seats in a 3-3-3 layout. The first 10 rows of the economy cabin are designated “Economy Space,” offering a seat pitch of 35 inches rather than the standard 31 inches.

Not your usual livery 👀 ✈️ See the making of our special edition @etihad x McLaren Racing livery 🧡 #McLarenF1 #BeyondBorders pic.twitter.com/I2SaS0hyR7

We didn’t have to wait long to find out how American Airlines is shaking up its route map in Los Angeles.

Just minutes after TPG reported the carrier was planning a route announcement at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), American revealed its plans. And there’s both good and bad news for AA flyers in Southern California.

Most notably, the carrier plans to bolster its service on four routes to major U.S. cities.

It’s also bringing back a route to Colorado that it hasn’t offered in a half-decade.

Plus, American will end service to two cities from LAX.

All told, Friday's changes cover nine routes from its West Coast hub. Here's what to know.

American confirmed it’s bringing back service to Grand Junction, Colorado, for the first time in five years.

It will operate seasonal regional service from LAX between May 27 and Aug. 9 with a Bombardier CRJ700.

American last operated LAX service to Grand Junction Regional Airport (GJT) in 2021, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

In 2027, this route will effectively replace American’s flight to Colorado’s Aspen/Pitkin County Airport (ASE), which will be closed next summer for construction.

American will fly its LAX-GJT route with one of its smaller CRJ-700 aircraft.

Elsewhere, American will turn to two routes it’s previously offered seasonally — and sporadically —from LAX into more regular service:

Both routes will operate with an Embraer 175 regional jet.

Starting next spring, American will also add extra daily flights from LAX to several major U.S. cities.

Denver, Las Vegas and Seattle will all get additional frequencies. Plus, American will double its daily service on one transcontinental route — from LA to Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

Starting in May, American will offer twice-daily Dulles service. That’ll make the IAD-LAX routes a stronger complement to AA’s cross-country Los Angeles service from nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

American will cut ties with its LAX route to Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) effective Feb. 11.

That same day, it will also end service to Des Moines, Iowa.

This network revamp in LA comes a day after American executives said the carrier was rethinking the routes it offers at its Southern California hub.

American’s LAX service today sharply lags the flight offerings it had at the airport in 2019.

Speaking Thursday, American’s chief commercial officer, Nat Pieper, said the airline would aim to offer more flights from LAX to major U.S. cities in a push to win more L.A.-based flyers.

"We’re going to grow and we’re going to invest in the local market,” he said, speaking Thursday at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York.

That expansion, Pieper noted, will be gradual — and ramp up — as infrastructure work at LAX progresses over the next two years.

#6092. Global Airlines Liquidating: The Senseless A380 Dream Finally Dies

Over the past few years, I’ve extensively covered Global Airlines, the strange “airline startup” that had a single Airbus A380, with which it wanted to bring back the “golden age” of travel. The carrier’s A380 has been parked since the spring of 2025, and just several months ago, I covered how the company faced several winding up petitions. Well, there’s now an update, which seems long overdue…

Public records in the UK show that Global Airlines has finally been given winding up orders, which is the equivalent of liquidation. This is in response to a petition that was filed on May 29, 2026, and a court approved that order on November 4, 2026. This has only been added to public records today, as there seems to be a one week period between when these decisions are made, and when they’re published for the public.

This means that a government officer from the Insolvency Service will now become the liquidator, and take control of the company, investigate its affairs and the conduct of directors, and collect whatever assets still exist for creditors. This means that the directors no longer have control of the company.

What’s amazing about this entire story is that in the spring of 2025, the company actually operated two roundtrip flights to New York out of Europe, for reasons that most of us couldn’t really make sense of. For that matter, this was part of a wet lease agreement with Portuguese charter company Hi-Fly, given that Global Airlines lacked its own operating certificate.

James Asquith, founder of Global Airlines, gate crashes travel guru Simon Calder's interview with Mike Graham.@james_asquith: "Did you get a cupcake?"@Iromg | @SimonCalder pic.twitter.com/etMVj1TcPu

Shortly after the A380 operated those flights, it entered long term storage, as it needed to undergo heavy maintenance, which costs millions of dollars. The company’s founder, James Asquith, had insisted that the reason the plane was parked for so long was due to delays with being able to get heavy maintenance.

Just months ago, Asquith suggested that the airline would be flying to the Maldives before the end of 2026, despite no progress having been made on the heavy maintenance front.

A post shared by Robyn Asquith (@robynasquith)

Obviously on the surface, the whole Global Airlines thing sounds a bit odd. But let me simply say that the public knows only a tiny fraction of what was really going on here. That’s true both in terms of what Asquith was showing investors to get them onboard with the concept, and also what he claimed the goals for the company were.

My skepticism with this concept wasn’t because I don’t like to see other people succeed, or because I’m against innovation, or anything like that. Instead, it’s because things aren’t always what they seem, and when you’re raising millions of dollars of other people’s money and selling them a dream, there has to be some chance of that actually becoming a reality.

Keep in mind that in 2025, Asquith appeared on The Times’ 40 richest people under 40 list, which claimed he had a net worth of £183 million, making him richer than Adele. Right.

I’d encourage those who just went along with Asquith to be a little introspective here. For example, when you have publications like SimpleFlying that publish things about Global Airlines without even an ounce of skepticism, and then you have people like Captain Chris who latch on to people like Asquith as if they’re Richard Branson (which he literally compared him to, while pointing out that he was proving the doubters wrong), that’s a problem.

A post shared by Captain Chris | Aviation Life (@captainchris)

Many people lost many millions of dollars on this venture. Now, I’d also encourage them to perhaps be a bit more careful next time. And if you just want to make a donation to someone with no expectation of any return, I’m also happy to wire you my bank account details. 😉

It’s the end of the road (or runway) for Global Airlines, as the A380 “airline” has had its winding up petition approved, meaning the company will now be liquidated. It was only a matter of time before this was going to happen, so I don’t think anyone will be surprised. Hopefully one day the entire story can come to light…

What do you make of Global Airlines liquidating?

#6091. FAA Orders Nationwide Ground Stop

Flights were grounded across the U.S. Friday afternoon over suspected air traffic control communications issues.

The FAA issued a highly unusual mass ground stop shortly after 3 p.m.

“Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety, attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped,” the agency said in an advisory. “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis.”

In a separate statement, the FAA said a communications issue affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers is to blame. Agency technicians are now investigating the issue.

According to ABC News, this is only the second time since the 9/11 attacks that departures across the country have been stopped. Flights currently in the air are believed to still be in contact with ATC.

National media outlets showed footage of commercial airplanes queued up but not moving at numerous major airports, including Los Angeles, Boston, Reagan National, New York-LaGuardia, Houston Bush, Dallas/Fort Worth, and Raleigh–Durham.

The ground stop will almost certainly cause a cascade of cancellations and delays lasting into the weekend.

The first Cabinet-level official to comment in person on the incident was Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who spoke to reporters outside the White House. Mullin said there is no indication that the outage is a cyberattack, or connected to the recent Microsoft outage.

The situation is close to “unprecedented,” the secretary added, but there is no threat to public safety or reason to panic. Mullin said it is still too early to say when the problem will be resolved.

It was not immediately clear if the outage is connected to ongoing upgrades on ATC systems and infrastructure. The FAA has been moving rapidly to replace outdated equipment, such as old radios and floppy disks, and install more automated technology. The agency is also ripping out old copper wiring and replacing it with fiber optic cables.

#6090. In Pictures: Riyadh Air’s First Airbus A321neo In Bedouin-Inspired Pearl Livery

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

The first of Riyadh Air's Airbus A321neos have rolled out of the paint shop, debuting the airline's signature pearlescent livery. This is the first of 91 Airbus aircraft for the Saudi carrier. It marks another important step in the airline's evolution and fleet expansion as it builds on the Kingdom's aviation ambitions.

This latest milestone will add to Riyadh Air's mixed fleet of Airbus and Boeing aircraft, supporting its domestic and international growth ambitions. The jet, which will eventually be registered as HZ-RXFA, emerged from the Airbus paint factory in Hamburg, Germany, on Friday, and the airline shared photos on its LinkedIn page.

The plane carries a modern-inspired livery from traditional Saudi heritage, which combines flowing lines that are influenced by traditional Bedouin tents. This includes elements that reflect Arabic calligraphy. On the exterior of the plane, there are shades of indigo and lavender, while inspired patterns dress the fuselage toward the rear.

For the A321neo, it will now undergo a series of test flights in the coming weeks, before it is officially delivered to Riyadh Air. This jet will complement the existing Boeing 787 Dreamliners that are set to form the backbone of the airline's widebody expansion plans. For those interested in the inside cabin configuration and design of the Airbus jet, these are set to be formally debuted in the coming weeks.

Simple Flying reached out to Riyadh Air for comment on its newest aircraft on Saturday; however, an airline spokesperson could not immediately be reached.

As already implied, the plane will now undergo a series of test flights under German Airbus test registration D-AZWL. The plane, which will then carry HZ-RXFA, should be delivered to the airline in the coming months. This Airbus A321neo is the first of 60 of the type to be delivered to the new airline, which aims to revolutionize how passengers travel to and from the Saudi Kingdom.

With ambitions for the airline to serve up to 100 destinations by the end of the decade, these narrowbody aircraft will support thinner, niche routes, or shorter international services, building on the long-haul expansion plans that the carrier is already exploring with its fleet of 787 aircraft.

Riyadh Air is the second flag carrier for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. It operates domestic and international flights and plans to serve 100 destinations in six continents relatively quickly. The airline began commercial operations in October 2025 and is owned by the Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF).

The aircraft will be part of the static display lineup at Le Bourget alongside other Airbus types throughout the Paris Airshow.

Riyadh Air is not part of any major airline alliance. It has signed cooperation and codeshare agreements with several airlines.

Paris Charles de Gaulle, Amsterdam Schiphol

Atlanta; Detroit, Minneapolis/St. Paul, New York-JFK, Salt Lake City, Seattle

The airline currently has just ten active 787-9 aircraft, with one leased from Oman Air and used as a technical spare and training aircraft. The airline has an order for more than 40 of the widebody jets, which will eventually be complemented by 31 Airbus A350-1000s.

With the first of 60 Airbus A321neo aircraft set to begin deliveries to Riyadh Air very soon, these narrowbody aircraft will fly short- and medium-haul routes of up to five hours, likely to other Gulf countries and India, feeding passengers through Riyadh.

#6089. Wild: Stolen Delta Bag Tracked From JFK To DC Bus Stop, Thief Nabbed By Police

It’s not totally uncommon to see bags stolen (or perhaps in some cases accidentally taken) from baggage claim belts at airports. In the past that was basically a lost cause, but thanks to things like AirTags, they can often be tracked.

Here’s an absolutely wild version of such a story, where someone in the miles & points community had their bag stolen, and then someone else tracked it down… hundreds of miles away, and with the help of police!

JT Genter is Editor-in-Chief of AwardWallet and a member of the miles & points community who travels full time. On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, he took to social media to share that his checked bag had been stolen off the Delta baggage claim belt at New York Kennedy Airport (JFK) Terminal 4.

He filed a Delta missing bag claim and police report, and pointed out how “so many irreplaceable memories” were lost in the bag, including all his clothing, medicines, all his toiletries, etc. And he claimed that Delta agents didn’t seem like they gave a you-know-what.

God. So many irreplaceable memories lost in that bag. All of my clothing. Medicines. All my toiletries. Literally so many of my worldly possessions stolen right off Delta's baggage claim belt.And @Delta agents couldn't give less of a shit. Acted like it must happen all the time

That’s obviously incredibly frustrating, though this is a story that had a happy ending less than 24 hours later. JT did have a tracker in his bag, so could keep an eye on the movements of the bag, but he just didn’t say so initially. Apparently the person had pretty quickly taken Amtrak down to DC.

But this is where the story gets truly wild. Jamie Larounis, an Upgraded Points contributor and another member of the miles & points community, coordinated with JT to help. Let me just share Jamie’s version of events:

This might be a story for the history books. Man steals backpack in NY. He takes Amtrak train to DC. I decided to play detective and found the thief with the backpack sitting at a bus station. He boards a bus, but luckily I caught the bus number. I found 2 extremely helpful cops to assist and they found the thief a few blocks away and they nabbed him. They asked me to get in the cop car to ID the thief, and we headed to the police station to retrieve the items.

Gotta say, I didn’t have being in a Metropolitan Police cop car on my bingo card today, but with a little perseverance we got this thief locked up!!! Huzzah!

And by "we", I mean @TheForwardCabin! Jamie used the Tile tracking location to get a visual on our bag and found DC police who were ready to protect and serve.What an incredible end to this story!https://t.co/LvFthwBMqt

When asked what was missing from the bag after it was recovered, JT shared that the guy ditched some clothing, supplies, and custom medical equipment, plus “irreplaceable memories.”

When you consider the volume of bags that are checked, obviously a fair number get lost, stolen, etc. In theory, stealing a bag from a baggage claim belt is really easy — you just take it and leave. However:

Publicly, we of course don’t know anything about this thief. Are we to assume that he wasn’t actually flying, and was just there to steal a bag? And of all the bags he could steal, why did that black backpack catch his eye? And was he planning to travel to DC anyway, and if so, was that the plan all along, or was that just the “escape” plan with the stolen goods?

I recognize that people stealing bags off of baggage claim belts probably aren’t the most sophisticated criminals, but in this day and age, you’d think that checking every pocket of the bag for a tracker would be a best practice, given how common they are.

A traveler had their backpack stolen off of a baggage claim belt at JFK after a Delta flight. Fortunately he had a tracker, which showed that the bag was taken down to DC on Amtrak. After posting about this online, someone else coordinated and played detective, and found someone with the bag at a bus station in DC, and with the help of police, it was recovered.

It’s nice when a story like this has a positive ending, and it’s also a good reminder to put some sort of a tracking device in your bag, for situations where your bag gets lost or stolen.

What do you make of this checked bag recovery mission?

Some of the most aspirational business-class award redemptions are increasingly hard to find, even for the most experienced points and miles enthusiasts.

Cathay Pacific is a prime example. It's harder and harder to find award availability in the Hong Kong-based airline's premium cabins, especially with partners.

But one trick still works: Look for award availability when airlines launch new routes or bring back old ones.

I was able to fly from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points. That is a screaming deal. But there was only saver-level availability for a limited time when the schedule was first loaded.

It turned out to be a fantastic redemption, with excellent service, delicious food and a comfortable lie-flat seat for the long journey across the Pacific.

I'll have more details later in this story on how to find some of these incredible deals in business class, but first, let's talk a bit more about this flight.

Here's what my experience was like aboard Cathay Pacific's Airbus A350-900 and how you can use a similar strategy to find these elusive business-class awards.

Cathay Pacific relaunched its service to Hong Kong from Seattle in March 2026, after suspending the route during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The route originally launched in March 2019 and was canceled in November of the following year. The airline's CEO told TPG that the carrier had always wanted to restore the route, which was Seattle's first nonstop service to Hong Kong since the pandemic.

The plane was a nine-year-old A350-900 with the ship number B-LRL, with 38 business-class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 214 economy seats.

It was a very comfortable way to cross the Pacific and opens up fun new ways to get to Asia from the U.S. West Coast. It also adds another way to use points and miles to fly to Hong Kong, though as you'll read below, it's no easy task to find the lowest-level award availability.

Business-class guests on Cathay Pacific are invited to use The Club at Seattle in the South Satellite area, which is connected to the main terminal by an underground train.

The Club SEA is an independent lounge that participates in Priority Pass. It offers a buffet of hot and cold food items and free drinks. It's basic, and it doesn't hold a candle to Cathay Pacific's own lounges in places like San Francisco and Hong Kong (no noodle bar here). However, it will do the trick for a quick drink and bite.

It was crowded during my quick visit, and I didn't spend much time at this lounge, since I'd had access to the beautiful Alaska Airlines lounge in the N Concourse. I grabbed a bite there before heading to the S Concourse, which is about to get a major, modern $2.5 billion renovation. It should be a much nicer place to hang out once the renovations are done.

Cathay Pacific has 38 business-class seats, split between two cabins. I was in the forward cabin with 30 seats arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration. There is a smaller cabin with just eight business-class seats behind a small galley/boarding area, which looked like a good option for a more intimate experience.

The seats fold down to 75 inches in length to become fully flat beds, though the footwell is a bit narrow.

Cathay Pacific gave out British lifestyle brand Bamford amenity kits that had moisturizer, cooling body gel, pillow mist, an eye mask, earplugs, a toothbrush and toothpaste and mouthwash. There were also noise-canceling headphones and a bottle of water at the seat.

The seat had lots of little storage areas, along with slippers (but no pajamas, as Cathay only has pajamas on select planes with first class).

Bathrooms are plentiful, with two in the front of the main business-class cabin and one more behind. The coolest thing was that the two bathrooms in front have windows — something you don't see that often on airplanes. Amenities were provided by Bamford and included a moisturizing spray and lotion.

The inflight entertainment was great, with an 18.5-inch HD touchscreen and plenty of movies and entertainment. I was able to choose from hundreds of movies and television shows (including a documentary on Cathay Pacific's 80th anniversary). There was also a tail camera and a moving map. A handheld controller is available to navigate the screen.

Cathay Pacific provides free Wi-Fi for business-class passengers, and I found it worked well on my flight. It's not as fast as Starlink, but it was still easy for me to get some work done.

I really like Cathay Pacific's business-class seats on these planes, though I'm excited to try one of Cathay's newer Aria Suite business-class products someday. Those suites are currently being installed on their Boeing 777-300ER fleet.

I'm especially hoping to see it on flights to and from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), which the airline has hinted could come as soon as next year. (The timing of that rollout remains to be confirmed.)

A friendly and attentive crew, delicious food and good bedding made for a great flight across the Pacific. I had especially good service with flight attendants Mei, Amanda and Elsa, all of whom were super friendly and chatty.

Service wasn't as formal as some Asian airlines I've flown, and the crew was fun to be around.

A predeparture beverage of orange juice or water was served during boarding.

Not long after takeoff, flight attendants served drinks. I went with a nonalcoholic Cathay Delight, the airline's signature nonalcoholic drink, made with kiwi, coconut and mint.

That was followed by a lovely amuse-bouche of a deviled egg. I could have happily eaten 20 of them.

The egg dish was served with a Betsy Free, Cathay Pacific's nonalcoholic version of its signature Betsy beer, in a vintage-style Cathay Pacific beer can.

That was followed by an absolutely delicious lunch: a roast carrot soup with a selection of breads, a hearty buffalo mozzarella and rocket pesto salad with grilled radicchio and toasted hazelnuts, and a roasted chicken breast in a maple-chipotle barbecue sauce, served with corn on the cob, creamed spinach and garlic mashed potatoes.

The dessert cart was filled with things like cheese and fruit plates, a yogurt panna cotta, ice cream, or a raspberry tiramisu and, of course, port or wine.

The flight attendants saw me snapping a ton of pictures, so they ended up letting me sample a little bit of almost everything. What a feast!

As if that weren't enough, flight attendants later brought around a chocolate sampler.

There were also snacks set out in the area between the two business-class cabins.

I was able to pre-select a second meal before the flight, and went with a classic beef burger.

There was a nice set of options available on the pre-order menu.

That meal was served after I'd gotten a few hours of shut-eye. Cathay Pacific is well-known for its burgers, and this one didn't disappoint.

I'm not sure how they managed to make a burger served at 30,000 feet taste good, but they did.

The flight attendants helped make my bed with a Bamford-branded mattress pad, duvet and large pillow. I managed to get about five hours of sleep — not too bad.

Before landing, there was yet another meal.

Breakfast was a more traditional Chinese meal of congee with shrimp dumplings and siu mai. Honestly, at that point, I was so full that I didn't eat much of it, but I did enjoy about four cappuccinos.

I'll tell you one thing: Come hungry when flying international on Cathay Pacific.

I was able to score that business-class seat on Cathay Pacific's newly resumed flight to Hong Kong for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points and $5.60 in federal security tax. You can also book Cathay flights with American Airlines AAdvantage miles.

Unfortunately, low-level award space has been increasingly hard to come by using partners lately. That's why I always look when a new or newly resumed route goes on sale. I've often found low-level awards when the route first comes up for booking.

That also happened recently when American Airlines announced new service to Prague and newly resumed flights to Budapest,. The airline made business-class redemptions widely available for just 55,000 Alaska Atmos Rewards points.

So when a new route starts or resumes, check award availability as soon as the seats go on sale.

Related: 9 flight award booking hacks every traveler should know

Of course, you'll likely find more availability using Cathay Pacific's own program: Asia Miles. Cathay Pacific often releases more award availability to its own members. You can transfer miles 1:1 from multiple Cathay Pacific banking partners — including Bilt and Citi ThankYou Rewards, among others — directly to Asia Miles. American Express Membership Rewards also transfers to Asia Miles but at a reduced 5:4 ratio.

Award search tools are increasingly a big part of my deal hunt. Some of my favorites include Seats.aero, ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG parent company, Red Ventures) and Roame.travel. I also rely on the Points Path award tool, which runs in my browser, so I can see award availability when I search on Google Flights.

Flexibility is another key to finding award availability like this. You'll often need to travel whenever a seat is available, not on a specific date. If you're open to multiple destinations, you'll also have better luck finding the cheapest awards, especially to destinations like Asia. Consider using wherever you find the best redemption as a jumping-off point to see other destinations in the region.

Business class on Cathay Pacific's A350-900s may not have all the excitement of its newer Aria Suite, but it's still a super-compelling product, as my recent flight from Seattle to Hong Kong showed. This trip proved once again why Cathay Pacific is one of my favorite airlines, and the newly resumed service from Seattle adds another option for American travelers.

Friendly service, a great seat, and incredible food and beverages made this trip one to remember. The best part was getting all that for just 75,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points.

Keep an eye out for newly launched (or relaunched) routes when you are looking for your next great redemption. You might get a happy surprise.

The Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ is Chase’s premium business card. While the card has a steep annual fee, it also has strong perks, and for many people, will prove to be more than worthwhile.

We’re currently seeing a highest-ever Sapphire Reserve Business bonus, which matches the best bonus we’ve seen on this card. I’d like to recap the details of the offer, including talking about eligibility, and why the card could be worth it. While this is a limited time welcome offer, the end date hasn’t been published.

Link: Learn more about the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠

The Chase Sapphire Reserve Business currently has a limited time highest-ever welcome offer of 200,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards after spending $30,000 within the first six months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus on this card is worth $3,400, which is incredible, among the best welcome offers out there. Admittedly the spending requirement is big (you need to average $5,000 per month in spending over six months), but so is the bonus.

For context on the Sapphire Reserve Business bonus history, when the card launched in 2025, we saw the same offer that’s currently available, for 200,000 points. Then in early 2026 we saw an offer for 150,000 points, before the offer for 200,000 points returned. If you’re trying to understand general Chase business card restrictions, the Chase Ink cards probably give you the best sense of what you can expect in terms of eligibility. You don’t need a corporation to apply for the Sapphire Reserve Business, as a sole proprietorship would qualify as well. So even a side gig (like freelancing or having a rental property) would potentially qualify you for the card.

There’s not a specific credit score you need to get approved for the Sapphire Reserve Business, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that goes into deciding on approvals.

The $795 annual fee Chase Sapphire Reserve Business is a pretty compelling business card. As is the case with many premium cards, the idea is that the annual fee can be justified based on a combination of the rewards structure, benefits, and airport lounge access, among other things.

#6086. Why Doesn't The World's Fastest Commercial Aircraft Have Winglets?

Josh is an avgeek and pilot based in the United Kingdom. He started at Simple Flying as a Commercial Aviation Journalist before taking a less writing-focused role as Content & Growth Lead for Simple Flying's Flight Tracker.

The Boeing 747-8 is the largest, newest, and most aerodynamically advanced 747. The aircraft has a wingspan stretching 224 feet 7 inches (68.4 m) and features redesigned airfoils and raked wingtips that reduce induced drag and improve fuel efficiency by up to 16% compared with the 747-400.

Per Boeing’s data, the 747-8 can carry 467 passengers in a typical three-class layout while maintaining Code F airport compatibility. This enables operations at major international hubs including Frankfurt Airport (FRA), Hong Kong International Airport (HKG), and Dubai International Airport (DXB). In this article, we will compare the 747-8’s wing design, structural efficiency, and operational impact with those of the Boeing 747-400.

By examining raked wingtips, span extensions, and improved lift distribution, we will also explain why Boeing opted for integrated aerodynamic solutions over traditional vertical winglets. For airlines worldwide, these improvements translate into longer nonstop routes, lower fuel burn per passenger or per mass of cargo, and greater flexibility for both passenger and cargo operations across intercontinental networks.

Winglets are vertical or canted extensions added to the ends of wings to reduce induced drag, an unavoidable byproduct of generating lift. Put simply, as a wing moves through the air, it creates a pressure difference: low pressure above and high pressure below. Air naturally tries to equalize this difference by flowing around the wingtip from high to low pressure, forming swirling currents called wingtip vortices.

These vortices represent energy loss and tilt the lift vector slightly backward, so some of the lift is effectively turned into drag. Winglets work by disrupting and reshaping this airflow. They act as a barrier that weakens the formation of vortices and smooths how air transitions off the wingtip.

By reducing the strength of these vortices, winglets allow more of the aerodynamic force to act upward rather than backward, improving the aircraft’s lift-to-drag ratio. This leads to greater aerodynamic efficiency, particularly during cruise, where even small reductions in drag can have a meaningful impact over long distances and long flight times.

In practical terms, this improved efficiency results in lower fuel consumption, increased range, and in some cases better climb performance. However, winglets come with trade-offs: they add weight and increase structural stress at the wingtip.

They can also introduce additional parasite drag (the resistance an aircraft experiences as it moves through the air) at higher speeds. Because of these factors, their overall effectiveness depends on the aircraft’s design, intended mission, and operating conditions, making them one of several possible solutions rather than a universal fix.

From an aerodynamic standpoint, one of the most efficient ways to reduce induced drag is to increase the aspect ratio of the wing. A longer wing, or a wing with a higher aspect ratio (span relative to chord), distributes lift more evenly across its span, which reduces the pressure difference at the tips and weakens the formation of wingtip vortices at their source.

Gliders are a prime example of this principle: their long, slender wings minimize induced drag, allowing them to maintain lift with very low energy loss. In practice, however, aircraft design is heavily constrained by real-world operational limits. Airports are built around standardized gate sizes, taxiway clearances, and runway spacing.

All of these impose strict limits on how large an aircraft’s wingspan can be. If an aircraft exceeds these limits, it may not be able to access many airports, which significantly reduces its flexibility and commercial value. This is why aircraft are designed to fit within specific airport classification systems, balancing aerodynamic efficiency with infrastructure compatibility.

For example, the Boeing 777X uses folding wingtips, allowing it to have a very high-aspect-ratio wing for aerodynamic efficiency in flight while folding the tips on the ground to fit existing airport infrastructure. Winglets emerged as a clever engineering compromise within these constraints. Instead of extending the wing outward, they redirect airflow upward.

This partially replicates the aerodynamic benefits of a longer wing without increasing the actual span. This makes them particularly valuable for retrofitting older aircraft or for designs that must remain within strict size limits. In that sense, winglets are not just an aerodynamic feature: they are a solution shaped equally by engineering physics and the practical realities of global airport infrastructure.

How can split scimitar winglets help airlines and aircraft manufacturers achieve their ambitious sustainability goals?

The Boeing 747-8 represents a significant aerodynamic redesign compared to earlier 747 variants. One of the most important changes is its all-new wing, which is not just a refinement of the older design but a fundamentally updated structure. It features a greater wingspan and redesigned airfoil profiles for better lift distribution.

The use of more advanced materials improves strength and efficiency while managing weight. The wingspan of the 747-8 was increased enough to move it into the Code F airport category, the same classification used by the largest commercial aircraft. This shift gave Boeing engineers far more flexibility.

Specifically, it allowed them to prioritize aerodynamic performance rather than being tightly constrained by legacy airport compatibility limits. Earlier 747 models had to balance efficiency improvements against stricter size restrictions, which limited how far their wing designs could evolve.

Because the wing is both longer and more aerodynamically refined, it naturally produces less induced drag without relying on vertical winglets. Instead of adding devices to fix inefficiencies, the 747-8’s design minimizes those inefficiencies from the start. This results in a cleaner, more integrated aerodynamic solution that better suits the aircraft’s long-haul, high-efficiency mission profile.

Rather than using vertical winglets, the Boeing 747-8 employs raked wingtips, long, tapered extensions that sweep backward from the main wing. These tips effectively increase the wingspan while preserving a smooth, continuous aerodynamic surface. Instead of adding a distinct vertical structure, the wing itself is extended and refined, making the design more integrated and aerodynamically clean.

Raked wingtips reduce induced drag by allowing airflow to leave the wing more gradually, which weakens the formation and intensity of wingtip vortices. Because they extend the wing horizontally rather than redirect airflow upward, they more closely replicate the ideal aerodynamic solution: a longer, more efficient wing. This makes them particularly effective for large aircraft operating over long distances.

They are especially effective at high subsonic cruise speeds, where long-haul aircraft spend most of their flight time. Additionally, raked tips avoid the abrupt geometric transition of a vertical winglet, resulting in smoother airflow and reduced interference drag. This combination of aerodynamic efficiency and structural elegance is why raked wingtips are widely used on modern widebody aircraft designed for long-range performance.

We unravel the secrets of the 777's wingtips.

When comparing winglets and raked wingtips, the differences extend well beyond simple drag reduction. While winglets can be very effective at reducing induced drag, they act as vertical extensions at the wingtip, creating a lever effect that increases bending moments at the wing root. This additional stress requires structural reinforcement, which adds both weight and complexity to the wing.

For aircraft designers, this trade-off must be carefully balanced against the efficiency benefits. Raked wingtips, by contrast, distribute aerodynamic loads more smoothly along the wing because they extend backward and horizontally rather than purely vertically. The horizontal orientation reduces the lever effect and the associated structural stress.

This allows the wing to achieve aerodynamic gains with less added weight. In practical terms, this can make a significant difference on very large aircraft, where even small structural savings translate into improved efficiency and payload capability. There is also a speed-related consideration. At higher cruise speeds, vertical surfaces like winglets can generate additional parasite drag.

This reduces some of the efficiency gains achieved from induced drag reduction. Raked wingtips tend to perform better under these conditions, making them particularly well-suited for large, fast, long-haul aircraft like the 747-8. The result is a wing design optimized not only for efficiency, but for efficiency in the specific flight regime the aircraft is designed to operate in.

The 747-400, introduced decades earlier, incorporated winglets because its wing design and operational constraints limited options for reducing drag. The 747-400’s wings were based on an older design that could not be easily extended without significant structural redesign. Additionally, airport compatibility requirements at the time imposed stricter limits on wingspan.

As such, any major extension could have restricted the aircraft from operating at many key airports around the world. Winglets offered a practical, cost-effective solution. By redirecting airflow and reducing wingtip vortices, they improved fuel efficiency without requiring a complete redesign of the wing.

During an era when fuel costs were rising sharply, even modest efficiency gains could translate into substantial operational savings for airlines. Winglets allowed the 747-400 to achieve these benefits while maintaining its existing footprint and performance characteristics. The transition from the 747-400 to the Boeing 747-8 reflects a broader evolution in aerospace engineering: moving from add-on efficiency solutions to fully integrated aerodynamic optimization.

Advances in computer modeling, new materials, and flexible airport infrastructure enabled Boeing to design wings that inherently minimize drag, reducing the need for retrofitted features such as traditional winglets. This evolution highlights how aircraft design has become more holistic, optimizing efficiency at the source rather than correcting it after the fact.

#6085. American Airlines Concierge Key: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. In this post, I’d like to take a close look at this elite status, and talk about what it is, how you can earn it, what the benefits are, etc. The truth is that very little is officially published about this, so we mostly have to go off of data points.

The reality is that these invitation-only elite tiers are kind of genius from the perspective of airlines. That’s because a not-insignificant portion of the frequent flyer community finds this status to be rather “sexy,” and will go out of their way to earn it. Since the qualification requirements aren’t published, it keeps people on the hamster wheel, booking as many expensive tickets as possible.

On the most basic level, Concierge Key is American’s invitation-only elite status level. There’s no published criteria to earn it, and it has to be renewed every program year, so you can earn it one year and lose it the next.

Going back many years, Concierge Key was completely separate from the AAdvantage program, but that’s no longer the case. Nowadays Concierge Key is a formal part of the AAdvantage program, and it’s a tier above Executive Platinum status (American’s highest elite tier with published qualification criteria).

I think it’s also worth mentioning that Concierge Key is perhaps the most well-known invitation-only elite status in the industry, as it was a major theme of the popular 2009 movie “Up In The Air,” starring George Clooney. Ugh, I can’t believe that was over 15 years ago.

The criteria to earn Concierge Key is not published, but generally there are a few ways to earn it.

One way is to spend a ton on American Airlines travel. We’re talking $50,000+ of spending per year. That’s not to say that spending $50,001 will get you Concierge Key status, but rather that if you spend less than that, don’t assume you have any real chance of being invited. As a matter of fact, nowadays you might need to spend significantly more than that. So you absolutely can earn Concierge Key purely through your own travel, and that’s probably the most common way it’s earned.

We don’t fully know what American looks for in this regard, though. Does the airline care purely about the dollar amount you spend, the typical fare classes you fly in (consistently full fare first class, for example), or something else? There are also some indications that the qualification criteria vary based on markets, so you have a better chance of earning it if you’re not living in a major hub city of American.

In other words, on some level it’s competitive, and you’re ranked against other travelers in similar markets. Expect that it takes more effort to earn Concierge Key if you primarily fly out of Charlotte (CLT), Dallas (DFW), or Miami (MIA), rather than out of Atlanta (ATL), Seattle (SEA), or Tampa (TPA).

Keep in mind that nowadays American Airlines elite status is based on the Loyalty Points program, so you can even earn elite status through credit card spending. So, does non-flying activity similarly count toward Concierge Key status? The reports I’ve seen suggest that it does, but you need to engage with the program a lot. For example, I’ve heard of people earning Concierge Key through credit card spending, but we’re talking about many hundreds of thousands of dollars in spending, if not over a million dollars.

You can also earn Concierge Key through the influence you have over others’ travel. Sometimes American Airlines will give Concierge Key nominations as part of a big corporate contract, or to key travel planners who have influence over a lot of others’ travel.

American Airlines is even known to comp Concierge Key to some “influencers.” For example, going back several years, YouTuber Casey Neistat was comped Concierge Key status and was really unhappy when it was taken away.

For avoidance of doubt, I’ve never been offered Concierge Key status, and I’m totally fine with that. 😉

Just for context on how these requirements compare to Executive Platinum, that requires 200,000 Loyalty Points per year. All AAdvantage members earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on credit cards, and Executive Platinum members earn 11x Loyalty Points per dollar spent on flights. So Executive Platinum requires $200,000 in credit card spending or around $18,200 in spending on flights.

American Concierge Key has quite a few published benefits, but some would argue the biggest benefit of the status is better “soft” treatment in the event of irregular operations.

The first thing worth understanding is that Concierge Key automatically comes with all Executive Platinum benefits. This includes everything from oneworld Emerald status, to space available first class upgrades, to complimentary Main Cabin Extra seating, to 120% bonus miles on flights, to three free checked bags, to a free drink & snack in economy, to priority services, to same day flight changes & standby.

This also includes access to the Loyalty Point Rewards program, allowing members to select additional perks, ranging from systemwide upgrades to bonus miles. Beyond that, benefits of American Concierge Key include the following:

Assistance during irregular operations is probably both potentially the most valuable perk, and also the most inconsistent one. On a good day, Concierge Key members may get proactive rebookings when flights are canceled and delayed.

American even has a fleet of cars at hubs for Concierge Key tarmac transfers, so during a short connection you may be picked up planeside and driven to your connecting flight. At the same time, there are also instances where you’ll likely be disappointed, because Concierge Key agents aren’t going to deliver 100% of the time.

If you’re looking to at least get Concierge Key levels of airport support with a particular trip, keep in mind that American offers Five Star Service, which is a paid program for more attentive service at the airport.

In the interest of being thorough, let me also mention some perks that Concierge Key used to offer, but no longer does:

American Airlines understandably hasn’t revealed how many Concierge Key members there are, so the best we can do is speculate. If I had to guess, I’d say there are somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 Concierge Key members. To be more exact, my assumption is that the number is roughly in the middle of that range.

In 2019 there was a clue — American worked with a company to send out chocolate to Concierge Key members, and the company posted that 11,300 packages had been prepared. Now, not all Concierge Key members received this chocolate, suggesting to me that there are more members than that.

If you’re curious how other elite ranks compare, I’d guess the number of Executive Platinum members is maybe 4-5x as high as the number of Concierge Key members. Again, that’s purely speculation on my part, and with the Loyalty Points system nowadays, the number may be even higher than that.

It’s hard to say whether something like Concierge Key is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Concierge Key varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

If you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Flagship Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal — you’ll get to board first, but there’s not necessarily all that much more to it.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including Delta 360 and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, though, I’d say that Concierge Key is probably the strongest of the tiers, in terms of the number of perks, including additional lounge access to the carrier’s most premium lounges. A couple of thoughts, though:

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. It gives you priority over Executive Platinum members for just about everything, lounge access, and also (hopefully) proactive help in the event of irregular operations. However, don’t expect it to earn it if you don’t spend at least $50,000 per year on American Airlines flights, and even then it’s not a sure bet.

Is the status life changing? While I’ve never had it, I’m inclined to say “no.” But others certainly may disagree…

If you’re a Concierge Key member (or have been one in the past), what has been your experience with the status? How does it compare to Executive Platinum status?

#6083. Richard Avedon, Fashion Guru, Does Old Age

A moving, incisive photography exhibition in Toronto and Montreal explores the way of all flesh.

Left: Richard Avedon, Gloria Swanson, actor, New York, September 4, 1980, gelatin silver print. Right: Richard Avedon, The Duke and Duchess of Windsor, Waldorf Astoria, suite 28A, New York, April 16, 1957, gelatin silver print.

© The Richard Avedon Foundation, courtesy of the Museum of Modern Art, New York, Committee on Photography Fund

Old faces — some seem to crease and crumble as we watch — were a specialty for Richard Avedon (1923–2004), the photographer famous for his fashion work for Vogue, Harper’s Bazaar, Revlon, and Elle, magazines not known for plugging geezers. I didn’t know this, so I learned something new in my first minutes in Richard Avedon Immortal: Portraits of Aging, 1951–2004, finishing its tour next month, when it goes to The Image Center in Toronto and the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts. Avedon was a pioneer in presenting cool, stark, tough beauty — he gave us a nude Nastassja Kinski with a boa constrictor licking her earlobe, Brooke Shields in jeans, and lots of movie stars and potentates at their peaks. But old age? Shades of decadence are one thing, but decrepitude?

The Image Center is Canada’s premiere photography museum and part of Toronto Metropolitan University. The exhibition there is similar to Montreal’s edition and displays 100 Avedon portraits. Avedon died more than 20 years ago, and the show spans 50 years, so the subjects are from another era. That said, old age is timeless as well as time-limited. On view are superstars such as Gloria Swanson, Ronald Reagan, the Duke and Duchess of Windsor, and the Dalai Lama. Then there are the period pieces like Dorothy Parker, Oscar Levant, Ezra Pound, and Coco Chanel.

Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.
