#6082. Which Hotel Credit Cards Offer Free Night Awards, And Are They Worth It?

Hotel credit cards are among the most underrated out there. Understandably a lot of people get cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) to maximize the rewards they’re earning for their spending, and that’s a great idea. These cards offer valuable bonus categories, no foreign transaction fees, great travel coverage, and more.

But I think supplementing one of those cards with hotel credit cards can make a lot of sense. That’s because hotel credit cards largely offer some incredible perks that more than justify the annual fee, including free hotel elite status, and even some free night certificates. So even if you’re not loyal to a hotel group, it’s easy to get outsized value.

In this post, I’d like to specifically look at which credit cards offer free nights as part of their rewards structure, how you can earn them, and if they’re worth it.

There are hotel credit cards issued by Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, and World of Hyatt, which offer the opportunity to earn free night awards. To be clear, I’m not talking about the ability to earn points, but instead, the ability to earn free night awards that can be redeemed at a set of properties.

These free nights come in different forms — some free night awards are offered for spending a certain amount on a card, and some free night awards are offered as an annual benefit just for having a card, with no spending required.

So let’s take a look at the details of how these free night awards work, and then we’ll talk about whether they’re worth it. Note that I’m focusing specifically on cards that offer free night awards on an ongoing basis (rather than as part of a welcome offer), and am also limiting this to cards that are open to new applicants.

Hilton Honors has two credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Hilton Honors free night awards are my single favorite hotel free night awards out there, given that they have no category caps, and they’re valid for 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Hilton points at 0.5 cents each.

Hilton free night awards can be redeemed for standard rooms at properties costing up to 250,000 points per night, and there’s only a small list of excluded properties. They’re even valid at Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) properties that are part of the Hilton Honors partnership. It’s easy to redeem these at properties costing $1,000+ per night.

IHG One Rewards has three credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

IHG One Rewards free night awards are also potentially quite valuable, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value IHG points at 0.5 cents each.

While IHG free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, what I really like is how you can top them off with an unlimited number of points. So if a hotel requires 100,000 points, you could use a 60,000 point free night certificate, and then top it off with 40,000 points.

Marriott Bonvoy has four credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Marriott Bonvoy free night awards are also extremely lucrative, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Marriott points at 0.7 cents each.

While Marriott free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, you can top them each off with up to 25,000 points, to redeem at more expensive properties. So you could book a hotel costing 60,000 points per night by redeeming a 35,000 point free night award, and then redeeming 25,000 additional points.

World of Hyatt Honors has one credit card that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

World of Hyatt free night awards are valuable, but definitely the most restrictive of the bunch. Free night awards issued with the card expire 12 months after they’re issued. I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

Category 1-4 covers a lot of Hyatt properties (these can cost up to 25,000 points per night), but the catch is that you can’t use these certificates to redeem at more expensive properties by topping them off. Still, it should be very easy to get outsized value.

I’ll let my credit card portfolio speak for itself — I have quite the selection of hotel credit cards. They’re not necessarily cards that I spend a ton on, but instead, they’re cards I largely have because of the very strong perks that they offer, which to me, more than justify the annual fee. Let me just give a few direct examples…

I have the Hilton Honors Aspire Card, and it’s my single favorite hotel credit card. The card offers a massive number of perks, but in particular, the free night alone more than justifies the annual fee for me. I try to use this at properties that would retail for $1,000+ per night, so it’s pretty awesome to get that, along with all kinds of other perks, just for having the card.

I also think there’s merit to spending $60,000 per year on the card, if you can swing it. That spending would earn you a minimum of 180,000 points (since you earn at least 3x points per dollar spent with the card), plus two additional free night awards, potentially worth up to 500,000 points. So this is a great card to consider if you’re making a big purchase.

In the case of Marriott Bonvoy, I have both the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card and Marriott Bonvoy Business Card, which get me free night awards worth 85,000 and 35,000 points, respectively. These also in and of themselves more than justify the annual fees on the cards. I generally redeem the larger free night award for a luxury hotel stay, while I redeem the lesser free night award for a stay at a mid-range property.

Lastly, I also have the World of Hyatt Credit Card, and that free night award also more than justifies the annual fee in and of itself. Admittedly I wish the free night award cap would be increased to reflect inflation, but even so, I get a ton of value out of this. At an absolute minimum, I use it when I have an overnight near JFK to stay at the Hyatt Regency JFK, which typically costs $300+ if paying cash.

There are potentially lots of great benefits to hotel credit cards, including big welcome bonuses, easy opportunities to earn hotel status, generous rewards structures for spending, and more.

The best part is that most issuers let you have multiple credit cards, meaning you can potentially earn more than one free night certificate per year. In the case of just about all of the above cards, I’d say the free night certificates more than justify the annual fees.

What’s your favorite hotel credit card free night certificate?

#6081. Update: FAA Lifts Ground Stop

After a roughly five-hour freeze on virtually all commercial aircraft departures, the FAA has lifted its nationwide emergency ground stop.

The FAA canceled the ground stop around 8:20 p.m., and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed it at a press conference at the White House Friday night. He said it will take some time for flights to restart but emphasized that the air space is safe.

According to Duffy, FAA personnel began to see inconsistencies in air traffic data around 3:30 p.m. Friday, and, out of an abundance of caution, the decision was made to ground flights not already in the air. He said old analog ATC communications switches were overwhelmed and “went down,” causing the inconsistency.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the failure was triggered by an attempted technology update, which caused the system to reboot and crash.

There is no evidence of a cyberattack or terrorism, Mullin emphasized, and passengers were never in any danger.

Duffy said travelers should contact their airline for information about potential cancellations and delays. He said his department is in contact with the major carriers and will work with them to restore normal operations.

A small number of mostly international flights were cleared for takeoff at airports such as New York-JFK, Washington Dulles, Reagan National, and Detroit Friday afternoon during the ground stop, but most remained grounded until the FAA reversed its order.

#6080. Nationwide Ground Stop Caused By Same Firm That Left Trump’s Boeing 747-8 With Security Gaps

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

The four-hour ground stop that halted flight departures across the United States triggered more than 10,000 flight cancellations on Friday alone. The routine telecommunications upgrade was being completed by L3Harris Technologies, the same defense and aerospace contractor that was hired by the Pentagon to retrofit the Qatari-donated Boeing 747-8 Air Force One.

During the morning briefing, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that L3Harris, which owns and operates the legacy telecommunications network for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), was working on a remote site for the administration when the system collapsed on Friday, causing chaos in the aviation industry.

According to FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, and alongside Duffy, the two explained how the outage unfolded during an L3Harris crew switching the aging copper telecommunications line to fiber-optic cabling at a remote facility. This caused the router involved to flood other routers across the private air traffic control (ATC) network.

Preliminary findings suggest that the Cisco 600-series routers, which were manufactured a quarter of a century ago, then became overwhelmed and were feeding out-of-sync data pockets into the wider network.

With an estimated 1,000 connection attempts every few seconds, 45 minutes of instability was experienced across 17 of 22 enroute air traffic control centers, affecting voice radio communications with pilots and altering radar feeds, resulting in the rare move by the FAA to order a nationwide shutdown of departing flights out of an abundance of caution.

The ground stop was issued for all departing flights to, from, and within the US. Flights already enroute and in the sky were permitted to continue to their destination, with 1,000's of airplanes able to land safely. All departing flights were grounded for up to four hours until the ground stop was lifted. This sent a ripple effect to flights across the world, with many US-bound services delayed at the gate until the all-clear was given to resume flights later on Friday at 8:15 PM EST.

Duffy and Bedford have stressed that there was no sign of a cyberattack or link to the FAA AI controller tool. Investigators are now looking to determine whether the failure stemmed from the defective router or an installation error by the L3Harris technicians. This would not be the first time a fiber transition to the new network has failed; a 2009 incident also disrupted up to 129 FAA facilities.

As a result, more than 10,000 flights were canceled on Friday, and many more delays and cancellations are expected to linger across the weekend as airlines work to reposition thousands of affected crew, passengers and aircraft.

The agency cited communication problems for the halt.

L3Harris has a connection to the Trump-influenced Boeing 747-8 VC-25B Bridge. The FAA worked with L3Harris on a rapid retrofit of the Qatari-donated 747-8, which is set to serve as an interim aircraft until the delivery of new Air Force One aircraft expected in 2028. L3Harris worked with the administration to fast-track modifications for the interim aircraft.

The rapid overhaul focused on basic communication and livery, instead of the full suite of hardened electronic countermeasures that are installed on the legacy VC-25A aircraft. These defensive gaps were highlighted during the aircraft swap Trump was forced to undertake after a security threat in Ankara, Turkey, where it is alleged Trump was moved from the 747 to a catering truck and then into a waiting Air Force C-32A for a trip to the UK. Following this incident, the 747-8 was taken offline for additional security upgrades to the aircraft.

As highlighted on Friday, aging ATC infrastructure is under immense pressure in the US, and Duffy has called on Congress to rapidly approve up to $50 billion to fully replace the nation's air traffic control system.

#6079. What Amenities Make An Airport Lounge Good? Here’s My Take…

I write a lot about airport lounges on the blog, ranging all the way from domestic lounges in the United States, to the best business class lounges, to the best first class lounges. When I rank the lounges that I like the most, some readers understandably have very different takes.

I thought it would be fun to start a discussion about basic expectations of airport lounges, and what makes them exceptional.

Obviously lounge standards should differ depending on whether you’re using Priority Pass to access a lounge or are traveling in international first class, so we’ll get into more detail on that below.

Broadly speaking, what I’m looking for in a lounge is a (relatively) quiet place to sit, connect to Wi-Fi, recharge electronics, use a clean bathroom, and maybe have some water or coffee. Other things are good to have, but not something I necessarily expect.

There are also some deal killers for me when it comes to airport lounges. Personally, if a lounge is packed, I have no interest in being there, and that largely reflects that over the years, terminals have become much better places to spend time:

I figured I’d share my expectations for lounges, and I’ll break it up into three tiers of lounges (admittedly some of the lines are blurred here):

I think it’s also important to note that everyone is looking for different things in lounges:

I think the two below videos from Cathay Pacific from several years ago oh-so-beautifully sum up what makes lounges great. The commentary in the videos is almost poetic.

With that out of the way, let me share my basic expectations of various types of lounges, and admittedly these reflect my preferences and biases.

My expectations for Priority Pass lounges, airport contract lounges, airline membership lounges, and credit card lounges, are pretty simple. I’m happy if I can actually consistently get in and have a quiet place to sit. Sadly that’s not as straightforward as it may sound, with so many stories of lounges denying entry to club members, Priority Pass members, etc.

What sets a “basic” lounge apart? I’d say showers, bathrooms that are significantly nicer than in the terminals, workstations, a good food selection (ideally with hot food), good coffee, and employees who actually make you feel welcome.

Just to give some examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be exceptional:

My expectations are a bit higher for purpose-built international business class lounges. In addition to what I expect from the more “standard” lounges above, I hope that international business class lounges will have hot food, a more premium drink selection, showers, and workstations.

What sets an international business class lounge apart? I’d say a la carte dining, nap rooms, barista-made coffee drinks, and generally elevated decor.

Just to give a few examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be quite good (we’re actually pretty lucky in North America):

International first class lounges are as premium as they get, so expectations should be high. In international first class lounges I expect a la carte dining, barista-made coffee, some sort of an area to rest, a truly tranquil environment, and staff who make you feel welcome.

What sets an international first class lounge apart? Dining that’s (high-end) restaurant quality, an amazing drink selection, individual nap rooms, spa treatments, and a ground experience that extends beyond the lounge. That’s to say either tarmac transfers or an escort to the gate, and that’s no doubt an area where many airlines fall short.

I’ve reviewed the world’s top first class lounges in detail, so it’s no secret what my favorite options are the Air France La Premiere Lounge Paris and Lufthansa First Class Terminal Frankfurt.

We’re all looking for different things from airport lounges, and I think that’s totally fair. Standards should differ based on what kind of a flight you’re taking, how you access the lounge, what you’re trying to accomplish by visiting a lounge, etc.

Everyone will have a different take on which lounges are great vs. just okay, and that’s fine. While I care about tranquility and good coffee, others care about great food and drinks.

I’m curious to hear from OMAAT readers — what makes a lounge great, in your book?

#6078. Elizabeth Warren’s Plan to Abolish Credit Cards

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D., N.Y.), and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D., Mass.) host a roundtable on housing affordability and accessibility on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., January 7, 2026.

Elizabeth Warren, never short on annoyances, thinks that interest on consumer credit cards is too high.

The average rate currently hovers around 21 percent. Her solution: Pass a law to cap interest rates at 10 percent. She says she has a bill ready to go, and like-minded lawmakers have signaled their support for controlling rates.

Like any other price ceiling, an interest cap would create a shortage of the product it attempts to make more affordable. With only a tiny fraction of credit cards now offering interest at 10 percent or less, capping rates at that level would force lenders to dramatically restrict accounts — requiring borrowers to put up collateral or limiting access to people with exceptionally good credit — or eliminate them outright.

To progressives, interest on credit cards is nothing but usury — the exploitation of poor borrowers who can’t afford to pay their bills on time. Warren’s sales pitch implies that, under her bill, people would enjoy the same credit just at a lower cost. In reality, almost everyone would see their current credit cards disappear.

Regrettably, Warren may also find allies for her proposal among Republicans. She claims she is open to working with President Trump, who called in 2024 for a temporary cap on credit card interest of “around 10 percent.” Senator Josh Hawley (R., Mo.), a right-wing progressive of sorts, recently joined hands with Bernie Sanders to translate that thoughtless musing into legislation.

Interest rates are not some arbitrary number. They are the price for lenders to provide liquidity on the promise, but never the certainty, that it will be repaid. To issue loans through a credit card, banks must first obtain the money by borrowing it themselves, either from depositors or other financial institutions. Interest must be paid on that debt and passed through to cardholders.

It’s true that rates on credit cards, as well as other consumer loans, are typically much higher than those for mortgages and businesses. That is because personal credit is one of the riskiest kinds to extend. Unlike secured loans, repayment depends wholly on borrowers’ creditworthiness. That often fails to hold up: 13 percent of credit-card balances are seriously past due, and approximately 5 percent of debt is never repaid. Higher interest rates exist to compensate for these losses.

Rates also vary based on individual creditworthiness. Borrowers with poor credit history, or people just starting to build their history after leaving childhood or moving to the country, have the most to lose from interest caps. They must accept costlier rates to obtain any credit whatsoever, and if lenders can’t adjust for their added risk, they will simply be cut off. Those in need of funds will instead have to turn to pawnshops or illegal loan sharks.

The credit card industry could always use more competition to keep interest rates at their fair market level. Ironically, the Dodd-Frank Act that Elizabeth Warren championed likely reduced the availability of consumer credit by increasing lenders’ regulatory burden. She also despises credit reporting agencies for tracking borrowers’ repayment histories, even though they replaced a far more discretionary and intrusive system in which bankers evaluated applicants’ personal reputations. For someone so appalled by alleged discrimination in finance, Warren should love objective credit reports.

By and large, Americans like their credit cards and wish to keep them. In trying to rescue consumers from their own financial decisions, Warren would deprive them of their plastic and consign them to infinitely more treacherous alternatives.

#6076. American CFO Lays Out Vision For Becoming ‘Premium Global Airline’

The chief financial officer of the world’s largest airline said the carrier is positioning itself to be a “premium” option at the global level.

Speaking at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York on Thursday, American CFO Nat Pieper said the airline is investing in and improving its highest leverage points.

“That is an ongoing effort. So many different steps to the travel process. But I think we’ve made good progress. I feel like we’ve got momentum and we’re optimistic about where we’re going,” he said.

Customer experience, loyalty, network strength, and premium products will be leading priorities, he added, since they encourage customers to stick with the airline over time.

Pieper also said the airline is focusing on optimizing operations at LAX.

“Local yields are better than connecting traffic. If you’re going to win and jump on markets, you’ve got to focus on the local market. That’s what we’re going to do in Los Angeles,” he said.

“It’s going to be a gradual build as we get to the end of ’28, when T4 and T5 will be ready to roll, we’ll have 30 gates there,” he continued. Terminal 4 and 5 are undergoing an extensive $1.6 billion modernization.

When it comes to the financials, Pieper said the best way to maximize cash flow is to invest in the product.

“The ultimate goal for American is generate as much cash flow as we can… You can pay your balance sheet and get it into the shape that you want it, as well as generate enough cash to be able to reinvest in your product and have people continue to want to fly your airline,” he said.

#6074. Why Breeze Airways Is Taking Spirit Airlines' Leftover Leisure Markets But Avoiding Big Trunk Routes

The collapse of Spirit Airlines in May has created opportunities across the US aviation market, leaving several airports without commercial service and removing an important source of low-cost competition on popular leisure routes. While other airlines have been cautious about taking over these abandoned markets, Breeze Airways is moving quickly.

It has been targeting destinations where passengers have lost convenient nonstop connections and where existing airline competition remains relatively limited. However, Breeze Airways is not attempting to recreate the network that Spirit Airlines once operated. Instead, its expansion reveals a much more selective strategy.

It is concentrating on smaller regional airports, holiday destinations, and point-to-point international services rather than competing directly on the country's busiest routes. From Latrobe, Pennsylvania, to Tampa, Florida, the airline is choosing opportunities that fit its operating model, suggesting that the most attractive parts of Spirit Airlines' former network are not necessarily its biggest routes.

Spirit Airlines officially ceased operations on May 2, 2026, following its unsuccessful attempts to reorganize under Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection and its subsequent move towards Chapter 7 liquidation. Rising fuel prices, which exceeded $4 per gallon amid geopolitical disruptions affecting energy markets, placed additional pressure on an already financially troubled business.

The deteriorating economics made its restructuring plans increasingly difficult to sustain. Its departure immediately created gaps in several markets where ultra-low-cost airlines had been the only commercial operator. Smaller airports were particularly exposed because they lacked the passenger volumes and competing airlines that could make replacing lost services relatively straightforward.

For communities accustomed to affordable nonstop flights, the shutdown meant losing more than an airline; it meant losing convenient access to important leisure destinations. Breeze Airways has identified these abandoned markets as potential opportunities, particularly where passengers previously depended on Spirit Airlines for direct holiday connections.

Rather than simply copying its former competitor's entire network, Breeze Airways is selecting individual routes that appear compatible with its aircraft, operating costs, and passenger demand. This distinction is important because not every route previously operated by Spirit Airlines necessarily offers attractive economics.

The airline's approach also reflects the competitive environment following Spirit Airlines' departure. Average fares have increased considerably on routes no longer served, demonstrating how the removal of an ultra-low-cost competitor can affect ticket prices. Breeze Airways therefore has an opportunity to attract price-conscious passengers without necessarily matching every fare previously offered by Spirit Airlines.

One of the clearest examples of this strategy is Arnold Palmer Regional Airport (LBE) in Latrobe, Pennsylvania. The airport lost all commercial passenger service when Spirit Airlines departed, leaving an important gap for residents of Westmoreland County and surrounding communities.

The consequences extended beyond passengers, with the airport also facing employment and economic challenges following the withdrawal of its only commercial airline. In the 12 months leading up to Spirit Airlines' collapse, data from the US Bureau of Transportation Statistics shows that the busiest three routes from the airport were those detailed in the table below.

Breeze Airways will restore scheduled commercial service with twice-weekly flights to Myrtle Beach International Airport (MYR) beginning February 9, 2027, followed by service to Orlando International Airport (MCO) from May 26, 2027. Both destinations appeal strongly to leisure travelers, offering straightforward connections to popular vacation markets.

Crucially, as well, they do not require passengers to travel through Pittsburgh International Airport (PIT) or another larger airport. The advertised introductory one-way fares make the routes particularly interesting. Myrtle Beach flights have been promoted from $49, while Orlando services start at $59. These prices position Breeze Airways competitively for families and travelers who previously relied on Spirit Airlines.

However, additional charges and changing availability mean the advertised starting fares will not represent every passenger's final ticket price. Latrobe also offers infrastructure advantages that make the opportunity more attractive. Its approximately $28 million terminal expansion introduced additional gate capacity and improved passenger facilities.

This created an airport environment capable of supporting renewed airline operations. With a relatively uncomplicated operating environment and limited direct competition, Breeze Airways can establish a presence without immediately entering the expensive competitive battles associated with major metropolitan airports.

They are from ten of the carrier's 12 Florida airports. See them all here!

Breeze Airways' selection of Myrtle Beach and Orlando illustrates why leisure markets are central to its expansion strategy. Both destinations attract substantial holiday demand, particularly from families and travelers planning trips around school holidays, seasonal breaks, and longer weekends. Their appeal is also relatively easy to communicate to passengers.

This makes them suitable destinations for an airline building awareness in previously underserved communities. Unlike large business-oriented markets, leisure routes can often be developed around concentrated periods of demand. Passengers traveling to Florida or South Carolina may be more willing to arrange their schedules around particular departure days.

This allows an airline to operate limited weekly frequencies instead of committing substantial capacity to daily service. This flexibility can be particularly valuable when testing a relatively new market. Breeze Airways is also expanding its presence at Tampa International Airport (TPA), where the airline is building a growing network of holiday connections.

Beginning December 16, it plans to introduce service to St. Thomas, followed by Cancún on December 18 and Montego Bay on December 19. These destinations provide additional opportunities to attract passengers seeking direct access to popular Caribbean and Mexican vacation markets.

The busiest destinations from Tampa International Airport last year are outlined in the table above. The wider appeal is that Breeze Airways can connect passengers with destinations they actively want to visit without necessarily competing for the same customers as major network airlines.

Leisure travelers often prioritize convenient departure airports, affordable tickets, and nonstop journeys over extensive connecting networks. By concentrating on these preferences, Breeze Airways can develop a recognizable market position while avoiding some of the pressures associated with traditional hub-based competition.

Although Breeze Airways is particularly interested in smaller airports, its expansion at Tampa demonstrates that the airline is not exclusively pursuing underserved regional communities. Tampa International Airport provides access to a much larger passenger market, a strong leisure-travel base, and opportunities to develop international services that would be difficult to support from smaller airports.

The most significant addition is Santo Domingo (SDQ) in the Dominican Republic, with year-round flights scheduled to begin June 18, 2027. The service will operate twice weekly using the Airbus A220-300, giving passengers a nonstop alternative for traveling between Tampa and the Dominican Republic's capital. It will also become Breeze Airways' sixth international destination from Tampa.

This expansion is significant because it demonstrates how Breeze Airways can use an established operating base to support international growth without attempting to challenge the largest airlines across their most important domestic markets. Tampa already offers the airline a foundation of existing routes, aircraft operations, and passenger recognition.

This makes additional international destinations a more logical extension of its network. As detailed in the table above, Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ) was the busiest international destination from Tampa International Airport last year. The Caribbean additions also create opportunities to distribute aircraft utilization across different markets.

St. Thomas, Cancún, Montego Bay and Santo Domingo appeal to different passenger groups, but they share an important characteristic: each offers a recognizable leisure or VFR market. This gives Breeze Airways several opportunities to build demand while maintaining a network focused on relatively straightforward nonstop journeys.

The startup airline has some unique strategies that are driving its profitability.

The absence of an aggressive push into major trunk routes is arguably the most revealing part of Breeze Airways' expansion strategy. Routes connecting cities such as New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, and Atlanta can generate enormous passenger volumes, but they also involve intense competition, expensive airport operations, and established relationships between major airlines and corporate customers.

Entering these markets is not automatically attractive simply because passenger demand is substantial. Major airlines, including American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and United Airlines, have extensive networks, established frequent-flyer programs, and substantial connecting traffic. Competing directly against these advantages requires more than inexpensive tickets.

A smaller carrier must also generate sufficient demand, maintain attractive schedules, and withstand the pricing pressure that established competitors can apply when defending important markets. Breeze Airways' operating model is better suited to identifying gaps between cities where passengers currently face inconvenient connections or lengthy surface journeys.

These routes can offer a meaningful convenience advantage without requiring the airline to build a massive operation at a major hub. Smaller airports may also provide more manageable operating environments, helping the carrier concentrate on delivering its intended passenger experience. There is also a financial consideration.

Specifically, operating frequent services on heavily contested trunk routes requires considerable aircraft capacity and consistent passenger demand throughout the week. Breeze Airways can instead introduce selected routes with limited weekly frequencies, observe booking patterns, and adjust its capacity accordingly. This approach does not eliminate commercial risk, but it offers greater flexibility than immediately committing significant resources to an established competitive corridor.

By focusing on city pairs largely ignored by other airlines, Breeze's network serves markets with limited competition and relatively stable demand.

Aircraft selection is another important part of understanding Breeze Airways' approach. Its Airbus A220-300 fleet provides a combination of operating efficiency, passenger capacity, and range that supports the airline's preference for connecting smaller markets with popular leisure destinations. The aircraft is particularly useful for an airline seeking to operate routes that might not justify larger narrowbody aircraft.

The A220-300 also gives Breeze the flexibility to serve domestic and international destinations from its existing network. Its capabilities support services from regional airports as well as longer leisure connections, allowing the airline to pursue opportunities without relying on a single aircraft type for substantially different operating requirements.

This flexibility is particularly relevant as its network continues expanding. The latest data from ch-aviation shows that Breeze Airways currently has 66 Airbus A220s in its fleet, making it the third-largest operator of the type, as detailed below. Breeze Airways expects to serve approximately 95 cities and operate more than 300 routes by mid-2027, representing a substantial expansion from its original network.

However, the number of destinations is only part of the story. The airline's ability to maintain profitable frequencies, manage fuel expenses, and generate consistent passenger demand will ultimately matter more than how quickly its route map grows. The experience of Spirit Airlines provides an important reminder that low fares and substantial passenger numbers cannot guarantee financial sustainability.

Fuel prices, aircraft utilization, competitive pressure, and operating costs all influence whether a route can generate sufficient returns. Breeze Airways appears to be approaching the opportunities left behind with that lesson in mind, selecting markets where nonstop leisure demand, manageable competition, and its A220-300 fleet can work together economically.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6073. The Fight Over Obamacare’s Phantom Enrollees

The Trump administration is right to take on the problem of improper enrollment.

Administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Dr. Mehmet Oz speaks during a press conference on anti-fraud initiatives at the White House campus in Washington, D.C., September 22, 2026.

More than a dozen Democratic senators are criticizing the Trump administration’s efforts to address the problem of phantom enrollments in Obamacare. In a letter to insurers, the senators accuse the companies of “colluding” with the administration to terminate coverage for more than 760,000 enrollees. Their criticism gets insurers’ financial incentives backward and overlooks the extensive safeguards the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) employed before terminating these highly suspicious enrollments.

Insurers have little incentive to drop phantom enrollees. For years, insurers have been the biggest beneficiaries of the expanded Obamacare subsidies — reaping tens of billions of dollars in higher subsidies. By making millions of plans free to consumers, Democrats created powerful incentives for improper and phantom enrollment. Given these incentives, the administration was right to scrutinize suspicious enrollments.

Brian Blase is the president of the Paragon Health Institute. He was special assistant to the president for economic policy at the White House’s National Economic Council, 2017–19.

#6072. How To Redeem World Of Hyatt Points For Best Value, Maximize Award Chart

I write a lot about the value of hotel loyalty programs, and in this post, I’d like to talk about World of Hyatt. What are the best ways to redeem World of Hyatt points, how many points do you need for a free night redemption, how does the award chart work, etc.?

Let’s start by talking about the basics of redeeming World of Hyatt points — how much should you expect to pay for free nights, are there blackout dates, how much are World of Hyatt points worth, etc.?

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each. There’s no science to that, but rather I think that’s a fair, conservative valuation for what the points are worth. In other words, I won’t redeem points for a hotel stay with Hyatt unless I’m getting well over 1.4 cents of value per point (and that has to factor in the points I’m forgoing by redeeming rather than paying cash, etc.).

It’s important to come up with a points valuation for yourself (it can be different than mine), so that you can decide whether to pay cash or redeem points for a hotel stay.

I have lowered this valuation a little recently, in light of the World of Hyatt award chart devaluation we’ve seen, where Hyatt has gone from three tiers of pricing within each category to five.

World of Hyatt has no blackout dates, which is to say that if a standard room is available for sale with cash, it can also be booked with points.

Now, the important thing to keep in mind is that some hotels have a very small pool of “standard” rooms, and a vast majority of rooms at a hotel may be considered “premium.” If a hotel has 150 rooms, it’s possible that only 10 rooms are considered “standard,” so that’s the major issue you’ll run into when redeeming points at some properties.

Unfortunately in the hotel industry overall, we’ve seen a reduction in the number of standard rooms at many properties that are popular for redemptions, which is essentially a way for hotels to create indirect capacity controls.

Keep in mind that Hyatt has a great points availability calendar, which at least makes it easy to find the nights that are available with points, for those properties that are challenging.

Hopefully this isn’t an issue anyone runs into, but just keep in mind the World of Hyatt points expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. Any points earning or redemption activity resets the expiration of your points by a further 24 months.

Unlike Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt continues to publish award charts for award redemptions (the exception is Mr & Mrs Smith properties, which I’ll talk more about in a bit).

The catch is that at this point, World of Hyatt has five tiers of award pricing for standard room redemptions — Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper, and Top — and the variance within each category is huge. So while I appreciate that there’s not technically dynamic pricing, when a Category 1 hotel can cost 3,000 or 9,000 points, and a Category 8 hotel can cost 35,000 or 75,000 points, you’re not exactly getting a lot of assurance.

The standard award chart applies at a vast majority of properties globally, including most Hyatt branded properties. There are eight categories of hotels, and 40 different pricing tiers, given the five pricing bands within each tier. Pricing ranges from 3,000 points for a Category 1 property during the “Lowest” period, and 75,000 points for a Category 8 property during the “Top” period.

Next, World of Hyatt has an all-inclusive award chart, which applies to an ever-growing number of properties across Hyatt’s all-inclusive brands. Hotels fall into one of six categories, with the similar five bands of pricing, all based on double occupancy. Pricing ranges from 12,000 points for a Category A property during the “Lowest” period, to 85,000 points for a Category F property during the “Top” period.

Lastly, World of Hyatt has an award chart for Miraval properties, which are Hyatt’s super-luxurious wellness resorts. Pricing varies based on single or double occupancy, and then there’s also the five bands of pricing.

Note that unlike Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt doesn’t offer a fifth night free on award redemptions. So you’ll pay the points that correspond to the number of nights you’re staying.

World of Hyatt is the only major hotel loyalty program that lets you efficiently redeem your points for suites. This can come in the form of free night redemptions, or in the form of an upgrade award. Unlike with standard room availability, there are capacity controls on suite redemptions, so these won’t always be available just because a suite is for sale.

You can find the standard suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, the premium for a standard suite can range from around 20% to 100%, so there’s quite a bit of variance here. In many situations this could represent a good deal. Of course the ways that hotels choose to designate suites differs by property, so in some cases this can represent a huge upgrade, while in other cases it doesn’t.

You can find the premium suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, there’s also quite a bit of variance here in terms of how much of a premium you’re paying.

World of Hyatt also lets you upgrade to club rooms, suites, and premium suites, using points. You can find the chart for that below, though note that this is only possible when booking a fully paid stay at the flexible rate directly with Hyatt. This requires a rate code, so it’s not even combinable with Hyatt Privé rates.

There are also more capacity controls here than you’d have if redeeming Hyatt suite upgrade awards, which are issued through the Milestone Rewards program.

World of Hyatt offers Points + Cash awards, whereby you can book a stay at a hotel using a combination of points and cash. This might sound appealing to those who want to reduce the cash cost of a stay using points, or those who don’t have quite enough points for a stay.

Points + Cash redemptions follow an award chart. The way this works, you can redeem 50% of the standard points required, plus you’ll receive around 50% off the cash component of a stay, in comparison to the flexible rate.

It’s always worth taking a look at this, though more often than not I don’t find this to be as good of a deal as just outright redeeming points. Also note that Points + Cash redemptions have capacity controls, unlike free night redemptions.

Hyatt acquired luxury travel company Mr & Mrs Smith, and you’ll find that many Mr & Mrs Smith properties are bookable through Hyatt channels. This is an opportunity to earn and redeem Hyatt points for stays at all kinds of independent luxury properties that you’d not otherwise have access to with a major loyalty program.

While the opportunity to earn points is potentially exciting, the catch is that points redemptions largely represent a bad value. Award pricing is fully dynamic, and you’ll find that in many cases, points only get you around a cent each toward a stay. That’s significantly less than I value them, so I wouldn’t recommend redeeming that way.

While I wouldn’t say it’s my favorite use of points, World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, whereby you can redeem points toward a folio credit that can be applied to on-property dining and spa awards. With this, you’ll get anywhere from 1.0 to 1.54 cents of value per point.

While there are some restrictions to be aware of, this is still something that has the potential to be useful for those with lots of points, who are looking to splurge on incidentals during a stay.

With the Milestone Rewards program, World of Hyatt members can earn Guest of Honor certificates. This extends World of Hyatt Globalist status benefits over the course of a stay, for up to seven nights. These can be applied to any eligible revenue stay or points stay, and offer lots of value.

Those booked with a Guest of Honor certificate receive the standard Globalist perks, including complimentary breakfast, suite upgrades subject to availability, and much more. This is one of my favorite loyalty perks out there.

World of Hyatt has a generous policy when it comes to letting members transfer or combine points between accounts. World of Hyatt members can transfer points between accounts at a 1:1 ratio.

Members can transfer a minimum of 1,000 points, and can transfer in increments of 500 points above that. Members can transfer up to 525,000 points per transaction, and may transfer or receive up to that many points across accounts per calendar year. World of Hyatt accounts must be at least 60 days old in order to send or receive points.

World of Hyatt members are also limited to making one free points transfer every calendar month, and six free points transfers every calendar year. Transfers generally happen within 24 hours, but in rare cases could require additional review, and could take up to 10 business days.

This can be a great way to combine points in order to have enough for a particular redemption, or even to transfer points in order to make a booking out of an elite member’s account, or using a Guest of Honor award.

Nowadays many properties charge resort fees or destination fees, which are essentially a money-grab. All World of Hyatt members don’t have to pay these when redeeming points, which can add significant value. Furthermore, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay these even on revenue stays.

As a further perk, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay for parking on award stays (however, non-Globalist members do have to pay for parking).

World of Hyatt has three elite tiers — Discoverist (10 elite nights), Explorist (30 elite nights), and Globalist (60 elite nights). While status isn’t quite as easy to earn as with some other hotel groups, there are still some opportunities to earn status with credit cards. World of Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards include the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more). You can earn elite qualifying nights and status with these cards:

Even if you’re not a Hyatt loyalist, the great news is that earning World of Hyatt points is pretty easy. However, the ratios aren’t as consistently good as in the past.

In addition to being able to earn World of Hyatt points with the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you can also transfer points from both Bilt Rewards and Chase Ultimate Rewards:

On top of that, World of Hyatt frequently has promotions for purchasing points. The reason this matters is because there are lots of situations where you could get outsized value simply by buying points from Hyatt and then immediately redeeming them for a hotel stay.

With the above basics out of the way about redeeming World of Hyatt points, how do you get the most value with your points? Let me share my approach to redeeming Hyatt points.

As a Hyatt Globalist member, I exclusively redeem my points for free night award redemptions in standard rooms. While I think there can be value in redeeming points for standard or premium suites, my general strategy is to redeem for standard rooms, and then use suite upgrade awards to confirm suites.

The reality is that I get huge value with my World of Hyatt points throughout the award chart, and not just at aspirational properties. Generally I decide to redeem points if I’m getting at least two cents of value per World of Hyatt point. There are several things I factor into that, though. When deciding whether to redeem points:

With World of Hyatt charging such vastly different amounts across the five bands of pricing, in some cases you’ll get the most value per point when redeeming during an off-peak period, while in other cases you’ll get the most value when redeeming during a peak period. You of course always want to compare the cash rates to the points redemption rates.

With a little bit of effort, I have no issues redeeming a vast majority of my Hyatt points for well over two cents each, in comparison to the cash cost.

Ultimately the reason I collect airline miles and hotel points is for aspirational redemptions. I try to redeem for things that I typically wouldn’t pay for in cash, where I’m getting outsized value.

So just as airline miles are best redeemed for first & business class travel, hotel points are often best redeemed for five-star properties that would cost a lot in cash. So the main reason I earn Hyatt points is to be able to redeem at properties belonging to brands like Alila and Park Hyatt. From Alila Napa Valley, to Alila Ventana Big Sur, to Alila Jabal Akhdar, to Park Hyatt Kyoto, to Park Hyatt Milan, to Park Hyatt Paris, I’ve had some amazing award redemptions over the years.

World of Hyatt is my all-around favorite hotel loyalty program. I greatly value the elite perks I receive as a Globalist member, and I also consistently get great value with my points, especially for aspirational properties. I also love how World of Hyatt points can efficiently be transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, providing an easy pathway to racking up this currency.

Personally my favorite use of World of Hyatt points is for stays at Hyatt’s top luxury hotels, where you’ll almost consistently get the best value, assuming you can find award availability. However, I’ve gotten great value at lower end properties as well.

Now, in fairness, the value of Hyatt points is definitely decreasing a bit at the moment, and on top of that, the reduced transfer ratio from other currencies is frustrating, and definitely eats into the value a bit. That being said, that’s true of the industry at large, as we’ve also seen endless devaluations with Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy. I do still get the most value with Hyatt.

What has your experience been with redeeming World of Hyatt points?

Membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

When it comes to most frequent flyer and hotel loyalty programs, my philosophy is simple, If it gets too complicated, just walk away. People need to put a value on their time. If you're spending hours trying to figure out how to maximize a benefit, at some point it simply isn't worth it. The complexity often works in favor of the programs, not the customer. At the end of the day, when you factor in the time, effort and frustration, you end up losing more than you gain. So I've gone back to the good old fashioned approach of simply finding the best highly rated property at my destination, with attributes that matter to me, regardless of loyalty program. It takes far less time, and I'm discovering and enjoying some wonderful hotels that I would never even have considered in the past. It's been a refreshing change. When loyalty is no longer rewarded, it pays to stop being loyal.

Flight cancellations are on the rise in 2026. Since Jan. 1, U.S. carriers have canceled roughly 2% of all flights, according to FlightAware, putting this year on pace for the highest cancellation rate since 2022. And delays remain common: About one in four departures nationwide was delayed between Memorial Day and Labor Day, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

While most flights leave on time, delays and cancellations remain a reality of air travel — whether due to bad weather, mechanical issues, scheduling problems or other unforeseen circumstances, including the recent nationwide ground stop.

In case you experience flight delays or cancellations, here are tips on how to decrease your chances of getting stuck and increase your odds of arriving at your destination as quickly as possible. Plus, check out our advice on how to potentially get reimbursed for unexpected expenses due to your flight delay or cancellation, depending on the reason that caused the delay.

In this era of full flights and easily available information, don’t wait for the airline to tell you there is a problem. You can keep an eye on general flight trends across the country by using FlightAware, which gives you a good overview of how a day in the sky looks.

FlightAware’s “MiseryMap” focuses on delays. In the 24 hours before travel, you can manually check the status of your flight on your airline’s website. If possible, be sure to check the plane's origin. Even if the conditions are clear where you are, there’s a good chance your plane won’t get to you on time if it’s sitting in a snowstorm somewhere else.

It’s also a good idea to sign up for flight notifications from your airline. Here are details on how to opt in to that process with American Airlines and United Airlines.

You can also get flight status updates sent directly from FlightAware. TPG staffers are also fond of the Flighty app, which offers a reliable "Where's My Plane?" feature to track your plane starting 25 hours before your flight.

Be sure to download your airline’s app on your phone, too. Many airlines will show you where your incoming plane is currently. In fact, your airline’s app often has more up-to-date flight departure information than what’s on the departure and arrival boards at the airport.

This can be a tricky one. If your flight is still listed as “on time” in the app, leave for the airport according to the original schedule.

Even if your flight shows as delayed in the app, that status is subject to change. So, in most cases, it’s best to be at the airport ready to go at the originally scheduled time. We’ve certainly heard stories of flights being delayed only to depart sooner than expected, leaving some passengers behind.

Sometimes, you’ll receive confirmation well in advance, letting you know if your flight will be significantly delayed. Say you are at an airport that isn’t a hub for the airline you are flying (meaning there's less chance of spare planes and crew), and the plane that's supposed to operate your flight is nowhere close to arriving at the airport. In that case, it's likely that your posted delay will be a real delay. However, it’s still safer to be at the airport, just in case.

Bad weather can sometimes cause a temporary ground stop at the airport. As soon as the weather improves and the stop lifts, airlines will try to get their flights off the ground ASAP. So, it’s best to be close by should things change on short notice.

Related: 3 things to do if your flight is delayed

It’s important to know your rights as an airline passenger, which have been changed in recent years.

For instance, if your flight is canceled or significantly delayed and you choose not to travel, you’re entitled to a refund, no matter the reason for the disruption. According to current rules from the U.S. Department of Transportation, passengers on domestic flights that are significantly changed, including arriving three or more hours late, and international flights arriving six or more hours late are entitled to automatic refunds if they choose not to travel and don't accept alternative transportation or travel credits. Those refunds must be issued within seven days for credit card purchases and 20 days for cash payments.

However, if you get stranded overnight, you may also be able to recoup costs for extra meals, hotel nights and ground transportation, depending on the reason for the delay. A widespread FAA ground stop, for example, is unlikely to be a covered reason.

You’ll find these and other passenger rights guarantees on flightrights.gov, the DOT’s dashboard.

On that website, you’ll find a rundown of what airlines guarantee in the event of “controllable” delays and cancellations — disruptions within an airline’s control. Keep in mind that these controllable situations typically exclude weather-related problems.

When looking at the dashboard, you’ll quickly see that some airlines promise to do more than others regarding overnight hotel stays, ground transportation, credit vouchers and rebooking on partners. Give that list a look not only when you’re deciding which airline to book with but also in the event of a long, controllable delay or cancellation. This way, you’ll know what the airline has promised to do in those situations. You can file a complaint with the DOT if the airline doesn’t hold up its end of the bargain.

Monitor weather patterns a few days before your flight to see if any major systems are anticipated. It’s vital to check the forecast the night before and on the day of travel to see how any issues could affect your departure and arrival airports.

Again, be sure to opt in to receive updates on your flight’s status. If you know bad weather is coming later in the day, ask for an earlier flight if you can. Alternatively, leaving the night before the weather arrives is a good idea if you want to minimize the risk of delays.

Many airlines will issue travel advisories during (and ahead of) severe weather, such as blizzards, ice storms or even heavy thunderstorms. These advisories allow travelers to make changes even when flying on a restrictive ticket that typically can’t be altered — like some basic economy fares. In some cases, the airline may even proactively change your flight.

If you know bad weather is on the horizon, visit your airline’s website and look for an advisory notice or call the airline to discuss options. If an airline gets ahead of weather issues, you may be able to reschedule your flight by a few days in either direction with no fees. Additionally, you can try asking for a nonstop flight if the weather jeopardizes your connecting flight.

However, if the airline hasn’t issued its own advisory, you might need to pay out of pocket for any fare differences if you really want to be proactive in changing plans.

Standing in a long line at the airport or waiting on hold by phone is usually no longer the most efficient (or most enjoyable) way to rebook when a flight is canceled or delayed.

Most major airlines will allow you to rebook yourself using a mobile app. You may be able to rebook for a new time or even to a new nearby origin or destination city. For that reason, the airline app should probably be your first stop when you learn of a hiccup in your travel plans.

United will even let you standby for up to three flights if something happens to your originally scheduled flight, while maintaining your original seat.

That said, there are times when automated rebooking systems are not your best option. Sometimes, the only automated option is a red-eye flight or a flight several days later that will head to your destination. That’s especially true when many flights are full.

If you can’t locate what you need on the app, find an airline employee who can work the ticketing desk. Check their uniforms and name tags to ensure you get a ticket agent, versus a baggage handler or a similarly outsourced contractor who is less likely to be able to help.

If the U.S. call center has long hold times (which can happen during widespread issues), you can try dialing an international number for faster service. You can often find those numbers on the airline’s website. You might also find success reaching out to an airline on the social platform X or other social media channels when customer service lines are busy.

For example, when the first leg of an American Airlines flight from New York to Arkansas, scheduled just before Christmas, was delayed, TPG Managing Editor Madison Blancaflor missed her connection. She contacted American Airlines on X to help ensure she was rebooked on the earliest possible flight. She still had to endure a long layover in Charlotte, but it was better (and less stressful) than rushing to the customer service desk to try to rebook upon arrival.

Additionally, some airlines offer live online chat or text options that can be quicker than calling.

If there are no reasonable booking options left with your carrier, ask whether there are options available on another airline. If the delay is weather-related and you are on a basic economy ticket or are flying on a low-cost carrier, there might not be other airline options at your fingertips. Still, it’s worth asking — and, if possible, presenting options you have researched yourself.

Related: Don’t wait on hold: Here’s how to reach airline customer service quickly

If you have airline lounge access at a United Club, a Delta Sky Club or something similar, you can head there for help from experienced agents with potentially shorter lines. Use it as a spot to gather your thoughts, charge your phone and make level-headed decisions. The agents there might be able to help you change or track your flight, as there are usually agents with that knowledge and ability in the airline lounges.

In third-party lounges, such as an American Express Centurion Lounge, you won’t be able to get that type of airline-specific assistance, but you’ll probably be in a better spot to wait out the storm than in a crowded terminal.

Related: Best credit cards for airport lounge access

Sometimes, if you really need to get home, you may need to do the work and pay for a new flight yourself.

In some of our prior experiences, the airlines we originally booked with couldn't get us home within 24 hours of our flights being canceled. In cases like these, you may be able to book a nonstop flight with at least one last seat available on another carrier.

Keep in mind, though, that rebooking yourself is typically not covered by any insurance provider or carrier. Still, you should be able to get a refund for your original ticket, which will at least offset some of the pain of a new one. The extra work may be worth it to control your own destiny and avoid being stuck as options narrow.

Your credit card’s built-in trip delay or trip cancellation coverage can help with many unexpected expenses in the face of delays and cancellations, but a brand-new flight home isn’t likely to be one of them. Still, in some cases, it may be the only way home for a while, so you’ll have to weigh the pros and cons.

Fortunately, many airlines now allow you to cancel main cabin tickets and, at the very least, get airline trip credit; you can use this credit to book a future flight — even if you are being proactive to try and avoid possible delays and, ultimately, your originally scheduled flight does not experience a delay. (This does not necessarily apply to basic economy fares or low-cost carriers' flights.)

Related: Should you get travel insurance if you have credit card protection?

While thinking through what to do in case of a flight delay or cancellation, consider your options at airport hotels; they can fill up during major delays and cancellations. Sometimes, it is best to call it a day, get some rest and try again in the morning.

Airport hotels are generally pretty affordable on points, but cash rates can skyrocket when demand surges. Accommodations are typically covered by trip delay protection in the event of cancellations or very long delays via cards like the (see rates and fees) and .*

*Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Related: Why my favorite use of Hyatt points is a Category 1 airport hotel

If you know in advance that your flight will be canceled or delayed, heading to the airport early could score you a same-day standby flight that gets you to your destination on time.

For example, one TPG staffer used this strategy to avoid getting stuck overnight when a hiccup with his flight from Austin to New York would have caused him to miss a connection in Dallas. He arrived at the airport a bit early and was placed on the standby list for an earlier flight connecting to a different city.

Getting on the standby list isn’t foolproof, especially if the earlier flight is almost full. This is a case where having elite status can help since you’ll have priority over non-elite travelers. Additionally, some airlines charge non-elite travelers a fee to be added to the standby list for an earlier flight.

Related: The best credit cards to reach elite status

The hard truth is that in the event of airline delays and cancellations caused by weather, the airline itself is not going to help you out with the extra expenses you incur due to the change in plans, since the weather is outside its control. Travel insurance may have your back if you purchased it, but beyond that, the credit card you booked your flight with may also be able to reimburse you for unexpected expenses due to your flight delay or cancellation — even if it was caused by weather.

Many rewards credit cards confer valuable travel protections when you have a delayed or canceled flight (if you used one of them to book your flight). Below are just a few examples of cards that provide some built-in coverage:

*Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Related: Best credit cards with travel insurance

To highlight how valuable this can be, a couple of years ago, one TPG staffer's flights home from Colorado during the busy winter holiday season were canceled due to a snowstorm.

She was faced with an unexpected $1,100-per-night hotel stay during peak season in a pricey ski town, based on what was still available at the last minute. Ultimately, her eligible Chase card covered not only the $1,100 unexpected hotel stay but also the unexpected car service and meals during the delay. Within 26 days of the unexpected cancellation and delay, she had a check for $1,401.74 in her hand, thanks to using the right credit card to book the flight.

Unfortunately, some situations are not covered by the built-in trip delay and trip cancellation protections that commonly come with some rewards credit cards, but it never hurts to save receipts and try.

Last but not least, we recommend being decisive when making travel decisions amid delays or cancellations.

The longer you wait to switch flights or book a hotel, the greater the chances you’ll be at the mercy of whatever dwindling options are left as hundreds (or thousands) of other passengers rebook their plans.

Most of the time, your flight will get you where you need to be, close to when you want to be there. Still, flight delays and cancellations are a reality of air travel. If your flight is delayed by an hour or two, there’s not usually much to do other than be patient. However, when facing a long delay or cancellation, it’s good to have a plan to reduce the odds of getting stuck.

Given the common theme of full flights these days, acting quickly, researching options and making a speedy decision will put you ahead of the pack.

#6070. Former Hyatt Renovation Halted After Inspectors Find Families Living Inside—And Rooms Chained From The Outside

Inspectors entered the closed former Hyatt Regency Dearborn and found families living upstairs. Hotel room doors on the property were chained and padlocked from the outside. Two days later, police searched. The families were gone. Officers closed the case after about a two hour search. On September 22, inspectors found, On the 12th floor: Dozens of people, including young children, with groceries, suitcases, puppies and dog feces. On the 10th floor: Doors chained and padlocked from outside, apparently impossible to unlock from within. In a hallway: Packaging for a large machete (though no machete was seen). A project manager initially suggested a worker’s family was visiting for lunch. A guard said up to 100 people had lived there over the previous year, and his bosses told him to ignore residents. The hotel’s owner denied knowing families were living there. Police said the locked rooms secured workers’ equipment and their search found no criminal activity, such as human trafficking. This is the Edward Hotel and Convention Center which once had a revolving restaurant and a monorail connection to Fairlane Town Center. It left Hyatt in 2012, and the city shut it down in 2018. The property was acquired in 2016 for $20 million. That owner faced criminal charges in Canada that were ultimately withdrawn. It was sold in 2021 in a forfeiture sale for $18.25 million. The buyer defaulted on the mortgage and in 2024 it was auctioned by the sheriff for $9.85 million, but apparently an auction of the distressed note and sheriff’s deed ended at $5.925 million. According to Dearborn City Council materials from October 2024, Hyatt had expressed interest in returning if sufficient capital investment could be secured. This exterior photo is from September 2024, by Warren LeMay via Wikipedia. But Wait, It Gets Worse According to a local activist a supposed immigration agent had thrown someone to the floor and killed a dog by throwing it through glass. She later reached an injured woman inside, who told her: “I don’t know how to get out.” The activist also said workers reported wages withheld because employers supposedly used the money to bribe immigration agents and being told: “Look, we’re keeping ICE away from you. Now you have to work for free.” Immigration and Customs Enforcement denies conducting enforcement at the hotel. A Detroit councilwoman’s office says Mayor Abdullah Hammoud was alerted September 18, four days before the inspection. Reportedly police failed to review the hotel’s surveillance video before closing the investigation. The Hotel Was Supposed To Make A Comeback Dearborn has sunk subsidies into the hotel’s redevelopment plans. In December 2025, the city approved a 12-year property tax exemption and a 30-year brownfield plan for a redevelopment involving a $45 million rehabilitation, plus acquisition costs. The project would combine hotel rooms, apartments and convention space. In January, the mayor said the hotel would return as a Hilton, with a hoped-for opening by the end of 2026. Here’s a walk-through of the property from before the current state of affairs: I don’t think the former Hyatt Regency Dearborn is re-opening as a Hilton in 2026. It strikes me that the city isn’t adequately investigating issues at a redevelopment site that it’s subsidizing.
