#6069. How Delta Air Lines' Boston Expansion Became A Safer Bet Than Its Postponed Atlanta–Riyadh Launch

Delta Air Lines is taking two very different approaches to international growth in 2027. At Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), it is adding seasonal European destinations and increasing frequencies on established routes, including daily service to Reykjavík, four weekly flights to Venice, and daily service between Boston and Milan. The airline is also launching a daily Austin–Paris link and a new Detroit–Athens connection. In Atlanta, however, Delta has postponed its planned launch to Riyadh until March 2027 after deadly attacks near King Khalid International Airport (RUH) raised security concerns. The contrast shows why the airline’s near-term network strategy is more straightforward in Europe than in the Middle East.

The Boston expansion builds on an existing hub with substantial local demand, established transatlantic traffic, and partner connections across Europe. Riyadh offers a potentially valuable new market, particularly as Saudi Arabia invests in tourism and international business, but the route depends on a security environment that Delta cannot control. The airline is therefore pursuing growth where demand and operating conditions are more predictable while waiting for a safer opportunity to introduce a strategically significant long-haul service.

Delta’s Boston expansion for summer 2027 adds Reykjavík and Venice, while increasing Boston–Milan to daily service. Reykjavík begins April 12 and operates daily through October 30 using Boeing 757-200 aircraft. Venice starts May 7 with four weekly flights on Airbus A330-300s, while Milan’s frequency increase gives passengers more options on a route Delta already serves. With Reykjavík included, the airline says Boston will have 14 unique long-haul destinations during the peak summer season and 16 international destinations overall.

The growth is supported by Boston’s existing scale. Delta carried 5.6 million passengers from Logan in 2025, approximately 200,000 more than its closest competitor, and says it has increased seat capacity there by 50% since 2019. The airline averages around 170 daily departures from the airport and has invested in facilities such as its Delta One lounge. These figures indicate that the new international routes are being added to a substantial operation rather than relying on a newly established market.

Delta’s position also gives it access to a mix of local business and leisure travelers, as well as passengers connecting from other US cities. Its Boston network is particularly useful for transatlantic flying because the city is geographically closer to Europe than many other major US gateways.

Delta’s return to Boston–Reykjavík comes after low-cost carrier Play ceased operations in September 2025. Play had offered a lower-cost option between the cities, and its departure left an opening for another airline to attract travelers seeking nonstop access to Iceland. Delta’s schedule is designed around the spring-to-autumn travel season, when demand for Iceland’s landscapes, outdoor activities, and connecting travel is strongest.

However, Boston is not an unserved market. Icelandair continues to operate between Boston and Reykjavík, meaning Delta will join an existing competitive route rather than create a monopoly. The Points Guy noted that the airline also previously flew the route in 2021, before discontinuing it later that year. Its 2027 return therefore represents a renewed attempt to establish a sustainable presence, now supported by a larger Boston operation and a broader range of connecting itineraries.

The aircraft choice reflects the market’s scale and the route’s relatively short transatlantic distance. Delta’s 757-200 offers Delta Premium Select, Comfort, and Main cabins, but no Delta One lie-flat business-class product. That is a more limited premium proposition than the A330-300 assigned to Venice, which includes Delta One. The configuration suggests Delta is matching capacity and product to a route where leisure demand is likely to be significant, rather than deploying its most premium aircraft.

They're from three hubs and focus cities. Find out more here!

The 2027 expansion is not confined to Logan. Delta plans to launch daily Austin–Paris service on March 27 using an Airbus A330-900neo, giving Austin its first nonstop connection to the French capital. The route also creates one-stop access to nearly 70 destinations across Europe, India, and Africa through the airline’s joint venture with Air France-KLM. This is a broader network proposition than simply serving local demand between Texas and France.

Detroit–Athens will begin June 8 and operate three times weekly through October 28 on an Airbus A330-200. Athens will become Delta’s 12th unique long-haul destination from Detroit during the peak summer season. The frequency is more cautious than Austin–Paris, reflecting a seasonal leisure market and a route that does not need daily capacity in its first year. Meanwhile, Boston–Venice will use a widebody with Delta One and Premium Select, indicating a higher premium-cabin emphasis than Reykjavík.

These additions demonstrate Delta’s preference for measured growth in markets where it already has a hub, connecting feed, or established transatlantic presence. The airline is also extending some existing European services into shoulder seasons and increasing frequencies where demand supports it. Rather than relying on one large international launch, Delta is distributing capacity across several gateways and matching aircraft size to anticipated demand.

Delta had planned to launch nonstop Atlanta–Riyadh service on October 23, 2026, marking its first direct connection to Saudi Arabia. The route was designed to operate three times weekly on an A350-900, with daily flights during its opening week. Through Atlanta, passengers from across Delta’s domestic network would have gained access to the Saudi capital, while the airline would have established a direct link to a market central to the kingdom’s economic diversification plans.

The launch was postponed to March 2027 after missile and drone attacks struck the Riyadh area, including King Khalid International Airport. The attacks reportedly killed at least 13 people and prompted airlines to reconsider operations in the region. Delta said it was monitoring developments in coordination with government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, and emphasized that customer and employee safety guided the decision.

Unlike the Boston additions, the obstacle is not simply whether enough passengers will buy tickets. Airlines must assess airspace restrictions, airport security, insurance exposure, crew safety, and the reliability of onward operations. The FAA issued a caution notice for US operators flying to or over Saudi Arabia through December 10, 2026, citing threats associated with military activity and navigation-system interference. Reuters reported that other airlines also adjusted Saudi and regional schedules after the attacks.

The routes are spread across Europe, the Caribbean, Mexico and Central America, South America, and Oceania.

Delta’s latest financial results help explain why the airline is investing in routes with different cabin and aircraft profiles. In the third quarter of 2026, ticket revenue from premium products reached $6.82 billion, narrowly exceeding the $6.80 billion generated by main-cabin tickets. Premium revenue rose 18% year over year, compared with 12% growth in main-cabin ticket revenue. Across the first nine months of 2026, premium ticket revenue also edged above main-cabin revenue, at $19.10 billion versus $19.068 billion.

These figures cover Delta’s overall ticket sales, not international routes alone, but they show why the airline is emphasizing premium seating across its network. Boston–Venice and Austin–Paris offer Delta One, while Detroit–Athens provides a full long-haul cabin mix. Reykjavík, by contrast, uses a 757 without lie-flat business class, keeping a premium-economy option while avoiding a more expensive widebody deployment. Delta can therefore pursue several customer segments without assigning identical capacity to every route.

The fleet strategy also matters. Delta is introducing newer widebodies, including the A330-900neo and A350 family, while continuing to use older aircraft such as the 757 where their economics and capacity remain appropriate. Its September-quarter financial release documents the premium revenue trend. The airline’s challenge is to convert that willingness to pay for upgraded cabins into sustained returns without adding more capacity than each market can support.

Delta’s Boston expansion is the safer near-term investment because it builds on an established operation, benefits from existing transatlantic demand, and uses seasonal schedules to manage capacity. The Riyadh route has greater geopolitical exposure, but postponement does not necessarily undermine its long-term commercial rationale. Saudi Arabia’s investment in tourism, business, and international connectivity could still create demand for a nonstop US service once operating conditions become more predictable.

The next test will be whether Delta can turn its Boston additions into durable routes beyond their opening seasons. The Reykjavík route faces direct competition from Icelandair, while Venice and Milan will need to sustain premium and leisure demand across a concentrated summer market. If those services perform well, Delta may have room to add frequencies or extend schedules. For Riyadh, the March 2027 target should be treated as a reassessment point rather than a guarantee. The airline’s ability to launch will depend on security conditions, regulatory guidance, and confidence among its partners. Together, the two strategies show Delta pursuing growth without treating every attractive destination as ready for immediate service.

#6068. FAA Issues Nationwide Ground Stop, Shuts Down The Skies: What’s Going On?

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop, which is pretty unprecedented. Admittedly we’ve had our fair share of air traffic control issues in the United States over the years. But this is really on a different level, unlike anything we’ve seen since 9/11, in terms of operational disruptions. I guess it’s fitting that this is happening on Friday the 13th.

At 3:54PM ET today (Friday, November 13, 2026), the FAA issued a ground stop for flights across the country, as pilots received the following message:

DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY. ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED. ALL DEPARTING TRAFFIC SHOULD REMAIN GROUND STOPPED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. INBOUND INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS WILL BE MANAGED ON A CASE BY CASE BASIS.

As of now, the ground stop is through 11:30PM ET, though it’s possible that it’s lifted before then. That timeline clearly reflects the extent to which the current situation is a complete mess, and this won’t be an easy fix.

As usual, JonNYC was among the first to break the news, and he even reported on this before the official ground stop was issued, when airports in the Northeast started having issues, prior to this going nationwide.

Kind of major, started at approx 3:15pmBoston Center, New York Center, Chicago Center, New York Approach have all lost numerous frequencies. All facilities are in ATC Alert. Some sectors in New York Center are unable any traffic currently. Numerous— I mean NUMEROUS frequencies…

“All airspace is currently being sterilized and centers are preparing for ATC Zero operations. Airborne’s should NOT be majorly effected— i.e, at least for now, this is not a “9/11 type of event” where airbornes are being forced to land at the closest airport available. All…

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed this development a while later, sharing that there were “communication issues impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” and he stated that “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.

As of now, there’s no timeline for this ground stop ending. To my knowledge, I believe this is now the most significant ground stop we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years (since 9/11).

If you’re flying this weekend, expect that things will be a mess. To those flying right now, good luck. Ford is on a flight that was supposed to depart at 3:59PM, so suffice it to say that he had some pretty bad luck here, as they pushed back, and then this happened. I hope not too many others are in the same situation.

There’s a major issue when you have flights landing but flights can’t depart, since you have way more planes than gates. So get ready to be patient if you’re onboard a flight, given the complicated logistics.

What could explain an air traffic outage of this scale? As of now, all we can do is speculate, though there are a few interesting things to point out.

First, it remains to be seen if this is related, but the FAA reportedly began its rollout of the new AI-powered air traffic management tool this week, known as SMART (which stands for “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories”).

Timing-wise, it seems like there’s a possibility this could be related. At the same time, you wouldn’t assume this leads to communication issues, which is what seems to be going on here. So it’s worth pointing out the timing, but we have no reason to believe the two things are related.

Yes the FAA began its nationwide rollout of the SMART AI for ARTCCs to use this week. It’s not clear at this time if the rollout is related to this outage, but if it’s a rolling communications issue, it’s much more likely it’s within already established equipment pilots-ATC use https://t.co/PXqSFdOA1q

One can’t help but wonder if a cyber attack might be to blame. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin insists that there are no indications of this being a cyber attack. However, if they’re still investigating the cause, it seems hard to rule anything out.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the agency had no indications of outages being tied to a cyberattack or potential terror threat, adding that the nationwide ground stop was “just a telecommunications outage." https://t.co/cb8xON9Xrz

If this is truly “just a telecommunications outage,” then that represents a major failure. How can air traffic control nationwide have that issue, rather than it just being isolated to one region? Are there no redundancies?

I don’t want to be a conspiracy theorist, but it sure feels to me like some very unusual things are going on. We just saw a huge Microsoft outage, and it has been a very strange week in general. Those two things can of course be completely unrelated, but you can’t help but point it out.

The FAA has grounded flights nationwide, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” For nearly two hours now, no flights have taken off in the United States, making this the largest outage since 9/11, to my knowledge.

It remains to be seen what the cause of this was, and whether this is a tech glitch, a cyber attack, or what. To those flying now (or this weekend), good luck… you’re going to need it!

What do you make of this strange ATC outage?

The gate agents do not know what is going on and won't answer questions. As I go to the Admirals Club I get a notice that I'm rebooked MIA/SAN, then SAN/PHX on AS and then the next day PHX/TUS. An agent at the Admirals Club indicates the status of the MIA/PHX flight is "Cancellation in Progress" and her 35 years she's never seen that status. But I'm rebooked. Then my original flight boards ten minutes later, not cancelled.

At MIA this morning. About 500 people standing in the rebooking line. Most of the 6AM-9AM flights seem to be cancelled. Assuming there's a crew my 11AM flight should go. The FL is pretty crowded.

Not sure if I misheard, but they let slip in the press conference exactly what the issue is. They connected new equipment to the old legacy and overwhelmed it. This was clearly an IT screw up whilst trying to incrementally upgrade the infrastructure. No more complex than that..... Or somebody plugged a laptop into the network and tried to pre-load GTA6 :-)

#6067. FAA Ground Stop: Every U.S. Airport Departure Halted As Air Traffic Control Communications Fail

The FAA has ordered departures stopped at every U.S. airport after a communications failure hit air traffic control centers across the country. Planes are being held on the ground as Friday afternoon travelers head into the weekend, with no announced time for flights to resume. Aircraft already in the air are being allowed to continue and land. There isn’t a general order to put every plane down at the nearest airport, like 9/11. The FAA says inbound international flights will be handled individually. The agency’s national ground stop advisory, issued at 3:54 p.m. Eastern on November 13: DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY. ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED. ALL DEPARTING TRAFFIC SHOULD REMAIN GROUND STOPPED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. INBOUND INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS WILL BE MANAGED ON A CASE BY CASE BASIS. The FAA’s status board lists the reason as “EQUIPMENT / OUTAGE.” This is in place “until further notice.” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirms a communications issue affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers, with FAA technicians investigating. These are the facilities that handle aircraft flying between airport areas. Secretary Sean Duffy’s statement — November 13, 2026 Aviation watchdog JonNYC reported widespread frequency failures before the nationwide order. His initial reports named Boston Center, New York Center, Chicago Center and New York Approach, with Boston Approach also experiencing problems. Some New York Center sectors reportedly couldn’t accept traffic. Then things spread. Chicago O’Hare and Midway were placed under ground stops before the nationwide halt. JonNYC’s reports of air traffic control frequency failures — November 13, 2026 A cockpit message shared by JonNYC tells crews: ATTENTION ALL CREWS- PER FAA GUIDANCE, ALL DEPARTURES ARE STOPPED NATIONWIDE. PLEASE STANDBY FOR FURTHER INFORMATION. UPDATE IN 15 https://t.co/XQvj5neLF2 — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 13, 2026 A Software Upgrade Issue Has Been Reported The New York Post reports that an unnamed source points to a possible software upgrade behind the disruption. The FAA hasn’t identified the failed system or what triggered the outage. However, controller and pilot message boards have several more specific accounts. In Reddit’s air traffic control forum, one commenter writes, “Allegedly all [backup emergency communications] sites on the east coast went out at the same time. They’re trying to figure out why.” Another commenter describes those backups as a third radio system, with separate radios, antennas, power and communications links. If the reported simultaneous failures are accurate, the behavior of those backups becomes a particularly important part of the investigation. In a second controller forum, a poster reports, “A lot of the frequencies and landlines in the Houston area started going hot on their own randomly over the past hour.” That adds a report of unexpected activity on both radio and telephone connections. In the flying forum, a commenter says the word they’re hearing is a communications problem between en route facilities. Others report hearing controllers announce the nationwide stop in Seattle and Redmond. JonNYC reports facilities preparing for “ATC Zero,” the status used when a facility can’t provide air traffic services. The FAA Has A Long History Of Technology Failures The closest recent comparison is the January 11, 2023 nationwide ground stop, when the system that provides safety notices to pilots failed. The FAA later traced that outage to contractors accidentally deleting files while trying to correct synchronization between the primary database and a backup. That was only the second nationwide ground stop, after 9/11. In March I covered an overheated circuit board that disrupted five Washington area airports. Transportation researcher Bob Poole reported that the board was part of a 25 year old voice switch, describing an FAA maintenance policy that allowed equipment to run until it failed, with fewer technicians and inadequate training to keep old systems going. The FAA’s own equipment photos illustrate what they’ve been working with: When I reviewed the administration’s air traffic control overhaul, the plan called for replacing 25,000 analog radios and 800 voice switches, along with moving thousands of sites off legacy telecommunications connections. My criticism was that the same organization that spent decades failing to deliver upgrades would be asked to deliver another one. The FAA regulates itself, both running the system and regulating its safety, while long term capital projects depend on annual congressional appropriations. Buying equipment doesn’t fix bad incentives or project management. Earlier today, the administration asked Congress for another $30.1 billion in aviation funding, including $10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization. Congress approved $12.5 billion last year. The new request also includes money for control towers and airport projects. They want taxpayers bailing out the system, rather than airlines and passengers. Even a quick repair won’t immediately put the airlines back on schedule. Planes held now will be late for their next flights, connecting passengers will miss departures, and crews can run out of permitted duty time. Then with planes out of position, disruptions continue. #6066. An Intellectual History of California’s Proposition 40

How a French academic research project and an elite public university nearly took down the Golden State’s venture capital economy with a wealth tax

People attend a rally in support of Proposition 40 and in opposition to Propositions 41 and 42 ahead of the midterm elections in Los Angeles, Calif., October 5, 2026.

On November 3, California voters narrowly rejected Proposition 40, a 5 percent tax on the net worth of the state’s billionaires. That outcome was not assured. In September, the measure led 52 percent to 46 percent in the Public Policy Institute of California’s survey of likely voters. Had it passed, the state that received 62 percent of all U.S. venture capital dollars in 2025 would have begun taxing founders on the paper value of companies, potentially driving them elsewhere.

The union that sponsored Proposition 40, SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, supplied the signatures and most of the campaign money. The idea came from an intellectual movement that began with the French economist Thomas Piketty, found an institutional home at the University of California, Berkeley, and received financing from the foundation of a Boston insurance executive.

People attend a rally in support of Proposition 40 and in opposition to Propositions 41 and 42 ahead of the midterm elections in Los Angeles, Calif., October 5, 2026.

#6065. Beond Airlines Suspends Flights For The Rest Of The Year: Better Luck In 2027?

Back in April 2026, we saw Beond Airlines suspend all scheduled operations for the summer, as the airline claimed it would resume flights as of late October. Then in October, it announced it would return in December. There’s now another update, as the airline has just announced that it will resume flights in January. That doesn’t sound so good, does it?

Beond Airlines launched operations in 2023, and it brands itself as the world’s first premium leisure airline. The company is headquartered in Dubai, but primarily operates flights to and from the Maldives. I reviewed the airline in 2024, and the onboard product was super pleasant. The airline currently has a fleet of two aircraft, including one A319 and one A321.

Anyway, in mid-April 2026, the company announced that it would suspend its scheduled operations for the entire summer. The airline promised to resume flights in October, for the winter season.

Then in October, the airline announced that it would suspend operations through November 30, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of December 1, 2026. Then just yesterday, the airline announced that it would suspend operations through December 31, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of January 1, 2027.

So I guess it remains to be seen if we actually see a resumption of flights as of January, or if the timeline will get pushed back again. If you can’t make all-business class flights to the Maldives work for the festive season, then prospects seem pretty grim.

Beond Airlines does have its “commitment” to customers when plans change, which includes the ability to change destinations or travel dates, receive a travel credit valid for 18 months, or to receive a full refund. A change of destinations or dates, plus a travel credit, isn’t worth a whole lot for an airline that keeps pushing back its relaunch.

Interestingly, but perhaps not surprisingly, earlier this year the airline deleted its customer promise webpage, which used to guarantee rebooking on another airline in business class in the event a flight is canceled, or else the airline would offer a free flight. That page is now gone, and there’s no mention of rebooking on another airline.

So the airline will “support you every step of the way,” unless you actually want to take the vacation you booked, in which case you’re out of luck (which is less than ideal, given that many Maldives properties have very strict cancelation policies).

While Beond Airlines’ business plan was questionable under the best of circumstances, the crisis of this year makes matters worse:

So I feel bad for Beond, and I’m not trying to do a “told you so, I was right” thing, because these are of course exceptional circumstances. The thing that made me suspicious about Beond for so long is that the airline would repeatedly make outlandish growth announcements, only to rarely follow through on them. That’s neither here nor there, though.

Keep in mind that since operations were initially suspended in April, we’ve seen some interesting developments:

My assumption is that Saudi Arabia is to some extent funding the Red Sea flights, given how the country is throwing money at any airline willing to fly there. However, one wonders if that’s enough money to make the math work, or if Beond even has the general funding right now to keep things operating.

It’s just all so strange, because it feels like half of the announcements from Beond Airlines are really targeting prospective investors, constantly promoting how it’s going to open new subsidiaries all over the world, launch dozens of new routes, etc.

As I said in April, I didn’t think it was a sure bet that flights would resume in October. Now we’ll see if flights actually resume in January. I wouldn’t count on it. One bizarre angle to this is that Beond has claimed it will launch flights to London Heathrow (LHR). Best I can tell, there’s no public record of the airline getting slots for that. And if the airline did have slots, it would be under a “use it or lose it” clause, so not operating the route would make the airline lose them.

In the spring of 2026, all-business class airline Beond suspended scheduled operations through October 2026. Then the airline announced it would resume flights in December 2026. Now the airline claims it will relaunch flights in January 2027. Over the summer, we learned that the airline wasn’t paying many staff for months, and the airline is now pivoting to operating service via Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Airport.

We’ll see what happens in the coming weeks. Presumably the Red Sea service gets the airline some money from the Saudi government, but it remains to be seen if that’s enough to keep this operation afloat.

It’s understandable that the current situation is really challenging, between the price of jet fuel, plus overall sentiment about the Middle East. However, I have to imagine the airline didn’t have great financial health before this whole mess started, and suspending flights in some ways only makes things even worse.

How do you see this playing out for Beond?

#6064. Emirates Pokes Fun At US’ Aviation Disaster From Ground Stop & Microsoft Outage

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Dubai-based Emirates has taken a poke at the US aviation disaster that unfolded this week, posting on its social media channels that 'the skies are always open'. The original post, which included a lighthearted nod to the Microsoft Outlook and cloud outage, was then followed up with a 'was it something we said?'

This comes as, on Friday, a rare nationwide ground stop was issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration after an L3Harris router malfunction stopped the FAA's air traffic control network in its tracks, forcing thousands of aircraft to be grounded and preventing flights from departing to, from, or within the US.

The post, on X, has racked up 613,000 views at the time of writing and continues to increase. The Middle Eastern airline has shared this across other social media channels, but has only reached 2,400 likes on Facebook.

Due to the four-hour delay in US flight operations, this had a ripple effect on airlines around the world, grounding US-bound services. This affected several Emirates flights, from Dubai to destinations across America. While flights already airborne were permitted to land, those still at the gate were forced to wait until final clearance was provided, and services resumed at 8:15 PM EST on Friday.

Emirates services were eventually able to operate to the US, with slight delays on some flights. There were no blanket cancellations or major disruptions to US-bound services. In the US, thousands of flights were canceled on Friday and Saturday, with delays expected to linger in the coming days as local airlines return to normal operations and clear the passenger backlog.

Experienced by airlines around the globe, flight departures were marginally delayed until clearance was given for services to resume. This had no major impact on non-UAE flight operations, and neither Emirates nor neighboring Etihad Airways or Qatar Airways saw any major displacement of aircraft or crew, unlike the thousands of canceled flights and crew timeouts experienced in the US.

Simple Flying reached out to Emirates for comment on the Microsoft Outage and ground stop; however, an airline spokesperson could not immediately be reached.

A ground stop of this magnitude in the US has not been seen in more than a quarter century. The last time the FAA ordered a nationwide halt to all flight departures was briefly in January 2023, due to a malfunction in its Notice to Air Missions system (NOTAM). The last major ground stop was in 2001, following the September 11 terrorist attacks.

"Your email might be down, but the skies are always open" was a light-hearted jab at the Microsoft Outlook and cloud outage that disrupted millions of users of Microsoft cloud-based services and software suites worldwide. This affected Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams and Copilot users.

The multi-region technical failure knocked out key collaboration and email tools for millions of users across 74 countries. Microsoft confirmed this was not a cyber attack, security breach, or AI malfunction, but instead stemmed from a technical issue that was introduced during a network capacity upgrade. Microsoft's services were fully restored later on Thursday, but many were left in the lurch without access to these vital software systems. The global outage indirectly affected Emirates by disrupting the airline's corporate communications and internal office and email tools, while also hampering customer support channels, as confirmed by Gulf Business.

Emirates is a large international airline that operates a robust network of international flights from its home at Dubai International Airport (DXB). The airline operates a fleet of Airbus A350s, A380s, and Boeing 777s. It is the world's largest operator of the A380 and 777, and handles more than 3,600 flights per week, in excess of 500 per day, to and from the Middle East, and several unique fifth-freedom routes.

It's going to be a rough weekend at airports, as the U.S. air travel system rebounds from one of the most significant disruptions in decades.

Thousands of flights have been canceled for Saturday, continuing fallout from the Federal Aviation Administration's move to halt most takeoffs and landings across the country for about four hours Friday evening.

Airlines were cleared to resume service at 8:15 p.m. EST Friday evening, but travelers will face significant disruptions into the weekend — especially Saturday.

As of 4:35 p.m. EST Saturday, flight cancellations for the day topped 5,300, according to data from FlightAware. And cancellations already extended into Sunday, with 200 flights preemptively grounded. Of those, United accounted for the most (48) followed by JetBlue (33), Delta regional affiliate Endeavor Air (22) and American (20).

Nationwide, nearly 13,000 flights have been scrubbed since Friday.

“This morning, the system remains stable, and our airline partners are working through the operational recovery,” FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said at a Saturday morning press conference alongside Transportation secretary Sean Duffy. “Of course, we have crews and aircraft that are out of position.”

That came after most departing flights in the U.S.were grounded indefinitely late Friday afternoon after the FAA reported communication issues impacting air traffic control centers.

The fallout for travelers has been severe, stranding travelers across the country and forcing hundreds of flights to divert.

Airkines have been racing to reset their operations — and get planes and crewmembers back to where they're supposed to be so schedules can get back to normal.

The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop late Friday afternoon after discovering a communications outage affecting air traffic control.

It happened as crews were working to upgrade critical FAA equipment, apparently overloading the system amid a switch from copper wiring to fiber at one of the agency's facilities.

“This was an FAA system that didn’t meet the moment," Duffy said at the Saturday press conference. "Our contractor didn’t meet the moment, or the equipment didn’t meet the moment and caused the outages.”

The disruption marked only the second time since 9/11 that a ground stop affecting the entire nation had been issued.

All told, airlines canceled more than 9,000 flights on Friday, according to FlightAware. Another 7,000-plus were delayed.

Some international flights and service within Alaska and Hawaii continued, despite the outage.

But the vast majority of domestic departures on Friday evening were affected.

With the ground stop lifted, airlines can now begin the complex process of resetting their operations.

That means getting aircraft, travelers, crews and baggage to the right destinations.

"Our airline partners are working through that," Bedford said Saturday. "So we will still have delays and cancellations today, but that will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow. And based on everything that we’re hearing from our airline partners, they believe that they’ll be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday."

Airlines issued travel advisories in the midst of the travel chaos. These waivers typically allow passengers with flights booked more flexibility to change their itineraries:

If your flight is affected by this weekend's disruptions, stay glued to your airline app — you may be able to search for a new flight and rebook yourself without waiting on hold or in line at the airport.

Don't see a good flight option for days? Keep checking back: with a lot of passengers shifting plans across the country, it's still possible seats will open up.

Passengers whose flights are canceled or significantly delayed are entitled to a refund if they choose not to travel or accept a rebooked flight, regardless of the reason for the disruption.

Under U.S. Department of Transportation rules, a significant delay generally means arriving at your final destination at least three hours late on a domestic itinerary or six hours late on an international itinerary. For passengers who decide to not travel on those flights, airlines must provide refunds to the original form of payment, not just travel credits.

In large-scale travel disruptions like this, rental cars and hotel rooms at or near airports can book up quickly, so it can make sense to act fast if you want to secure a backup option.

If you have airline miles you can use to book a flight for this weekend, that can also be a good self-insurance policy in case the disruption isn't resolved quickly. Just make sure you understand the cancellation and refund rules before booking a backup ticket.

Because this disruption was due to issues outside airlines' control, carriers are unlikely to reimburse stranded passengers for hotel, ground transportation and meal costs.

Some rewards credit cards do offer built-in trip delay or cancellation protection if you used them to book your original airline tickets.

However, it's not guaranteed that those benefits will cover FAA groundings of this nature. Still, save your receipts for any unexpected expenses in case you're eligible for reimbursement.

#6061. Duffy And Mullin’s FAA Ground Stop Press Conference: Self-Praise, A $50 Billion Ask, And Conflicting Stories

Yesterday, we saw the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issue a nationwide ground stop, which wasn’t fully lifted for over four hours. This represents the single biggest grounding of flights in the United States since 9/11, so the scale of whatever happened is pretty wild.

At around 8PM last night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference to update people on the state of things. I can’t help but cover this, because it felt like something between an SNL skit and a shakedown, and they couldn’t even keep their story straight… all while praising themselves for doing an unprecedented job!

Below you can find the press conference last night regarding the FAA shutdown, which happened around the time that the ground stop was lifted. First Mullin and Duffy spoke for around 10 minutes, and then they took questions for around 20 minutes.

The gist of the story is that they claim there were no signs of this being a cyber attack, and basically they broadly blame the outdated air traffic control system.

Mullin didn’t speak for long, and his primary comment was this:

“This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like, by the organization and team he has put together. We are built to handle crises like this, and that’s exactly what we’re doing. We’re moving at an unprecedented pace, as a whole of government, to make sure we’re doing the public justice by making sure everyone is safe, which everyone is.”

Isn’t this a little self-congratulatory, especially while he’s also claiming that they don’t fully know the cause here? Just objectively, the pace was indeed unprecedented… it was the longest ground stop since 9/11!

Then you have Duffy speak, and this basically just turned into a demand for Congress to give him $50 billion to modernize our aviation infrastructure, while not actually being honest about the state of things:

“The President, for the last year, has been asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a new air traffic control system.”

That’s just not accurate at all. In July 2025, Congress authorized $12.5 billion for modernizing air traffic control, which Duffy described as a “down payment.” Since then, the size of the request kept changing, and the formal ask only went to Congress this week, when Duffy asked lawmakers for $30.1 billion for air traffic control and airport upgrades.

So it’s a bit rich to claim that Congress has been uncooperative over the past year, especially when you consider Republicans have controlled the White House, House, and Senate.

He then tried to explain what happened, which just feels like a complete deflection to me, as it’s about an overall need to modernize ATC, rather than what actually went wrong here:

“What happened is that our switches, actually got overloaded with data, and they went down… I shouldn’t say they went down… they started to give us inconsistency with the data from those routers, and because of that, we shut the system down. Now, I have already replaced some of those switches with President Trump, and our new IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down, and I think the question for the American people is, ‘do you want your Congress to fund this?'”

“I think the Congress at a point looked at the history of the FAA, and said ‘we don’t trust you.’ Well with President Trump, and what we’ve done, I think they do trust, because what we’ve done with that first tranche of money.”

“I’ve asked the President to ask for $30 billion. I want $50 billion.”

Obviously our air traffic control technology is really outdated and does need updating, there are no two ways about it. However, what was different yesterday, and caused an outage to this scale?

You can see I quoted Duffy above as saying that he claimed that “what happened is that our switches, actually got overloaded with data,” and that this caused the shutdown. I’m not a tech expert, but how exactly does that happen and cause the systems nationwide to have issues? At most, you’d assume it would be regionalized, no?

So this is where the questions from reporters come in handy. Mullin seemingly threw Duffy under the bus, saying:

“What it appears to be right now is that as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches in the system, they were putting new equipment, and new technology, and that new equipment and new technology was overwhelming the older system.”

You can see Secretary Duffy’s reaction as Secretary Mullin says the newer technology was overwhelming the system. pic.twitter.com/IeoW5nM4aY

Duffy was then asked what was different yesterday, given that the system had been in place for years. As you’d expect, there was no good answer.

Initially Duffy made it sound like they knew exactly what happened, but then he backtracked on that, and said “we’re still working on the details of what went wrong, I’ll be happy to give you more information, but I don’t want to give you the wrong information.”

Very good set of questions from Luke Radel for Secretary Duffy and Secretary Mullin. pic.twitter.com/f6tlfDtbJG

I also appreciate how someone actually asked the question about this being blamed on Congress, given that the Republicans have had full control for the past two years. As you’d expect, Duffy’s response was first to ask what network the person was from.

DUFFY: How many times does this have to happen before congress gives the money to fix it?R: You’ve been in office almost two years now, Republicans controlled both chambers of congress and still do.DUFFY: What your network are you from? pic.twitter.com/xuX5arTwjl

What’s amazing to me is the overall tone of the press conference. They feel bad for themselves, with Duffy pointing out that he hopes he doesn’t have to give another press conference after 8PM. You know what’s not mentioned once, though? Thanking travelers for their patience throughout all of this, or apologizing to the public for the disruption. Not once.

I’m 100% in support of funding and modernizing air traffic control. But when you have the biggest outage you’ve had in over 25 years, it seems a bit rich to say “give us $50 billion” and “we’re doing an unprecedented job.” And again, if Mullin is to be believed, the system updates that were put in place were to blame.

Breaking – All flights nationwide have beengrounded – the #FAA is facing a computer outage.Yet another major blow to incompetent Transportation Sect Mayor Pete and people who get important jobs with no experience to check some identity politics boxes.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference last night about the nationwide ground stop, and it just struck me as being incredibly tone deaf and off base.

You had Mullin congratulating the Trump administration for their “unprecedented” response, you had Duffy claiming the outage was due to switches getting overloaded with data, and you had had Mullin then claim this happened because of the system updates that Duffy put in place. Oh, and the focus was also on demanding that Congress give them $50 billion, suggesting they’ve been dragging their feet for the past year.

There was zero tone of accountability or apology. There was no “thanks to everyone traveling for their patience,” but instead, self-pity for the fact that they had to be there after 8PM on a Friday, when they’d probably rather be at home… or a bar, maybe.

What do you make of this press conference?

#6060. Hawaii Airport Video Shows Japanese ‘Hostess’ Handcuffed—Then Deported On A Flight Leaving In 30 Minutes

A Japanese woman screams “Help me!” and “SOS!” as border officers handcuff her at Honolulu airport. Her Hawaii trip ends with a rush to get her onto a flight back to Nagoya leaving in 30 minutes because missing it would mean spending the night in federal detention. Newly circulating footage of the incident comes from Frontline Crime uploaded in July, and is from an episode of Airport Security: USA that appears to have come out two years ago. A report on the clip describes the woman as a Japanese ‘hostess’. View the airport footage shared by Grit Hiro The woman refused to cooperate with a request to move to secondary inspection. Officers restrain her as she cries out and insists she’s visiting on vacation. An officer says they were asking basic questions when she accused them of suspecting her of prostitution. He treats that reaction as evidence that she has something to hide. Questioning eventually turns to who paid for her airfare and hotel. She says a man covered the trip, but she doesn’t know where he is and hasn’t contacted him. The narrator first says officers suspect he has ties to a Japanese criminal organization, then reports an organized crime connection. The officer declares she hasn’t overcome the presumption that she intends to immigrate, and tells her she’ll be sent back to Japan because that makes her ineligible to enter as a temporary visitor. If she intended to work in a Hawaii club, even just serving drinks and talking with customers would be a problem because she was entering as a tourist and not someone work authorized. On Japanese Twitter, Hiroyuki Nishimura mocked the idea that refusing questions and making a scene would get her admitted. I’ve covered Molly Hill, who said she was strip searched and jailed after flying to Hawaii to visit her boyfriend. She had a ticket home after 88 days. Officials suspected she intended to stay, and she was brought back through the airport in handcuffs on her birthday. And in 2022, an Australian traveler was detained in Honolulu over an onward-ticket problem. Jack Dunn said he was strip searched, placed in a cell, and left to sleep on a concrete floor with a paper bag for a pillow. Topics on this pageAirport securityDaniel K. On Japanese Twitter, Hiroyuki Nishimura mocked the idea that refusing questions and making a scene would get her admitted.

I’ve covered Molly Hill, who said she was strip searched and jailed after flying to Hawaii to visit her boyfriend. She had a ticket home after 88 days. Officials suspected she intended to stay, and she was brought back through the airport in handcuffs on her birthday.

And in 2022, an Australian traveler was detained in Honolulu over an onward-ticket problem. Jack Dunn said he was strip searched, placed in a cell, and left to sleep on a concrete floor with a paper bag for a pillow.

#6059. 5 Military Aircraft Powered By Engines Found On Commercial Airliners

David Monniaux | Wikimedia Commons | Simple Flying

Many military aircraft use commercially derived powerplants. This is especially true for transports, tankers, and maritime patrol aircraft. These uses share many engine characteristics that are also useful in commercial aviation. Examples include reliability, low maintenance costs, and fuel efficiency. It also avoids manufacturers having to spend a vast amount on engine development.

A Boeing spokesperson explained the benefits to Simple Flying.

“Using commercial-derived engines lets manufacturers and operators leverage existing design maturity, production capacity and global maintenance infrastructure. That translates into lower development risk and cost, faster fielding, more abundant spare parts and established MRO networks—while still allowing mission-specific adaptations to meet durability, fleet performance and mission capability.”

F117 is the military designation for the Pratt & Whitney PW2000. The engine is used exclusively by the C-17 Globemaster III. The transport aircraft uses four of these engines, each rated at 40,400 lbf (180 kN). This power is enough for the aircraft to carry a payload of up to 160,600 lb (72,800 kg) with a range of 2,400 nautical miles (4,400 km). Perhaps the most impressive attribute the engine gives the Globemaster is its ability to take off fully loaded from a runway 7,600 feet (2,300 meters) long. Likewise, the aircraft can land at airfields under 3,000 feet (900 meters) long. The aircraft achieved 22 world records during its testing. Another unique feature of the engine is its thrust reversers, which can be deployed in flight, allowing it to reverse up a two-degree slope.

The F117 has gradually been improved during the Globemaster's operation and has reached a reduced-temperature configuration (RTC). This configuration uses single-crystal turbine materials that improve reliability and have lowered operating temperatures. Pratt & Whitney claims that these improvements have resulted in increased time on-wing.

The F117 is closely tied to the PW2000. In commercial operations, the engine is used for the Boeing 757 and the Ilyushin Il-96M, which first flew in 1993. The PW2000 produces 38,400 to 43,734 lbf (170.81 to 194.54 kN) of thrust with a thrust-to-weight ratio of 5.41 to 6.16.

The P-8 Poseidon is a maritime patrol and reconnaissance aircraft that was developed for the United States Navy as a derivative of the Boeing 737 Next Generation airliner. As a result, it uses the CFM56-7 series of engines, which also power the Boeing 737-600, -700, and -800. The same engine powers the other 737 NG-derived military aircraft in the US Air Force, including the Boeing E-7 Wedgetail and C-40 Clipper. Other Boeing aircraft using different variants are the E-3D Sentry, E-6 Mercury, and KC-135R Stratotanker.

The table below shows the specifications for the P-8 Poseidon, making use of data published by Boeing:

1,200 nautical miles (2,225 km), or around four hours on station

The CFM56-7 series first ran on April 21, 1985. It offered reduced fuel burn and maintenance costs compared with older engines in the series. It also allowed the 737 NG to achieve 180 minutes of extended-range twin-engine operations (ETOPS) certification from the US Federal Aviation Administration. This attribute is essential for maritime patrol aircraft like the P-8 Poseidon, which often fly in remote areas.

The CFM56 has helped the P-8 achieve an impressive level of commercial success, with almost 200 jets built. Operators outside the US include the Royal Australian Air Force, the German Navy, the Indian Navy, the Royal New Zealand Air Force, and the Royal Air Force. Canada also has 14 P-8s currently on order, and options for two more.

The C-17 Globemaster III's four-engine design holds the key to its unrivaled capabilities, but was this a choice of power or necessity?

The C-5 Super Galaxy is the largest strategic airlifter currently used by the United States Air Force. The 52 in-service aircraft have all been upgraded to the C-5M variant, which uses updated engines and modernized avionics. The Air Force hopes to keep this aircraft in service until at least 2040. The C-5M Super Galaxy uses CF6-80C2 engines. These jets are used on 15 widebody aircraft types, many of which are commercial. Examples include the Boeing 747-400 and McDonnell Douglas MD-11. The engine has ETOPS-180 certification for the Airbus A300, Airbus A310, Boeing 767, KC-767A/J, E-767J, and Kawasaki C-2.

The table below shows the specifications for the C-5M Super Galaxy. It uses data collected by Air Mobility Command:

The older C-5 Super Galaxy variants (C-5A, C-5B, and C-5C) were powered by four older General Electric TF39-GE-1 or TF39-GE-1C. Enthusiasts loved this engine because of its distinctive scream, which is no longer present in the newer C-5M engine. Unlike the CF6-80C2, this engine was developed specifically for the Super Galaxy. However, it was later modified into the General Electric CF6. The civilian engine entered service in 1971 with the McDonnell Douglas DC-10.

The new engine brings a host of improvements over the TF39. It delivers higher power, allowing for shorter takeoffs and faster climb rates. It is also more reliable and fuel-efficient, and produces less noise. This gives Super Galaxy operators more flexibility in using civilian airfields. Finally, wider use of the engine in commercial markets leads to an abundance of relatively affordable spare parts.

The KC-46 Pegasus is an aerial refueling and strategic transport aircraft developed and produced by Boeing. The manufacturer claims it is the world's most advanced aircraft in this role. It is capable of refueling friendly aircraft at a rate of 400 gallons per minute (1,500 liters per minute). The aircraft can also be configured for 58 passengers in normal operations or 114 as a maximum limit. In an aeromedical configuration, the aircraft can hold 54 patients, although 30 must be ambulatory. It also seats 15 crew members. In the transport configuration, the plane can hold 18 463L pallets.

The plane has been developed from the Boeing 767. As a result, it uses the PW4062, a variant of the Pratt & Whitney PW-4000-94. Other examples of civilian usage of this engine family include the MD-11, 747-400, A330, and the A300-600. The PW4000 has been in service since 1987, amassing 140 million flight hours.

The table below shows the specifications for the -94 variant of the engine, as is used by the KC-46 Pegasus. The data is from the FAA:

The primary benefit that the PW4062 brings to the KC-46 Pegasus is reliability. Pratt & Whitney claims that the engine averages 16,000 hours on-wing before requiring a shop visit. It says that this attribute greatly reduces the maintenance costs that the US Air Force has to pay to keep Pegasus in the skies.

The shift to a Modular Open Systems Architecture in the C-17's cockpit will enable faster upgrades and ensure long-term sustainability.

The US military calls the E-4 "Nightwatch," but it is popularly known as the "Doomsday Plane." It is a strategic command and control military aircraft used by the National Emergency Airborne Command Post (NEACP) program. A key purpose of this aircraft is to keep the US government operational in the event of nuclear warfare. In such a crisis, it would become a mobile command post for the President of the United States and the Secretary of Defense. Four E-4s have been built.

The E-4 is modified from the Boeing 747-200B. It is powered by four General Electric F103 turbofan engines. Each of them produces 52,500 lbf (234 kN) of thrust. This engine is derived from the General Electric CF6-50E2.

The engine was launched in 1969, used to power the DC-10. It also powered the A300 from late 1969 and the 747 from 1975. The CF6-45 variant of the engine was developed with 10% less thrust, used for a short-range variant of the 747. In military aviation, the engine is also used by the McDonnell Douglas KC-10 Extender.

When the aircraft first emerged, named the E-4A, four Pratt & Whitney JT9D powered it. The first two Nightwatch planes built used this engine. The third E-4 built used the F103 engine. This engine use was instituted for future E-4s built and standardized across the fleet. The advantage of this engine was that it was modified to run two constant speed drives (CSDs) and two generators per engine. These components produced enough electrical power to run a more advanced command-and-control suite.

#6058. Delta 360: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

All of the “big three” carriers in the United States have invitation-only elite status. I’ve written about how American has Concierge Key and United has Global Services, and in this post, I’d like to take a look at Delta 360, which is Delta’s invitation-only elite status. I’d argue it’s the most mysterious, least talked about, and perhaps the rarest, of the three.

What is Delta 360 status, how do you earn it, what are the benefits, and how many members are there? I’ll share everything I know…

Delta 360 is Delta Air Lines’ invitation-only elite status. It’s my understanding that this is the most exclusive of the invitation-only elite tiers, in the sense that there are the fewest members. Despite that, the benefits are actually pretty weak, at least on paper. For that matter, Delta 360 isn’t even a formal elite tier, which is to say that you separately still have to qualify for status in the Delta SkyMiles Medallion program.

For what it’s worth, here’s how Delta describes Delta 360 status on its website:

Delta 360° is an annual, invitation-only membership for our most loyal SkyMiles Members. A Delta 360° Membership offers Delta’s most premium suite of benefits and services exclusive to our top SkyMiles Members. Entry into Delta 360° will be extended to a very small percentage of Diamond Medallion Members. Considerations include, but are not limited to: overall Delta flight activity, premium product purchases (Delta One, Delta Premium Select, Delta First) and spending on Delta SkyMiles American Express Cards.

As is the case with the invitation-only status of American and United, the requirements to earn Delta 360 status aren’t published. However, based on the data points I’ve seen, the criteria are even more confusing. With American and United, as a general rule, you need to spend well over $50,000 per year to have a shot at the status. In the case of Delta, you probably need to spend even more.

As Delta officially states, getting an invitation to Delta 360 is for the “most loyal SkyMiles members.” Generally speaking:

Some suggest that you’d have to spend $100,000 per year on Delta flights to be invited as a Delta 360 member at major hubs, while the number could be much lower if you’re not based at a hub.

Note that qualification for Delta 360 is annual (so it expires at the end of the elite year), and criteria could change year-to-year. So it’s possible you have the same activity in two years, and earn Delta 360 one year, but not the other. There’s also no way to ask for or request the status (at least not in a way that will achieve the intended result). Instead, you’ll be contacted if you’re eligible, and you’ll see your account updated to reflect that.

There’s one other way to earn Delta 360 status. As part of the SkyMiles lifetime elite status program, you can receive Delta 360 status for life if you rack up five million lifetime miles. This metric is based on the number of eligible miles flown on Delta.

Just for some context on all of this, Delta’s top published tier is Diamond Medallion, and that requires earning 28,000 Medallion Qualifying Dollars (MQDs) in a program year. That would require $28,000 in spending on Delta tickets, or $280,000 to $560,000 in spending on select co-branded Delta credit cards.

Interestingly, Delta 360 isn’t a separate tier in the SkyMiles program. That’s to say that Delta 360 members still have to earn status in the SkyMiles Medallion program. Most Delta 360 members are also Diamond Medallion members, but in theory it’s possible to earn Delta 360 without being a Diamond Medallion member.

This is different than American AAdvantage and United MileagePlus, where Concierge Key and Global Services are separate tiers, above the published top tier levels.

What are the benefits of Delta 360 status?

Those are all the Delta 360 benefits that I’m aware of. There’s no upgrade priority for Delta 360 members beyond their standard Diamond Medallion status, so Delta 360 doesn’t factor into upgrade priority. Furthermore, any confirmed upgrades would be earned through the standard Choice Benefits program, as this is how you can earn Global Upgrade Certificates (GUCs) and Regional Upgrade Certificates (RUCs).

So the benefits of Delta 360 are weak, though I’d imagine that the “soft” treatment is very good — Delta has great service to begin with, and I imagine it’s even better for Delta’s best customers.

I also think it’s noteworthy how Delta is much quieter about this status than American and United. There’s just not as much public acknowledgement of invitation only status at Delta as at American and United (and that might be by design).

This is a real mystery, and all I can do is speculate. For context, I’ve speculated that there are 10,000-20,000 American Concierge Key members, and I’ve speculated that there are 15,000-25,000 United Global Services members.

This is purely a guess on my part, but I think the number of Delta 360 members is probably in the 5,000-10,000 range. That’s simply because the status seems to be more difficult to earn. Like I said, this is purely a guess on my part, and I could be wrong. If anyone has any data or info, I’d love to hear it.

It’s hard to say whether something like Delta 360 is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Delta 360 varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

If you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Delta One Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal, above and beyond what you’d otherwise get.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including American Concierge Key and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, I’d say Delta 360 probably offers the fewest official perks of the three tiers. The one exception is that Delta One Lounge access is an absolutely awesome benefit, given the quality of lounges (though the lack of free guests limits the usefulness for those not usually traveling alone).

Here are a couple of thoughts on the comparable status tiers at American and United:

Delta 360 is Delta Air Lines’ invitation-only elite tier. It’s the US airline status that’s probably hardest to earn. Historically the benefits have been weaker than comparable status with American and United, though with access to Delta One Lounges, that’s perhaps no longer the case. Delta 360 offers dedicated customer support, a Sky Club membership, Delta One Lounge access, good odds of tarmac transfers, and more.

To earn Delta 360, be prepared to spend a lot on Delta flights, especially if you’re based out of a Delta hub.

Are any OMAAT readers Delta 360 members? If so, what has your experience been like?

A former DL 360 member mentioned that he spent 91k to get an invitation but when he ‘only’ spent 41K and 68K he did not get invited back. #6055. United CEO Scott Kirby Says “100%” Chance Merger With American Airlines Would Get Approved

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby says he’s “100%” convinced a merger with American Airlines could get approved. He says he’s even more confident than he was this spring, when news of the talks came out, and he sees getting American to agree as the biggest obstacle. But ‘get approved’ doesn’t mean what he seems to suggest. A friendly Justice Department signing off would still leave any such combination with state attorneys general, foreign governments and two competing sets of international airline partnerships to deal with. Speaking at Yahoo Finance Invest, Kirby said: “It wouldn’t be easy.” “We’d have to do some divestitures, but I 100% think it could get approved.” His argument is that bringing United’s service, technology and operational performance to more passengers would make them better off. He thinks critics misunderstand the deal because they treat airline seats as interchangeable. Contra Kirby, better service is actually a core part of DOJ merger guidelines recognizing quality, innovation and choice. Plus, United service isn’t that good! And while their operations are better than they used to be, they aren’t industry-leading. They’re consistently modestly better than American’s but the difference is hardly vast. Kirby Hasn’t Given Up On The Airline That Fired Him When I covered Kirby’s merger pitch in April, the appeal to United was obvious: American would give them a much bigger New York presence, more strength in Los Angeles, a southeastern hub and a powerful Latin America network. Kirby later said he’d build a Miami hub if he could get 40 or 50 gates. He also wants more at New York JFK than United’s planned return will provide. American rejected merger discussions, arguing that combining the airlines would hurt consumers and competition. Any antitrust case – even at the state level – would just quote American’s own release. As I covered October 31, Kirby described conversations he thought were continuing until American blindsided him with that press release. In any case, American can make investments without being bought. They’ve already made real progress over the past 21 months towards improving their product almost across-the-board. The Justice Department Doesn’t Get The Only Vote I laid out the problems beyond Washington back in April. Getting the administration to support a deal isn’t even close to enough. States can bring their own case. A federal settlement doesn’t bind state attorneys general who aren’t parties to it. Private plaintiffs can sue, too. The Clayton Act allows injunctions against threatened antitrust harm. Closing doesn’t automatically end the risk. The merger notification statute preserves later challenges. Letting the federal waiting period expire isn’t permanent antitrust immunity. He’d Have To Untangle Two Competing Global Networks American and US Airways needed European Commission clearance for their merger. The London–Philadelphia remedy included slots for a competing daily flight. Two U.S. companies combining doesn’t make the transaction solely an American matter. United and American also have joint ventures that let them coordinate prices, schedules and revenue with different foreign airlines. Among those arrangements: Market United’s Partners American’s Partners Atlantic   Lufthansa Group and Air Canada   British Airways, Iberia, Aer Lingus and Finnair Japan   All Nippon Airways   Japan Airlines South Pacific   Air New Zealand   Qantas A combined airline couldn’t assume it could keep these competing arrangements unchanged. Moving American’s flying into United’s partnerships would change the competition analysis. Ending American’s existing deals would also change the connecting traffic and economics Kirby is buying. The Transportation Department’s alliance approvals are another process, separate from Justice Department merger review. And foreign oversight is already an issue: Britain. American’s existing Atlantic partnership already faces slot remedies for London–Boston, London–Chicago and London–Miami, plus protections for London–Dallas passengers. In February, the British competition authority announced approved slot agreements for Delta on Boston and Virgin Atlantic on Miami. Buying American could create new hurdles for either transatlantic joint venture the combined carrier participated in. The European Union would have its own merger review, too. Japan. United and American have separate immunized partnerships with Japan’s two major network airlines. The merger would also raise questions about their scarce Tokyo Haneda access. Japan might not approve a combined American and United in either partnership. Keeping both carriers’ Haneda slots aren’t necessarily in the DOT’s view of the public interest. Australia and New Zealand. Australia renewed the American–Qantas alliance authorization on October 14. New Zealand renewed it in March, and separately authorizes United’s cooperation with Air New Zealand. Combining the American partners in those competing relationships would give both governments new questions to consider regardless of which airline they decided they wanted to keep a partnership with. Canada. United and Air Canada announced an expanded transborder agreement last month and submitted it to Transport Canada for approval. Combining that operation with American’s Canada seems almost impossible on its own. What Would United Have To Give Up? Chicago is the biggest domestic problem. United and American operate competing hubs at O’Hare. New York, Los Angeles and Washington raise challenges as well. United has Newark while American considers the combined LaGuardia and JFK a hub; both airlines have hubs at LAX, and United has a hub at Washington Dulles while American is the dominant carrier at Washington National. And surely American’s debt is a poison pill? It ended September with $29.6 billion in debt and finance leases (without operating leases and pension obligations). The “100% approved” isn’t at all credible, unless he means only at the federal level and because he’s had assurances from the President (who could change his mind!). Scott Kirby is starting to believe his own delusional statements – if the Courts & DOT would not approve the JetBlue-SPIRIT Airlines merger (which resulted in the demise of SPIRIT), then how the heck does he believe they will approve a merger between these 2 mega giants. Perhaps Kirby should invest his time in his current responsibilities and stop trying to put himself in the spotlight. His rhetoric is clearly to feed his ego versus promoting a rational cause. STFU already.

Scott Kirby is apparently modeling his strategy after Frank Lorenzo. He is getting more aggressive with his desire to wipe American Airlines off the face of Aviation today. And just why he is not happy to run the Airline he already has is pure revenge. And he appears to think that because his name is prominent in the Airline Industry, that he would have no problem getting all that he desires approved.

I personally am getting a little sick of hearing about his greed and desire for revenge . He should be thankful for what he has instead of constantly seeking to demolish another airline.

Follow the money. He’s pandered to the Trump administration and the merger would hurt competition but line pockets without providing a better service to passengers plus need to be paid for through lower costs and redundancies. Remember Continental and US Air? Did things get better post merger?

I like American as they are, stay away Kirby leave American alone, they are not perfect but they are my Airline of choice. Take care of your own house.

I think you can apply the Colonel Klink rule from Hogan’s Heroes. Whatever he says, the opposite is likely to be true.

Kirby said recently that Doug Parker advised him he would be promoted to CEO. Six weeks later, Parker fired Kirby.

Now, the media reported that Kirby kept asking the Board when Parker would retire or relinquish the CEO title. The Board got fed up and fired Kirby.

Someone is not being 100% truthful, and I think it’s Kirby.

Consider this. Kirby has not sold his house in the Metroplex or purchased a house in Chicagoland.

He typically works out of his house in the Metroplex, forcing United executives to fly to DFW for meetings.

If Kirby does fly to Chicago for meetings at United HQ or to mouth off to the Chicago press, he flies American and not United.
