#6054. United CEO 100% Sure A Merger With American Would Get Approved. I’m 99% Sure He’s Wrong.

I’ll admit that there’s probably collectively a little too much reporting on what United CEO Scott Kirby says. The issue is, he’s a really bright guy, and I’d argue he’s the most impactful leader in the US airline industry since Richard Anderson at Delta. At the same time, on some level that seems to have gotten to his head, and I just feel like he’s making claims that are completely indefensible, at least if you approach them with any level of objectivity.

In April 2026, news broke about how United CEO Scott Kirby reportedly approached the Trump administration about the concept of merging with American, and forming a “flag” carrier for the United States.

Days later, American management publicly rejected this concept, which caused Kirby to publicly make his case for a merger with American. Months later, it came out that Kirby had also approached Delta about the concept of a merger. Ever since, Kirby has continued to insist that this is a great idea, and that those who oppose it are just misunderstanding his vision.

The widespread belief (among other industry executives and the public) is that such a deal wouldn’t get approval, because it shouldn’t… it would be really bad for competition! However, View from the Wing flags Kirby’s latest comments on his merger dream, which I can’t help but find to be interesting:

“I think the biggest impediment is having a willing partner. I am more convinced today than I was when I wrote my note six months ago that it could get approval. It could get approval because it is good for customers. So many people look at that kind of a merger through what has been the traditional airline commodity lens, that air travel is a commodity, and it doesn’t matter which airline flies. But customers care about the service, the product, the technology, the reliability. It wouldn’t be easy. We’d have to do some divestitures, but I 100% think it could get approved.”

So Kirby claims he’s 100% certain that a merger between two of the three biggest US carriers would get approved by regulators. No, he’s not 80% sure, or 90% sure, or 99% sure. He’s 100% sure. Now, in fairness to him, he acknowledges that some divestitures would be required, but I think he’s underestimating the scale of divestitures that would be required for anything like this to get approval.

Maybe this is a hot take, but I think American management should call United’s bluff. Come to a deal that’s good for American shareholders, and create an absolutely massive breakup fee in the event it doesn’t get approval. There would only be upside for American, and then Kirby can put his money where his mouth is.

We know that Kirby has an axe to grind with American, since he was fired there, and then went on to work at United (which probably ended up being the best thing that could happen to him, because he sure seized that opportunity). So I can’t help but feel like a large motivation for his merger dream is based on wanting to get revenge, and that’s maybe clouding reality for him a bit.

Fundamentally, I disagree with Kirby’s merger dream on two levels — he overstates United’s greatness, and he understates the competitive implications of a merger of this scale.

United has absolutely improved massively under Kirby’s leadership. But Kirby acts like United is Singapore Airlines, while Delta and American are Air Algerie and TAAG Angola Airlines, by comparison.

Is Kirby forgetting that United is still catching up with Delta, and in the number two spot in the US industry? He acts as if the only way to have a pleasant flight on a US carrier is to fly with United, which just seems extreme. He seems to believe that, though, since he has called United “the best airline in the history of aviation.”

For that matter, from a consumer perspective, does Kirby not realize that the positive changes at United are now forcing American to make positive changes? American is getting seat back TVs, Starlink Wi-Fi, improved lounges, etc. That strong competition helps consumers, and it doesn’t hurt them.

Obviously eliminating one of the “big three” carriers would have huge implications for competition, and pricing power for airlines (especially when airline executives keep talking about how they want fare increases to stick around even after fuel prices decrease).

Kirby’s emphasis has long been on how it’s not just about offering the best price, but also about offering the best overall experience and value. While there has definitely been some decommoditization of airfare (in other words, more people are brand loyal), that still represents the minority of consumers. United is a publicly traded company that’s there to maximize shareholder value, and you can bet the airline will charge the highest fares it possibly can — if they didn’t, Kirby should be fired, because he’s not doing his job.

Even if you were to claim that domestic competition would be preserved (it wouldn’t be, in my opinion), what about internationally? The way global aviation has evolved is that the “big three” US carriers have helped create “big three” joint ventures, where they all partner with different airlines across the Atlantic and Pacific, allowing them to coordinate fares, schedules, etc. Abandoning an entire set of joint ventures would horribly hurt the competitive landscape.

United CEO Scott Kirby has for months been talking about how great it would be if United and American could merge, and he talks about how positive it would be for consumers. The issue is that such a deal would be unlikely to get regulatory approval, given the competitive implications.

Kirby disagrees, and he’s 100% certain that such a deal would get approval. I couldn’t disagree with him more, because the competitive implications would be massive (and negative). I kind of wish American would call his bluff and agree to a merger with a huge breakup fee, so that Kirby can be forced to actually stand behind his claims.

What do you make of Kirby’s merger “guarantees?”

#6053. Overworked? Leaked ATC Schedule Reveals Mandatory Overtime & 10-Hour Shifts

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Air traffic controller (ATC) work schedules have been scrutinized and show the reality behind the shortage of air traffic controllers in the United States. The schedule, obtained by The Washington Examiner's Anna Giaritelli, noted that controllers are scheduled to report to their facilities every single day for two weeks straight.

These rosters surfaced after the standoff between controllers and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), where a 2.8% pay rise was approved but stalled by Administrator Bryan Bedford. The roster shows that the controller worked from September 20 to October 3, with the only nominal day off on a Friday, but began on a midnight shift.

With 14 consecutive days on duty, the schedules indicate that the break immediately followed a Saturday night shift, beginning the evening prior at 9:00 PM. This resulted in controllers reporting every calendar day for two weeks.

Within a single week, there is a Rattler Shift, which has controllers starting at 1:00 PM and working mandatory overtime throughout the week. Across other rosters, mandatory overtime turns a five-day standard rotation into a six-day workweek, with backwards rotating start times dropping from afternoon shifts to early mornings within a matter of days.

The shortfall of more than 3,000 controllers needed across the country highlights the deficit, with the staffing levels falling below the 85% minimum threshold at 20 of the 26 busiest airports and facilities.

Chronic understaffing results in long shifts across consecutive days. Pushing controllers to their limit. This has led fatigue rules to mandate a minimum of ten hours off between standard shifts, and 12 hours off before midnight shifts. Despite this, controllers and union leaders have warned that relentless overtime will leave too little time for individuals to rest.

Tensions have continued to strain since the 2.8% pay rise was withheld, with controllers being told to spend at least five hours of an eight-hour shift actively working traffic positions. It has been argued that controllers should spend more time on each shift on radar or tower scopes.

National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA) and controllers have pushed back, noting that the non-scope time is required for mandatory weather briefings, training, and federally mandated recuperative breaks following high-stress radar sessions. Withholding the raise after years of mandatory six-day workweeks has accelerated retirements and attrition in the agency as it struggles to rebuild the workforce.

FAA ties delayed pay to efficiency metrics that demand more on position time amid a 3,000 controller shortfall.

Controller staffing and fatigue can directly shape daily airline reliability and the system's resilience if a disruption hits. At understaffed facilities, an absence of just one or two workers could force the FAA to limit arrival or departure rates at major airports, like New York, Newark, Los Angeles, or Atlanta. These limitations can force ground stops or ground delay programs even on clear-weather days.

The compounding strain during these outages sees the FAA already operating to its limit of staffing capacity and facing legacy systems and aging telecommunications infrastructure that is vulnerable, as highlighted by the Friday nationwide router outage that left airlines grounded across the country, displacing millions, canceling more than 10,000 flights, and leaving airline crew timed out and aircraft stranded. With a 3,000-controller shortfall and a stalled 2.8% raise, airports continue to operate at the limit of required staffing thresholds. The intense work schedules put into question how these professionals continue to work to a high standard in high-pressure environments.

Aging infrastructure, a long-standing deficit, federal government shutdowns, and a rigorous multi-year training pipeline show the vulnerability of the air traffic control system. The massive communications and radar failure on Friday led to the historic nationwide ground stop, which affected millions of passengers. Less than 10% of US airport control towers remain fully staffed.

#6052. Why Airlines Schedule Flights To Take Longer Than They Used To—Even Though It Costs Them More

Former Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost says his flight to Washington’s National Airport still takes about 50 minutes, but the published schedule has grown to an hour and 42 minutes. He thinks he’s figured out why: airlines get to look more on-time by giving themselves longer to arrive. He’s right that the schedule determines whether a flight counts as on time. But airlines pay for those extra minutes, and they generally have good reasons to avoid adding more than they need. My flight to DCA takes about 50 minutes. It used to be listed as an hour & change. The *posted* flight duration keeps getting longer, now 1hr 42 min. Still takes 50 minutes. I can only conclude that these posted durations are used in determining on-time statistics. — Dave Yost (@DaveYostOH) November 12, 2026 The Schedule Includes Time On The Ground Airlines publish block time: the time scheduled from leaving the departure gate to reaching the arrival gate. That includes taxiing, waiting for a runway, flying, and getting to a gate at the other end. And National airport is a particularly odd place to dismiss congestion. In a January update, the Federal Aviation Administration explained that it had reduced the airport’s hourly arrival rate from 36 to 26 after the January 2025 collision, before increasing it to 30. The airport could handle more – if the air traffic control system hadn’t had such challenges. More demand concentrated into busy periods, limited runway and gate capacity, controller shortages and equipment problems all affect how long the trip takes. The problem also isn’t just the average. It’s how much travel time varies. An airline needs a schedule that works when there’s a normal amount of congestion, not just when the plane gets straight to the runway and encounters no delay at the other end. If that variability grows, the schedule can need more time even when the flight takes 50 minutes in the air. I made this point when covering claims about increased schedule padding in 2023. Airport and air traffic control bottlenecks make trip time less predictable. Airlines build that uncertainty into their schedules. Airlines Pay For Those Extra Minutes I’ve been pushing back on the simple ‘they’re juking the stats’ explanation since at least 2015. Making flights look longer is an expensive way to improve a scorecard. Crew costs. Scheduled time can determine pay even when a flight arrives early. American Airlines flight attendants, for instance, receive flight time pay based on the greater of scheduled or actual block time for each flight. Less productive airplanes. Add time across the day’s flying and there’s less room for another revenue flight. The airline can wind up needing more airplanes and crews to operate the same service. Less attractive itineraries. Longer trips can lose bookings to faster connections, competing airlines, or driving. Airlines want to sell you a convenient schedule. Back in 2015, I cited Southwest Airlines’ estimate that adding just a couple of minutes of block time across its schedule would cost the equivalent of 8 to 10 airplanes’ daily flying. You can’t just push flights later in the day, because airlines need to schedule flights when people want to fly. And airlines help create some of their own congestion through banked schedules at hubs. Packing flights into connecting waves makes more itineraries possible, but it also puts more demand on gates, runways and employees at the same time. Longer Schedules Can Improve More Than The Statistics The government counts an arrival as on time when the plane reaches the gate less than 15 minutes after its scheduled arrival. But if an airline keeps missing its arrival times by small margins, increasing block time can be a sensible first step toward fixing reliability. It’s acknowledging how long operating the flight actually takes, including the delays that occur often enough to plan for. American announced longer block times alongside a redesign of their Dallas operation, moving from 9 large connecting waves to 13 smaller ones in April. I explained why that investment could pay for itself through fewer missed connections, delayed bags and disrupted aircraft and crews. In April, American’s Dallas hub chief reported that missed connections were down 50%. At United Airlines’ 2019 media day, an executive explained that 25% of their flights were expected to arrive 10 minutes early. That gave them room to hold some departures for connecting passengers and still arrive on time through their ConnectionSaver program. United had started improving its reliability with longer block times. Arriving Early Can Create A Gate Problem Of course, extra time in the schedule doesn’t create extra gates. Get in early and the gate assigned to your flight may still have another airplane on it. An empty gate may belong to another airline, be unsuitable for your aircraft, or lack the employees needed to bring you in and operate the jetbridge. I covered Doug Parker explaining this problem in 2018: American used essentially all its hub gate capacity at peak times, and a few airplanes failing to leave could leave arriving flights with nowhere to go. So you can land early, sit waiting, and reach the terminal around the originally scheduled time. The government’s arrival clock keeps running until gate arrival. Regardless, it’s not all a conspiracy to juke the stats. Often it’s just a realistic expectation for how long the airline thinks on average it’ll take to travel, though sometimes they beat those expectations. The real solution isn’t just tightening schedules, it’s improving throughput – more capacity in air travel control and at airports. But if an airline keeps missing its arrival times by small margins, increasing block time can be a sensible first step toward fixing reliability. It’s acknowledging how long operating the flight actually takes, including the delays that occur often enough to plan for.

American announced longer block times alongside a redesign of their Dallas operation, moving from 9 large connecting waves to 13 smaller ones in April. I explained why that investment could pay for itself through fewer missed connections, delayed bags and disrupted aircraft and crews. In April, American’s Dallas hub chief reported that missed connections were down 50%.

At United Airlines’ 2019 media day, an executive explained that 25% of their flights were expected to arrive 10 minutes early. That gave them room to hold some departures for connecting passengers and still arrive on time through their ConnectionSaver program. United had started improving its reliability with longer block times.

Of course, extra time in the schedule doesn’t create extra gates. Get in early and the gate assigned to your flight may still have another airplane on it. An empty gate may belong to another airline, be unsuitable for your aircraft, or lack the employees needed to bring you in and operate the jetbridge. I covered Doug Parker explaining this problem in 2018: American used essentially all its hub gate capacity at peak times, and a few airplanes failing to leave could leave arriving flights with nowhere to go. So you can land early, sit waiting, and reach the terminal around the originally scheduled time. The government’s arrival clock keeps running until gate arrival. Regardless, it’s not all a conspiracy to juke the stats. Often it’s just a realistic expectation for how long the airline thinks on average it’ll take to travel, though sometimes they beat those expectations. The real solution isn’t just tightening schedules, it’s improving throughput – more capacity in air travel control and at airports. #6051. How To Tell Different Airplanes Apart, From 737s To A380s: An AvGeek’s Guide

The miles & points world has all kinds of different enthusiasts — some people are only interested in miles & points in order to save money on travel, while others are interested in miles & points because they love airplanes. I know there are plenty of people who are very frequent flyers but can barely tell the difference between an Airbus A380 and Boeing 747.

In this post, I’d like to share how I easily identify planes in a split second. Of course there are lots of methods for doing this, but I’ll share my techniques (and maybe other hardcore avgeeks can chime in with their methods in the comments section).

To keep things simple, I’ll just stick to the most popular mainline, commercial aircraft, and I’ll be talking about each “family” of aircraft in a particular section. Let’s start with Boeing aircraft, and then we’ll cover Airbus aircraft.

The Boeing 737 is the most common commercial aircraft in service. To me, there are a couple most obvious signs that a plane is a 737, as opposed to an A220 or A320.

One method is to look at the cockpit windows. The 737 has six cockpit windows (which is standard), and the window at the far end on each side “slopes up” at the bottom, so the window doesn’t go as far down as on other jets. Furthermore, when you look at the tail of the 737, you’ll see that it connects with the rest of the plane with an extended slope, much more so than on the A220 or A320 (below you can see a 737 in the front and an A321 in the back).

What can make identifying the 737 challenging is that there are so many different variants. Let’s differentiate between the 737 NG (the older version of the jet), and the 737 MAX (the newer and more controversial version of the jet).

There are three most obvious ways to tell if you’re traveling on a 737 MAX. The 737 MAX has the zig-zag pattern at the back of the engines, which I’ll talk more about below, as you’ll also find this on 787s and 747-8s.

Furthermore, the 737 MAX has the split winglet, which is large going both up and down, and the edges remain flat and straight. While some 737 NGs have split scimitar winglets, the upper and lower edges of the winglet are sloped.

Lastly, the 737 MAX has perfectly round engines, while the 737 NG engines flatten out a bit at the bottom, or look more oval.

How can you tell the difference between the variants? In terms of fuselage design, there’s the 737-700, 737-800/737 MAX 8, and 737-900/737 MAX 9 (with the 737 MAX 7 and 737 MAX 10 entering service soon). The 737-700 is the smallest variant, and the easiest way to identify it is based on the single exit on each side over the wing.

The 737-800 and 737 MAX 8 have two exits over the wing on each side, in addition to the exits at the front and back of the aircraft. The only exception would be the 737 MAX 8200, which is operated by some ultra low cost carriers, where there’s an extra exit in the back, with nine windows behind it.

Then the 737-900 and 737 MAX 9 have two exits over the wing, plus they have an additional door plug (as opposed to an actual exit) between the wing and rear exit, which is why the window spacing is a little weird in the back.

While Boeing’s modern narrow body aircraft is the 737, there are still a fair number of 757s flying around. The 757 is sort of like a flying pencil, as it’s quite long and the fuselage is narrow.

Unlike most other narrow body planes, the 757 has 10 wheels, as it has two wheels in the front, and two sets of four wheels in the back, which differentiates it from the 737, A320, etc., as those planes typically only have six wheels. The 757 also has a “proper” exit door behind the forward section, plus two overwing exits.

There are two variants of the 757 — the 757-200 and 757-300. The way to tell them apart is easy. The 757-200 does not typically have an additional exit between the overwing exits and the rear door.

Meanwhile the 757-300 does have another full exit in the rear section, with roughly a dozen windows on each side between it and the rear door. The 757-300 looks so long that you’d think it would break in half (don’t worry, it won’t).

As far as I’m concerned, the Boeing 747 will always be the queen of the skies. While the Airbus A380 has overtaken it in terms of size and passenger comfort, it can’t compete with the 747’s curves. The 747 has a full lower deck and then a partial upper deck, making it easy to identify.

While the passenger version of the 747 is becoming increasingly rare nowadays, there are two types that are most common — the 747-400 and the 747-8 (and no, it’s not the 747-800).

How can you tell the difference between the two planes? For one, the 747-400 has traditional winglets that stick “up.” On top of that, the 747-400 has a smaller upper deck. Behind the upper deck exit row, there are only seven windows on each side.

As a point of comparison, the 747-8’s wingtips gradually go up, and the upper deck is bigger, with 15 windows on each side behind the upper deck exit row.

The rear of the 747-8’s engines are also similar to those of the 787, with a zig-zag pattern, as I’ll explain below.

From a distance, it’s not unreasonable to think that a 767 and 777 look alike. I even sometimes make that mistake. It’s especially tricky since there’s the 767-300 and 767-400, and they’re roughly proportional to the 777-200 and 777-300 in terms of their dimensions.

What makes identifying the 767 especially tough is that many airlines have “modified” them. Some airlines have winglets on the 767, while others don’t. Some airlines have two doors on each side of the 767-300, while others have three doors.

So let me make this simple — at the base of each wing, the 767 has two sets of two wheels. In other words, on each side there are four wheels, for a total of 10 wheels on the plane (including the two nose wheels). Meanwhile the 777 has three sets of two wheels at the base of each wing, for a total of six wheels on each side. I know this might sound minor, but I’ve actually found it to be a very easy way to tell the planes apart.

How can you tell the difference between the 767-300 and 767-400? The 767-300 has at most three sets of doors on each side (and sometimes just two), while the 767-400 has four sets of doors on each side.

For me there are four identifying characteristics of the 777 — two huge engines, no winglets, a total of 14 wheels (two in the front, and six in the back on each side, with three rows of wheels there), and a vertically flat and boxy tail cone below the tail (as opposed to a rounded one on most other jets).

But how do you tell the difference between a Boeing 777-200 and a Boeing 777-300?

A Boeing 777-200 has just four doors on each side of the aircraft (one in the very front, one in front of the wing, one behind the wing, and one in the very back).

Meanwhile the 777-300 has five doors on each side of the aircraft (one in the very front, one in front of the wing, one immediately above the wing, one behind the wing, and one in the very back).

The easiest way to identify the 787 is by the zig-zag “cut outs” in the back of the engine, known as chevrons (designed for noise reduction). Also, the wings have a unique shape. While there aren’t abrupt winglets, the wings “stretch” pretty high up.

If you’re staring right at the front of the plane, there’s another easy identifier. The 787 is the only wide body jet to have four cockpit windows, rather than six.

How do you tell the difference between the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10? Personally I can eyeball it pretty easily, but it can be tough for some people to do, since all versions of the plane have four exits on each side, similar wings, the same number of wheels, etc.

The only real difference between the planes is the length — the 787-8 is 186 feet long, the 787-9 is 206 feet long, and the 787-10 is 224 feet long. That’s a pretty significant difference, as the longest version is over 20% longer than the shortest version.

I think a 787-8 is pretty easy to spot, because it looks quite small from the outside. Usually I look at the number of windows between the first and second set of doors. If there are 10 or fewer windows on each side (including ones that are “blacked out”), it’s a 787-8.

Meanwhile if there are more than 10 but fewer than 15 windows on each side between the first and second set of doors, it’s the 787-9.

If there are more than 15 windows between the first and second set of doors on each side, it’s the 787-10.

The Airbus A220 is one of the most pleasant narrow body aircraft to fly. This is a fairly small, sleek, and modern looking aircraft. I know this might sound silly, but to me, it looks like an Airbus A350 that shrunk.

There are a few easiest ways to tell this apart from other jets. For one, unlike the 737 and A320, the A220 has four cockpit windows, rather than six. You’ll also notice that the nose of the aircraft is straighter and longer, compared to the more rounded nose of the A320.

The plane also has distinctive winglets, at least among narrow body planes. The winglets exclusively go up, and are pretty straight. They’re not as curved or vertical as on the A320.

There are two variants of the A220 — the A220-100 and A220-300. If you ask me, the easiest way to tell them apart is by how many windows there are between the forward door and the emergency exit over the wing. The A220-100 has roughly 12 windows on each side in this area, while the A220-300 has roughly 17 windows on each side in this area. You can also usually just eyeball it — the A220-300 looks a lot more stretched.

Much like with the 737, there are lots of A320 variants. There’s the A320ceo (the older version of the jet) and the A320neo (the more modern version of the jet, with “neo” standing for “new engine option”). Then you also have several variants, including the A319, A320, and A321.

Let’s start with the difference between the A320ceo and A320neo, which largely comes down to the engines, as you might have guessed based on the “neo” name. Not only does the A320neo have bigger engines than the A320ceo, but the A320neo also has extensions at the rear of the engine at the top and bottom. In simple words, you’ll notice how the engine looks more “open” in the back, unlike on the A320ceo, where it looks like it “closes” more.

Now let’s talk about how to tell the variants apart. The A319 is smaller than the A320 and A321, and an easy identifier is that it typically has only one exit over the wing on each side.

Meanwhile the A320ceo and A320neo have two exits on each side over the wing, but no other exits between the forward and rear doors.

Lastly, the A321ceo and A321neo are the largest variants of the jet, and just generally look stretched. These planes have an extra set of exits, beyond the forward and rear doors, plus the two exits on each side over the wing. So you’ll either notice an extra door, or some weird window spacing toward the back of the plane. The A321LR and A321XLR are just variants of the A321neo, and from the outside, there’s not an obvious way to tell them apart.

The major challenge with identifying the A330 is that there are two very different types of these planes — there’s the A330-200/300, which is the original version of the plane, and then there’s the A330-800/900neo, which is the new version of the plane. To some people, the A330-900neo may look more like an A350-900 than an A330-300.

Let’s start with the A330-200/300. This plane is pretty “proportional” looking, and can easily be identified by the fact that it has two engines and the most “traditional” winglets out there. The winglets are an easy way to differentiate it from the other twin-engine wide bodies out there. Furthermore, the plane has four doors on each side.

The A330-800/900neo has a similar body style, except the winglets are different. While the A330-200/300 winglets are wide and point almost straight up, the A330-800/900neo winglets get narrower, and curve a bit more.

The A330neo and A350 have similar general designs, though there is a big difference in the wingtips, as you’ll see below when I cover the A350. If anyone has any other easy ways to spot the difference between the two planes, please let me know.

The A340 is a single deck plane with four engines, which makes it pretty easy to identify, since it’s the only non-double decker that has four engines. But how do you tell the difference between the A340-200/300 and A340-600? Okay, truth be told there aren’t a lot of these planes flying anymore, so there aren’t many situations where you’ll have to do that. With Lufthansa having just retired the A340-600, you’ll barely find the plane outside of Iran nowadays. But still…

The A340-200/300 has engines that looks disproportionately small (like, are these things gonna propel us through the sky at 500 miles per hour, or dry my hair?), and also has just four doors on each side of the aircraft.

Meanwhile the A340-600 is a gorgeous, beastly work of art. It’s so long, so skinny, and has appropriately sized-looking engines. There are also five doors on each side of the aircraft. Personally after the 747, I find the A340-600 to be the most beautiful plane. However, like I said, you won’t find it in the skies of most countries anymore.

The Airbus A350 has two main identifying characteristics — an extremely sleek design (especially near the nose, and with the Batman-looking cockpit windows), and very “steep” winglets (they’re not gradual, unlike the 787).

How do you tell the difference between the A350-900 and A350-1000? There are two main differences.

For one, the A350-900 has 10 wheels, while the A350-1000 has 14 wheels. The difference comes from the base of each wing having six wheels (three rows of two) rather than four wheels (two rows of two). That’s because the A350-1000 is the stretched version of the A350-900.

The easiest other way to tell the difference is based on the number of windows between doors one and two. The A350-900 has somewhere around 15 windows on each side between the first two sets of doors.

Meanwhile the A350-1000 has over 20 windows on each side between the first and second set of doors.

I don’t think anyone has trouble identifying this whale-jet, given that it has two full decks.

Understandably not everyone can spot the difference between airplanes, because, well, to most people it doesn’t actually matter. That being said, for us avgeeks it’s often a favorite pastime. Hopefully the above is a simple guide that can help people tell apart planes, should they be interested in learning a bit more.

While there are lots of other differences, I figure it makes sense to highlight some of the most “obvious” tricks, as opposed to studying each plane in great detail.

To fellow avgeeks, I’d be curious to hear how you easily tell planes apart!

#6050. Bitter Christmas: A Bah Humbug to Moviemaking

Almodóvar’s loss of creativity and camp is cause for alarm.

Pedro Almodóvar’s Bitter Christmas explores his own recent creative crisis. Using a prismatic structure, Almodóvar tells three stories that reflect one another with diminishing returns. These interwoven tales never blend due to the blockage suffered by gay male Spanish filmmaker Raul (Leonardo Sbaraglia, styled with a storm of gray-white hair to resemble Almodóvar himself). Viewers must do a meta reading about the nature and purpose of filmmaking and artistic expression.

Almodóvar makes the mistake of introducing Raul’s imaginary stories before revealing their real-life source. As Bitter Christmas becomes more and more convoluted and uninvolving, it undeniably reflects a peculiar Millennial crisis: the internalized post-Covid repression that has paralyzed many filmmakers. Once the most exciting filmmaker of the late 1980s, Almodóvar now suffers the same malaise that has also befallen comparable colleagues Martin Scorsese and Steven Spielberg. You don’t have to be a cinephile to realize that most contemporary filmmakers are bereft of fresh ideas and genuine inspiration.

Before getting to that core Raul/Almodóvar narrative, Bitter Christmas first presents stories in which a female filmmaker Elsa (Bárbara Lennie) imagines the drama of a woman, Patrizia (Victoria Luengo), who feels her same maladies and longs to escape an unhappy marriage, and then another woman, Natalia (Milena Smit), who is deep in mourning. This narrative contraption is the worst example of a gay male’s feminine empathy that Almodóvar has ever contrived. Unlike Law of Desire and Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown, this film lacks the camp buoyancy that made Almodóvar a comic hybrid of Jean Cocteau and Luis Buñuel, putting him at the vanguard of the world’s evolving sexual sophistication.

Now foregrounding his identification with female experience, Almodóvar seems to cater to political correctness rather than flout it. That a once-major pop artist can no longer make irresistible movies but instead succumbs to patronizing political trends is a cause for alarm more significant than any particular misbegotten film.

In one subplot, Raul is told, “You can lie in your life but not in your fiction,” referring to how he mistreats his partner Santi (Quim Gutiérrez) while also exploiting his assistant Mónica (Aitana Sánchez-Gijón) as fodder for his newest script.

This contorted set-up suggests that Almodóvar feels pressure to join the global progressivism that a former bad boy of the Spanish underground is now obliged to endorse. That’s why the ultra-bourgeois Bitter Christmas lacks comedy and eroticism. Raul’s sex life is transferred to the shallow, quasi-porn of Elsa’s relationship with boytoy Bonifacio (Patrick Criado), a firefighter and part-time stripper (probably an homage to the superior João Pedro Rodrigues satire Will-O’-the-Wisp.

Almodóvar has lost audacity. Sadness pervades the movie. Its title comes from “Amarga Navidad” (“Bitter Christmas”), a ranchera (folk torch song) performed by Chavela Vargas. But this is the least impassioned film Almodóvar has made; its emotions are distanced by artifice — in imagination, storytelling, and performance. The projection of Raul/Almodóvar’s true feelings into fakery distances real life so much that the melodrama is drab. It’s not fabulous or funny (despite ornamental design and another urgent Alberto Iglesias score), but arid like Lanzarote, the black-sand volcanic island where make-believe characters Elsa and Victoria retreat into a dull version of Ingmar Bergman’s Persona — another go at Almodóvar’s insipid The Room Next Door. None of these meta-antics result in moral summation like Fellini’s masterpieces La Dolce Vita and Otto e mezzo.

Although Almodóvar avoids obvious political pronouncement like those that ruined Killers of the Flower Moon, West Side Story, and Disclosure Day, the twisted autobiographical aspects of Bitter Christmas still indicate that he suffers a similar personal liberal panic. (Unlike Spielberg and Scorsese, Almodóvar has made foolish partisan comments on American politics.) Almodóvar can’t escape the private anxiety that Scorsese and Spielberg experience along with the rest of us. Almodóvar’s inability to disentangle primal emotional need from political confusion is evident on screen in Bitter Christmas and ultimately unsatisfying.

Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

#6049. American Airlines Reverses Its Original New York Strategy—Wants Local Customers Back In Major Cities

American Airlines says focusing on local customers has produced “material margin improvement” at LaGuardia. They’re doing better in New York by focusing on the needs of New Yorkers. Meanwhile, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said at at Thursday’s Skift Aviation Forum that he sees Chicago’s biggest opportunity in winning corporate traffic, and he’s working on Los Angeles schedules that better serve the people who live there too. That’s a full rejection of the New York strategy American laid out in 2014, immediately after the US Airways merger. They wanted to bring passengers to New York, rather than offer a schedule for New Yorkers. That was dumb. They thought they couldn’t compete in New York, and they walked away from the credit card spending of New Yorkers. American Chose Not To Be The Airline For New Yorkers The original post-merger strategy was building schedules around people coming to New York for business and then going home. Arriving in the morning and leaving in the evening works for an out of town visitor. A New Yorker making a day trip wants the reverse. American dropped LaGuardia service to Cleveland, Minneapolis and Atlanta while adding cities like Roanoke and Wilmington, North Carolina. They were using scarce New York slots to strengthen their appeal to customers they believed were underserved elsewhere in the country, instead of building a schedule to take people who lived in New York to the places they needed to go. It was an extension of the old US Airways playbook of avoiding direct competition. By 2018, Robert Isom was pitching a boutique business airline for New York, built around London, premium transcons and a limited collection of other routes. That was already a change from the original inbound strategy. It still missed that the person buying a business class ticket to London also takes their family on vacation. And by not providing either a better product or a more well-rounded schedule, they were setting themselves up to be a ‘spill carrier’ taking business only when offering a lower price that competitors wouldn’t meet. The JetBlue partnership demonstrated what a broader network could do. In October 2021, I reported American’s fastest growing markets for AAdvantage signups were its JetBlue and Alaska partnership cities. Doug Parker Explained The Credit Card Math Problem In March, I wrote about former American CEO Doug Parker’s explanation of how airlines allocate credit card revenue to routes. He described assigning the money to flights where customers redeem their miles. That accounts for the seats being used. It doesn’t tell you which flights caused the customer to get the card and put spending on it in the first place. A New Yorker might use their miles for Hawaii. But they chose American because it worked for their trips to Chicago, London and Miami. If American stops being useful for those trips, the customer may switch airlines and cards. Crediting the Hawaii flight doesn’t capture what the New York schedule was doing for the business. That was my criticism of American’s retreat seven and eight years ago: cutting a flight can improve its route accounting while making the company worse off by losing the customer’s other business. You can’t count the card revenue twice, but you need to count what disappears when the customer leaves. Chicago And Los Angeles Need The Same Rethink This is also why the O’Hare fight matters beyond departure counts and Scott Kirby’s desire to beat American. At the employee meeting I covered in January, Pieper reported 20% growth in Chicago loyalty enrollments and 20% growth in card acquisitions over the preceding nine months. As I explained when Chief Financial Officer Devon May addressed Chicago profitability in March, allocated overhead, network effects and credit card economics can produce very different answers to whether a hub makes money. May said their usual flight profitability systems don’t directly capture all those card effects. Meanwhile, American withdrew Los Angeles long haul flying and became less useful to local customers. In October I contrasted the old network strategy with Pieper’s plans to reverse it. He’d told Brett Snyder at Cranky Flier: I fundamentally believe we need to fly our own airplanes to the big markets in the world In his Skift comments, he describes schedule changes continuing through 2027 toward a 2028 terminal rebuild and a 30-gate operation. Yet in his October 12 interview with Cranky Flier, the plan was 25 gates across terminals 4 and 5, while Pieper wanted all 30. American’s fifth lease amendment, approved by the City Council on December 10, 2025, provides for 25 preferential use gates after Terminal 5 reopens: all 15 in Terminal 4 and 10 in Terminal 5. LAWA’s 30-gate description is for the entire two-terminal complex, not American’s allocation. American has been using 5 Tom Bradley terminal gates, but those are temporary replacements during Terminal 5 construction. American can seek additional Bradley, but they aren’t assured five permanent extras. The lease also ends LAWA’s obligation to accommodate American at the remote Eagle’s Nest when the rebuilt Terminal 5 opens. So 25 is the documented allocation in terminals 4 and 5, and 30 is the larger operation Pieper wants. It’s not clear to me how he’s able to say that they’ll have them – I hope they will! The Alaska Partnership Fits This, Too American nearly threw away its Alaska partnership for a related reason. As I reported when Parker explained the reversal in February 2020, American had seen Alaska’s purchase of Virgin America as creating more route overlap, turning a partner into a competitor. But Alaska had strength in Northern California and the Pacific Northwest that American lacked. Those customers could make American’s flights more valuable, and a broader combined offering could win corporate accounts neither carrier could serve as well alone. The original plan had American operating long haul flights from Seattle, supported by Alaska. Bangalore and Shanghai never started. London started and then disappeared. Alaska bought Hawaiian and began building the international airline American hadn’t delivered. As I wrote in September, bringing Alaska into the Atlantic joint venture with British Airways and partners, and the Pacific venture with Japan Airlines, would change the incentives. American would have a financial interest in selling Alaska’s international flights, while the foreign partners could bring customers from the other end. They could coordinate schedules rather than merely put a codeshare on an existing flight. More Flights Aren’t Enough To Win Scott Kirby was explaining the network and credit card connection back in 2017. United needed better domestic schedules to win customers, who would then become prospects for its card. American needs to repair the parts of its network that prevent it from earning a customer’s broader business. But I also pushed back on Kirby’s assumption that network size would win the card business. The competition includes bank cards with transferable points and cash back, not just another airline’s card. American’s newer Citi relationship makes the network and product investments more consequential. As I wrote last month about its ambition to approach $10 billion in annual loyalty partner payments, acquiring a cardmember, keeping them, and getting them to spend are different tasks. That’s why it matters tremendously that American is working to build a better airline. And it matters that they preserve the quality and advantages of their AAdvantage program. Without either of those, the gambit gets expensive fast but doesn’t deliver the hoped-for results. Meanwhile, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said at at Thursday’s Skift Aviation Forum that he sees Chicago’s biggest opportunity in winning corporate traffic, and he’s working on Los Angeles schedules that better serve the people who live there too.

That’s a full rejection of the New York strategy American laid out in 2014, immediately after the US Airways merger. They wanted to bring passengers to New York, rather than offer a schedule for New Yorkers. That was dumb. They thought they couldn’t compete in New York, and they walked away from the credit card spending of New Yorkers.

The original post-merger strategy was building schedules around people coming to New York for business and then going home. Arriving in the morning and leaving in the evening works for an out of town visitor. A New Yorker making a day trip wants the reverse. American dropped LaGuardia service to Cleveland, Minneapolis and Atlanta while adding cities like Roanoke and Wilmington, North Carolina. They were using scarce New York slots to strengthen their appeal to customers they believed were underserved elsewhere in the country, instead of building a schedule to take people who lived in New York to the places they needed to go. It was an extension of the old US Airways playbook of avoiding direct competition. By 2018, Robert Isom was pitching a boutique business airline for New York, built around London, premium transcons and a limited collection of other routes. That was already a change from the original inbound strategy. It still missed that the person buying a business class ticket to London also takes their family on vacation. And by not providing either a better product or a more well-rounded schedule, they were setting themselves up to be a ‘spill carrier’ taking business only when offering a lower price that competitors wouldn’t meet. The JetBlue partnership demonstrated what a broader network could do. In October 2021, I reported American’s fastest growing markets for AAdvantage signups were its JetBlue and Alaska partnership cities. Doug Parker Explained The Credit Card Math Problem In March, I wrote about former American CEO Doug Parker’s explanation of how airlines allocate credit card revenue to routes. He described assigning the money to flights where customers redeem their miles. That accounts for the seats being used. It doesn’t tell you which flights caused the customer to get the card and put spending on it in the first place. A New Yorker might use their miles for Hawaii. But they chose American because it worked for their trips to Chicago, London and Miami. If American stops being useful for those trips, the customer may switch airlines and cards. Crediting the Hawaii flight doesn’t capture what the New York schedule was doing for the business. That was my criticism of American’s retreat seven and eight years ago: cutting a flight can improve its route accounting while making the company worse off by losing the customer’s other business. You can’t count the card revenue twice, but you need to count what disappears when the customer leaves. Chicago And Los Angeles Need The Same Rethink This is also why the O’Hare fight matters beyond departure counts and Scott Kirby’s desire to beat American. At the employee meeting I covered in January, Pieper reported 20% growth in Chicago loyalty enrollments and 20% growth in card acquisitions over the preceding nine months. As I explained when Chief Financial Officer Devon May addressed Chicago profitability in March, allocated overhead, network effects and credit card economics can produce very different answers to whether a hub makes money. May said their usual flight profitability systems don’t directly capture all those card effects. Meanwhile, American withdrew Los Angeles long haul flying and became less useful to local customers. In October I contrasted the old network strategy with Pieper’s plans to reverse it. He’d told Brett Snyder at Cranky Flier: I fundamentally believe we need to fly our own airplanes to the big markets in the world In his Skift comments, he describes schedule changes continuing through 2027 toward a 2028 terminal rebuild and a 30-gate operation. Yet in his October 12 interview with Cranky Flier, the plan was 25 gates across terminals 4 and 5, while Pieper wanted all 30. American’s fifth lease amendment, approved by the City Council on December 10, 2025, provides for 25 preferential use gates after Terminal 5 reopens: all 15 in Terminal 4 and 10 in Terminal 5. LAWA’s 30-gate description is for the entire two-terminal complex, not American’s allocation. American has been using 5 Tom Bradley terminal gates, but those are temporary replacements during Terminal 5 construction. American can seek additional Bradley, but they aren’t assured five permanent extras. The lease also ends LAWA’s obligation to accommodate American at the remote Eagle’s Nest when the rebuilt Terminal 5 opens. So 25 is the documented allocation in terminals 4 and 5, and 30 is the larger operation Pieper wants. It’s not clear to me how he’s able to say that they’ll have them – I hope they will! The Alaska Partnership Fits This, Too American nearly threw away its Alaska partnership for a related reason. As I reported when Parker explained the reversal in February 2020, American had seen Alaska’s purchase of Virgin America as creating more route overlap, turning a partner into a competitor. But Alaska had strength in Northern California and the Pacific Northwest that American lacked. Those customers could make American’s flights more valuable, and a broader combined offering could win corporate accounts neither carrier could serve as well alone. The original plan had American operating long haul flights from Seattle, supported by Alaska. Bangalore and Shanghai never started. London started and then disappeared. Alaska bought Hawaiian and began building the international airline American hadn’t delivered. As I wrote in September, bringing Alaska into the Atlantic joint venture with British Airways and partners, and the Pacific venture with Japan Airlines, would change the incentives. American would have a financial interest in selling Alaska’s international flights, while the foreign partners could bring customers from the other end. They could coordinate schedules rather than merely put a codeshare on an existing flight. More Flights Aren’t Enough To Win Scott Kirby was explaining the network and credit card connection back in 2017. United needed better domestic schedules to win customers, who would then become prospects for its card. American needs to repair the parts of its network that prevent it from earning a customer’s broader business. But I also pushed back on Kirby’s assumption that network size would win the card business. The competition includes bank cards with transferable points and cash back, not just another airline’s card. American’s newer Citi relationship makes the network and product investments more consequential. As I wrote last month about its ambition to approach $10 billion in annual loyalty partner payments, acquiring a cardmember, keeping them, and getting them to spend are different tasks. That’s why it matters tremendously that American is working to build a better airline. And it matters that they preserve the quality and advantages of their AAdvantage program. Without either of those, the gambit gets expensive fast but doesn’t deliver the hoped-for results. I’m not surprised to hear AA talking about wanting to be more competitive in New York, Chicago, and Los Angeles. They’ve been running a promo, seemingly targeted at travelers who have flown American for business, offering bonus miles for segments to/from/through NYC/ORD/LAX.

AA is finally starting to learn the lesson that George Costanza learned. Every instinct that they have had for the past 10 years has been wrong. So, just do the opposite.

You really do have to wonder how much longer Devon May can survive. He’s been on the wrong side of every product decision at AA and been the key voice against product improvement.

But it’s also a very AA phenomenon — keeping bad leaders who have never shown a shred of strategic thinking.

Speaking from the position of a +40 year ~4 million-mile Platinum Pro A/Advantage customer, when American began abandoning New York for both transcontinental and international flights, I began abandoning American and it will take a lot to bring me and many other top tier former loyal NYC area customers back. Unfortunately, the airline has been mismanaged and mistreated loyal customers since Bob Crandell left in 1998 and both shareholders and loyal customers have suffered. It’s time for a major overall of both senior management and the Board and a new attitude/approach from American’s current poor customer service team.

Day by day Nat and Heather are fixing the Vasu, Parker and Isom effups.

They can reshuffle the existing fleet to serve both segments…early morning locals departing the hub and early morning visitors to the hub.

This is good to see and it is reflected in the schedules (for example, JFK-ORD is now 4 x daily) and the resumption of JFK-SEA with 2 x daily (which will be complemented by the AS flying). AA has some holes to fill in its NY portfolio. It should fly from JFK to SAT for example, and continue to pick up markets that B6 is walking away from. Eventually, American will have the majority of the B6 portfolio to themselves and that will unlock their ability to be a competitive force in the NYC market. AA must still continue to refine and improve its offering and maintain and grow the pivot to premium. The money is in the NYC, Chicago, and LA markets, not in the sunbelt.

@Gary–This article is an excellent analysis. I agree that flight times are important to local passengers. When I visit NYC or Chicago, I like to depart such that I arrive in the mid to late afternoon. That allows me to check into a hotel upon arrival and have the evening to get a good meal, go to a show, erc. I like to come home on a late afternoon flight ti maximize my time on the trip. (That kind of scheduling appeals to leisure travelers as well as business travelers.). If I lived in NY or Chicago, I would like similar schedules if flying west.

@Joe–I agree that whenever possible, an airline should try to schedule in a way that works for both ends of the city pair.

@Peter – exactly right! Best post of the day.

I would add AA needs to add back a few non stop flights from NY and BOS to South Florida and Orlando. This is the key to winning the NY/ BOS domestic market.

Seems like Parker and Kerr (the US Airways CFO who served at AA until 2023, promoting May) were the ones who are most responsible for where we are now – finance ran the show. Vasu, and even Isom inherited a lot of the implications of their thinking.

And let’s not forget Kirby before he learned new ways at United – decisions in the early 2010s set up the fleet and network we have today

Southwest has a miniscule presence in New York. Delta has a miniscule presence in Chicago. Yet both are much more profitable than American. How can that be?

@DesertGhost – Delta has #1 at JFK/LGA and #1 at LAX. They themselves say the reason for AUS expansion is card revenue. Southwest is huge in California. Huge in Florida. And has lower costs. And their profits aren’t that much higher than American’s.

AA should also try to add SAN, maybe CPH and ZRH from JFK. Also should build more of a focus city at Boston Logan. There is card revenue there!

Is it possible AA could get from ~11% of JFK market share to 15-20%?

this is precisely why Scott Kirby is paranoid.

AA is coming back and UA can no longer count on revenue that AA has been bleeding for years.

DL’s focus on “stealing from” AA was largely pre-covid and at LAX during covid. DL is comfortable w/ its domestic size now and is not focused on market share and is reaping the profits accordingly even while continuing to take share from B6 in the NE.

AA is the largest domestic airline because of their size in a whole lot of small and medium sized cities.

AA steal carries a lot of low fare traffic it should not be carrying but it cannot get rid of it until it replaces it with higher quality revenue in coastal cities.

Speaking as someone who is now approaching 17 years of experience traveling with kids, having the right "stuff" matters more than you might think.

Something for the kids to do, something to keep the devices charged, something to hold all the stuff, something to hold the kid and something comfy to wear (with pockets!) throughout the process are just a few of the things that can make family travel a little easier along the way.

So, as we approach the holiday season, here are 11 of my tried-and-true recommendations for gifts, whether you're shopping for yourself or another family on the go.

Best for: Preschool-aged kids who fly frequently

If your family travels a lot and your preschool-aged kid wants a really cool piece of luggage all their own that matches yours, then the Away Kids Carry-On Luggage is a great choice. It's not only fun, but really well made.

It comes in colors such as berry pink and dragonfly blue — and there are even some limited-edition colors and collections, including a current Toy Story line. The handle adjusts to two heights: one for them and one for you when they ... decide to be done. Like the full-size models, it has a TSA-approved lock and a compression system.

Once your kiddos get much past the preschool years, they might be better off with full-sized Away Carry-On bags simply because they hold more. But there are a few good years when these bags are absolutely perfect for little frequent flyers.

TPG tip: Not only does Away sometimes run pretty decent Black Friday sales, but there are periodically Chase Offers that save you $50 or more on certain Away bag orders with cards such as the (see rates and fees).

Best for: Families with multiple devices they need to keep charged on the go

Phones, tablets, headphones — virtually everything requires power on the go these days, so having a good charger for the family is a must. Anker makes some of the best, and one that can be especially handy when you have a family's worth of devices to keep charged is the Anker MagGo Power Bank. It has a kickstand, shows you the battery percentage and time remaining to charge, can charge itself while recharging your devices and can get an iPhone to about 50% power in just 30 minutes.

TPG tip: Anker chargers are sold at many big retailers, so to earn bonus miles or cash back on this (and other) purchases, check CashBackMonitor.com before buying to see which shopping portal is offering the biggest reward for clicking through first.

Best for: Teens and tweens who like taking pictures and having something tangible to show for it beyond photos on their phones

Gen Alpha and Gen Z are into nostalgia — and with that comes photos you can hold in your hand instead of just viewing on your phone. Frankly, I'm here for it.

One of the mini cameras that makes this easy is the Fujifilm Instax Mini 13. It has two self-timer options, a cute design available in five colors and produces instant prints measuring roughly 2 by 3 inches. It's a fun way to give your kids physical memories of their travels instead of having every photo live somewhere in the cloud.

TPG tip: The camera typically does not come with film, so be sure to pick up Instax mini instant film to go with the gift.

Best for: Moms who want to be comfy on the plane but also a tiny bit on trend

Being comfortable when kiddos are involved is often priority number one, whether you're running around at home, navigating an airport or flying halfway around the world.

Enter one of my favorite brands: Vuori, which makes some of the most comfortable clothes I own.

My current favorite is the Vuori Halo Essential Wide Leg Pants in black. They go with almost everything, are cozy for the plane, are made with Vuori's DreamKnit material and have pockets — an absolute must on travel days. They also come in short, regular and long lengths, so you can find the right fit.

TPG tip: If you want even more comfy athleisure in your luggage or under the tree, remember that the comes with a quarterly up to $75 credit for Lululemon (enrollment required). And you can still check to see if Lululemon is on a site such as Rakuten to potentially earn some bonus points or cash back.

Best for: Ages 3 - 10 often love these, but they can really work for virtually any age who likes to hold a 'pen' and draw.

LCD drawing tablets are the definition of punching above their weight (er, price) class when it comes to how much entertainment they provide for how little they cost.

We've had tablets like these draw a crowd at a delayed boarding gate full of children before, especially when Grandma was smart enough to buy a few extras "just in case" since they are so affordable.

They're fun, mess-free, inexpensive and perfect for long flights or car rides. Plus, many are designed to be resistant to some inevitable drops and spills that come with traveling with kids.

TPG tip: Because they are so affordable, it might be worth picking up an extra one.

Best for: Travelers who want to stay organized (honestly, I think everyone who travels can benefit from these)

The list of reasons I recommend packing cubes for family travel is longer than The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King extended edition. But here's the abridged version: You can easily pack by person or by day, stay organized and often fit more into your bags than you could without packing cubes.

And a bonus reason I bet you wouldn't have guessed is that packing cubes can be a good way to help reduce the chances of bringing bed bugs home if you use them in your larger packing and unpacking strategy, as I do. Calpak makes very durable packing cubes that also come in really cute patterns and colors, such as polka dot and dark cherry, alongside classics like black.

TPG tip: Even if you don't pack for the whole trip by day, having a packing cube full of the first night and next full day's worth of clothes so you don't have to dig through all the bags right away is one of my favorite travel hacks.

Best for: Anyone with Apple devices who owns virtually anything they don't want to lose.

At this point, we probably almost all know and love AirTags. But with the second generation now offering improved range, they're even more useful, and honestly, I don't think you can realistically ever have too many.

Put one in each piece of luggage, your kids' backpacks, your sling bag, on your keychain, on your pet's collar, even in your carry-on bags you don't plan to be parted from ... just in case.

TPG tip: You can now share the location of the AirTag you put in your checked luggage with many airlines in case your bag is delayed, helping reunite you with your things faster.

Best for: Travelers who want a sleek, cool, functional bag that looks like it cost a lot more than it did.

I have luggage brands that cost double or more what this Quince bag costs, but it was just as light as those pricier brands I've tried and rolled at least as well with its 360° spinner wheels, had a very smooth and easy-to-use handle and came in a fun dark green color.

TPG tip: The Quince expandable carry-on is the one I was gifted by Quince to try out, and I love the extra space over the traditional carry-on size and it fit in the overhead bin just fine. However, be aware that some airlines (and certain gate agents) can be stricter than others about size limits on expandable luggage and may ask you to unexpand it.

Best for: Families with newborns and young babies

When I look back on our time with little kids, there's one purchase that I'd make a million times over: The Doona.

And I still see parents-in-the-know using it now more than ever for the same reason we loved it once upon a time. The Doona transforms from a car seat into a stroller in seconds, without even having to take your baby out of the seat.

It's fantastic for hopping in and out of cabs, navigating airports and bringing an approved car seat aboard a plane, all without having to lug both a car seat and a stroller.

One caveat: It's rated for babies weighing 4 to 35 pounds and measuring up to 32 inches tall, but in my experience, it isn't uncommon for kids to outgrow it well before their first birthday. For those early months when it works, though, it's fantastic.

TPG tip: You can typically fly with your Doona if you purchase your baby a seat, even though you typically don't have to have them in their own seat until they turn two.

Best for: Parents who love to travel with kids ages 2 to 6 who weigh under 80 pounds

There's an awkward phase of family travel when your kids might be too big for you to want to haul a stroller everywhere with you but still can't be trusted to walk through an airport at a reasonable pace for more than 30 seconds.

And for that phase, having luggage that little kids can 'ride' on can be both handy and fun. One of the brands that offers that is Younglingz with their ride-on suitcases that come in fun themes like unicorns, fire trucks and motorcycles. This way, you are getting your kids and their things through the airport even when the walk starts to get a little longer than you'd like.

TPG tip: If you are purchasing this (or anything) on Amazon, be on the lookout for periodic promotions that can save you $15 to $40 (or sometimes more) by using just a few Amex Membership Rewards points toward the purchase.
