#6047. How The Boeing 737 MAX, 747-8, & 787 Dreamliner's Engines Create Problems No Other Modern Jet Faces

Modern commercial jet engines are among the most refined pieces of engineering ever developed. They are quieter, more fuel-efficient, and dramatically cleaner than the engines that powered earlier generations of airliners. Yet three of Boeing’s most important aircraft families, the Boeing 737 MAX, 747-8, and 787 Dreamliner, carry an unusual design feature that introduces a problem almost no competing modern jet faces: serrated engine exhaust nozzles known as chevrons.

The distinctive sawtooth patterns visible on the rear edges of the engine nacelles were designed primarily to reduce noise. Boeing developed the concept alongside General Electric and NASA as airlines faced increasingly strict airport noise regulations and growing community pressure around major hubs. The system succeeded in making aircraft quieter during takeoff and landing, particularly on the Dreamliner. However, the solution came with a trade-off. The same aerodynamic mixing effect that lowers noise also creates drag and slightly reduces engine thrust during all phases of flight, including cruise, where noise reduction provides little operational benefit. Over time, Boeing itself began searching for alternatives, eventually abandoning chevrons entirely. The result is a fascinating engineering story about how one innovation solved a regulatory challenge while simultaneously creating a performance penalty that no other major aircraft manufacturer chose to accept.

Chevrons are serrated trailing edges built into the rear section of an engine nozzle. Instead of a smooth circular exhaust outlet, the nozzle edge features a repeating sawtooth pattern extending into the exhaust flow. Boeing introduced the technology commercially on the 787 before expanding it to the 747-8 and the 737 MAX family. Every 787 engine variant uses chevrons, regardless of whether the aircraft is powered by Rolls-Royce Trent 1000s or General Electric GEnx engines. The 747-8 and all 737 MAX variants also feature this design.

The engineering principle behind chevrons is relatively straightforward. Modern turbofan engines produce two separate exhaust flows: a hot, high-velocity core stream from the combustion section and a cooler bypass airflow generated by the fan. The interaction between these two flows creates turbulence, which is a major source of jet engine noise. Chevrons reduce that turbulence by generating controlled vortices that mix the exhaust streams together more gradually. The smoother transition lowers the acoustic intensity of the exhaust plume, particularly during high thrust operations such as takeoff and initial climb. NASA research conducted during the technology’s development confirmed measurable reductions in perceived engine noise around airports.

The concept emerged during a period when airport noise regulations were becoming increasingly restrictive worldwide. Airlines operating large fleets at densely populated urban airports faced growing pressure to reduce community noise exposure. Boeing saw chevrons as a way to improve compliance without fundamentally redesigning engine architecture. Visually, the feature also became associated with Boeing’s next-generation aircraft branding. The scalloped nacelle edges gave the 787 a distinctive appearance that emphasized technological innovation and acoustic refinement. For many passengers, the chevrons became symbolic of quieter modern air travel. Yet the aerodynamic realities behind the design created complications that became increasingly apparent over time.

The central problem with chevrons is that the vortices they intentionally create do not simply disappear once the aircraft leaves the airport environment. The aerodynamic mixing process continues throughout the entire flight, including cruise conditions where noise reduction is far less important. Those vortices slightly disrupt the exhaust flow and increase drag, which reduces overall engine efficiency and marginally lowers thrust output. Aviation analyst Petter Hörnfeldt, better known through Mentour Pilot, has estimated that the thrust penalty from chevrons is approximately 0.5%. While that figure appears small, aviation economics are built around extremely thin performance margins where even fractional efficiency losses matter significantly.

For high-utilization aircraft such as the 737 MAX, the effect becomes cumulative. Narrowbody airliners often perform multiple short-haul sectors daily, so a minor efficiency penalty applied continuously across thousands of annual flights translates into meaningful fuel burn increases over the lifespan of the aircraft. This creates the core engineering contradiction behind chevrons. The system addresses a problem most critical during takeoff and landing, but imposes its aerodynamic penalty continuously. Unlike deployable aerodynamic devices that activate only when needed, chevrons are fixed structures permanently protruding into the exhaust stream.

The issue becomes especially relevant during cruise flight. At high altitude, engines operate in carefully optimized conditions designed to minimize drag and maximize fuel efficiency. Any disruption to exhaust flow can slightly degrade propulsion efficiency. Airlines closely monitor these performance margins because fuel remains one of the largest operating expenses in commercial aviation. The penalty also affects thrust generation. While passengers would never perceive a half percent reduction in performance directly, aircraft manufacturers compete intensely over efficiency metrics. Modern airliner programs are often marketed around fuel burn improvements measured in single digit percentages. In that context, a permanent efficiency loss becomes strategically important. As noise regulations evolved and engine technology improved independently, the industry began exploring whether chevrons were still the best solution available.

Engine chevrons have become a defining feature of modern aircraft, but do they really pose a problem for performance?

One of the most revealing aspects of the story is that Airbus never adopted the technology on any of its competing modern aircraft programs. The European manufacturer chose an entirely different path for noise reduction, relying instead on nacelle acoustic treatments, advanced fan designs, and high bypass ratio engines. Initially, Boeing’s patented chevron design prevented competitors from using the concept commercially. That patent protection remained in place until 2021.

However, even after the patent expired, Airbus still showed no interest in integrating chevrons into aircraft such as the Airbus A350 or Airbus A320neo family. The company’s reasoning was unusually direct. A350 Chief Engineer Dougie Hunter publicly explained that Airbus found no compelling advantage in the technology. According to Hunter, Airbus engineers determined that chevrons did not provide sufficient noise benefits to justify the associated specific fuel consumption penalty.

That statement highlights an important philosophical difference between Boeing and Airbus during the development of next-generation aircraft. Boeing embraced a visible mechanical solution to tackle airport noise. Airbus instead prioritized improvements inside the nacelle and engine architecture itself, reducing noise without altering external exhaust geometry.

High-bypass turbofan engines already produce significantly less noise than older designs because more thrust comes from slower-moving bypass airflow rather than the high-velocity exhaust core. Airbus engineers concluded they could meet regulatory requirements without introducing additional drag-inducing structures into the exhaust stream.

The divergence also reflects how aircraft manufacturers balance competing priorities differently. Boeing accepted a measurable efficiency compromise to secure stronger community noise performance. Airbus decided the operational costs outweighed the acoustic gains. Over time, Boeing itself appeared to move closer to Airbus’ position.

The clearest evidence that Boeing recognized the limitations of chevrons emerged during the development of the Boeing 777X and its GE9X engines. Despite the feature appearing prominently on the 787, 747-8, and 737 MAX, Boeing abandoned chevrons entirely for its newest flagship widebody. Instead, Boeing and General Electric developed a radically different nozzle architecture using ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs. These advanced materials tolerate extremely high temperatures while remaining substantially lighter than traditional metallic structures. Their thermal resistance allowed engineers to create a more compact and aerodynamically efficient mixed exhaust nozzle without relying on serrated trailing edges.

The result achieved a similar acoustic performance while reducing drag and weight simultaneously. GE9X Chief Project Engineer Terry Beezhold explained that the new nozzle technology provides equivalent cabin and community noise levels but with lower drag and lighter construction. The GE9X nozzle system is reportedly around 20% lighter than older designs. This transition is significant because it effectively acknowledges the trade-offs associated with chevrons. If the technology represented the optimal long-term solution, Boeing likely would have retained it on the 777X. Instead, the company invested heavily in eliminating the feature while preserving its acoustic benefits.

The move also illustrates broader trends in engine development. Modern aerospace engineering increasingly favors integrated aerodynamic efficiency over external add-on solutions. Advanced materials, computational fluid dynamics, and improved nacelle shaping now allow manufacturers to address noise problems more elegantly than was possible when chevrons first emerged. In many ways, the 777X represents Boeing’s attempt to solve the same challenge without inheriting the same penalties.

Discover why the Boeing 777X depends entirely on the GE9X, the world’s largest and most advanced commercial jet engine ever built.

Despite their drawbacks, chevrons were not necessarily a mistake, particularly on the Dreamliner. Boeing found a secondary advantage that partially offset the performance penalty and made the overall trade-off more acceptable for that aircraft specifically.

Because the engines were substantially quieter externally, Boeing was able to reduce the amount of sound insulation material installed throughout the fuselage. Reports indicate the company eliminated up to 600 pounds, or roughly 272 kilograms, of acoustic insulation compared with what otherwise might have been required. That weight reduction improved fuel efficiency and helped compensate for the thrust and drag penalties created by the chevrons themselves. On a long-range aircraft such as the 787, where weight savings compound significantly across intercontinental missions, the trade-off became economically viable.

The Dreamliner’s broader design philosophy also supported the decision. Boeing engineered the aircraft around aggressive efficiency goals using composite materials, advanced aerodynamics, and next-generation engines. The chevrons fit within that larger optimization strategy, even if they were not an aerodynamically perfect solution in isolation. The equation was less favorable on smaller aircraft such as the 737 MAX. Narrowbody jets generally lack the same opportunities for large-scale insulation weight savings, while their high cycle utilization amplifies fuel burn penalties over time. This partly explains why criticism surrounding chevrons became more pronounced as the technology spread across Boeing’s lineup.

Still, the system undeniably succeeded in one important area: noise reduction. Airports and communities benefited from quieter operations, and airlines operating at noise-sensitive hubs gained regulatory and operational advantages. The problem was never that chevrons failed technically. The issue was that they solved one problem while creating another.

Boeing’s use of engine chevrons on the 737 MAX, 747-8, and 787 Dreamliner represents one of the more unusual engineering compromises in modern commercial aviation. Developed alongside NASA and General Electric to reduce airport noise, the serrated nozzle design successfully lowered acoustic output by improving exhaust flow mixing.

Yet the same vortices responsible for quieter operations also introduced drag and reduced engine efficiency throughout every phase of flight. That trade-off created a challenge virtually unique among major modern airliners because Airbus rejected the concept entirely, preferring alternative acoustic technologies that avoided continuous performance penalties. Boeing itself eventually moved away from chevrons on the 777X, replacing them with a more advanced low-drag nozzle architecture built around ceramic matrix composites.

The story illustrates how aviation engineering rarely produces perfect solutions. Every design decision involves balancing competing priorities, including noise, fuel efficiency, weight, emissions, maintenance, and regulatory compliance. Chevrons solved a real operational problem during a critical period in commercial aviation development. But over time, advances in engine and materials technology revealed that quieter aircraft did not necessarily require permanent aerodynamic compromises.

#6046. Which Credit Cards Give You Hotel Elite Status, And Are They Worth It?

Hotel credit cards are among the most underrated out there, thanks to the strong perks that they offer. In this post, I’d like to specifically focus on credit cards that offer hotel elite status, and talk about under what circumstances they could be worth it.

I’ve already written about the best hotel credit cards offering free nights, either as an annual benefit or as a reward for reaching certain spending thresholds. In many cases, these anniversary free night certificates can more than justify the annual fees on cards, given that they can be redeemed at some great hotels.

Nowadays it’s possible to earn elite status with most major hotel group through credit cards, so let’s talk about the options there are, and under what circumstances this is actually worth it.

I’d like to take a look at all the ways that you can use US-issued credit cards to earn elite status with a hotel loyalty program. In some cases, you get status just for having a card, and in other cases, a certain amount of spending is required.

There are potentially all kinds of benefits to hotel elite status, ranging from free breakfast to late check-out to bonus points to suite upgrades. Obviously the higher your status, the better the perks.

Here are all the options, going in alphabetical order based on the name of the loyalty program. Note that I’m only including credit cards that are only open to new cardmembers.

Choice Privileges has two credit cards that can help you earn elite status.

The following card can earn you Choice Privileges Gold status (which ordinarily requires 10 qualifying nights per calendar year):

The following card can earn you Choice Privileges Platinum status (which ordinarily requires 20 qualifying nights per calendar year):

There are no cards that offer Choice Privileges Diamond status.

Hilton Honors has several cards that can help you earn elite status.

The following card can help you earn Hilton Honors™ Silver status (which ordinarily requires 10 qualifying nights, four qualifying stays, or $2,500 in qualifying spending, per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn Hilton Honors™ Gold status (which ordinarily requires 25 qualifying nights, 15 qualifying stays, or $6,000 in qualifying spending, per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn Hilton Honors™ Diamond status (which ordinarily requires 50 qualifying nights, 25 qualifying stays, or $11,500 in qualifying spending, per calendar year):

There are no cards that offer Hilton Honors Diamond Reserve status.

IHG One Rewards has several cards that can help you earn elite status.

The following card can help you earn IHG One Rewards Silver status (which ordinarily requires 10 qualifying nights per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn IHG One Rewards Gold status (which ordinarily requires 20 qualifying nights or 40,000 base points per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn IHG One Rewards Platinum status (which ordinarily requires 40 qualifying nights or 60,000 base points per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn IHG One Rewards Diamond status (which ordinarily requires 70 qualifying nights or 120,000 base points per calendar year):

Marriott Bonvoy has several cards that can help you earn elite status. One important thing to understand upfront is that some Marriott credit cards outright offer a certain elite tier, while other cards offer a certain number of elite nights toward elite status, and some cards offer a combination of the two. So the below reflects all of those factors.

Note that each Marriott Bonvoy member can earn at most 40 elite nights per year from credit cards, with 25 elite nights coming from a personal card, and 15 elite nights coming from a business card.

The following cards can help you earn Marriott Bonvoy® Silver Elite status (which ordinarily requires 10 qualifying nights per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn Marriott Bonvoy® Gold Elite status (which ordinarily requires 25 qualifying nights per calendar year):

The following card can help you earn Marriott Bonvoy® Platinum Elite status (which ordinarily requires 50 qualifying nights per calendar year):

There are no cards that offer Marriott Bonvoy® Titanium Elite Status or Marriott Bonvoy® Ambassador Elite status.

World of Hyatt has several cards that can help you earn elite status. This both comes in the form of outright receiving status, and also in the form of receiving elite nights that count toward status.

The following cards can help you earn World of Hyatt Discoverist status (which ordinarily requires 10 qualifying nights or 25,000 base points per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn World of Hyatt Explorist status (which ordinarily requires 30 qualifying nights or 50,000 base points per year):

The following cards can help you earn World of Hyatt Globalist status (which ordinarily requires 60 qualifying nights or 100,000 base points per year):

Wyndham Rewards has a few cards that can help you earn elite status.

The following card can help you earn Wyndham Rewards Gold status (which ordinarily requires five qualifying nights per calendar year):

The following card can help you earn Wyndham Rewards Platinum status (which ordinarily requires 15 qualifying nights per calendar year):

The following card can help you earn Wyndham Rewards Platinum status (which ordinarily requires 40 qualifying nights per calendar year):

If you’re going to stay with a certain hotel group, it goes without saying that having some elite status is better than not having elite status. At the same time, I don’t want to overpromise, and suggest that being an elite member is going to get you the most amazing treatment on earth.

After all, if you get elite status just for having a credit card, you can assume that you’re not alone in pursuing this strategy. 😉 That being said, there are definitely some credit card elite status opportunities that are more lucrative than others.

My single favorite hotel credit card for elite status is the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card (learn more), as it offers Diamond status in the Hilton Honors program. This gets you 100% bonus points, room upgrades subject to availability, breakfast (or a food & beverage credit in the US), lounge access at select brands, etc.

As is common with the major hotel groups, the further from the United States you get, the better the elite treatment, and the better the shot of a good upgrade. Hilton Honors is my third preferred hotel group, and the Diamond status on the card does the trick for me. Given all the card’s other perks, I also find it really easy to justify.

My second favorite hotel credit card is the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more), as it offers Platinum status in the Marriott Bonvoy program. This gets you 50% bonus points, room upgrades subject to availability, the option of selecting breakfast as your welcome amenity at most brands, lounge access at most brands, guaranteed 4PM check-out at non-resorts, etc.

Don’t expect all that much when it comes to upgrades (at least in major markets), but the guaranteed perks, like late check-out, breakfast at most brands, etc., really do add up.

Beyond that, I think there should be a special mention for all the cards offering Hilton Gold status, given how easy it is to earn. Most crucially, it offers breakfast at properties outside the United States (and a food & beverage credit within the United States), so at least it offers something in the way of guaranteed benefits, compared to other comparable tiers.

It’s pretty remarkable that nowadays you can earn valuable status with Hilton, Marriott, and Wyndham, just for having a credit card (without a spending requirement), and with Hyatt and IHG you can earn valuable status with credit card spending.

On top of that, there are many mid-range credit cards that offer status just for having the card, which can be valuable as well. For example, it’s really easy to earn Hilton Gold elite status, and that gets you perks like free breakfast at most brands, bonus points, and more.

If you are going to spend money on your hotel credit card to earn status, just make sure you consider the opportunity cost of that spending.

Which credit cards do you find to be most valuable for earning elite hotel status?

#6045. United Raises Credit Card Bonuses To 100,000 Miles—Cardholders Earn More On Flights And Pay Less For Awards

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. United and Chase have raised initial bonuses on all four personal credit cards, with offers now reaching 100,000 miles. That’s worth considering because United has made its credit card much harder to skip: eligible primary cardholders earn more miles for flying, then pay fewer miles to book United awards. Even elite status doesn’t eliminate the disadvantage of going without one.

I’ve written about United cutting mileage-earning for customers without a card while giving cardholders more. If you’re active with the airline and MileagePlus, you need to look at the cost of a card against the miles you’re giving up without it. And with the annual fee cards, you don’t have to put all your spending on one to get the better flight earning and award pricing.

Here’s the current lineup. Each offer has a spending component plus another 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user (an employee card on the business products) within three months of account opening. Card    Initial Bonus    Purchases In First 3 Months    Annual Fee United GatewaySM Card (See rates and fees) 40,000 after $1,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user50,000 total $1,000 $0 UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees) 70,000 after $3,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user80,000 total $3,000 $0 first year, then $150 United QuestSM Card (See rates and fees) 80,000 after $4,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user90,000 total $4,000 $350 United ClubSM Card (See rates and fees) 90,000 after $5,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user100,000 total $5,000 $695 UnitedSM Business Card (See rates and fees) 90,000 after $5,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user100,000 total $5,000 $150 There are also elite status incentives: Quest: 500 Premier qualifying points after your first purchase. Business: 2,000 Premier qualifying points after the same $5,000 in purchases within three months that earns the mileage bonus. The extra 10,000 miles for adding a user are awarded once per account, and that user must remain on the account when the bonus is fulfilled. What You’re Giving Up Without A Qualifying Card For United tickets purchased on or after April 2, 2026, here’s what the airline awards for flying. The cardholder column applies to the primary holder of an eligible annual fee card. The United GatewaySM Card requires spending to qualify. MileagePlus Status    Without A Qualifying Card    With A Qualifying Card General member 3 miles per dollar 6 miles per dollar Premier Silver 5 miles per dollar 8 miles per dollar Premier Gold 6 miles per dollar 9 miles per dollar Premier Platinum 7 miles per dollar 10 miles per dollar Premier 1K 9 miles per dollar 12 miles per dollar These rates apply to base airfare and carrier-imposed surcharges and exclude taxes. Basic Economy and other base-option fares have different earning rules. This is mileage earned from flying, separate from whatever the card you use to buy the tickets earns. A general member earns twice as many flight miles with a qualifying card. A 1K doesn’t double their earning, but still picks up three more miles per eligible dollar. Spend $5,000 on eligible fares and that’s 15,000 additional miles at either status level. Then there’s the redemption side. United gives eligible primary cardholders: At least 10% off United and United Express award prices without Premier status. At least 15% off with Premier status. Access to additional Polaris business class Saver award inventory. More seats at the lower price can matter more than the percentage discount. At the minimum discounts, an award with a base price of 100,000 miles becomes 90,000 miles for a cardholder without status, or 85,000 for a cardholder with status. The discounts don’t cover partner-operated flights, Money + Miles bookings, or taxes and fees. You need to book through the primary cardholder’s MileagePlus account. Adding someone as an authorized user doesn’t give their MileagePlus account these benefits. The award pricing benefit can take up to five weeks after card issuance to become available. The No Annual Fee Card Has A $10,000 Spend Requirement To Unlock Benefits United GatewaySM Card‘s offer is 50,000 miles with just $1,000 in purchases and an added authorized user. That’s a record bonus and a low spending requirement. Chase is right to call it the card’s best offer ever. However, Gateway requires $10,000 in purchases in a calendar year to unlock the higher flight earning and cardmember award pricing. Once earned, the award pricing benefit lasts for the rest of that calendar year and the following one. I actually think that UnitedSM Explorer Card (which has a $0 annual fee the first year) and the UnitedSM Business Card are both better options. Which Offer Makes The Most Sense? UnitedSM Explorer Card is the base personal card. You get up to 80,000 miles and the better MileagePlus earning and award prices without a first year annual fee. It also comes with Group 2 boarding, two United Club one-time passes each year, and a free first checked bag for the primary cardholder and one companion on the same reservation. The bag benefit generally requires buying the tickets with the card. Club passes are subject to admission restrictions and capacity. The UnitedSM Business Card is especially attractive if you qualify. It matches the 100,000-mile maximum on the Club cards, adds 2,000 qualifying points, and costs $150 a year. It offers a $125 United travel credit after five United flight purchases of at least $100 each in a calendar year. And you get 5,000 anniversary miles when you also hold a personal Chase United card. United QuestSM Card has strong benefits if you’ll use them. The $350 annual fee buys $200 in United TravelBank cash after opening and at each anniversary, plus a 10,000-mile award flight discount starting at the first anniversary. It also provides 1,000 qualifying points annually starting the calendar year after opening. If the $200 credit replaces airfare you’d otherwise buy, you’re left evaluating $150 of the fee against the remaining benefits and that’s the annual fee of Explorer. The United ClubSM Card is for people who will use the lounges. It has a $695 annual fee and includes United Club membership. #6043. How the Electoral College Dies

Blue-state activists are about to be perfectly positioned to execute an end run around the constitutional system.

In the wake of the 2026 midterms, we are on the cusp of a total transformation of the U.S. election system. After decades of Republican dominance in state legislatures, Democrats now control enough state governments to push the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact past its 270-vote activation threshold and dismantle the Electoral College from below.

But it seems like the right has barely realized the importance of the fight that’s about to begin.

Inez Feltscher Stepman is a senior policy and legal analyst at the Independent Women's Forum.

It's that time of year again — holiday shopping season.

I’m the friend everyone comes to for gift ideas, and I take that VERY seriously (in fact, my nickname during the holiday season is "Santa Bella"). Between way too many hours scrolling on my FYP and my group chats, I always know what's trending and actually worth the hype. This year, I'm also lending my gift giving expertise to all of you with a guide on all of the trending gifts you should get the chronically online loved one in your life. These are all gifts I guarantee won’t end in the back of someone’s closet.

You'll find everything from viral skincare, plushies everyone is collecting and a few wellness upgrades people have been eyeing all year. And since the upcoming Black Friday/Cyber Monday holiday is the best time to get a deal, every gift also comes with a TPG tip to help you get rewarded on the gifts you give.

Best for: Skincare lovers or those who need a hydration boost

The Medicube PDRN Collagen Gel Mask is viral for a reason. Put it on, leave it for a few hours, and peel it off once it turns clear. I absolutely love using this before a big event or after a long flight. It leaves my skin looking plump and hydrated. You can purchase this on Ulta, Amazon, Target, or on Medicube’s site.

TPG tip: Sign into Ulta Rewards before checking out as every purchase counts towards dollars you can redeem. Bonus tip: make sure you use Rakuten for extra cash back.

Best for: The plushie lover and collector

Jellycats are everyone’s favorite plushy, and definitely not just for kids. I have a ton of friends who collect them. The designs are adorable and the quality is great and some are country-exclusive (I really want the aviation one you can only get in London). Buying in person is half the fun, especially at FAO Schwarz in NYC. You can find them also in Nordstrom or Bloomingdales.

TPG tip: Join Nordstrom’s Nordy Club and log in before you buy to earn points towards a future purchase.

Best for: Anyone who wants to be wrapped up in a ball all winter.

This might be the most viral blanket ever! They have a 4-way stretch that makes it softest blanket you will ever own. They often offer discounts throughout the year, including a big discount when you sign up, so be sure to get one then. Bonus: the founders donate blankets every month to women going through breast cancer. Shop the blankets on their site or at Bloomingdales.

TPG tip: Wait for it to go on sale or sign up for their site to get 35% off the first order. Also make sure to use Rakuten to get cash back!

We grew up with Legos and somehow never outgrew it. Legos are the perfect gift for ANYONE. There are so many options from plants to planes, so there is one for literally everyone. I love that they can also act as decor in your home once you complete it. You can buy these almost anywhere, from the Lego Store itself to Best Buy.

TPG tip: Join LEGO Insiders to earn points on purchases from LEGO directly. If you are buying elsewhere, look at Rakuten’s cash back offer and check your card offers for a bonus.

Best for: Skincare lovers ready to level up their routine.

A face-sculpting tool for your jawline, cheekbones, and under-eyes. Hot and cold contrast therapy across six temperatures helps depuff, and a ton of people use it for muscle tension too! You can get it from Sephora, Ulta, Best Buy, Kohls, Amazon, and more!

TPG tip: Make sure you are logged into any of the above loyalty programs and get cash back from Rakuten.

Best for: The person who finally wants to tackle their wellness in 2027

The wellness tracker everyone wants. The newest design features a slimmer band, which was a dealbreaker for a lot of people last time. It tracks your overall health including your sleep and can actually predict you getting sick (wild!).

TPG tip: Use your for the up to $200 annual statement credit. Enrollment required.

One of my all time favorite under eye patches. I absolutely love these when I have an event coming up or getting off of a long flight because they depuff and brighten so I actually look awake. Some even wear it all day as an accessory. I love the brand too: science-backed, sustainability-first, and made with every skin tone in mind.

TPG tip: Sign up for their rewards program to earn perks like birthday rewards and even a shot at one of their iconic brand trips. Sephora Beauty Insiders members can also purchase through Sephora.

These are one of my all time favorite gifts to give (and get). These Sephora Favorite fragrance sets come packed with samples plus a certificate to redeem for a full size, so you never have to guess someone’s scent. There is truly something for everyone, and the minis are perfect for traveling.

TPG tip: Wait for a Sephora sale, when you get discounts depending on your Beauty Insider tier. Stack it with Rakuten or your card’s shopping portal for extra cash back or miles.

Shop Sephora fragrance favorites for men and women

Best for: Someone who loves to document every moment

You can’t scroll on Instagram or TikTok without seeing a sign to get a digital camera. Viral for a reason: the soft, nostalgic look, perfect sunset shots, and it’s small enough to toss into your bag. I shoot on the Canon G7x, which is nearly impossible to find right now, but there are plenty of comparable options for a fraction of the price.

TPG tip: Purchase from whatever store gives you the highest cash back on Rakuten. Since these cameras are offered in a ton of stores, check your card offers to see if a store offers a larger mile multiplier.

Everybody loves a good water bottle and right now, Bink is my favorite. The designs and colors are so cute, and since wellness is at the top of everyone’s mind, having a glass or stainless steel one is key. They’re dishwasher safe and yours breaks, they will replace it (you just cover the shipping).

TPG tip: Make sure to use a credit card that earns on online shopping to maximize your purchase.

#6041. Southwest Pilot Calls Out Nationwide Flight Shutdown As A Government Control Plot

A pilot, reportedly with Southwest Airlines, says he flew from Cancún to Phoenix without any communications problems. He’s concluded that Friday’s nationwide flight shutdown was a government operation to control people. He calls the whole thing “a big farce.” He managed to successfully complete his own flight, which was already in the air by the time trouble began, and claims that proves the whole thing was a scam. The video is from @mike4flight, the profile of Mike McHugh. Standing in a parking garage in uniform, he lists the facilities he spoke with and says they all worked fine. Then he offers his theory: So whatever’s going on, I think it’s designed to create fear and disruption and chaos, because that’s how the government gets control of things, controls people. Watch the pilot’s video He never explains how this advances the government’s goal, what additional control it gains, or why it wants that control. Which power are stranded passengers supposed to surrender? The government already decides whether planes can take off. Keeping people at the airport for hours accomplishes what, exactly? And how does costing airlines hundreds of millions of dollars in a day advance its goals? He says “I don’t know what’s going on,” but instead of then keeping quiet he decides to tell the world it’s a government operation. His fight went fine, but that doesn’t mean everything was actually fine. Some communications worked, others didn’t. Radar information could become unreliable even while a pilot could hear a controller. A pilot hears the frequencies he’s assigned at the times he’s using them. That doesn’t say much. The decision to let aircraft already airborne continue while stopping departures isn’t a contradiction. Limiting the number of flights controllers had to work given the conditions they faced made sense. Every landing reduced the workload. Every new departure would have added another aircraft needing instructions, separation and handoffs between controllers. Remaining capacity could be reserved for aircraft already flying. Working frequencies and contingency procedures could help bring those flights in without supporting a normal stream of new departures. The FAA’s ground stop rules cover facilities that are only partially unable to provide service. You don’t wait until every radio goes silent before reducing traffic. In fact, depending on when he flew, the ground stop may have helped make his trip uneventful. Fewer planes competing for the remaining capacity would make his experience easier. He may be pointing to the benefit of the restriction as evidence it wasn’t needed in the first place. Friday’s nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and was lifted around 8:15 p.m. It lasted over four hours. By early Saturday morning, there were more than 12,500 cancellations across Friday and Saturday. Trouble moving that information interrupts a controller’s radio audio and radar display. Apparently the break down came in Cisco 600-series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin managed to throw Duffy under the bus while trying to defend the administration. He calls the whole thing “a big farce.” He managed to successfully complete his own flight, which was already in the air by the time trouble began, and claims that proves the whole thing was a scam.

The video is from @mike4flight, the profile of Mike McHugh. Standing in a parking garage in uniform, he lists the facilities he spoke with and says they all worked fine. Then he offers his theory:

So whatever’s going on, I think it’s designed to create fear and disruption and chaos, because that’s how the government gets control of things, controls people.

He never explains how this advances the government’s goal, what additional control it gains, or why it wants that control. Which power are stranded passengers supposed to surrender? The government already decides whether planes can take off. Keeping people at the airport for hours accomplishes what, exactly? And how does costing airlines hundreds of millions of dollars in a day advance its goals?

He says “I don’t know what’s going on,” but instead of then keeping quiet he decides to tell the world it’s a government operation.

His fight went fine, but that doesn’t mean everything was actually fine. Some communications worked, others didn’t. Radar information could become unreliable even while a pilot could hear a controller. A pilot hears the frequencies he’s assigned at the times he’s using them. That doesn’t say much. The decision to let aircraft already airborne continue while stopping departures isn’t a contradiction. Limiting the number of flights controllers had to work given the conditions they faced made sense.

The FAA’s ground stop rules cover facilities that are only partially unable to provide service. You don’t wait until every radio goes silent before reducing traffic.

In fact, depending on when he flew, the ground stop may have helped make his trip uneventful. Fewer planes competing for the remaining capacity would make his experience easier. He may be pointing to the benefit of the restriction as evidence it wasn’t needed in the first place.

Friday’s nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and was lifted around 8:15 p.m. It lasted over four hours. By early Saturday morning, there were more than 12,500 cancellations across Friday and Saturday.

Looks like some stuck travelers got a concert from the singer of Hoobastank during the national air traffic shut down https://t.co/xWW5yE9JaP

— Jennie Taer (@JennieSTaer) November 14, 2026

According to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, legacy telecommunications switches and routers became overloaded, producing inconsistent radar information and communications at en route centers and airport approach facilities. He said the newer internet protocol switches hadn’t experienced these problems.

The L3Harris-operated FAA telecommunications network carries voice and surveillance information between facilities. Trouble moving that information interrupts a controller’s radio audio and radar display. Apparently the break down came in Cisco 600-series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin managed to throw Duffy under the bus while trying to defend the administration. Standing beside him at the briefing, Mullin said the apparent problem involved Duffy and the FAA installing patches, equipment and technology that overwhelmed the older system. The new tech was “overwhelming the older system.” Duffy’s defense was that the new equipment hadn’t failed.

Watch Markwayne Mullin explain the apparent cause beside Sean Duffy

When I reviewed the administration’s modernization plan, I warned that compressing decades of hardware replacements, software integrations and transitions into 36 months brought risks of service disruption.

Duffy used the briefing to press Congress for $50 billion. He wants more taxpayer money rather than user fees to prop up an agency that’s failed to modernize with the billions given to it before, without explaining why only money – and not fixing project management, budgeting and leadership at the agency – is all that’s needed.

I wouldn’t want this nut case to be the pilot on any flight I happen to be on.

Southwest has way more than their fair share of nut jobs. Case and point.

Airlines pay for FAA “services” by the airport fees and fees (taxes) placed on passenger tickets. General Aviation pays for FAA services with a high “fuel tax”. All of this money goes into the “kitty” for use by the FAA. BUT…Congress (both parties!!) will steal this money for pet projects…kinda like the “bridge to nowhere” in Alaska. The FAA doesn’t/won’t take any advice from the NTSB to fix issues related to aviation safety. The DCA regional jet/Army helicopter crash is a PRIME example of complete incompetence. The NTSB says, “get your communications fixed”, “don’t let helicopters fly in KDCA airspace”. Does the Congress or FAA comply? HELL NO! There are those that proffer “privatizing” the FAA. EVEN WORSE! Canada’s private “FAA” NAV CANADA charges for EVERYTHING. A student wants to shoot “touch & go’s”…there’s a charge to your credit card or FBO. You want to shoot several instrument approaches…same thing. You want to fly cross country…a charge. That’s why Canadian student pilots come to the US for training. While the hourly rate may be higher in USD, it’s offset by not being nickel & dimed to death. If you want to point a finger, point it at both senators and your congressman. THEY are the problem!

Did anyone watch the 1997 movie Conspiracy Theory? Crazy conspiracy theories are nuts, unless they are true. Of course, I think the Southwest Pilot is unlikely in the extreme. However, his theory is more likely than my theory that I am going to win $1 billion in the lottery. Just saying.

More serious comment. Cisco routers from 2001 to 2006. I think that is Window XP level technology. Since then, Microsoft forced me to buy a Windows 7 computer. Then a Windows 10 computer. I am being forces to shop for a Window 11 computer. No wonder the update didn’t work.

As an IT professional for several decades (financial institutions, oil&gas businesses and supply chain management for the world’s largest food company), I have never known critical systems to be patched or updated during normal business hours. That just never happens. Don’t know what really happened yesterday nor with the Microsoft outage but the stories that are being told that it was updates gone bad, are lies.

There is an element of truth. Project 2025 has a section that discusses dismantling the FAA and privatizing the system. And in general, yes, fascist regimes do sow chaos and distrust in existing systems as a form of control over the population.

Back in 1984 Charles Perrow wrote a book called, “Normal Accidents”. His contention is that as systems get more complicated thy are more likely to have points where failures magnify through the tightly coupling of various parts. Eventually these can cascade into a catastrophic collapse of the entire system. These situations may be reduced, and to some extent mitigated with good designs and training, but by the very nature of complexity will still occur in totally unexpected ways. In fact, building in redundancies can sometimes be counter-productive as it makes systems even more complicated and prone to failure.

We may have reached this point in air traffic control, made worse by old equipment and a sluggish bureaucracy that reacts rather than is proactive in avoiding accidents. You don’t need a vast plot (though I admit that I wondered if this was the start of a coup) to have a total system failure. One thing does seem likely, and that is more such events will occur, and without intelligent action they will be more frequent.

#6038. Combat Took on America’s Socialism Fever

The National Review newsletter captured a time in which revolutionary violence tried to join the mainstream.

Young men raise their fists and chant slogans during the “Days of Rage” demonstrations organized by the Weatherman to protest the Chicago Seven trial and “to bring the war home” in Chicago, Ill., in 1969.

Socialism looks in 2026 a lot like bell bottoms: tried on, worn out, and out of fashion.

Decades ago, Germany, Russia, Cambodia, Ethiopia, and points beyond tried socialism to disastrous results. Many American leftists, as judged by the election returns, believe in an American exceptionalism of sorts, too. They think that socialism in the United States will be different. We won’t need a world war, societal collapse, or the obligatory charitable single and accompanying global benefit show to save us from its consequences. Socialism, for its true believers, amounts to salvation and not that from which people living under it require deliverance.

#6037. Airlines Are Giving Passengers ‘Hoe Bags’—But You May Be Owed More When Your Luggage Goes Missing

A Southwest Airlines passenger says her luggage went missing on a flight to Detroit, and the airline handed her what she calls a “hoe bag”: a plastic bag containing a toothbrush, razor, mouthwash and deodorant. “This is a care package for hoes.” Comedian Delo Brown, who posts as @keepitonthedelo, says Southwest lost her luggage “last week.” She expected a voucher or some sort of credit. Instead, she got toiletries to use while they looked for her belongings. “Take this hoe bag and be happy.” Watch Delo Brown’s Southwest Airlines toiletry kit unboxing. Then she starts pulling out the contents. There’s a brush, facial pads and cotton swabs, a toothbrush, a razor, wipes, mouthwash and a tiny deodorant. The razor gets a particularly enthusiastic explanation of what it might be used for. By the end, she’s sold: “This is the best hoe bag I have ever received in my life. This is a caring hoe bag. This is a care package for hoes. I love this. Thank you, Southwest, for my hoe bag.” A “hoe bag” means a bag with the overnight essentials you’d bring when you might wind up spending the night at somebody else’s place. Toothbrush, deodorant, something to clean up with, perhaps fresh underwear. A couple of the better comments: “I used to leave those in the top drawer of nightstand on the other side of my bed.” “Got your hoe bag but still missing a WHOLE BAG.” Other commenters think the plain plastic bag and generic toiletries look more like a hospital admission kit or something handed out in jail. Several compare it to the $148 Skims advent calendar that drew complaints over its inexpensive accessories. These are meant to get you through a night without your checked bag, whether your luggage didn’t arrive or a disrupted trip leaves it somewhere you can’t get to. You’d get the at the baggage service office. And you’ll find them at other airlines, too. In a 2009 comparison of airline overnight kits, Wired actually picked Southwest as best overall. Its kit came in a reusable bag with pockets and a hanging hook, and included Speed Stick, Colgate, Scope, Pert Plus and TRESemmé. That was a much more elaborate kit than the plastic bag in this video. Passengers still need their bags back. Expenses in the meantime may be covered by the credit card they used to purchase the ticket, and airlines have to reimburse reasonable, documented expenses caused by delayed baggage. That can include necessary toiletries and replacement clothing. Hotels can help, too. Ask the front desk before buying a toothbrush, toothpaste, razor, shaving cream or comb. Many have complimentary basics, while deodorant, mouthwash, makeup wipes and other items depend on the property. A hotel’s lobby shop often isn’t the only option. I wrote about “Hyatt Has It” when it launched in 2013. What I liked was that Hyatt would actually tell guests what was available and invite them to ask. At participating full service hotels, they’d deliver the items, knock and leave the bag on the doorknob. Hyatt still advertises the program, including requests through the World of Hyatt app. Holiday Inn’s “Forget Something?” service can offer complimentary toothbrushes, toothpaste, shaving cream, razors and combs. Of course, some hotels would rather sell you the basics. I covered a stranded Marriott Ambassador member who said the Detroit Metro Airport Marriott wanted $12 for deodorant and another $12 for mouthwash. Their shuttle would take him anywhere within a mile, but the drugstore was 1.1 miles away. He moved to a Hyatt Place and got the toiletries for free. I’m on the road about half the year on assignment for TPG and on any given week, you might find me browsing the jade market in Taipei, window-shopping through Galerie Vivienne in Paris or strolling through the San Telmo market in Buenos Aires on the hunt for collectibles.

I can’t tell you how many times I’ve seen a souvenir, piece of art, sweet treat or other little curio and thought, “Wouldn’t this make a great gift for so and so?”

The only trouble is, I travel light, so there’s nary a nook or cranny in my carry-on to fit a gift, let alone several.

I do, however, make a mental inventory of potential gifts I see so that I can order them for friends and family later. Here are a few of my favorite recent finds that might be perfect for someone on your holiday gift list, all inspired by my travels.

Best for: Armchair travelers who like to keep cozy

There’s a lot I love about 1 Hotels — their sustainable ethos, the Bamford bath amenities, in-room filtered water taps, the smattering of hyperlocal, destination-specific activities on offer to guests, bustling public spaces with unique dining concepts and…the bathrobes. I’m not usually a bathrobe kind of guy, but I can’t resist donning one of these ultracomfortable numbers anytime I’m a guest at one of these properties. Simple and soft, with a gray jersey-knit lining and a loose hoodie, they’re perfect for lounging with a cappuccino while you try to stave off jet lag.

TPG tip: You might want to make this purchase at an actual 1 Hotel boutique so you can earn more points per dollar with a credit card that offers a travel or hotel category bonus.

Best for: The Japanophile you want to impress

Like an unstoppable force meeting an immovable object, my delight in purchasing travel souvenirs is only impeded by the limited space in my small city apartment. That’s why I love the little lacquerware boxes and trays from Zohiko, a boutique in Kyoto’s Nakagyo Ward that traces its history back to the 17th century. I especially love the finely filigreed Kirikane style, where patterns or shapes are cut out in gold or silver leaf and pressed into place. I purchased a glossy black box with gold inlay of cherry blossoms and autumn leaves on my last visit, and I keep it on my nightstand to hold my wedding ring and watch.

TPG tip: Make a trip to Japan out of it and browse the physical Zohiko boutique (you can also enjoy tax-free purchases if you’re visiting) while checking out some of Kyoto’s exciting new hotels.

Best for: Folks who appreciate colorful, culturally significant crafts

Inevitably, every time I’m traipsing around Bogotá, I find myself drawn to this gorgeous little boutique in the city’s upscale Chapinero neighborhood, which sources fair-trade handcrafted pieces of art and decor from small communities around the country, including woven baskets starting at just $18. I am personally drawn to carefully carved wooden Tamo bowls from the coastal Nariño region, decorated with brightly dyed strands of wheat or barley fiber, but you can find everything from woven baskets to hammocks, jewelry and even pieces of furniture.

TPG tip: While you can often haggle for handicrafts in Colombia, prices in this boutique are as marked, so save your negotiating skills for street vendors.

Best for: Helping a friend spruce up their interior decor game

Although long popular with backpackers and river cruisers, Luang Prabang still feels like an under-the-radar find in mountainous Laos, sitting on the confluence of the Mekong and Nam Khan Rivers. It’s also a hotbed of fair-trade arts and crafts. A standout atelier in town is Ock Pop Tok, an art school, store and restaurant that aims to revive, support and teach traditional Lao artistic techniques. Visitors can take classes in silk-weaving, batik-dyeing and embroidery, among other offerings. I am always tempted to buy out the textile section of the boutique, but I usually limit myself to a vibrant wall hanging or two.

TPG tip: Don’t just make a purchase; spend a few days as a student at Ock Pop Tok to pick up a new craft yourself.

Best for: Travelers who like their perfumes with a hint of historical luxury

Of course, I’d suggest visiting the original Florence flagship of this bath and beauty purveyor, which dates back to 1221. It feels a little like visiting Ollivanders Wand Shop from “Harry Potter,” with antique cases bursting with all-natural unguents and elixirs whose formulas were originally developed by Dominican friars. But if you can’t get there, there are also locations around the U.S., including those in West Hollywood, California, Soho in New York City and Bal Harbour, Florida. I tend to keep it simple and go for the pure sweet almond oil, but you could also go regal and buy a bottle of the perfumery’s citrusy Acqua della Regina, created for Catherine de' Medici as a gift for her husband, the future king of France, back in 1533.

TPG tip: It can sometimes be less expensive to purchase these products from the original store in Florence, so why not make a trip out of it?

Best for: The fashionable cowboys at your rodeo

I love an eye-catching accessory, and belts are my statement pieces of choice. So on my last visit to Buenos Aires, I stopped by Arandu Talabarteria’s tony boutique in Recoleta. The whole store is inspired by a romanticized version of gaucho life on the pampas. You can find sturdy leather boots, billowy bombacha pants, cozy ponchos and my favorite: woven belts with intricate threadwork and high-quality leather. They start at $45 and can range into the hundreds of dollars, depending on the level of detail and craftsmanship. Best of all, you can ship to the U.S., so you don’t have to cross the equator to stock up.

TPG tip: They also have dog collars for your faithful canine companion.

Best for: The high-flying #avgeek in your life

If you’ve followed me for the past few years, you know I’m pretty much obsessed with KLM’s tile Delft houses, the little replicas of actual historical buildings around the Netherlands that the airline hands out to long-haul business-class passengers. I’ve attended the unveiling of each year’s new house for several years now, and my own collection has grown into a veritable village. If you have an equally #avgeeky member of your gifting circle and are looking for the perfect present, then you might want to consider buying one of these beauties for them. Historian Mark Zegeling’s “Little Kingdom by the Sea” book set, which delves into the history of all 107 of the houses, is a great accompanying gift as well.

TPG tip: Be sure to use a credit card that waives foreign transaction fees so you don’t get dinged with a 1-3% surcharge when buying your house.

Best for: Swanky sunseekers who want to make a splash

How do you tell me you summer on the French Riviera without telling me you summer on the French Riviera? You simply tote around a sunshiney yellow-and-white-striped beach bag from the iconic Carlton Cannes, the first luxury hotel to open in the city, way back in 1911. A lot has changed since then, but the simple design is meant to evoke the Côte d’Azur of yore, when you might have found Cary Grant and Grace Kelly sunbathing on the plage between scenes of “To Catch a Thief.”

TPG tip: Make your purchase in person and use an IHG One Rewards credit card to earn multiple points per dollar.

Best for: International imbibers with a sweet tooth

You might find it hard to remember your visit to Singapore, let alone pick up some souvenirs as gifts for friends, after you’ve had a few Singapore Slings at the Raffles Hotel’s iconic Long Bar. That’s why it might come in handy to pick up a keepsake Singapore Sling glass for your friends from the hotel’s online boutique. It’s like taking a sip of history with you. The nation’s signature drink was invented by Ngiam Tong Boon back in 1915 and is an intoxicating (and sweet!) mix of gin, grenadine, cherry liqueur, Benedictine, Curacao and both pineapple and lime juice. Even a sip can transport you back to a sultry Southeast Asian evening.

TPG tip: Pick a card that earns bonus rewards on everyday purchases, like the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, so you’re making the most of your spending.

#6035. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6033. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.
